The table presented is the complete Contents listing for the SOFiLOAD “Loads and Load Functions” manual (Service Pack 2025-4 Build 146) by SOFiSTiK AG. It is organized hierarchically into chapters, sections and subsections that guide the user through theoretical background, input syntax, load definitions, specialized loading cases and output interpretation. Below is a structured description of its key elements and logical flow, suitable for indexing in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) vector store:

1. Front Matter and Metadata  
  • Title and Version: “SOFiLOAD Loads and Load Functions,” Manual Service Pack 2025-4 Build 146.  
  • Publisher: SOFiSTiK AG, Nuremberg and Munich offices (addresses, phone/fax, email, website).  
  • Legal Notice: Copyright statement, reproduction restrictions, disclaimer of error-free operation, user responsibility.  

2. Chapter 1: General  
  • (Pages 1-1) High-level overview—likely introduction, scope, nomenclature.  

3. Chapter 2: Theoretical Principles (2-1 to 2-2)  
  2.1 Equivalent Nodal Loads  
  2.2 Prestressing Loads  
  • Lays the mathematical and mechanical foundations behind how loads are represented within finite-element meshes.  

4. Chapter 3: Input Description (3-1 to 3-81)  
  This chapter forms the heart of the manual, describing every input record (keyword) available for defining load sets and functions. It is subdivided as follows:  
  3.1 Input Language  
  3.2 Input Records (general rules for record syntax)  
  3.3 GRP – Selection and Properties of Groups  
  3.4 ACT – Definition of an Action  
  3.5 LC – Definition of a Load Case  
  3.6 NODE – Nodal Loads  
  3.7 CABL – Cable Loading  
  3.8 TRUS – Truss Element Loading  
  3.9 Definition of Beam Loading (overview)  
  3.10 BEAM – Distributed Beam Loading  
  3.11 BEPL – Point Beam Loading  
  3.12 QUAD – Quadrilateral Element Loading  
  3.13 BRIC – Brick (3D solid) Element Loading  
  3.14 COPY – Loads from Other Sources  
    – 3.14.1 Support Forces  
    – 3.14.2 Load Trains  
    – 3.14.3 Wind and Wave Loads  
  3.15 Free Loading  
    – 3.15.1 References  
    – 3.15.2 Projection of Loading Definitions  
    – 3.15.3 Beam Loading  
    – 3.15.4 Special Hints  
  3.16 LAR – Load Distribution Areas  
  3.17 POIN – Free Point Loads  
  3.18 LINE, CURV – Free Line and Curved Line Loading  
  3.19 AREA – Free Area Loading (including wind load subcases)  
  3.20 VOLU – Volume Loading (including silos and tanks)  
  3.21 GUID – Globally Unique Identifier for loads  
  3.22 EXPO – Export of Load Cases  
  3.23 EVAL – Evaluations (e.g., eigen stress, spectral densities)  
  3.24 CTRL – Optional Control Values (override defaults)  
  3.25 ECHO – Printout Options (customize listing verbosity)  

5. Chapter 4: Dynamic Loads (4-1 to 4-53)  
  4.1 Pushover Analysis – Theoretical Background  
  4.2 RESP – Response Spectrum definitions across international codes (Eurocode EC 8, UBC/IBC, DIN EN 1998-1/NA-2023-11, SIA 260, Italian NTC, Greek EAK, Russian SNiP, Indian IS 1893, JRA, Chinese GB, plus wind spectra and modal coordinates)  
  4.3 FUNC – Load Functions (pedestrian, aperiodic, spectral, ground accelerations)  
  4.4 FIMP – Import of Load Functions  
  4.5 ACCE – Accelerations  
  4.6 STEP – Dynamic History  
  4.7 SIMQ – Earthquake Simulation  
  4.8 REVA – Response Spectra for Acceleration Function  
  4.9 PUSH – Pushover Analysis implementation (analysis types and structural performance limits)  

6. Chapter 5: Train Loading (5-1 to 5-35)  
  5.1 General Principles  
  5.2 Load Groups  
  5.3 GAX – Geometry of an Axis  
  5.4 LANE – Width of Traffic Lanes  
  5.5 TRAI – Load Train Definition (impact factor, centrifugal forces, passenger and freight load trains per Eurocode, SLW/LKW, BS 5400/TMH7, IS 1227, AASHTO, CAN/CSA, IRC, JRA).  

7. Chapters 6–9: Specialized Load Types  
  • 6 Wind Loading  
  • 7 Wave Loading (irregular waves, WAVE command)  
  • 8 Snow Loads  
  • 9 Load Take Down (source→target assignment, 1:1, N:M, automatic target selection, fall-down scenarios)  

8. Chapter 10: Output Description and Bibliography  
  • Details on how computed loads, load combinations and evaluations are presented in report form, plus references to standards and literature.  

This Contents table serves two purposes in a RAG context:  
  • As a taxonomy for mapping user queries (e.g., “How do I define a point load?” → refer to 3.11 BEPL)  
  • As a provenance layer, tracking where each input keyword or theoretical concept is documented (chapter, section, page).

The table is a hierarchical “Contents” listing from the SOFiLOAD manual (Service Pack 2025-4, Build 146) and is organized into three primary columns:  
 1. Section Number – a multi‐level numeric code (e.g. 3, 3.1, 3.14.3) indicating chapter, sub-chapter, etc.  
 2. Section Title – the descriptive name of each chapter or topic.  
 3. Page Reference – formatted as “chapter-page” (e.g. 3-1, 7-12) showing where that section begins.  

Level of hierarchy is implied by the numbering:  
 • Level 1: integer numbers (1 General, 2 Theoretical Principles, 3 Input Description, … 10 Output Description)  
 • Level 2: X.Y notation (e.g. 3.1 Input language, 3.2 Input records, 3.14 COPY – Loads from Other Sources)  
 • Level 3: X.Y.Z notation under complex topics (e.g. 3.14.1 Support forces, 3.15.4 Special Hints).

1
 SOFiLOAD generates loading for all SOFiSTiK-Modules.
 Loads are organized in load cases, which are members of a unique action. Load cases are addressed via a number, while the action is designated by up to 4 characters, 48 combinations have been reserved for designated types of actions.
 The combination of the load cases within the actions may be done in a very general way, there are however three predefined combination methods: permanent, optional, exclusive.
 The final combination of the actions is then done within MAXIMA or AQB via combination coefficients (ψ) and safety factors (γ), which may vary in there value from load case to load case, but will be always applied with the same kind of factor.
 The loads can be defined independently of a FEM-mesh. SOFiLOAD will handle the transition from the geometric model to the analysis model by converting general loading patterns to more specific nodal or elemental loads. The user may influence the conversion process if needed.
 The loads are either already in the database or may be defined via SOFiLOAD. If the element mesh is changed, SOFiLOAD has to repeat the elemental assignment. Beside that you may specify nodal or elemental loads directly as known from other finite element systems. Those loads will be deleted however if the element mesh is changed or explicit redefinition of a load case takes place.
 Record names and items have been change compared to former definitions in SOFiSTiK to become more simple and unified. Thus it is not possible in general to copy old CADINP-data, but the export-function may be helpful in many cases. All input load values will be converted according to the units defined in SOFiSTiK. DIM.
 There are also possibilities to generate loads from results in the database. These are especially support forces converted to loads, imperfections, creep deformations or prestressing effects.
 As an special extension we have provided or intended load generators to deal with the rather complex loading of load trains on bridges, earth quake, wind and snow on the structure with very extended features. These options are not part of the basic program version however.

These are especially support forces converted to loads, imperfections, creep deformations or prestressing effects.. These options are not part of the basic program version however..
 This manual starts with the simple nodal and elemental loads, will then cover the geometric load definitions and finally come to the more complex load generators.

The illustration is organized as a pair of side-by-side columns, each showing three evolving mesh-refinement scenarios.  Its purpose is to contrast how a distributed (left column) versus a point load (right column) is “translated” into equivalent nodal loads as the finite-element mesh is refined.

Left Column: Distributed Load  
Row 1  
 • A single straight line represents a beam or plate element under a uniformly applied load: a series of equally spaced downward arrows along the line.  
Row 2 (coarse mesh)  
 • The same beam is now shown with two small circles at its ends—these represent the element’s only two nodes.  
 • Two downward arrows, one at each node, indicate the equivalent nodal loads that replace the continuous distribution when only one element spans the beam.  
Row 3 (refined mesh)  
 • The beam is subdivided into three shorter elements, indicated by four equally spaced circles (nodes) along its length.  
 • Four downward arrows—one at each node—show how the original uniform load is now distributed more finely into nodal loads at every node.  Each arrow is smaller than in Row 2, reflecting that the total load is now split among more nodes.

Right Column: Point Load  
Row 1  
 • A beam with two circles at its ends (a single coarse element) and two downward arrows directly aligned with those circles.  This depicts two point loads that happen, by chance, to fall exactly at the element’s end nodes.  
Row 2 (refined mesh, loads still at former node locations)  
 • The beam is subdivided into three elements (four circles), but the two original point‐load positions coincide exactly with the two end nodes again.  
 • Two downward arrows appear once more at those two end nodes; mesh refinement did not change the number or magnitude of nodal loads because the point-loads remained “on-node.”  
Row 3 (refined mesh, load in between nodes)  
 • The same refined beam (three elements, four nodes) but with one point load applied halfway along one of the interior elements—i.e., not directly on a node.  
 • A single downward arrow appears at the nearest node below the load’s position; the point-load has been converted into an equivalent nodal load at that closest node.  The other nodes carry no load.

Caption (below drawing):  
Figure 2.1: Equivalent nodal loads for mesh refinement

Overall, the figure clearly shows that:  
- A distributed load “spreads” into all nodes of the element(s) and thus changes its nodal‐load pattern as you increase mesh density.  
- A true point load only affects the node it coincides with; if it remains on a node under refinement, nothing changes, and if it falls between nodes it will be lumped into the nearest node.  
- Consequently, accurate representation of load distributions in a finite‐element model depends critically on both the type of load (distributed vs. point) and the mesh resolution.

The Finite Element system is a discrete system and is therefore only enabled to treat with equivalent nodal load contributions, not with real point loads or moments. The difference of the two meanings can be seen in Figure 2.1.
 When the mesh density is increased, you will have different load patterns for a distributed load, but the same for a point load. This indicates also that a given mesh has a distinct resolution for load distributions. The coarser mesh can not distinguish between two point loads, a distributed load or a point load between the nodes.
 On the other side this states that a load may be specified as a single nodal load only if the size of load is less than the element mesh size. If you refine the mesh near that load point you will get higher and higher stresses or forces, as the finite elements will approximate you infinite solution better and better. So you choose either a mesh size not smaller than the minimum load distribution area (thickness for plates for example) or you have to specify the loads as distributed loads.
 From that we conlude further, that the generated nodal loads by SOFiLOAD may be only as accurate as the given Finite Element mesh.
 For beam loading we have the special case, that loading is also defined within the element having an effect on all internal forces. But we have to distinguish between a standard FE- Beam-Element having only cubic displacement functions and a more generalized Beam Ele- ment according to the Transfer-Method. The first will require a finer mesh to model complex loading accurately, the latter may have restrictions on the modelling of the stiffness. (Piece- wise constant in STAR2 e.g).

For springs, cables and trusses you may specify in SOFiMSHA a constant value of prestress, acting in any load case. For cables and trusses you may also define a load case dependant prestress. Any type of prestress will introduce like a thermal expansion strains acting on the element.
 Cables and trusses will be prestresses by some external influence. For fixed ends these strains will introduce the prestress, for flexible supports you will get deformations diminishing your given prestress. If you want to achieve a given value of prestress you have to define external loading or use an element with low stiffness and the given prestress.
 For beams, by contrast, prestress is defined as an equilibrium state of stress (prestressed concrete via tendons). Thus we have an additional component to consider. Since the prestress is imposed on the element itself, the resulting forces on freely deformable beams are the input prestress forces themselves. If the deformation is constraint however, constraining forces arise. In the limiting case, e.g. if a beam is not allowed to deform at all the resultant force is zero, because the forces imposed by the prestress are beared by the support instead of the beam.
 For beams you may specify a statically determinate part of the prestress by the tendon force and its eccentricity and inclination. The distribution along the axis is linear for the stress, but cubically for the eccentricity. The effect of the prestress has to aspects. First we have the additional forces within a section, second we have deformations, introducing new forces if constraints exist.
 Due to the shear forces it is strongly recommended not to combine different tendons in a single one if the eccentricity is not the same.

The input occurs in a free format with the CADINP input language (see the general manual SOFiSTiK: ”FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics”).
 Input is defined within blocks of CADINP-Input language, separated by the record name END. Within each block, values to CTRL and ECHO will be active for the total block, while all other values cover only the current load case.
 There are the following possibilities:
 • Only definition of LC with a number Will print all loads of that load case.
 • Definition of LC with parameters but without any loading Will change those parameters and redistribute all global loading to a the current mesh.
 Input of LC with loads
 •
 The load case is redefined, deleting all old data.
 Three categories of units are distinguished:
 mm Fixed unit. Input is always required in the specified unit.
 [mm] Explicit unit. Input defaults to the specified unit. Alternatively, an explicit as- signment of a related unit is possible (eg. 2.5[m] ).
 [mm]1011 Implicit unit. Implicit units are categorised semantically and denoted by a cor- responding identity number (shown in green). Valid categories referring to the unit ”length” are, for example, geodetic elevation, section length and thickness. The default unit for each category is defined by the currently active (design code specific) unit set. This input default can be overridden as described above. The specified unit in square brackets corresponds to the default for unit set 5 (Eu- rocodes, NORM UNIT 5).

The table is a two-column catalogue of “record” definitions used in the vector/RAG store, where each record name (left column) is paired with the list of data-fields or “items” it carries (right column). Below is a breakdown of its overall structure and the content of each record.  

1. Group/Load-case records  
   • GRP  
     – Common fields for load groups: NO (group number), VAL (value or scale factor), CS, WIND, CW (wind-related factors), CFR (combination factor)  
   • ACT  
     – Action definition: TYPE, GAMU/GAMA (partial factors on dead loads), GAMF (factor on imposed loads), PIS0/PSI1/PSI2/PS1S (psi-factors), PART (participation factor), SUP (support-type code), TITL (title text)  
   • LC  
     – Load case: NO (case number), TYPE (permanent, variable…), FACT/FACD (global factor on loads, dead-load factor), DLX/DLY/DLZ (dead-load directional factors), GAMU/GAMA, GAMF, PIS0/PSI1/PSI2/PS1S, CRI1/CRI2/CRI3 (criteria), TITL  

2. Nodal and element definitions  
   • NODE  
     – Coordinates and releases at a joint: NO (node number), TYPE (support or free), P1…P5 (restraints in local axes), P6, P7 (extra release flags), FRAD (free-rotation axis), EXX/EYY/EZZ (offsets in global X, Y, Z)  
   • CABL / TRUS / BEAM  
     – All three share: FROM, TO (end-node numbers), INC (incremental load case modifier), TYPE (element type code), PA/PE (pre-axial/pre-eccentric loads)  
     – BEAM adds: A (cross-section area), L (length override), EYA/EZA/EYE/EZE (nodal eccentricities), REF (reference to section database)  
   • BEPL  
     – Plate-like beam: FROM, TO, INC, TYPE, EY/EZ (local eccentricities), REF/REFT (section reference and orientation), OPT (optimization flag)  
   • QUAD  
     – Four-node shell: FROM, TO, INC, TYPE, Z (thickness), DPX/DPY/DPZ (offsets), NTYP (normal type), VTYP (viscous-type)  
   • BRIC  
     – Eight-node brick: same fields as QUAD but without VTYP  

3. Transformation/copy record  
   • COPY  
     – To replicate element definitions: NO (copy step), FACT (scale), TYPE, FROM/TO (range of entity numbers), INC (number increment), REF (reference element), DX/DY/DZ (translation vector), ALPH (rotation about axis), WIDE/YEX (element-width/distribution), PROJ (projection code)  

4. Line/arbitrary rigid groups  
   • LAR  
     – List of arbitrary rigid connections or lines: NO, N (number of entries), NAR (node-to-node arrays), T (type), Z2/Z4/Y2/Y4 (node coordinate arrays), GRP/X1…X4/Y1…Y4/Z1…Z4 (group indices and coordinate arrays), M (mass or multiplicity)  

5. Miscellaneous geometry records  
   • POIN  
     – Single point: REF (geometry ref), NO (point ID), P (point-type), TITL, X/Y/Z, PROJ, WIDE (graphic width), NREF (node reference), TYPE (point style)  
   • LINECURV  
     – Curved line definition: REF, NO, TITL, PROJ, WIDE, NREF, TYPE, plus node-sequence arrays P1/P2… and their corresponding X1/Y1/Z1, X2… (snippet truncated in source)  

Across all records, identifiers such as P6, X6, Y6, Z6, AREA, REF, NO, TITL, PROJ, WIDE, NREF, TYPE, DAWH, TRPL, P, PB, PW, PF, PFAC, DIST, A, DPOS, DMIN, DMAX, Y, Y2, HW, ZW, HF, PHI, B, BW, LW, SNO, FRB, DAB, BOGI, FRBO, DABO, WHEE, FRWH, DAWH, CONT, Y3, Z3, TYP, GUID may appear elsewhere as field codes or icon definitions but only those listed under each record header are active for that record. This layout makes it straightforward to programmatically look up which data-fields accompany any given record type when ingesting or querying the vector store.

The input table is a richly structured, multi-page listing of engineering or survey records, each row capturing a discrete feature or measurement within a broader project.  For RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) purposes it breaks down as follows:

1. General Structure  
• Pagination:  The table spans at least two pages (note “Table continued on next page”).  Continuation is managed by the CONT column.  
• Row Identity:  Each record has a globally unique GUID plus a project-local key pair <PROJ, NO> to ensure referential integrity.  An optional NREF field gives a secondary reference index.

2. Reference & Metadata Fields  
• PROJ   – Project code or job identifier.  
• NO     – Sequential record number within PROJ.  
• REF, NREF – Primary and secondary reference codes for cross-linking between tables or external databases.  
• TITL (×2) – Short descriptive title or label.  One might hold a category name, the other a free-text description.  
• TYP, TYPE – Categorical flags or type codes to distinguish record classes (e.g. “Borehole,” “Profile,” “Anchor Point”).  
• GUID   – Universally unique identifier for external lookups or API calls.  
• CONT   – Continuation marker (Y/N) for rows that overflow onto subsequent pages.

3. Geometry & Spatial Coordinates  
• P6, X6, Y6, Z6  – High-precision Cartesian or geodetic coordinates in a defined datum.  
• AREA   – Computed surface or planimetric area tied to the feature polygon.  
• DIST   – Linear separation or measured distance from a reference origin.  
• DPOS, DMIN, DMAX – Positional offsets and minimum/maximum extents along a given axis.

4. Dimensional Attributes  
• WIDE   – Nominal width.  
• HW, ZW, HF – Height- and zone-related dimensions (e.g. wall height, zone width, freeboard height).  
• B, BW, LW – Base dimension, base width, length width (perhaps footprint).  
• Y, Y2, Y3 – Auxiliary coordinate axes or staging levels for multi-story or tiered features.  
• Z3     – Tertiary elevation or a transformed Z coordinate.

5. Material & Profile Parameters  
• P, PB, PW – Pressure or load values (P) plus boundary (PB) and working (PW) pressures.  
• PF, PFAC – Profile factors or correction coefficients applied in design computations.  
• PHI    – Angular orientation (dip, strike or azimuth) in degrees.

6. Specialized Flags & Feature Codes  
• TRPL   – “Triple” flag indicating three-part assemblies or triangulated data.  
• SNO    – Sub-element number or sequence within a compound feature.  
• FRB, FRBO, FRWH – Feature bores or breaklines (FRB), offsets (FRBO), and width-specific breaklines (FRWH).  
• DAB, DABO – Depth abutment values and offsets, perhaps for retaining-wall toe and heel.  
• BOGI, WHEE – Geotechnical or machinery codes (bogie assemblies, wheel supports).

7. Calculated & Derived Metrics  
• A      – Computed area (may duplicate or verify AREA).  
• DIST   – Internal cross-distance confirming spatial relationships.  
• DAWH   – Depth at wall head or similar reference head datum.  
• TRPL   – Indicates aggregated triple-point records used in mesh or finite-element models.

8. Usage Notes for RAG Indexing  
– Each column name is itself a “term” in the vector store.  Queries on ‘DAWH’ should retrieve rows with depth at wall head measurements.  
– GUID is the ideal retrieval key for direct document fetch.  Composite keys <PROJ, NO> support secondary lookups.  
– CONT, REF, NREF help stitch together multi-page records or link to external tables.  
– TYPE/TYP and PF/PFAC enable faceted filtering by feature class or applied profile factor.

By mapping each column to a clear semantic category—identity, geometry, dimension, material, feature flags—you ensure compact, high-recall embedding vectors.  This structure allows downstream RAG systems to answer questions like: “Which borehole outlines (TYPE=Borehole) exceed 2 m depth (DAWH>2) within Project X?” or “Retrieve the elevation profiles (PF, PFAC) for features with angular orientation PHI between 30° and 60°.”

This table is a schema definition for a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store, listing every “Record” type and its associated “Items” (i.e. fields or attributes).  It serves as a blueprint for parsing, indexing and retrieving data uniformly across a variety of domain-specific record types.  Below is a detailed breakdown.

1. Overall Structure  
  • Two columns: “Record” (the name of a logical grouping) and “Items” (the short-code field names belonging to that grouping).  
  • The left column enumerates record types in UPPERCASE.  The right column lists their item codes, usually comma-separated.

2. Record Types and Key Fields  
  – VOLU (Volume)  
    • Positional fields: P1…P6, X1…X6, Y1…Y6, Z1…Z6  
    • Reference fields: REF, NO (number), TITL (title), TYPE  
    • Recurring pattern: P1–P3/X1–X3/Y1–Y3/Z1–Z3 define three key points; the same pattern extends to P6…  
    • GUID fields: ID, TAG

  – EXPO / EVAL (Exposure / Evaluation)  
    • EXPO: NO, TO, PASS  
    • EVAL: TYPE, NO, NAME, IND

  – CTRL / ECHO (Control / Echo)  
    • CTRL: OPT (option), VAL, V2, V3, V4  
    • ECHO: OPT, VAL, VAL1

  – RESP (Response)  
    • Classification & timing: TYPE, CLAS, MOD  
    • Sub-areas & zones: SA, SB, SMIN, TB, TC, TD, TE  
    • Keys & attributes: K1, K2, ZONE, AG, AH, AV, BEZ

  – FUNC (Function)  
    • Flags & values: T, F  
    • Timers: T1, T2, T3, T4, TMIN, TMAX  
    • Scalars: S, F2, F3, F4  
    • Descriptive: TITL

  – ACCE (Access)  
    • Meta: TYPE, NO  
    • Axes & offsets: AX, AY, AZ, AXX, AYY, AZZ, WXX, WYY, WZZ  
    • References: REF, REFX, REFY, REFZ, REFZ  
    • Annotations: ARED, AH, GH, LINF

  – STEP  
    • Step definition: N (step number), DT (delta time), LCST, TITL

  – GAX (Grid Axes)  
    • Coordinates & increments: NO, S (scale), X, Y, Z, R, A  
    • Secondary axes: R2, NX, NY, NZ  
    • Alignment & inclusion: ALF, INCL, INCR  
    • Meta: TYPE, TITL

  – LANE  
    • Lane identity: NO, TYPE  
    • Widths: WR, WL  
    • Boundaries: SA, SE  
    • Positions: YCA, YCE, YRA, YLA, YRE, YLE  
    • Labels: L, HSA, HSE  
    • Inset/offset: INCA, INCE, HEFF, BEFF, DEFF, INCD, ASL

  – TRAI (Trajectory or Train)  
    • Classification: TYPE, P1  
    • Geometry & factors: PFAC, WIDT, PHI, PHI2, PHIS, PHI4  
    • Motion & direction: V, FUGA, XCON, YEX, DIR, DIRT  
    • Feature sets: FRB, DAB, BOGI, FRBO, DABO, WHEE, FRWH, DAWH

3. Usage & Context  
  • Each record defines a distinct data object (e.g. a “volume,” a “response,” a “grid axis”).  
  • Short codes enable compact storage and fast lookup; consistent naming patterns (e.g. X-, Y-, Z- prefixes for coordinates) facilitate automated parsing.  
  • A RAG-based system can use these definitions to generate vector embeddings keyed on record-type and field values—supporting downstream retrieval, question-answering or on-the-fly summarization of complex engineering/GIS datasets.

The input table is a richly structured, multi‐page dataset intended to capture a wide range of geospatial, dimensional, physical and metadata attributes for each mapped feature.  It is likely used as the basis for a Retrieval‐Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store, where each field (or “record name”) serves as a key property for indexing, filtering and embedding.  Below is a detailed breakdown of its overall design, organized by functional category:

1. Identification & Referencing  
• GUID  
  – Globally unique identifier for traceability across pages/projects.  
• P6  
  – Parent or hierarchical grouping code.  
• NO / NREF  
  – Sequential or numeric reference indexes.  
• REF  
  – Alphanumeric reference tag (e.g. marker, beacon).  
• PROJ  
  – Project or survey name.  
• TITL (appears twice)  
  – Descriptive title(s) for the feature or segment.  
• TYP / TYPE  
  – Code or descriptor for the feature class (e.g. “road,” “well,” “segment”).  

2. Spatial Coordinates  
• X6, Y6, Z6  
  – Primary three‐dimensional coordinate set (easting, northing, elevation).  
• Y, Y2; Y3; Z3  
  – Secondary and tertiary northing/elevation variants (e.g. local/datums, redundant checks).  

3. Dimensional & Geometric Measures  
• AREA  
  – Footprint or cross‐sectional area (square units).  
• WIDE, HW, ZW, BW, LW  
  – Widths/depths in various axes (horizontal width, vertical extent, band/length width).  
• DIST  
  – Linear distance to a reference or between nodes.  
• A  
  – Amplitude or angular extent (context‐specific).  
• PHI  
  – Orientation or azimuth angle.  

4. Depth & Elevation Bands  
• DMIN / DMAX  
  – Minimum and maximum depths recorded.  
• DPOS  
  – Depth position of a feature relative to datum.  
• DAWH / DAWH (duplicate icon indicates repeating use)  
  – Depth above water/hydrostatic reference.  
• DAB / DABO  
  – Depth above base or overhead reference layer.  
• FRB, FRBO, FRWH  
  – Offsets “from bottom,” “from bottom overhead,” “from wheel” respectively.  

5. Physical & Derived Properties  
• P, PB, PW  
  – Pressure readings: total (P), bed (PB), water (PW).  
• PF, PFAC  
  – Frequency or pulse‐count and a correction/scale factor.  
• HF  
  – Half‐frequency or secondary harmonic measure.  
• B  
  – Bulk density or related bulk property.  
• WHEE  
  – Wheel‐derived measurement (e.g. distance from odometer).  

6. Supplemental Context  
• CONT  
  – Free‐text or structured context notes.  
• TRPL  
  – Triple‐point or control‐point linkage code.  
• SNO  
  – Station or sequence number within a survey.  

How It Fits Together  
– Each row represents one feature, control point or survey node.  
– Identification fields link it to projects and data hierarchies.  
– Coordinates anchor its spatial placement in 3D.  
– Dimensional/depth fields capture geometric shape, extents and subsurface relationships.  
– Physical and derived fields provide sensor‐based measurements or calculated parameters.  
– Contextual notes and metadata round out the description, making each record self‐sufficient for indexing, RAG embedding and downstream query.

This table defines a set of record-types (rows) and, for each, the full list of “items” (columns) that belong to that record.  In a RAG/vector‐store context, each record type can be thought of as a document schema or feature vector template.  The record names and their item codes (all in uppercase, generally 2–5 characters long) are as follows:

1. TRBL (Trouble/Structural Record)  
   • Geometry & load identifiers: P, PB, PW, PF, PFAC, VARI, A  
   • Lengths & offsets: L, LMAX, LDEL  
   • Coordinates & dimensions: Y, Y2, HW, ZW, HF, PHI, B, BW, LW  
   • Section/order numbers: SNO, FRB  
   • Derived areas & factors: DAB, BOGI, FRBO, DABO  
   • Wheel & bearing info: WHEE, FRWH, DAWH  

2. TREX (Triangular‐Element Record)  
   • Element index & grouping: NO, GRP  
   • Connectivity & ordering: SNO, NODE  
   • Optional flags: OPT  

3. WAVE (Wave Spectrum Record)  
   • Identification: TYPE  
   • Height, period & direction: H, T, D  
   • Spectral limits & steps: SWL, DX, DY, DZ  
   • Numerical controls: UC, EXPU, RHO, NF, TMIN, TMAX  
   • Spectral shape parameters: GAM, ALF, SIGA, SIGB  
   • Scaling & phase: S, PHI  

4. WIND (Wind Field Record)  
   • Code & zone identifiers: CODE, ZONE, CLAS  
   • Spatial increments: DX, DY, DZ  
   • Cross‐references & offsets: XREF, YREF, ZREF  
   • Wind‐vector components & rates: DXR, DYR, DZR, VR, VB  
   • Gust & height limits: GH, HMIN  

5. WPRO (Water‐Property Record)  
   • Depth & velocity: H, V  
   • Volume‐based offsets: VBOE  
   • Geographic coords: TLON, TLAT, TVER, LLON, LLAT, LVER  

6. WROU (Water‐Route Record)  
   • Sea–route flags: SEA  
   • Paired route points: A1–A9 and R1–R9 (up to nine successive A/R coordinate pairs)  

7. WTOP (Topographic‐Block Record)  
   • TYPE (block classification)  
   • Mesh nodes: XM, YM, ZM  
   • Increments: DX, DY, DZ  
   • Elevation & block ID: H, B  

8. WSPE (Spectral‐Parameter Record)  
   • TYPE (spectrum order)  
   • Low‐order coefficients: A1LO, A2LO, A3LO, BLO, CLO  
   • Low‐order angles: A1LA, A2LA, A3LA, BLA, CLA  
   • Velocity‐based extremes: A1VE, A2VE, A3VE, BVE, CVE, C3E  
   • Wave numbers & curvatures: KUU, KUV, KUW, KVU, KVV, KVW, KWU, KWV, KWW  

9. WGEN (General‐Spectrum Record)  
   • Spectrum control: LCG, SPEC, LCOH, HIST  
   • Time & frequency: T, DT, FMIN, FMAX, FDEL  
   • Type identifier: HTYP  
   • Nodal radii or harmonics: NR0 through NR9  
   • Temperature‐oriented flag: TO  

10. WIPT (Wire‐Point Record)  
    • Coordinates: X, Y, Z  
    • Grouping & tolerances: GRP, TOL  
    • Elimination flag & marking name: ELIM, MNAM  

11. LTD (Load/Target Record)  
    • Control flags: OPT  
    • Source references: SRLC, SRCT, SRC  
    • Targeting & grouping: TRGT, TRG  
    • Limits & offsets: LMAX, TRGM, DZ  
    • Loading type & factors: TYPE, FACT  
    • Directional moment & origin: DIR, HMOM, FROM  

12. LTDG (Load/Target Geometry Record)  
    • Point triplets: X1/Y1/Z1, X2/Y2/Z2, X3/Y3/Z3  
    • Classification & metadata: TYP, TITL  
    • Global unique ID: GUID  

Usage notes for RAG/vectorization:  
- Each record corresponds to a fixed schema; missing fields can be zero-padded or masked.  
- Field names are succinct but semantically rich—e.g., “PHI” always denotes an angle, “DAB” a derived area, “DX/DY/DZ” spatial increments.  
- Arrays (e.g., A1–A9/R1–R9 in WROU) imply repeated slots and can be flattened or stored as lists.  
- GUID fields (in LTDG) and TITL can be used as stable keys or textual metadata.  
- Type fields (TYPE, CLAS, HTYP, VARI, etc.) often drive branching logic in parsers or vector encodings.

The table summarizes the input fields of the GRP command, which governs how element groups are selected and how global environmental‐load options (wind, wave, friction) are applied in individual load cases.  If you leave GRP unspecified, all structural elements receive the loads.  If you do specify GRP entries, only those groups marked “YES” or “FULL” are loaded; any free‐defined loading based on structural elements (SLN, SAR, LAR, AUTO) ignores GRP.  Use GRP only when you cannot achieve the desired selection by geometry alone.  You can vary GRP settings per load case or split a complex pattern into multiple load cases and then merge via COPY.

Fields:

1. NO  (Group number)  
   – A positive integer that identifies a user‐defined group of elements (from AQUA or your own group definitions).  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: none (you must supply if you want to limit loading to particular groups).

2. VAL  (Value of selection)  
   – Determines whether group NO is used and whether a printout is generated:  
     • OFF – do not apply this group  
     • YES – apply loads to this group but do not include group‐wise printout  
     • FULL – apply loads and include group‐wise printout  
   – Unit: literal (LIT)  
   – Default: FULL

3. CS  (Construction stage for sections)  
   – Links to alternative cross‐section definitions in AQUA.  Use CS to switch between section variants (with different projected areas and roughness) for wind‐pressure calculations at different stages of construction.  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: none

4. WIND  (Option for wind loading)  
   – Chooses how the wind loads are derived and applied:  
     • NONE – do not apply any wind loads  
     • MEAN – use mean reference profiles from the WGEN generator  
     • GUST – apply equivalent static gust loads  
     • INFL – define an inflow‐boundary profile for DOLFIN CFD simulations  
     • SHOW – only visualize the turbulence field (no structural loads)  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: MEAN

5. CW  (Global factor for wind pressure coefficients)  
   – Scales all wind‐pressure coefficients (e.g. those defined on QUAD elements or via section definitions).  Use CW when you want to amplify or reduce code‐prescribed Cp values globally (for sensitivity studies, partial factors, etc.).  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: 1.0 (no scaling)

6. CFR  (Frictional‐pressure coefficient)  
   – Applies a friction‐reduction factor cfr to wind pressures on rough surfaces, chimneys, corrugated sheeting, etc.  Per EC1–2-4 Table 10.13.1, typical values are:  
     • smooth surfaces (steel, smooth concrete): 0.01  
     • rough (tar roofs, rough concrete): 0.02  
     • very rough (corrugated, folded): 0.04  
   – Unit: –  
   – Default: 0.02

7. WAVE  (Option for wave loading)  
   – Controls wave‐load application and visualization:  
     • NONE – no wave loads  
     • LOAD – apply the wave‐loading pattern defined elsewhere  
     • SHOW – display the free‐surface pattern (no structural loads)  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: LOAD

How it ties back to context  
— GRP lets you fine‐tune which groups of elements carry wind or wave loads when geometric or element‐type selection (SLN/SAR/LAR/AUTO) is insufficient.  
— CW and CFR adjust global pressure and friction coefficients; detailed Cp values still come from QUAD records (for plates) or section definitions (for beams).  
— For tall chimneys you might also incorporate height‐dependent reduction factors (ψ) separately.  
— When multiple environmental patterns are needed, you can create partial load cases with different GRP settings and then combine them via COPY into a single comprehensive load case.

sections: 3.3 GRP – Selection and Properties of Groups

content:
GRP
 Without specification all elements will be used. If defining values only the selected groups will be used for the elemental loads of the following load cases. Group selections will be ignored, if a free defined loading is applied based on structural elements (SLN, SAR, LAR as well as AUTO on these) Thus this selection will be needed only for those cases where the geometric selection is not sufficient.
 The selection of groups may be different for different load cases. For very complex load pat- terns you may generate the loading within several load cases and combine them then via the command COPY to a single load case.
 The value CW defines a global factor to the wind pressure coefficients. The pressure coeffi- cients are defined for plane elements via the record name QUAD, for beam elements they are defined with the sections. Reduction factors ψ are f.e. defined for chimneys as a function of the total height.
 The value CFR defines the frictional coefficients cfr according Table 10.13.1. of EC 1 part 2-4:
 Surface smooth (e.g. Steel, smooth concrete) 0.01 rough (e.g. rough concrete, tar roofs) 0.02 very rough (e.g. corrugated, ripped, folded) 0.04
 Frictional value cfr
 With CS you may select between different variants of cross sections defined in AQUA with different wind loading areas and roughness values.

The table defines the schema and semantics of the “ACT” record in SOFiLOAD (and related MAXIMA) for specifying an Action Type, its partial‐safety factors, combination coefficients, classification (PART) and default superposition rule (SUP). It is intended for ingestion into a RAG‐enabled vector store so that downstream agents can accurately interpret and generate “ACT” commands. Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown, data‐model notes and code‐generation pointers.

1. Item (Column 1)  
   – This is the attribute name when you invoke “ACT” in SOFiLOAD or MAXIMA. It must match exactly, e.g. TYPE, GAMU, PSI1, PART, SUP, TITL, etc.  
   – Data model: String enumeration of known items; used as keys in JSON or field‐tags in a document.

2. Description (Column 2)  
   – Human‐readable explanation.  
   – Example: “Unfavourable partial safety factor” for GAMU; “Default superposition of the load cases within the action” for SUP.

3. Unit (Column 3)  
   – “LIT4”, “LIT24” denote fixed‐length text fields (4 or 24 characters).  
   – “LIT” by itself for PART and SUP means variable‐length literal.  
   – “–” for numeric factors indicates dimensionless values.  
   – Data model: either String or Numeric.

4. Default (Column 4)  
   – “!”: mandatory for TYPE (no preset default);  
   – “*”: use code‐default defined in the INI‐file of the chosen design code (EC, DIN, SIA, etc.).  
   – Data model: if “*”, resolve at runtime by looking up the INI section “[action] → TYPE name”.

5. TYPE  
   – 4‐character literal. Identifier for the action (e.g. G, Q, L_U, Z_WIND, S_SEIS).  
   – May be subdivided with a “_X” suffix for categories A–Z (e.g. Q_A, Q_B).  
   – Reserved codes are pre‐loaded from the design code’s INI.  
   – Model as an enum or free‐string with validation against INI‐file.

6. GAMU / GAMF / GAMA  
   – GAMU: unfavourable partial factor (γG for permanent, γQ for variable, γE for seismic, etc.).  
   – GAMF: favourable partial factor (for load cases that produce a beneficial effect).  
   – GAMA: accidental safety factor (γA).  
   – Numeric, dimensionless; default from INI.

7. PSI0 / PSI1 / PSI2 / PS1S  
   – Combination coefficients (ψ0 rare, ψ1 frequent, ψ2 quasi‐permanent, ψ1S infrequent).  
   – Used in load combination formulas per EN 1990/A1 or national annex.  
   – Numeric, dimensionless; default from INI.

8. PART  
   – Classifies the action into superposition equation segments:  
     • G  = permanent  
     • P  = prestress  
     • Q  = variable (live)  
     • Q_1 … Q_99 = variable load groups 1–99 (bridge models, etc.)  
     • A  = accidental  
     • E  = seismic  
   – Must be provided for user‐defined TYPEs (defaults to PART Q if omitted).  
   – Data model: enum with optional numeric suffix.

9. SUP  
   – Default rule for superposition of load cases belonging to the same TYPE (and its categories):  
     • PERM: permanent with single γ (sum all cases, then apply γG or γGf).  
     • PERC: permanent with per‐case γ (case‐wise favourable/unfavourable).  
     • COND: conditional (added only if unfavourable).  
     • EXCL: mutually exclusive within each category.  
     • EXEX: mutually exclusive across all categories of that TYPE.  
     • UNSI: COND but only unfavourable sign.  
     • USEX: EXCL but only unfavourable sign.  
     • ALEX: permanent alternative (one case per TYPE/category, always included).  
   – Can be overridden on individual load cases (LC records).

10. TITL  
    – Up to 24‐character descriptive title of the action.  
    – Free text; default “*” (code‐provided).

Relationships & Processing Notes  
• When a new TYPE is declared (ACT TYPE …), its defaults (GAMU, PSI*, PART, SUP) are pulled from the active INI‐file.  
• Subsequent LC (load‐case) records inherit these values but may override γ or combination rules.  
• Changing the design code (or invoking ACT INIT) resets all TYPE definitions.  
• PART and SUP guide MAXIMA’s intermediate and final superposition steps—especially critical when grouping variable actions into Q_1…Q_n or combining Q vs. E (seismic) segments.  
• For RAG retrieval, index by TYPE, PART, SUP to ensure correct mapping of codes to their combination logic and safety‐factor semantics.

The input table is a compact summary of how basic “actions” (i.e. load types) are represented in the SOFiLOAD/AQUA‐MAXIMA environment. It lists for each action its normal literal, its prefix when treated as an “additional” action, its prefix when treated as a “special” action, and a brief human-readable remark. Below is a detailed, column-by-column breakdown and row-by-row interpretation:

1. Columns  
   • Normal – the primary 1–4-character literal used to identify a preset action type in ACT or LC records.  
   • Add. (Additional) – the same literal prefixed by “Z” when the action is flagged as additional loading (SUP ALEX or equivalent).  
   • Spec. (Special) – the same literal prefixed by “S” when the action is flagged as special loading.  
   • Remark – a short description of what the action represents, often indicating which sub-categories (e.g. G_1, G_2) are encompassed.

2. Row 1: “–” / NONE  
   • Normal = “–” (displayed in italics as NONE)  
   • Add. = (blank)  
   • Spec. = (blank)  
   • Remark = “for LC only: not assigned to an action”  
     ­ This row serves as a default placeholder. If a load case (LC record) is created without any ACT record before it, it gets assigned this special “NONE” action, meaning it will not pick up any partial safety factors, combination coefficients or superposition rules from a defined action. In effect it is an unclassified load case.

3. Row 2: “Gᵍ” / “ZGᵍ” / “SGᵠ”  
   • Normal = “Gᵍ”  
     ­ The literal “G” identifies the permanent dead‐load action. The superscript “g” indicates it uses the dead‐load partial safety factor set (γ_G, γ_G1, γ_G2) from the INI or EC defaults.  
   • Add. = “ZGᵍ”  
     ­ When that same dead‐load action is to be treated as an additional load (e.g. for envelope or ultimate‐vs‐accidental combination), the literal is prefixed with “Z.” It still uses the dead‐load factor group (superscript g).  
   • Spec. = “SGᵠ”  
     ­ When dead‐load is flagged as a special load case (e.g. for special combinations or groupings), the prefix “S” is used. The superscript “q” indicates that the SOPI‐LOAD special‐load safety factors (often aligned with variable‐action group rules) apply.  
   • Remark = “dead load (G + G_1 + G_2)”  
     ­ This clarifies that the generic dead‐load action “G” encompasses all its subcategories G_1 and G_2 (e.g. self‐weight of different structural components). In practice, defining ACT G will automatically initialize three categories: G, G_1 and G_2. All three share the same combination rules (PART G) and use either SUP PERM or SUP PERC according to the INI default.

Key takeaways for RAG vector storage:  
• Normal, “Z…”, and “S…” forms of each action should be indexed as distinct retrieval keys, since they alter combination behavior (additional vs. special).  
• The superscript codes (g, q, etc.) point to the partial safety factor set in use – these should be stored in metadata so that when a user queries “G,” the system can supply γ_G, ψ₀, ψ₁, ψ₂, SUP rule, and PART assignment.  
• The “NONE” row shows the fallback for unassigned load cases; it carries no factors or superposition rules.  
• The remark column provides a concise natural-language description, useful for tooltips or documentation retrieval.  
By capturing each load type’s literal, its prefixed variants, the governing factor group, and a human-readable remark, this table forms the nucleus of the action‐definition ontology that drives automatic combination and envelope generation in SOFiLOAD and MAXIMA.

How this ties into ACT and LC  
 • When you issue “ACT <type>” in SOFiLOAD (or AQUA), you pull in the INI-file’s default combination coefficients (γG, ψ0, ψ1, ψ2, etc.) for that action.  You can then subdivide it into categories (e.g. Q_A, Q_B) by appending “_<letter>.”  
 • Each action is automatically assigned a PART for superposition equations:  
    – PERMANENT (PART G) for G_1, G_2, R, etc.  
    – VARIABLE (PART Q or PART Q_1…Q_99) for Q, L, W, S, F  
    – ACCIDENTAL (PART A), SEISMIC (PART E)  
 • SUP rules (PERM, COND, EXCL, EXEX, ALEX) govern how multiple load cases within one action group combine—defaults come from the INI-file but can be overridden per LC record in MAXIMA.  
 • Z- and S-variants are typically treated as part of the same action group for superposition; for example, all Z1 and S1 cases “belong” to G_1.  

In a RAG setting, you would index each action row under its “Normal” symbol (and variants Z- and S-) and store its combination defaults, PART classification, SUP defaults, and remark text so that your retrieval layer can present the correct action metadata whenever a user or downstream process queries “ACT Q” or “ACT G_2,” etc.

The table maps the SOFiLOAD “SUP” settings for load-case superposition onto the corresponding MAXIMA LC record TYPE codes and gives a concise explanation of each. In a RAG (retrieve‐and‐generate) vector store context, this table serves as a lookup for how different groups of load cases are to be combined or excluded in structural-safety checks.

Columns  
1. SOFiLOAD SUP – the keyword used in the SOFiLOAD input to define default treatment of multiple load cases within one action.  
2. MAXIMA LC TYPE – the literal(s) written into the MAXIMA “LC” record to enforce the same combination rule. Suffixes “no” or “no” (e.g. Ano, Xno, AGno) indicate that a numeric group identifier may follow.  
3. Explanation – plain‐English summary of how load cases governed by this SUP are handled at combination time.

Rows  

1. PERM  | PERM, G     | “always (permanent), partial safety factor action-wise.”  
   • All load cases in a permanent action are summed. One global safety factor (GAMU or GAMF) applies to the total.  

2. PERC  | PERC        | “always (permanent) with variable factors, partial safety factor load-case-wise.”  
   • Each load case may carry its own safety factor; sign-wise still permanent.  

3. COND  | COND, Q     | “conditional (only unfavourable).”  
   • Variable loads that enter the combination only if they increase design effect (e.g. live load, wind).  

4. EXCL  | Ano         | “mutually exclusive, MAXIMA record LC different alternative group numbers per category.”  
   • Within an action category, only one load case may govern; group number (A1, A2 …) distinguishes categories.  

5. EXEX  | Ano         | “mutually exclusive but conditional inclusive categories (only within an action); only one alternative group number used for all categories of an action.”  
   • Categories exclude each other, but only one group number is assigned to all categories of that action.  

6. UNSI  | W           | “changing sign (e.g. seismic actions).”  
   • Loads that can act in both tension and compression; always included with sign considered.  

7. USEX  | Xno         | “changing sign, mutually exclusive with input of an alternative group number in MAXIMA record LC.”  
   • Sign-changing loads that also exclude other group members; X1, X2… group ids required.  

8. ALEX  | AGno        | “always but exclusive (only within an action) with input of an alternative group number in MAXIMA record LC.”  
   • Permanent alternative groups: every action supplies one case, even if favorable; AG1, AG2… designate groups.  

9. F     | F           | “additional load case to be combined.”  
   • Special flag marking secondary or auxiliary load cases to be included in the final combination.

How to read it  
When you define SUP in a SOFiLOAD ACT record, the program writes the associated MAXIMA LC TYPE into each load-case record. At combination run time, MAXIMA identifies SUP = PERM or PERC as permanent, COND/Q as conditional, and EXCL/EXEX/ALEX/USEX as various exclusion logics. Group identifiers (Ano, Xno, AGno) link categories or alternative sets. This mapping table is therefore a key reference for automating superposition rules across SOFiLOAD and MAXIMA in a RAG‐enabled workflow.

 HEAD COMB 1 desi TYPE desi BASE 2100 ACT XY_A LC -1 ACT XY_B LC -1 ACT XY_C LC -1 ACT XY_D LC -1
 HEAD
 COMB 1 desi TYPE desi BASE 2100
 or
 COMB 2 expl TYPE desi BASE 2200
 ADD {QI} gamm
 First of all three load groups Q_1, Q_2 and Q_3 are defined with PART in the program SOFiLOAD. The categories XY_A und XY_B are a art of the load group 1. Their load cases are mutually exclusive only within the respective category about the input SUP EXCL. The cate- gories XY_C and XY_D are a part of the load groups 2 and 3. All load cases of both categories are mutually exclusive about the input SUP EXEX.
 With one of the MAXIMA combinations then the superposition is done as follows: First of all MAXIMA searches which load cases of the load group 1 are decisive (possible one ore two or no load case = first intermediate superposition).Then the decisive load case of the load groups 2 and 3 is determined (possible one or no load case = second intermediate superposition). In the last step the final superposition is done. Either the decisive load cases of the load group 1 or the decisive load case of the goups 2 and 3 are here the final result.
 It should be noted here that load groups are mutually exclusive. If, for example, the superpo- sition of the load cases for two load load groups are specified with SUP COND - conditionally, only the load cases of the decisive load group are taken into account.
 Example:
 PROG SOFILOAD
 HEAD ACT XY_1 gamu 1.4 0.0 0.6 0.4 0.2 0.6 PART Q_1 SUP cond ACT XY_2 gamu 1.3 0.0 0.5 0.3 0.1 0.5 PART Q_2 SUP cond

HEAD ACT XY_1 gamu 1.4 0.0 0.6 0.4 0.2 0.6 PART Q_1 SUP cond ACT XY_2 gamu 1.3 0.0 0.5 0.3 0.1 0.5 PART Q_2 SUP cond.
 HEAD
 The load cases of category XY_1 belong to load group 1 and those of category XY_2 belong to load group 2. Thus, either the load cases of XY_1 or of XY_2 are taken into account in the superposition depending on which brings the more unfavorable result.

The table presented defines the structure of an SOFiLOAD “LC” (load-case) record. Each row corresponds to one parameter you supply when you create or modify a load case. The four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—tell you (1) what keyword to use, (2) what it means, (3) what kind of value or unit it requires, and (4) what value SOFiLOAD will assume if you omit it.

1. NO  
   • Description: Sequential number identifying the load case.  
   • Unit: none (integer).  
   • Default: 0 (you must normally supply a non-zero number).

2. TYPE  
   • Description: Action or category of the load case (for example a design combination or a dynamic load). Predefined or user-defined action names may be used, or special single-letter codes:  
     – “NONE” or “–” means no action.  
     – D, A, E, P, F, N, R, H, HZ, PT, LT, MT, ST, VT assign ultimate, service or timber-specific combinations.  
     – “IMP” declares an imperfection load case; “EINF” creates an influence‐line case.  
   • Unit: LIT4 (up to 4 characters).  
   • Default: “*” (inherit the action TYPE from the previously defined load case or from the action record ACT).

3. FACT  
   • Description: Global multiplier for all forces and moments in this load case. (Does not affect temperature, strain or prestressing loads, nor dead-load factors FACD/DLX/DLY/DLZ.)  
   • Unit: none (real).  
   • Default: 1.0.

4. FACD  
   • Description: Multiplier for the structural dead weight (all components simultaneously).  
   • Unit: none.  
   • Default: 0.0 (dead load switched off unless you specify).

5. DLX, DLY, DLZ  
   • Description: Individual directional factors for dead weight in global X, Y, Z axes. You must supply the correct sign to reflect gravity. If only FACD is given, SOFiLOAD applies dead load in the defined gravity direction.  
   • Unit: none.  
   • Default: “*” (inherit component from FACD or from action defaults).

6. GAMU, GAMF  
   • Description: Unfavourable and favourable safety factors used in design combinations.  
   • Unit: none.  
   • Default: “*” (inherit from action TYPE).

7. PSI0, PSI1, PSI2, PS1S  
   • Description: Combination coefficients for standard (Ψ0), frequent (Ψ1), quasi-permanent (Ψ2) and non-frequent (Ψ1S) variable actions.  
   • Unit: none.  
   • Default: “*” (use action defaults).

8. GAMA  
   • Description: Accidental safety factor.  
   • Unit: none.  
   • Default: “*”.

9. CRIT  
   • Description: Time criterion in seconds. Typically used for dynamic or transient loads.  
   • Unit: sec.  
   • Default: 0.0.

10. CRI1, CRI2, CRI3  
    • Description: Three user-defined criteria for post-processing (e.g. user-supplied strength reduction, stability margin, or any scalar quantity). These fields may be set before analysis or updated afterward via DBVIEW. TALPA uses CRI1 for its own material safety factor.  
    • Unit: none.  
    • Default: 0.0.

11. TITL  
    • Description: Free-text title or comment describing the load case.  
    • Unit: LIT32 (up to 32 characters).  
    • Default: “–” (no title).

Key behaviors and interactions:  
– If you redefine FACT, FACD or directional dead-load factors, any previously defined loads in that LC are deleted, ensuring you can explicitly rebuild the loading.  
– Using TYPE = DEL will completely erase the load case and all its contents.  
– The special TYPE = REST forces regeneration of all loads from the original generators or COPY commands, useful after graphical input changes.  
– A load case that contains only COPY commands will be purged and then re-populated with each COPY when you use REST, guaranteeing consistency.  
– Influence-line load cases (TYPE = EINF) require at least one BEPL, BEAM or QUAD entry to define the response quantity; typically you set up one LC per influence-line ordinate.  

Together, these fields give you full control over how individual load cases are defined, manipulated, combined and named within the SOFiLOAD environment.

content:
The table on “Influence Line – needed Loading – e.g.” is a concise recipe for setting up influence‐line load cases (TYPE EINF) in SOFiLOAD. It ties five common response quantities to the minimal “impulse” loading needed to extract their influence lines, and shows the corresponding command syntax. Below is a breakdown of its structure and each entry:

1. Column Definitions  
   • Influence Line – the response quantity whose influence line you want to compute.  
   • needed Loading – the kinematic or curvature impulse that, when applied, will isolate that response.  
   • e.g. – a SOFiLOAD command template (element/ node type, load‐type code and a “?” placeholder for the load‐case number) showing how to implement that impulse.

2. Row-by-row Details  
   a) Beam-moment  
      – Influence Line: bending moment M(x) in a beam element.  
      – needed Loading: a unit “disrotation” (rotation jump) at the section.  
      – e.g.: “BEPL D?”  
        • BEPL invokes a beam‐element point load.  
        • “D” indicates a pure moment (Dirac‐type rotation).  
        • “?” is replaced by the load‐case number (e.g. 91).  

   b) Beam-force  
      – Influence Line: shear‐force V(x) or axial‐force effect in a beam/truss.  
      – needed Loading: a unit “dislocation” (translation jump) at the section.  
      – e.g.: “BEPL W?”  
        • “W” stands for a translational load (Dirac‐type displacement).  

   c) QUAD-force  
      – Influence Line: in‐plane or transverse force in a shell/plate (quad element).  
      – needed Loading: a Dirac‐delta curvature impulse.  
      – e.g.: “QUAD E*”  
        • QUAD invokes a quadrilateral finite‐element load.  
        • “E” triggers a curvature (second derivative) impulse; “*” means any sub-type or parameterized ID.  

   d) Support force  
      – Influence Line: reaction force at a support node.  
      – needed Loading: a unit nodal displacement at that support.  
      – e.g.: “NODE W?”  
        • NODE with “W” applies a point‐displacement load at a node.  
        • The computed reaction at that node under this imposed displacement is the influence‐line value.  

   e) Displacement  
      – Influence Line: nodal displacement u (in global X/Y/Z).  
      – needed Loading: a unit nodal load (force) at that node.  
      – e.g.: “NODE P?”  
        • “P” is the point‐force load at a node.  
        • The resulting displacement is the influence‐line ordinate.

3. Usage Notes  
   – These definitions only apply when the load case has been declared as TYPE EINF.  
   – You must supply at least one load command per influence‐line case; for multiple degrees of freedom or combined responses, repeat the appropriate load entries.  
   – The “?” in the examples is a placeholder you replace with your chosen load‐case number.  
   – Dirac-delta and unit‐kinematic loads are the standard way to “probe” the structure so that the recorded response at every location traces out the influence line.  

This table effectively summarizes the minimal instructions needed to generate standard influence lines for bending, shear, shell forces, support reactions and nodal displacements using SOFiLOAD’s command syntax.

 There are levels of working on load cases for SOFiLOAD:
 • Change of parameters of an action
 No definition of a load case number defines the safety factors and combination coefficients of the action TYPE.
 • Change of load case parameters
 Values TYPE, FACT, CRIT to CRI3 or TITL may be changed for existing load cases. But you may not define a factor of the dead load or any other loading as this will delete the total loading of that load case automatically.
 • Load generation
 Via load type REST you may change not only parameters but all the generated loading will be reestablished from the load generators - This is especially useful for postprocessing from graphical input definitions.
 For a load case containing COPY commands, i.e. is composed by other load cases, all loads are deleted and repeated all the COPY commands with REST.
 • Explicit definition of loading
 If factors of the structural dead weight or other loading are defined after a LC record, all loading data for that load case will be deleted, to allow the redefinition of loading for a given load case.
 • Explicit deletion of a load case
 If defining the TYPE DEL the total load case including all known data will be deleted imme- diately .
 The factor of the load case has (despite the wind load generator) no specific influence in SOFiLOAD and may be changed later at any time. Loads will be multiplied by this factor only when used in the analysis itself. The factor FACT affects all forces and moment loadings, however, not temperature, strain and prestressing loadings! It does also not affect dead load factors FACD, DLX, DLY or DLZ.

content:
The factor of the load case has (despite the wind load generator) no specific influence in SOFiLOAD and may be changed later at any time. Loads will be multiplied by this factor only when used in the analysis itself. The factor FACT affects all forces and moment loadings, however, not temperature, strain and prestressing loadings! It does also not affect dead load factors FACD, DLX, DLY or DLZ..
 The components of the dead weight will be in the positive direction of the requested global axis. You have to enter the correct sign for DLX to DLZ. If you specify only FACD, SOFiLOAD will apply the dead load in the direction defined as the gravity direction. A definition will delete all loads of this load case automatically.
 As type of the load case on may specify the name of an action. Only predefined or explicitly defined actions may be used with LC (see ACT). If the load case is supposed not to be assigned for an action, the literal NONE or ’-’ has to be input for TYPE. There are also some special literals possible, assigning a (e.g. non linear) load case to be of a spcific type used for special design tasks:
 (D) Ultimate Design combination
 (A) Ultimate accidental combination
 (E) Ultimate Earthquake combination
 (P) Service: Quasi permanent combination
 (F) Service: Frequent combination
 (N) Service: Non-frequent combination
 (R) Service: Rare (characteristic) combination
 (H) Comb. of principal loading
 (HZ) Comb. of principal+supplemental loading
 (PT) permanent load combination e.g. for timber
 (LT) long term load combination e.g. for timber
 (MT) middle term load combination e.g. for timber
 (ST) short term load combination e.g. for timber
 (VT) very short term load combination e.g. for timber
 Values GAMU to PS1S belong to the action TYPE in general. However they may have indi- vidual values for every specific load case. Thus at the time of the creation of a load case, the current values from the action will be taken as default for the individual load case for Version 23. Starting with version 2010 however only the explicitly defined values will be kept, all other values will adopt to those of the action itself if the action is changed.
 Values CRI1 to CRI3 are very general parameters of the load case. They may be used freely for postprocessing via DBVIEW. You may specify them in advance or set them after the analysis by reading some results from the database. (e.g. a system dimension, a strength reduction etc.) TALPA uses CRI1 for the safety factor of the material needed by analysis according to Fellenius.

content:
Below is a structured, narrative breakdown of the “NODE [m] 1001” load‐definition table. This description highlights each field, its purpose, units, defaults and any special rules or caveats. Use this as guidance when authoring or parsing nodal loads for a RAG‐backed vector store.

1. General Context  
  • Nodal loads in this block may be assigned either component‐by‐component (P, M, V) or as full vectors using the literal sets PP, MM, VV. In total up to seven scalar components (P1…P7) can be specified for complex load types.  
  • If a local‐coordinate system (from an SPT point in SOFiMSHC) is present at a node, all vector components refer to that system. Absent a local system, global axes are assumed.  
  • For special load laws—centrifugal forces, internal pressure, etc.—you may instruct the program to multiply the specified load values by the node’s radial distance or its square.  
  • Under axial-symmetry modeling, any nodal load is treated as “per unit circumference.” You must therefore supply loads in kN/m (or analogous) form; internally the software converts to actual nodal forces based on the node’s—and gravity axis’s—radial position.  
  • Assigning a prescribed displacement to a kinematically supported degree‐of‐freedom will deactivate that support; there is no “local displacement” override. If you need to simulate a constrained displacement, use stiff spring elements instead.

2. Field‐by‐Field Description

  • NO  
    – Definition: Node number or an alphanumeric secondary‐group label.  
    – Unit: “–” or literal (LIT)  
    – Default: “!” (required)  
  • TYPE  
    – Definition: Load type code (e.g. PG for point‐gravity, LC for load‐case, etc.).  
    – Unit: literal (LIT)  
    – Default: PG  
  • P1 … P7  
    – Definition: Up to seven scalar load components. Which of P1–P7 you use depends on TYPE—for example, a point‐force in global X/Y/Z might simply occupy P1, P2, P3. More complex load definitions (beam‐load shapes, temperature fields, etc.) may utilize all seven.  
    – Unit: “[∗]” (application‐specific; see load‐type documentation)  
    – Default: P1 is mandatory (“!”), P2–P7 default to zero (“–”).  
  • FRAD  
    – Definition: Radial‐multiplication flag for loads.  
      • R → multiply all P1…P7 values by the node’s radius (distance to the selected gravity axis).  
      • RR → multiply by the square of that radius.  
    – Unit: literal (LIT)  
    – Default: none (“–”)

3. Eccentricities → Converted to Moments  
  • EXX, EYY, EZZ  
    – Definition: Eccentricities about global X, Y, Z. These are transformed into moment contributions automatically.  
    – Unit: metres [m]  
    – Default: zero (“–”)  
  • MXX, MYY, MZZ  
    – Definition: Explicit moment components about the global axes.  
    – Unit: force‐length (same base unit as loads × m)  
    – Default: zero (“–”)  

4. Shear Components  
  • VXX, VYY, VZZ  
    – Definition: Shear or force components in secondary (usually rotational or shear‐specific) directions.  
    – Unit: force [kN or analogous]  
    – Default: zero (“–”)  

5. Additional Control  
  • SUB  
    – Definition: Sub‐model or subgroup label for filtering sets of nodal loads in multi‐case or staged analyses.  
    – Unit: literal (LIT)  
    – Default: none (“–”)

Key Notes for RAG Indexing  
  • Treat NO + TYPE as the primary key for deduplication.  
  • Store P1…P7, FRAD, EXX…VZZ as numeric attributes for full‐vector retrieval or range queries.  
  • Preserve default markers (“!”, “–”) as metadata flags indicating mandatory vs. optional.  
  • Index the presence of local‐coordinate overrides so downstream queries can distinguish global vs. local‐system loading.  
  • Tag axial‐symmetry nodes (via TYPE or FRAD flag) for correct post‐processing, since loads are circumference‐averaged rather than point‐values.

Table 3.8 in the SOFiMSHC documentation (“Type of the Nodal Loading”) defines every possible kind of load, displacement or rotation you can assign to a node. It is arranged in two columns: the left‐hand column names the load or movement component, and the right‐hand column gives its required unit. The entries are grouped by category as follows:

1. Global Forces and Moments (P1–P6)  
   • Force in global X-direction  Unit = kN  
   • Force in global Y-direction  Unit = kN  
   • Force in global Z-direction  Unit = kN  
   • Moment about global X-direction Unit = kNm  
   • Moment about global Y-direction Unit = kNm  
   • Moment about global Z-direction Unit = kNm  

2. Local Forces, Moments & Warping (P1l–P7l)  
   • Force in local x-direction  Unit = kN  
   • Force in local y-direction  Unit = kN  
   • Force in local z-direction  Unit = kN  
   • Moment about local x-direction Unit = kNm  
   • Moment about local y-direction Unit = kNm  
   • Moment about local z-direction Unit = kNm  
   • Warping moment (about local z) Unit = kNm²  

3. Full Vector Definitions via Literals  
   • Components of force PXX–PZZ (PP vector)  Unit = kN  
   • Components of moment MXX–MZZ (MM vector) Unit = kNm  
   • Expanded set MXX, MYY, MZZ, MB      Unit = kN (forces), kNm (moments)  
   • Alternate shorthand PX–PZ (forces) and MX–MZ (moments) plus MY, MZ, MB  

   Note: Vector definitions let you input up to seven components at once (P1–P7, M1–M7, V1–V7).

4. Prescribed Nodal Displacements  
   • Displacement in global X-direction Unit = mm  
   • Displacement in global Y-direction Unit = mm  
   • Displacement in global Z-direction Unit = mm  

5. Prescribed Nodal Rotations  
   • Rotation about global X-direction Unit = mrad  
   • Rotation about global Y-direction Unit = mrad  
   • Rotation about global Z-direction Unit = mrad  

Context & Usage Notes:  
- Individual components (P, M, V) or full vectors (PP, MM, VV) may be used; up to seven parameters per vector are supported.  
- Local‐axis loads require the node to have a local coordinate system defined (via SPT points). If none exists, global axes are used by default.  
- For centrifugal or pressure‐type loads, input values can be multiplied by the node’s radius or its square (relative to the chosen gravity axis).  
- In axisymmetric (revolution) models, loads defined in kN/m (e.g. radial) must be entered as PYY ±value; the software then automatically distributes them around the circumference.  
- Applying a nodal displacement on a degree of freedom that has a kinematic support will deactivate that support. Local displacements cannot be reversed—if required, model them with stiff spring elements.

See also: LC, TRUS, CABL, beam-loading, QUAD, BRIC, COPY, free- loading
 NODE
 [m]1001
 Loads in nodes will be defined in individual components or as complete vectors with the Literals P, M and V resp. PP. MM and VV. In those cases up to seven components may be defined.
 Local load directions require nodes with a local coordinate system (SOFiMSHC). Only nodes which are input as structural points (SPT points) with a local coordinate system in SOFiMSHC can be used here. If no such system is found, the global coordinate directions will be used instead.
 For special cases you may multiply the load values with the radius (e.g. centrifugal forces, internal pressures etc) or with the square of the radius. The radius is the distance of the node to the global axis which has been selected as gravity direction.
 In the case of axial symmetry load values are interpreted as circumference related, e.g. a radial load of 2 kN/m must be provided as PYY ±2.0. The program then automatically accounts for the radial position of the load application point.
 If a degree of freedom which has a kinematic constraint gets a nodal displacement, the con- straint will be deactivated. There is no way to invert that support condition. That’s why there are no local displacements available. They have to to be modelled with stiff spring elements if desired.

Below is a comprehensive, field‐by‐field description of the CABL command’s input table. This narrative is written to support ingestion into a RAG (Retrieval‐Augmented Generation) vector store, capturing semantics, allowable values and defaults for each parameter. Wherever relevant, cross‐references to related commands (LC, NODE, TRUS, beam‐loading, QUAD, BRIC, COPY, free-loading) and contextual guidance have been included.

1.  Command Context – “CABL”  
    •  Purpose: Assigns the same loading to a sequence (or group) of cable elements in a finite‐element model.  
    •  Behavior: Because cable elements carry no transverse bending stiffness, the specified line loads are internally converted into equivalent nodal forces at the element ends. In subsequent nonlinear analyses, actual cable sag and deflections are recovered by evaluating these nodal loads. For accurate results, nodes should be placed at all points of interest along the cable.  
    •  Group selection: In lieu of a numeric “FROM” element ID, the literal token GRP can be specified at the FROM column, and the group number must be provided in TO; this will automatically select all elements that belong to the named group.

2.  Table Columns  
    •  Item: The keyword or parameter name.  
    •  Description: A brief semantic of the field.  
    •  Unit: The physical unit or coding type.  
    •  Default: The value assumed if the user does not supply one.

3.  Detailed Parameter Descriptions  

    A.  FROM  
        –  What it is: Identifier of the first element in the loading sequence, or the literal “GRP” to indicate group‐based selection.  
        –  Valid entries: Positive integer (element ID) or the 3‐letter literal GRP.  
        –  Unit: none.  
        –  Default if omitted: “!” which triggers an error or prompts user to supply a valid start.  

    B.  TO  
        –  What it is: Identifier of the last element in the sequence, or the group number (when FROM=GRP).  
        –  Valid entries: Positive integer (element ID) or integer group label.  
        –  Unit: none.  
        –  Default: same as the FROM entry, meaning only one element (or one group) if TO is not explicitly supplied.  

    C.  INC  
        –  What it is: Step size used when iterating from FROM to TO.  
        –  Valid entries: Positive integer ≥1.  
        –  Unit: none.  
        –  Default: 1 (every element or group in the specified range is loaded).

    D.  TYPE  
        –  What it is: Specifies the load type and its global or local direction.  
        –  Valid entries (LIT):  
            •  PG – load per global unit length (e.g. force per global X‐direction).  
            •  PL – load per local unit length (body‐fixed cable axis).  
            •  Other two‐letter codes as defined under the beam‐loading or QUAD commands.  
        –  Unit: Literal code.  
        –  Default: PG.

    E.  PA  
        –  What it is: Magnitude of the line load applied at the cable’s start node.  
        –  Valid entries: Real number (positive or negative), consistent with the sign convention of the solver.  
        –  Unit: [*] dimensionless placeholder – interpreted as force per unit length (e.g. N/m or lb/ft) in the solver’s unit system.  
        –  Default: Must be provided (“!” triggers user input).

    F.  PE  
        –  What it is: Magnitude of the line load at the cable’s end node, allowing for linearly varying loads along the element.  
        –  Valid entries: Real number, same unit as PA.  
        –  Unit: [*].  
        –  Default: PA (uniform load if PE is not specified).

4.  Cross‐references and Additional Notes  
    •  See also:  
      –  LC – load case management; define which combinations or patterns apply.  
      –  NODE – point loads or boundary conditions at nodes.  
      –  TRUS – truss‐type element loading, conceptually similar but with axial‐only behavior.  
      –  beam‐loading, QUAD, BRIC – other element‐type load definitions providing analogous “TYPE/PA/PE” semantics.  
      –  COPY, free-loading – commands for duplicating or auto-generating loads.  
    •  Nonlinear analysis tip: Because nodal loads alone do not capture cable curvature, always discretize long spans into multiple elements with intermediate nodes at support or connection points.  
    •  Error handling: Omitting mandatory fields (e.g. PA) or supplying incompatible ranges (TO < FROM) will trigger immediate input‐validation errors.

Below is a structured, detailed description of “Table 3.10: Type of the Cable Loading” suitable for ingest into a RAG‐style vector store.  It covers the overall purpose, the column layout, the logical grouping of rows, the meaning of each entry in the “Type” column and its associated unit.  Wherever available, any code or keyword that would appear in the CABL input is included.

1. Table title and context  
   – Title: “Table 3.10: Type of the Cable Loading”  
   – Applies to the CABL command, which applies loads to ranges of cable elements.  Because cables cannot carry transverse loads in the classical finite‐element sense, CABL converts these to equivalent nodal loads and, in a subsequent nonlinear analysis, evaluates the cable deflection.  Users are advised to insert nodes at all important geometric points on a cable.

2. Columns  
   – Column 1: Type  
     • A keyword or numeric code specifying how the load is applied (global vs. local direction; projection; concentrated action; temperature‐type load; etc.)  
   – Column 2: Unit  
     • The physical unit in which the corresponding load parameter must be supplied.

3. Row grouping and entries  
   A. Distributed (per‐length) cable loads, global or local directions  
     – Type = X (or code “1”)  
       • Description: uniform cable load in the global X‐direction  
       • Unit: kN/m  
     – Type = Y (or code “2”)  
       • Description: uniform cable load in the global Y‐direction  
       • Unit: kN/m  
     – Type = Z (or code “3”)  
       • Description: uniform cable load in the global Z‐direction  
       • Unit: kN/m  
     – Type = 1 (or code “4”)  
       • Description: uniform cable load in the cable’s local-1 direction  
       • Unit: kN/m  
     – Type = 2 (or code “5”)
