The table shown defines the six parameters you must supply when issuing a TRUS command to apply loads to a series of truss elements.  TRUS automates the conversion of element-based loads into equivalent nodal forces (since trusses cannot carry transverse element loads directly).  In order to capture the correct distribution along each member, you should ensure that nodes exist at all points where loads or geometry change.  Below is a detailed, column-by-column and row-by-row description of that table:

Columns  
• Item: the keyword or parameter name you enter on the TRUS command line  
• Description: a brief explanation of what that parameter represents  
• Unit: the expected unit or data type  
• Default: the value assumed if you omit the parameter or use the “!” symbol  

Rows / Parameters  

1. FROM  
  ­– Description: “Number of first element or GRP.”  This is either the element ID at which to start applying loads or, if you enter the literal GRP, it flags that you will specify a group number instead.  
  ­– Unit: none (integer or the special literal GRP)  
  ­– Default: “!” (an exclamation point indicates you must supply a value; no internal default exists)  

2. TO  
  ­– Description: “Number of last element or group number.”  If you started with a numeric element ID, TO is the final element ID in the sequence.  If you began with GRP, TO is interpreted as the group identifier whose members all receive the same loading.  
  ­– Unit: none (integer or group ID)  
  ­– Default: the value of FROM (so if you omit TO, only the single element or group specified by FROM is loaded)  

3. INC  
  ­– Description: “Increment of element numbers.”  Defines the stride by which you step through element IDs (for example, an INC of 2 would load every other element between FROM and TO).  
  ­– Unit: none (integer)  
  ­– Default: 1 (load all elements in sequence)  

4. TYPE  
  ­– Description: “Load type and direction.”  Specify a two-letter literal (LIT) code that indicates how the load is oriented relative to the local truss axis (for example PG might denote “parallel to global Y,” etc.; see the TRUS reference for all allowed codes).  
  ­– Unit: literal (text code)  
  ­– Default: PG  

5. PA  
  ­– Description: “Load value at truss start point.”  The magnitude (and sign) of the force applied at the first node of each loaded truss element.  Units correspond to whatever force unit your model uses (e.g. kN, lb).  
  ­– Unit: [*] (model’s force unit)  
  ­– Default: “!” (you must explicitly enter a value)  

6. PE  
  ­– Description: “Load value at truss end point.”  The force magnitude at the second node of each element.  If you omit PE, it defaults to the same value as PA, producing a uniform load along the member.  
  ­– Unit: [*] (model’s force unit)  
  ­– Default: PA  

Additional Context  
• A single TRUS command can load an entire group of truss elements by using “GRP” in the FROM column together with the appropriate group number in TO.  
• Because truss members cannot resist loads perpendicular to their axis in their local element formulation, TRUS automatically converts any distributed or point loads into equivalent nodal forces.  
• For more advanced beam-style loading (bending, torsion), see the BEAM-LOADING and QUAD/CABL/COPY commands. For pure nodal point loads, use NODE. For free-loading or bracing elements, see FREE-LOADING or BRIC.

The table entitled “Table 3.12: Type of the Truss Loading” is a simple two-column listing of all of the legal TYPE settings for the TRUS command together with their physical units.  In the documentation these TYPE keywords tell the solver which form of load or action to apply to a range of truss elements; each row in the left-hand column is a different TYPE identifier (expressed here generically as “direction,” “length,” “reference,” etc.), and the right-hand column shows the corresponding unit.  Visually the table is broken into three logical blocks by horizontal rules:

1.  Distributed loads in the element’s local coordinate system  
    – Four rows, all with unit kN/m.  
    – These correspond to applying a uniform line‐load in each of the element’s principal directions (local 1, 2 and 3 axes, plus the element axis itself).

2.  Distributed loads measured in global projection  
    – Three rows, all with unit kN/m.  
    – These represent the same kind of per-length load, but projected onto the global X, Y or Z axes rather than the element’s local axes.

3.  Scalar or element-specific actions and parameters  
    – Shrinkage (“0/00”): a relative deformation or humidity-type strain specified in parts‐per‐thousand.  
    – Axial force (“kN”): a constant concentrated force applied along the member axis.  
    – Length (“mm”): the undeformed or reference length of the truss element.  
    – Temperature reference (“K”): the temperature change or reference temperature for thermal loading.  
    – Two additional rows (unit “–”) are placeholders for non-dimensional flags or internal qualifiers that do not carry a physical unit.

Because a truss can only carry axial force, any distributed‐load entry is internally converted into equivalent nodal forces at the element ends.  It is therefore good practice to insert intermediate nodes at points of interest.  When you invoke TRUS you supply FROM and TO to pick a continuous element range (or instead the literal “GRP” and a group number), then you specify TYPE (one of the 11 keywords above), an amplitude value in its associated unit, and link it to a load case.  On execution the software decomposes that setting into the proper nodal loads or element‐level actions according to the entries in this table.

Vertical tic marks identify the start and end node of each beam segment. Beneath the axis, two horizontal dimension lines are drawn: the first, labeled “A,” spans the combined length of Beam 1 and Beam 2; the second, labeled “L,” covers the full length of Beam 3. Break symbols (short zig-zag slashes) on the baseline at the right end of the “A” span and the right end of the “L” span indicate that these are input ranges rather than continuous plotted distances.

On Beam 3, a series of identical downward-pointing arrows represent concentrated loads distributed at regular intervals along its span. Each arrow originates on or just above the beam axis and points downward toward the beam, signifying a vertical load. All arrows carry the same label, “PA,” indicating a point load of magnitude PA applied repeatedly over the region covered by L. A single “PA” label floating above the cluster of arrows reinforces that this is a uniformly repeated point-load value.

No loads are shown on Beam 1 or Beam 2. The transition from unloaded to loaded region is exactly at the interface between Beam 2 and Beam 3, corresponding to the end of the “A” dimension and the start of “L.” The tic marks at both ends of Beam 3 emphasize that loading definitions (for example via BEAM or BEPL cards) can refer to element‐number ranges rather than individual nodes or sub-element segments.

Visually:
- A straight horizontal line with three equally thin stroke segments.
- Vertical ticks at the two interfaces: Beam 1→Beam 2 and Beam 2→Beam 3.
- Under the first two segments (“Beam 1” and “Beam 2”) the legend “A” spans their combined length.
- Under the third segment (“Beam 3”) the legend “L” spans its length.
- At the top of the right-hand segment, closely spaced vertical arrows all labeled “PA” point downward onto Beam 3.

Semantically, the figure illustrates:
  • How to define a load on a subset of beam elements (elements covering L) independent of the finite‐element mesh subdivision.
  • The use of a beam input command (BEAM … PXX A #H L PA #EMAX … REF YY or equivalent BEPL definitions) to assign a constant point‐load PA over the local coordinate range A→L.
  • The notion of referencing the load extent to the “total set of selected beam elements,” with local distances measured from the beginning node of the beam sequence (gravity center by default) or a user‐specified REF system.
  • That even though the beam geometry might be continuous in space, loading is specified by element number ranges and local beam‐axis coordinates.

This schematic is thus a compact visual guide to setting up uniform discrete loads on part of a continuous beam in a RASTRAN‐style preprocessor, highlighting the separation between geometry definition (BEAM CARDs, node connectivity) and load definition (PXX/PA/PE with local ranges and reference systems).

The diagram shows how a single straight beam element is embedded in a 3-D global coordinate system and how various reference directions (REF) are defined for applying loads. From a common origin (the “start node” of the beam), three thick arrows indicate the world axes:

  • x-axis: slanted upward and to the right, labeled “x”  
  • y-axis: slanted downward and to the right, labeled “y”  
  • z-axis: vertical downward, labeled “z”  

From that same origin, the beam itself is drawn as a heavy straight line extending obliquely into space. Midway along this line is the label “S,” denoting the beam’s own longitudinal axis, which serves as the local coordinate for defining loads when REF=S (i.e. along the true beam axis).  

Two additional vectors illustrate the orthogonal projections of the beam axis into global reference directions:  
  – “XY” is the projection of the beam’s S-axis onto the global XY-plane. It is drawn as a thinner line lying roughly in the horizontal plane.  
  – “YY” is the projection of the beam’s S-axis onto the global y-axis direction, shown as another thin line pointing down-right more steeply.  

At the beam’s far end, a vertical line drops down from the beam into space, capped by a thick downward arrow. This arrow represents a point load (as would be specified via BEPL or a BEAM … PA/PE command) acting at some point along the beam section, typically anywhere between the gravity center or an eccentric position (EYA, EYE, EZA, EZE).  

Under the sketch is the caption “Figure 3.3: Reference systems REF,” emphasizing that the user can choose any of these directions—S, XX/YY/ZZ (projection onto a single global axis), XY/XZ/YZ (projection onto a global plane), SS/SSS/LSS (ratios of continuous beam, support or free-span lengths), or GXX/GYY/GZZ (absolute world-coordinate lengths)—to define the start (A) and end (L) of a load span. Negative prefixes (“–”) flip the measurement to run back from the beam’s end node.  

By visualizing S, its projections, and the downward point-load arrow together, the figure makes clear how “REF” selects which coordinate direction or ratio the software uses when converting user-supplied load extents into local beam coordinates.

The two‐by‐two table you’ve provided governs how point‐ or distributed beam loads (as entered via BEAM/BEPL) get located in the section when you do or do not supply eccentricity offsets (EYA/EYE/EZA/EZE), and how that choice interacts with the beam’s “reference axis” setting (NP).  In Effect, it says:

  1. NP=0 (“centric” beam, gravity‐center reference)  
     • If you do *not* specify any excentricities, the resultant load is applied at the gravity-centre of the cross‐section.  
     • If you *do* specify excentricities, those EYA/EYE/EZA/EZE values are measured from the gravity centre.

  2. NP=–1 (“excentric” beam, sectional‐coordinate‐system reference)  
     • If you do *not* specify any excentricities, the load still ends up acting at the gravity-centre.  (No eccentricity → gravity‐centre action by default.)  
     • If you *do* specify excentricities, those offsets are measured from the origin of the cross‐sectional coordinate system (not from the gravity centre).

Put another way:

– “Load definition without excentricities” always means “action in the gravity centre,” regardless of NP.  
– “Load definition with excentricities” means  
   • For NP=0: shifts about the gravity centre;  
   • For NP=–1: shifts about the sectional‐coordinate‐system origin.

Why does this matter?  The NP flag changes the *zero point* for any EYA/EYE/EZA/EZE you give:

– NP=0 → zero point is the centroid of the section.  
– NP=–1 → zero point is the local (cross‐section) origin you would have defined with your section geometry (via SPT, VERT, CIRC, PLAT/PANE IDs, etc., or NULL/0000).

If you need a different baseline you can also use REFT to pick an explicit reference point in the section (e.g. the center of a circle or a specific thin‐walled element midpoint), but the table itself simply contrasts the two most common choices (NP=0 vs. NP=–1) and whether you’ve provided any excentricity data at all.

In practice you would see this in input like:

   BEAM 1001 1021 1 PXX A #H L #EMAX PE #EMIN REF YY REFT S

– If NP=0 and you omit PE, the line load runs through the centroid.  
– If NP=–1 and you give PE=10.0, the line load is offset 10 mm (or whatever units) from the sectional origin.  

This rule guarantees that your load’s “action point” in bending and torsion always matches your intent, either about the centroid or about your own section‐coordinate origin.

The table presented defines the syntax and defaults for the BEAM-loading input record used in a structural analysis program. It has four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and thirteen rows, one for each keyword or parameter. Below is a field-by-field breakdown:

1. Item: FROM  
   • Description: Specifies the first beam element number in the sequence to be loaded. Instead of a numeric element index you may also supply the literal “GRP” followed by a group number, or the identifier of a super-element line (SLN).  
   • Unit: “–/LIT,” meaning either a pure number (element index) or a literal keyword.  
   • Default: none (this is an obligatory field, marked “!”).

2. Item: TO  
   • Description: Defines the last element (or group/SNL identifier) to receive the loading.  
   • Unit: none.  
   • Default: equals FROM. If you omit TO, the load applies only to the element or group given in FROM.

3. Item: INC  
   • Description: Step increment for element numbering between FROM and TO—for example, INC 2 would load every second element.  
   • Unit: none.  
   • Default: 1.

4. Item: TYPE  
   • Description: Literal indicating the type of load and its local axis. Common options:  
     – UZS: primary lateral imperfection as a factor of total beam length (unit m/m)  
     – PNX: axial prestress force along local x (kN)  
     – PMY: prestressing moment about local y (kNm)  
     – PMZ: prestressing moment about local z (kNm)  
     – Other beam-loading types (e.g., PG for gravity loads, PT for temperature, etc.) are also allowed.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal).  
   • Default: PG.

5. Item: PA  
   • Description: Load magnitude at the start of the loading segment.  
   • Unit: generic “[∗],” meaning the unit depends on TYPE.  
   • Default: must be specified (“!”).

6. Item: PE  
   • Description: Load magnitude at the end of the loading segment.  
   • Unit: “[∗]” (same as PA).  
   • Default: PA (if omitted, end value equals start value).

7. Item: A  
   • Description: Distance from the beam’s start node to the beginning of this loading region.  
   • Unit: meters [m]. Subscript 1001 indicates the primary length unit.  
   • Default: user-supplied (“∗”).

8. Item: L  
   • Description: Length of the loading region along the beam.  
   • Unit: meters [m].  
   • Default: user-supplied (“∗”).

9. Item: EYA  
   • Description: Local y-offset of the line of action at the start of the load, measured from the reference axis.  
   • Unit: millimeters [mm]. Subscript 1011.  
   • Default: “ys” (the default y-eccentricity stored from a previous command).

10. Item: EZA  
    • Description: Local z-offset at load start.  
    • Unit: millimeters [mm].  
    • Default: “zs.”

11. Item: EYE  
    • Description: Local y-offset at the end of the load segment.  
    • Unit: millimeters [mm].  
    • Default: EYA.

12. Item: EZE  
    • Description: Local z-offset at the end.  
    • Unit: millimeters [mm].  
    • Default: EZA.

13. Item: REF  
    • Description: Reference system for interpreting the parameters A and L. Possible options are documented under “beam-loading” (for example, S = absolute stationing from start node, M = midpoint, etc.).  
    • Unit: LIT (literal).  
    • Default: S.

14. Item: REFT  
    • Description: Reference system for interpreting eccentricities EYA…EZE. Options:  
      – S: section centroid (neutral‐axis = 0)  
      – NULL: use the sectional coordinate system (user-defined)  
      – ID: a point ID within the cross-section profile (newline format).  
    • Unit: LIT.  
    • Default: inherited (“∗”).

How it all fits together  
– You invoke BEAM FROM … TO … INC … TYPE … PA … PE … A … L … EYA … EZA … EYE … EZE … REF … REFT to define one or more trapezoidal (or uniform, linear) loads, prestresses or temperature distributions along each beam element in the specified range.  
– The CONT literal (not shown in this table) can be used for TYPE, PA, PE, A and L to carry over defaults from the previous record, simplifying the definition of multi-span, piecewise‐linear loading.  
– Eccentric loads (P-type) generate bending moments if EYA/EZA offsets are nonzero, and for nonlinear analyses these contribute to geometric stiffness.  
– Temperature-profile loads (type PT, DTY, DTZ) may also be specified by ZA/ZE coordinates (see the “general temperature distribution” notes in the main text).  
– Prestressing entries (PNX, PMY, PMZ and the special BEPL tendon stress type) impose initial strains or curvatures; their resulting forces and moments adjust automatically depending on whether the element is fixed or deformable.

Below is a structured description of Table 3.14 (“Type of the Beam Loading”), which maps the various continuous‐loading categories you can enter with a BEAM record to their physical meaning and units. Use this description to guide extraction of “TYPE” entries, their interpretation, and unit consistency when ingesting BEAM‐loading data into your RAG/vector store.

1. Table Purpose  
   • Associates each “TYPE” keyword in a BEAM‐loading input with the kind of distributed load or moment it represents.  
   • Shows the engineering unit that must accompany each load distribution.  

2. Column Definitions  
   – TYPE (implicit in the left‐hand descriptions)  
       • Identifies what is being distributed along the beam (force or moment, and in which axis).  
   – Unit  
       • The physical unit for the distribution (force per length or moment per length).  

3. Rows (Load Categories)  

   3.1 Distributed Forces in Local Beam Coordinates  
     • qZ (often simply entered as “PZ” or “QZ”):  
         – Description: load per unit length acting in the local z-direction (perpendicular to the beam’s reference axis, i.e. “vertical” in the beam’s own coordinate system).  
         – Unit: kN/m  

     • qX (often “PX” or “QX”):  
         – Description: axial force per unit length, i.e. acting along the beam’s local x-axis (the beam length direction).  
         – Unit: kN/m  

   3.2 Distributed Forces in Global Coordinates  
     • qG (entered via global-direction variants of P or Q):  
         – Description: force per unit length resolved in one of the global X, Y, or Z directions, irrespective of beam orientation.  
         – Unit: kN/m  

   3.3 Distributed Moments  
     • mY (sometimes “MY” or “MAY”):  
         – Description: moment per unit length about the local y-axis (bending around the weak axis of the section).  
         – Unit: kNm/m  

     • mZ (sometimes “MZ” or “MAZ”):  
         – Description: moment per unit length about the local z-axis (bending around the strong axis).  
         – Unit: kNm/m  

     • mG (global-moment variants):  
         – Description: moment per unit length about one of the global Cartesian axes.  
         – Unit: kNm/m  

4. How This Table Ties Into the BEAM Command Syntax  
   – In the BEAM record you specify, e.g.:  
       BEAM 101   PZ  CEIL  5   L 10    → a uniform vertical qZ load of “CEIL” kN/m over the first 10 m  
   – You may also use “TYPE CONT” to repeat the last TYPE/unit without retyping it, facilitating trapezoidal or step‐wise definitions.  
   – All distributed loads (forces or moments) must be entered in the units shown above; the parser uses this table to validate and convert where necessary.  

5. Additional Context (from Section 3.9 et al.)  
   – Eccentricities: if you offset a qZ load by an eccentricity in local y/z, the model will automatically generate corresponding bending moments.  
   – Prestress vs. applied load: PNX, PMY, PMZ are special imposed‐strain load types (constant along the beam) rather than true distributed external loads; these use units of kN (PNX) or kNm (PMY/PMZ), not kN/m.

The table under scrutiny defines the syntax and semantics of the BEPL record, the SOFiLOAD command for assigning beam-sequence loads through the “Definition of Beam Loading” (section 3.9).  It has four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and each row corresponds to one field of the input record.  Below is a field-by-field walkthrough:

1.  FROM  
    •  Description: Identifies the first beam (element) to which this loading applies.  Instead of an explicit element number you may supply the literal GRP plus a group number, or the identifier of an SLN (span line).  
    •  Unit: none (–) or literal (LIT) when using GRP/SLN  
    •  Default: “!”  (i.e. mandatory—no default)  

2.  TO  
    •  Description: Identifies the last beam (element) in the sequence, again either as a numeric element, a group (GRP) or SLN identifier.  
    •  Unit: none  
    •  Default: FROM  (so if you omit TO, the load applies only to FROM)  

3.  INC  
    •  Description: Increment for stepping through element numbers between FROM and TO.  
    •  Unit: none  
    •  Default: 1  (every consecutive element)  

4.  TYPE  
    •  Description: Load type and direction.  This is a literal (LIT) code—PG, PNX, PRE, U, etc.—which selects whether the load is dead weight, prestress, imperfection, nodal force or special tendon force.  
    •  Unit: LIT  
    •  Default: PG  (self-weight)  

5.  P  
    •  Description: Magnitude of the load.  For point loads it’s the force or moment; for distributed loads it’s the intensity.  
    •  Unit: user-defined (asterisk `[∗]` means force units follow global settings)  
    •  Default: “!” (mandatory)  

6.  A  
    •  Description: Abscissa of the loading’s application along the total beam sequence, measured from the start or end.  
    •  Unit: [m]₁₀₀₁  
    •  Default: “*” (0.0 if unspecified)  

7.  EY, EZ  
    •  Description: Local transverse offsets of the load line in the beam’s y- and z- directions, measured from the reference axis (centre line unless otherwise defined).  Eccentric loads generate bending moments.  
    •  Unit: [mm]₁₀₁₁  
    •  Default:   
      – EY: “ys” (uses the standard section-axis offset)  
      – EZ: “zs”  

8.  REF  
    •  Description: Reference system for A and L (the abscissa and length parameters).  This is a literal code—options are detailed in the beam-loading section of the manual.  
    •  Unit: LIT  
    •  Default: S  (section-centre, NP=0)  

9.  REFT  
    •  Description: Reference system for the transverse offsets EY and EZ.  Valid codes are:  
      – S : Section-centre (NP = 0)  
      – NULL : Sectional coordinate system  
      – ID : A particular point ID within the section (see beam-loading).  
    •  Unit: LIT  
    •  Default: “*” (centre)  

10. OPT  
    •  Description: Additional options controlling the load distribution type or special behaviors.  For continuous beams (STEL), OPT selects standard distribution shapes:  
      – LINA / LINE / LINM = linear (max at start/end/midpoint)  
      – QUAA / QUAE / QUAM = quadratic (max at start/end/midpoint)  
      – CUBA / CUBE = cubic (max at start/end)  
      – SPLI triggers a general cubic-spline fit if you supply multiple TYPE CONT vertices.  
    •  Unit: “∗” or LIT  
    •  Default: “*” (constant distribution if no option is specified)  

Key Remarks and Context:  
–  BEPL gathers all records sharing the same load number into one combined loading definition (unlike STAR2, SOFiLOAD forbids duplicate load numbers without TYPE CONT).  
–  If only one vertex is given, two zero-value points are implicitly added at the start and end, yielding a linear or quadratic distribution depending on the vertex’s location.  
–  TYPE PRE draws prestress from tendon definitions (AQUA/TENDON), and TYPE U derives imperfection shapes from existing nodal displacements (e.g. buckling modes).  By specifying a negative factor, you can subtract previous imperfections.  
–  For PNX (eccentric prestress loads), cubic interpolation of EY/EZ produces shear forces and moments; distinct tendon geometries usually require separate definitions.  
–  Group-based selection (GRP) and continuous-beam loading via STEL enable you to assign uniform or varying loads efficiently over many beam elements.

The fragment shown is part of “Table 3.16: (continued)” and serves to summarize the elementary BEPL‐type loading quantities that can be applied to a run or sequence of beams.  It is organized into two conceptual blocks—force components and moment components—each with a short descriptive title, the symbolic names of the individual load parameters, and the engineering unit in which they must be entered.

1. Force Components (units: kN)  
   – Symbolic names run from PXXX, PYXX … all the way through PZZZ.  Here each three-letter code denotes a force acting on the beam sequence in one of the local or global coordinate directions:  
     • The first letter “P” flags that this is a pure force rather than a moment or other load type.  
     • The next two letters encode the plane or orientation of action and the axis on which the resulting effect is resolved (for example, “PXYX” would be the X–Y component acting on the local X axis).  
   – A note immediately below points out that you may also substitute a global-direction literal “gg” and then, by specifying “i,” select its i-th component for loading.  In practice this means you can call out a global load—say gravity in direction “G1”—and then pick out exactly its X, Y or Z portion to apply to the local beam system.

2. Moment Components (units: kNm)  
   Immediately following the force block, four moment‐type load quantities are listed, each again with its own three-letter code:  
   – MXXX  
     • Torsional moment about the local beam axis (pure torque).  
   – MXXY  
     • Primary bending moment in the principal bending plane.  
   – MYYX  
     • Secondary bending moment in the orthogonal bending plane.  
   – MXYZ (sometimes shown as “All directions”)  
     • A catch-all for moment components acting in any or all of the local coordinate directions.  

Each of these moment symbols carries the same first-letter convention (“M” for moment) followed by the two letters defining the bending plane or torsional axis, and finally the axis on which the moment is taken.  Because moments cause rotations rather than translations, their unit is kilonewton-meters (kNm).

Structure

      • Pulls prestress data for tendons from the CDB (Construction Database).  
      • All tendons defined with prestress stage = OPT become active.

      • The resulting load is output as a PNX‐type load (axial prestress with geometric eccentricities).

      • Unit: –

The table is the formal definition of the QUAD‐element load record in ASE. It defines, for each load entry, how elements are selected, what loading is applied, how it varies in space, and—if needed—how it is distributed through the element thickness. It is organized in four columns—Item, Description, Unit, Default—and can be parsed entry by entry as follows:

1. Element Selection (FROM / TO / INC)  
   • FROM  
     – Description: First element number or a group literal (GRP)  
     – Unit: none or literal flag (denotes GRP)  
     – Default: “!” (mandatory)  
   • TO  
     – Description: Last element number or group number  
     – Unit: none  
     – Default: same as FROM (i.e. a single element)  
   • INC  
     – Description: Step size between element numbers in the range  
     – Unit: none  
     – Default: 1  

   By using FROM and TO you select all elements in a numerical or group range; INC refines the selection. If you specify a literal GRP for FROM, TO may also be a group number. To print elements rather than load them, INC must explicitly be set to 1.

2. Basic Load Definition (TYPE / P / X / Y / Z)  
   • TYPE  
     – Description: Load type and direction (e.g. PXP, PYP, PZP, PRE, T, wind types: STD, CYL…)  
     – Unit: literal  
     – Default: PG (pressure in global coordinates)  
   • P  
     – Description: Load magnitude (can be scalar or pressure coefficient)  
     – Unit: dimensionless “[*]” (multiplies geometry/load units)  
     – Default: “!” (must be provided)  
   • X, Y, Z  
     – Description: Global reference point coordinates for “P”  
     – Unit: meters ([m] in unit system 1001)  
     – Default: 0.0, 0.0, 0.0  

3. Spatial Variation (DPX / DPY / DPZ)  
   • DPX, DPY, DPZ  
     – Description: Linear gradients so that p(x,y,z) = P + (x–X)*DPX + (y–Y)*DPY + (z–Z)*DPZ  
     – Unit: same as P (“[*]”)  
     – Default: 0.0 each  

   Use DPX–DPZ to impose global varying loads (e.g. hydrostatic pressure). Conversion to internal units uses the geometry unit code 1001.

4. Additional Options (NTYP / VTYP)  
   • NTYP  
     – Description: Literal or flag for special behavior (e.g. reference prestress number, wind‐inclination limit, roof inclination for PXP/PYP/PZP)  
     – Unit: literal or none  
     – Default: “–” (not used)  
   • VTYP  
     – Description: Numeric value associated with NTYP (e.g. max angle in degrees, pattern index)  
     – Unit: dimensionless “[*]”  
     – Default: “–” (not used)  

   Examples:
     – For PZP with NTYP 60, VTYP unused: only elements whose local normals point upward (positive Z component) and are within 60° of the XY-plane are loaded.
     – For PRE, NTYP = tendon stage, VTYP not used; P should be 1.0 to generate prestress loading of stage NTYP.

5. Through‐Thickness Distribution (Z0/F0 … Z15/F15)  
   You may define up to 16 (Z,F) pairs to describe how P varies along the quad’s local thickness direction:  
   • Zi  
     – Description: Coordinate from one face (lower or upper fibre) or mid-surface, depending on sign of ordinates  
     – Unit: millimeters ([mm], unit 1010)  
     – Default: first Z0 is mandatory (“!”), others “–”  
   • Fi  
     – Description: Scale factor for P at that Zi position  
     – Unit: none  
     – Default: 1.0  

   Interpretation rules (three cases):  
     1. All Zi positive → referenced to upper fibre  
     2. All Zi negative → referenced to lower fibre  
     3. Mixed signs or zero → referenced to mid-surface (scaled with warning if thickness mismatch)  

Cross-references: LC (load cases), NODE, TRUS, CABL, BEAM, BEPL, BRIC, COPY and free-loading routines; function TEMP or TBEAM for nonuniform thickness loads; wind codes STD, CYL*, CYLR, CYLF, CYLK with Reynolds/shape factors; prestress and influence area loads.

The input is a two-column reference table entitled “Table 3.21: Type of the QUAD-Element Loading.”  It serves as a concise dictionary of all the different load “literals” you can apply to four-node shell (QUAD) elements in ASE/CSM, together with the physical unit or dimension expected for each.  This table is one piece of a larger set of definitions (see also: LC, NODE, TRUS, CABL, beamloading, BEAM, BEPL, BRIC, COPY, free-loading) but focuses exclusively on the QUAD‐element case.

Structure  
• Column 1: Load type literal – the keyword you use in your QUAD record (e.g. GRAV, DPX, PXP, PRE, etc.).  
• Column 2: Unit – the physical unit in which the corresponding load value P (and sometimes NTYP or other parameters) must be entered.

Row-by-row summary of the most important entries:

1. GRAV (Gravity direction)  
   – Unit: kN/m²  
   – Applies self‐weight on the actual element area according to the global gravity vector.

2. GREF (Gravity with reference)  
   – Unit: kN/m²  
   – Like GRAV, but referenced to a specific direction or magnitude (user-defined reference).

3. GPROJ (Gravity to projection area)  
   – Unit: kN/m²  
   – Projects self-weight onto a specified projection plane (e.g. horizontal projection of an inclined slab).

4. DPX, DPY, DPZ (Global varying loads)  
   – Unit: kN/m²  
   – Earth or water pressure: P = base pressure; DPX–DPZ = incremental pressure gradients in X, Y or Z.  ASE will convert units via the geometry unit (1001).

5. PXP, PYP, PZP (Directional pressure loads with roof‐inclination filter)  
   – Unit: kN/m²  
   – Uniform pressure on element area, subject to an NTYP “roof‐pitch” veto: only elements whose normals lie within the NTYP angle of the load direction (and with the correct sign) are loaded.

6. SNOW (Snow load to projection area)  
   – Unit: kN/m²  
   – Uniform load on the projected plan area (for snow on inclined surfaces).

7. WINDFAC (Wind-loading factor)  
   – Unit: Factor  
   – Applies code‐based wind factors (e.g. internal/external, suction/pressure).

8. DAMPFAC (Damping factor)  
   – Unit: Factor  
   – Damping coefficient for dynamic analyses.

9. TEMP (Temperature for hot design)  
   – Unit: °C  
   – Uniform temperature change.

10. DTX, DTY (Temperature change in local x/y plane)  
    – Unit: K  
    – Linear thermal gradient along local in-plane axes.

11. DTDIFF (Temperature difference, below–above)  
    – Unit: K  
    – Through-thickness thermal gradient.

12. DTOLD (Value of old DT load type)  
    – Unit: 0/00  
    – Legacy thermal definition in ‰ units.

13. CURVX, CURVY, CURVZ (Curvature in local x, y, z)  
    – Unit: 1/km (for x,y) or mm (for z)  
    – Prescribes initial curvature per length in-plane, or out-of-plane kinematic offset.

14. PRE (Prestress from TENDON)  
    – Unit: Factor  
    – Introduces tendon prestress (NTYP selects prestress stage); P is normally 1.0, other values simply scale the response but do not alter the database.

Key usage notes (from the surrounding documentation):  
– You select elements via “QUAD FROM … TO …” (possibly using literal GRP and group numbers).  To print instead of load, an explicit INC=1 flag is needed.  
– NTYP often carries extra information: prestress stage, wind-pattern selection, maximum roof inclination, etc.  
– Special “T” (temperature) loads can be defined as a piecewise function over the element thickness (up to 16 thickness‐factor pairs), with reference to the top fibre, bottom fibre or mid-surface depending on sign conventions.  
– Cylindrical (CYL) and related load types for wind on circular members (based on Reynolds number or code tables) exist but are outside the QUAD table.

Together, this table enables the user to assemble any combination of mechanical, thermal, prestress or environmental loads directly on shell elements by invoking the appropriate literal and supplying its standard unit.

Below is a concise yet thorough description of the three‐column input table and how it fits into the broader QUAD‐element load definitions. Although the original table is small, each entry carries specific meaning in a finite‐element context—especially when you recall that QUAD‐element loads can be global pressures, hydraulic heads or fluid velocities, and that they may be prescribed directly or via increments in the principal coordinate directions (DPX, DPY, DPZ).

1. Table Structure  
   • TYPE  
     – A short mnemonic or literal used in the input deck to identify the physical quantity.  
   • Description  
     – A plain‐language name of what the TYPE stands for.  
   • Unit  
     – The unit in which the value is expected, ensuring consistency with the model’s length, force, and time units.

2. Detailed Entries  
   • CFDP  
     – “Pressure of fluid”  
     – Units: kilonewtons per square meter (kN/m²)  
     – Role in QUAD loads: CFDP corresponds to a pressure field that can be applied normally to QUAD element faces. In a global‐load record (DPX, DPY, DPZ), this value would map to P (the baseline pressure) plus directional increments if specified. CFDP is typically used to simulate hydrostatic or dynamic fluid pressures pressing against a structure.  
   • H  
     – “Piezometric head”  
     – Units: meters (m)  
     – Role in QUAD loads: H represents the energy head in fluid‐structure interaction or groundwater flow problems. When applied to an element, it can be converted internally (using the density and gravity field defined elsewhere in the model) into an equivalent pressure load. This allows you to specify water table or seepage loads in terms more familiar to hydraulic engineers.  
   • U, V, W  
     – “Velocity of fluids”  
     – Units: meters per second (m/sec)  
     – Role in QUAD loads: These three literals define the fluid’s velocity components in the global X, Y, and Z directions, respectively. In advanced analyses—such as fluid‐structure interaction or convective load cases—one might prescribe U, V, W to capture drag loads or momentum transfers. Those velocities can be translated into pressure/force on the QUAD elements via appropriate hydrodynamic relations or user‐defined functions.  

3. Integration with the QUAD‐Load Framework  
   – Global vs. Local Definitions: CFDP, H, U/V/W can be applied as global loads (using DPX…DPZ) or as local boundary‐condition fields. Each is subject to unit conversions based on the model’s “1001” geometry and load‐unit system.  
   – Incremental Loading: If you combine CFDP with DPX–DPZ, the main value P is the CFDP entry; the DPX/DPY/DPZ values become incremental changes in those orthogonal directions.  
   – Coupling with NTYP: For special actions—such as varying head over a surface due to snow melt or time‐dependent flood hydrographs—you can use NTYP to reference auxiliary data (flow tables or head‐vs‐time curves).  
   – Orientation Filters: Although CFDP and H act on all surfaces by default, velocity‐based loads (U, V, W) might be filtered through an NTYP “inclination” criterion, ensuring the load only acts when element normals have a specific relationship to the flow direction.  

4. Practical Notes  
   – Consistency: Always check that the global coordinate system, load‐unit system, and geometry units align with the table’s kN/m², m, and m/sec entries.  
   – Conversion: When combining piezometric head (H) with gravity loads, the software converts head into pressure via ρ·g·H.  
   – Advanced Use: U, V, W can drive user‐written subroutines for fluid coupling or be passed into “wind” or “water” patterns if the software supports MOBILE‐type definitions for dynamic loads.  

In summary, though compact, this table defines the fundamental fluid‐load parameters you can invoke across your QUAD elements. CFDP deals directly with pressure, H with hydraulic head (translated internally to pressure), and U/V/W with velocity fields—each plugged seamlessly into the DPX/DPY/DPZ loading scheme and filtered or modified by NTYP or additional functions as needed.

The table defines all of the keyword fields you must supply when issuing a “distributed‐load” command (often called BRIC in legacy documentation) to the RAG‐based vector store.  It is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit, Default—and two logical groups: element‐selection parameters (FROM, TO, INC) and load‐definition parameters (TYPE, P, X, Y, Z, DPX, DPY, DPZ, NTYP).

1. Element‐Selection Parameters  
   • FROM  
     – Description: Number (ID) of the first element to receive the load, or the literal “GRP” to indicate selection by group.  
     – Unit: none  
     – Default: “!” (mandatory—must be specified)  
   • TO  
     – Description: Number (ID) of the last element in the range, or if selecting a group, the group number.  
     – Unit: none  
     – Default: same as FROM (i.e. if omitted, only the single element FROM is used)  
   • INC  
     – Description: Increment between element IDs in the range. If you wish to print element IDs rather than apply loads to a group, you must explicitly set INC=1.  
     – Unit: none  
     – Default: 1  

   Any integer range is allowed—even if it extends beyond existing element IDs—so long as at least one element exists in the selected span.  To target all members of a predefined group, set FROM=GRP and TO=<group #>.

2. Load-Definition Parameters  
   • TYPE  
     – Description: A literal identifier (LIT) specifying the type of load (pressure, traction, point load, etc.) and the direction or component it acts in.  
     – Unit: LIT  
     – Default: PG (pressure‐type general load)  
   • P  
     – Description: Base load value at the reference point (X,Y,Z).  
     – Unit: dimensionless [*] (converted internally via the geometry unit code 1001)  
     – Default: “!” (required)  
   • X, Y, Z  
     – Description: Global‐coordinate reference point for P.  The load at any mesh point is computed relative to (X,Y,Z).  
     – Unit: meters ([m] with unit code 1001)  
     – Default: 0.0 each  
   • DPX, DPY, DPZ  
     – Description: Gradient (increment) of the load in each global direction.  The local load at point (x,y,z) is  
         p(x,y,z) = P + (x–X)*DPX + (y–Y)*DPY + (z–Z)*DPZ  
     – Unit: [*] (same dimensionless unit as P)  
     – Default: 0.0 each  
   • NTYP  
     – Description: Reserved for additional or custom options (e.g. special balance schemes in HYDRA/DOLFYN).  
     – Unit: none  
     – Default: “–” (unused unless explicitly defined)  

Additional Context & Cross-References  
• See also the commands LC (load case definition), NODE (nodal loads), TRUS, CABL, Beamloading/BEAM, BPEL (plate loads), QUAD, COPY, and free‐loading options.  
• Groups are handled via GRP syntax; individual-element printouts require INC=1.  
• DPX–DPZ allow modeling of global, spatially varying fields (e.g. hydrostatic pressure, earth loads).  
• All units for P and its gradients are internally converted by the software’s unit‐conversion factor (geometry unit 1001) to maintain consistency.

The input “Table 3.24: Type of the BRIC-Element Loading” is a two-column summary of all of the different load‐type codes available when prescribing element‐wise loads on 3D brick (BRIC) elements.  In a typical RAG input deck you refer to one of these load types by its numeric identifier (e.g. NTYP = 11 for a DPX load), and then you supply the appropriate magnitude (and, where required, direction or variation parameters).  Below is a breakdown of the table’s structure and entries, followed by notes on how it ties back into the broader BRIC loading syntax.

1. Table Structure  
   – Column 1 “Load Type”  
     ­– A mnemonic name or brief description of what physical effect this load corresponds to  
   – Column 2 “Unit”  
     ­– The engineering units in which the prescribed magnitude (and increments, where relevant) must be given

2. Row-by-Row Description  
   1. Gravity direction  
      • Load code: 1 (implicitly understood from BRIC load-type numbering)  
      • Description: Applies a uniform body‐force equal to ρ·g in the local “gravity” direction of each element.  It is often used to represent self-weight.  
      • Unit: kN/m³  

   2. Global directions (DPX / DPY / DPZ)  
      • Load codes: 11 (DPX), 12 (DPY), 13 (DPZ)  
      • Description: Defines a spatially varying load field in global X, Y, or Z.  You supply:  
         – P: the base value at the element’s reference point (X,Y,Z)  
         – DPX/DPY/DPZ: the gradient (increment) of that load in global X, Y, or Z direction  
        This construct is typically used to model fluid pressures (e.g. water or earth pressure) that vary linearly over the element’s extent.  The software automatically converts units based on the declared geometry and load units (see Unit ID 1001).  
      • Unit: kN/m³  

   3. Temperature change  
      • Load code: 21 (for spatially uniform ΔT)  
      • Description: A uniform nodal temperature change applied to the element.  The resulting strain is governed by the element’s thermal expansion coefficient.  
      • Unit: K  

   4. Principal direction  
      • Load code: 22  
      • Description: A directional multiplier (0/00) that reorients the temperature‐ or mechanical‐load effect along one of the element’s principal material axes.  Used when the element has anisotropic thermal or mechanical behavior and you must specify which material direction the load “rides” on.

      • Load code: 23  
      • Description: Fully user-defined anisotropic loading.  The user provides a 6×6 stiffness or compliance modifier matrix (in the anisotropy subroutine) to compute how the applied load resolves into stresses/strains.

3. How to Select Elements for Loading  
   – You can load individual element numbers, or you can specify a range “FROM … TO …” containing at least one element.

The table shown here documents the available input parameters for the “COPY” command in a structural‐analysis program. Copying re‐uses loading definitions (point, line, area, volume loads, self‐weight, nodal and elemental loads, etc.) from one load case (or action) into another, optionally filtered by element type, scaled by a factor, shifted or rotated in space, or restricted to particular element ranges. Below is a structured description of each column and row entry:

1. Columns  
   - Item  
     The keyword or parameter name the user must supply.  
   - Description  
     A brief explanation of what the parameter represents or controls.  
   - Unit  
     If a numerical quantity, the physical units expected (for example, meters [m] or degrees [grad]); “–” indicates dimensionless or not applicable.  
   - Default  
     The value assumed when the parameter is omitted.

2. Core Parameters  
   • NO  
     – Number of an existing load case or the name of an action whose loads are to be copied.  
     – Unit: –  
     – Default: mandatory (denoted by “!”).  
   • FACT  
     – A global scale factor applied to all copied loads (can also be used to build combination factors for nonlinear analysis).  
     – Unit: – / LIT (literal numerical).  
     – Default: 1.0.  
   • TYPE  
     – Filters which kinds of loads to copy. Accepts one of several literal tokens:  
       • ALL – every loading definition.  
       • POIN – free point loading entries.  
       • LINE – free line loading.  
       • AREA – free surface/area loading.  
       • VOLU – free volume loading.  
       • PSUP – supporting point loads (loads at support points).  
       • SUPP – vector of supporting‐load reactions.  
       • TRAI – load‐train definitions.  
       • ELLA – load‐train definitions as used by the ELLA module.  
       • INTE – all generated analysis‐type loads (e.g. nodal analysis loads).  
       • NODE, BEAM, TRUS, CABL, QUAD, BRIC – element‐specific loads for nodal, beam, truss, cable, quad (plate), and brick elements.  
       • WIND – wind‐pressure coefficients.  
     – Unit: LIT.  
     – Default: ALL.  
     – Note: To restrict TYPE to only user‐defined loads of that category, append “:E” (e.g. “NODE:E”).  

3. Element/Node Selection  
   • FROM  
     – Starting element or node number in a range.  
     – Unit: –  
     – Default: not defined (no restriction).  
   • TO  
     – Ending element or node number.  
     – Unit: –  
     – Default: not defined.  
   • INC  
     – Increment step for selecting every nth element or node.  
     – Unit: –  
     – Default: not defined.

4. Reference & Geometric Transforms  
   • REF  
     – Reference number for an axis system or a traffic lane (relevant for PSUP or TRAI loads).  
     – Unit: –  
     – Default: not defined.  
   • LEV  
     – Elevation or level at which point‐support loads (PSUP) are generated or applied.  
     – Unit: [m]  
     – Default: 0.0.  
   • DX, DY, DZ  
     – Global or local translational shift of the copied loads in X, Y or Z direction.  
     – Unit: [m]  
     – Default: 0.0 for each.  
   • ALPH  
     – Rotation angle (in “grad”) applied before the shifts.  
     – Unit: [grad]  
     – Default: 0.0.  
   • WIDE  
     – Projection depth parameter for generated (e.g. area‐to‐line) loads.  
     – Unit: [m]  
     – Default: 0.0.  
   • YEX  
     – Eccentricity offset for load‐train definitions (transverse shift).  
     – Unit: [m]  
     – Default: unspecified (“*”).

5. ELLA‐Specific  
   • CASE  
     – Identifies an evaluation case within the ELLA module when copying train loads.  
     – Unit: –  
     – Default: 1.

Usage Notes (from surrounding documentation):  
- COPY will import all defined loads from a specified “NO” load case into the current case, including self‐weight (unless already defined).  
- One can restrict COPY to nodal/element loads only, or to specific element‐type groups (NODE, BEAM, TRUS, etc.).  
- COMB may be used in place of NO to import a saved nonlinear‐analysis load combination.  
- The FACT parameter can optionally generate design‐combination loads using user‐supplied safety and combination factors (not a simple superposition).  
- Load functions (time or spatial functions) are never copied; each case must have unique functions.  
- If no project or database name is given, loads are read from the current model; otherwise, they come from the specified database.

Loading on areas with wind according to EN 1991 requires a lot of calculation steps, as the pressure coefficients are rather detailed and have to be specified dependent on the size of the area. SOFiLOAD facilitates this task by providing the following steps:
 • A reference load case contains all loaded areas with their real size as AREA loading of TYPE WIND. For more details see record AREA.
 • For a specific wind load case one has to specify with record WIND the direction of the wind and the profile of the wind speed along the height.
 • Then a COPY TYPE WIND (or the default ALL) will create the detailed pressure distribu- tions according to tables 4 to 6 of DIN 1055-4 resp. tables 10.2.1 to 10.2.4 of EN 1991-1-4 depending on the defined geometry and wind direction. A positive factor selects for those regions with changing sign the suction, a negative factor will select the pressure value. To define the loading areas the outer dimensions of the building are needed. As these values may not be derived from the load areas, SOFILOAD will use the outer box of all active groups to evaluate these values.
 Hint: The wind profile of the design codes define the air velocity along the height for the undis- turbed flow. For a slender building this distribution will be seen on the front side (region D according picture 7.5 of EN 1991-1-4), however the rear and the other sides (regions A,B,C and E according picture 7.5 of EN 1991-1-4) have a rather constant suction which is refer- enced to the nominal reference pressure at the top of the building. This is clearly stated in the remark of section 7.2.2. (1).
 For compact buildings (H/B < 1) the same effect is observed for the front side. The constant pressure is again referenced to the value at the top of the building which is accounted for.

For a slender building this distribution will be seen on the front side (region D according picture 7.5 of EN 1991-1-4), however the rear and the other sides (regions A,B,C and E according picture 7.5 of EN 1991-1-4) have a rather constant suction which is refer- enced to the nominal reference pressure at the top of the building. This is clearly stated in the remark of section 7.2.2. (1).. For compact buildings (H/B < 1) the same effect is observed for the front side. The constant pressure is again referenced to the value at the top of the building which is accounted for..
 The staggered wind loading according to picture 7.4 of EN 1991-1-4, which is introduced with "‘may"’ is not applicable in all cases and is not physical. Thus the default in SOFiLOAD is to use the continuous variation. If that special load pattern is required, this can be achieved by an input of:
 TVAR 'WIND_PATTERN' 2 SCOP 'LOADING'
 The possible values 0,1,2 select no variation, continuous variation, staggered load pattern.
 For the wave loading a COPY will create the loadings with the Morrison equation and the defined force coefficients. A shift off the wave kinematics may be specified by the global coor- dinates (DX,DY,DZ). However in this case an explicit scalar definition for DX (0.5[-] or 50[%]) will shift the wave by this fraction of the wave length.

 Free loading is a very convenient method to place loads at any location within the structure and let the program decide how to convert it. This is especially useful for the import of geometrically defined loading from a CAD model. The loads will be converted by SOFiLOAD to equivalent nodal and elemental loading. For this purpose the program will also work with pure geometrical elements having no stiffness at all like the outer hull of a frame work. Eccentric loading may create moments, but moments will not be transferred into a pair of forces by this approach.
 Free point and line loadings will be applied exactly once within a system. For area loading the algorithm for that would be extremely complicated, so it has not been implemented and there is the chance for an area loading to be applied more than once.

If not otherwise specified (e.g. beam loading) the loading will be distributed in general via quadrilateral elements, which may be taken from:
 • General QUAD elements
 • QUAD elements with NAR 0 (surface definition only)
 • QUAD elements from a load distribution area
 • Surfaces of BRIC elements These are defined by the active groups and with GFA the area references defined for the nodes. Surfaces without area reference or with an interior volume node will not be loaded with GFA.
 For all references one has to distinguish between group based types (BGRP, QGRP and VGRP resp FGRP) and the geometric references (SPT, SLN, SAR, SVO, GFA as well as LAR). The geometric reference will be defined automatically with SOFiMSHC, but may be also defined explicitly with SOFiMSHA. This information will be saved with the elements and the nodes.
 The load may be specified to act only on certain types of structure. It may be useful to specify if a load is intended to become a beam load or should be converted to nodal loads. For curved reference elements it also makes a difference and the total load sum if the eccentricities are taken relative to the curved reference axis/area or to the polygon edges of the elements.
 If no element type is specified (AUTO), the program will try to use all possible reference types. The difference is apparent for point loads, where a AUTO-load will always be attached to the nearest node in the end, while an area or linear reference may decide, that this load is now off the structure.
 For the search of possible elements, the following rules are implemented:
 • Explicit references are always unique. The load will be applied with particular reference to the selected element.
 • References on element types will choose fast and directly between all possible elements to find the best fit. For AREA loading this might create multiple loading within the same loading area, for point and line loads the elements nearest to the load will win, a definition

 • For a reference to a geometric item SOFiLOAD will search in a more demanding outer loop the structural references, followed with multiple inner loops on the elements. But if this fails it will switch to the corresponding finite element type. Thus SPT will become NODE, SLN to BGRP and SAR to QGRP.
 • For an automatic reference the program will work first on explicit load distribution areas LAR, then SAR resp QUAD, then on SLN resp. BEAM and last on SPT resp NODE ele- ments. The load must be within the dimensions of the element, only for the final loop over all nodes the value WIDE will become effective. The reference MOVE will not cycle over the nodes, thus it will discard all loads of a load train outside the structure. The LAR areas may be ignored if required with CTRL LAR 0.
 Loadings on TRUS and CABL elements are applied with a ranking following all beam elements, as these elements can not account corretcly for partial loadings or load excentricities. Thus some selection by a reference number, a group number or a limited value for WIDE is always necessary. This behaviour is manadatory to avoid loading on cables of an external tendon.

The image is labeled “Figure 3.7: Projective loading with WIDE” and consists of two schematic side-by-side sketches, each drawn over a common horizontal reference line.  Both illustrate how a user-specified projection window (denoted by the text “WIDE” on the baseline) picks up elements within a certain offset before and behind a load definition, independent of the direction in which the load actually acts.

1. Left-hand sketch:  
   • A straight horizontal line serves as the structural reference axis.  At its left end is a small “+” marker and at the right end a short vertical tic, but no further coordinate labels.  
   • Midway along this baseline there is a vertical line rising upward.  This line represents the “projected” location onto which a planar load is to be applied.  
   • Above and just to the right of the vertical line sits a right-angled triangular shape: its hypotenuse slopes upward toward the left, and its right angle is at the bottom-right corner where it meets the vertical line.  This triangle symbolizes a generic line or area load positioned at some offset from the structure.  
   • Directly beneath the portion of the baseline on either side of the vertical line the word “WIDE” is centered—signifying that all structural elements lying within this horizontal “wide” range will be selected for loading (regardless of their orientation), before projection onto the vertical plane.

2. Right-hand sketch:  
   • The same horizontal reference line continues, again annotated with “WIDE” under its central span.  At the far right this line terminates in a small downward dash matching the left-hand styling.  
   • Rising above the center of the “WIDE” span is a vertical dashed line.  This dashed line represents the normal (N) or reference axis of projection in the global coordinate sense.  
   • To the left of that dashed axis, an approximately 150°-arc of a circle is drawn thickly in black (resembling a curved beam or shell segment).  
   • On that curved arc, near its mid-span, there is a small rectangular “corner” symbol indicating a right angle—this denotes that, for curved load definitions without a global projection selected, the projection is taken perpendicular to the local tangent or loading plane.  
   • The arc and the right-angle cue together show that the user-defined load will be projected normal to the curved surface, selecting all elements whose centroids lie within the “WIDE” offset before or behind this projected curved plane.

Overall, the figure makes clear that “WIDE” is not a geometric cut or trimming of elements: it merely defines a logical distance range about the projection plane (whether flat or curved) within which the structural elements are loaded.  The actual direction of the load itself—global or local—remains separately definable and is not altered by this projection-range selection.

The optimum definition of loadings is exactly at the point where they are acting. But for some structures, it is easier to define the load position by a projection. This first projection has nothing to do with the load direction itself and should never be mixed up with that.
 If no projection in global directions is selected, a projection on the loaded structural element is assumed. For the interpolation and integration of the load values this projected geometry will be used. If such a possibility is not available, the projection is done perpendicular to the loading plane for LINE and AREA loadings.
 As there is a limit on the magnitude of the projection window WIDE for curved load definitions, it is required to specify the projection direction if a value for WIDE is selected.
 The load may be defined e.g. with a certain offset from the structure itself. It will then act on all elements within a certain range WIDE before or behind the load plane, even those which are perpendicular to the projection plane of the load. The load value will be interpolated within the plane of the load definition. WIDE will not cut through the elements, it will only select them by a logical decision to be within the range or not. In SOFiLOAD there are different methods to deal with loading for beam structures. The most general method is based on explicit load distribution areas LAR and will then distribute all loads, even point loads, on multiple beams.
 This method is based on load distribution influence areas, constructed from regions either al- ready subdivided in quadrilaterals or to be established automatically in simple cases of four edges. There is a tiny plate-bending FE-program involved creating the support forces for sup- ported edges or edges with a beam section. These values are permanently saved to the database.
 If now an arbitrary loading is defined it will be first converted to nodal loads for the distribution mesh of the distribution region and then within a second step it is converted to support forces and eventually beam loading along the edges of the area.
 The other methods will load only a single distinct beam for any created part of the loading area. For point and line loads there is a hierarchic search method, where beams are selected based on their distance to the load. In this sequence the load will be projected onto the beams, subdividing line loads if necessary. A point load will be always applied entirely on one beam.
 For area loading however a primary and secondary span direction is selected (automatically or explicitly). Loading will be distributed in the secondary span direction.

Coordinate definitions relative to nodes are best performed by putting the coordinates to a variable with COOR beforehand. For simple cases for all coordinates a specification of the literal GPT instead of the X-value and for the number of a geometric point or a node instead of the Y-value will directly use the coordinates of that point. It is also possible to specify all
 coordinates relative to a special nodal point, which is given with its number and the the item NREF for all loadings but VOLU.
 With the literals DXY, DYZ or DZX instead of an X-value it is possibel to specify coordinates relative to the first defined load point. With literals DDXY, DDYZ and DDZX the differences are taken relative to the last load point.
 It is not required to specify a load value in all load points. Missing load values will be interpo- lated before saving the load (e.g. linear variant load value along a complex geometric curve)
 The problem of multiple loading may occur if the user has defined overlapping elements or there are multiple nodes with the same coordinates. For Point and LINE-loads there is a rather easy way to assure, that no part of the loading will be applied more than once. However, for QUAD-elements this is a very difficult task. Therefore the program will load all possible elements. The user has to define a WIDE-value which defines all elements within a distance WIDE before or behind the load plane will be treated as loaded. For special cases a sound group selection may be helpful.
 For all loading the percentage of the active load area based on the defined loading area respec- tive length will be calculated and printed. A value deviating from 100 percent will be marked. With ECHO LOAD the generated loads may be printed and controlled.
 For numerical reasons tiny load components will not bes saved. load areas with a dimension less than the factored part of the total dimensions defined by CTRL STOL will be ignored.

The table shown defines the input parameters for the LAR (Load ARea) record in SOFiLOAD, which is used to generate load distribution areas for beam systems. Each row in the table corresponds to a single input field (“Item”) and gives its meaning (“Description”), the expected unit of input (“Unit”) and the default value or behavior (“Default”). Below is a field-by-field explanation:

1. NO  
   – Description: Identifier of the load distribution area. This number is used when referring to the area via an AREA REF LAR NO statement.  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: mandatory (no default).  

2. NAR  
   – Description: If you wish to select an existing geometric area (GAR) rather than defining one explicitly, enter its area number here.  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: 0 (meaning “no existing area selected”).  

3. GRP  
   – Description: Alternatively to NAR, you can select a group of QUAD elements (via a group name or index) to define the area.  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: “–” (none selected).  

4. GRP1, GRP2, GRP3  
   – Description: Specify which beam-group(s) should receive the distributed loading. You can group beams by orientation or other criteria.  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: GRP1 = all (all beam groups loaded); GRP2/GRP3 = “–” (unused).  

5. M, N  
   – Description: When defining an explicit structured area (i.e. no NAR or GRP specified), M is the number of subdivisions along the edge from point 1 to point 2 (or 3 to 4), and N is the number from point 2 to point 3 (or 4 to 1).  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: “*” (if omitted or mesh is too coarse, SOFiLOAD automatically chooses mesh sizes).  

6. T  
   – Description: Defines the relative application range of the load distribution along the beam. Values from 0 to 1 project the distributed area onto a portion of the beam.  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: 0.0 (full span).  

7. X1, Y1, Z1  
   – Description: Coordinates (in meters) of corner point 1 of the explicit area, or a GPT (grid point) reference if you specify “GPT nn” instead of direct numbers.  
   – Unit: [m] for X and Y; [m] for Z  
   – Default: 0.0.  

8. X2, Y2, Z2  
   – Description: Coordinates or GPT reference for corner point 2. Z2 may also be one of the literals DXY, DYZ or DZX, in which case SOFiLOAD interprets the remaining two axes as increments from point 1 within that plane.  
   – Unit: [m] or plane-literal for Z2  
   – Default: X1, Y1, Z1 (i.e. identical to point 1 if omitted).  

9. X3, Y3, Z3  
   – Description: Coordinates or GPT reference for corner point 3, with the same options as point 2.  
   – Unit: [m] or plane-literal for Z3  
   – Default: X2, Y2, Z2.  

10. X4, Y4, Z4  
    – Description: Coordinates for point 4 of a quadrilateral. For triangular areas the input for point 4 must equal point 3, causing the software to treat the shape as a triangle.  
    – Unit: [m]  
    – Default: X3, Y3, Z3.  

Additional notes / context:  
- If neither NAR nor GRP is specified, the explicit area defined by corner points 1–4 and subdivided by M×N is used.  
- A local positive z-direction is assigned based on the corner‐point ordering (right‐hand rule analogous to QUAD elements), which allows PZ-type loads (loads in local z).  
- For large or multiple‐span bridge models, you should avoid defining overly broad LAR areas (one per span with possible overhangs) to prevent unintended “deductional” support forces in adjacent spans.  
- To soften negative support reactions, use a CTRL LAR command (e.g. CTRL LAR 0.3).  
- Visualization and verification in the ANIMATOR before running loads is strongly recommended.  
- Example input files: sofiload_LAR_girder.dat, LAR_Rahm.dat.

The figure before you (labelled “Figure 3.9: Four-span girder with four load distribution areas”) is a schematic plan view of a continuous beam (girder) divided into four equal spans, with each span shown in turn carrying one explicit “load distribution area” (LAR). The drawing is composed of four horizontal rows: each row repeats the same four-span girder outline in bold blue, but highlights a different span by superimposing on it a semi-transparent, coloured mesh patch that represents the load distribution area assigned to that span.

Overall Layout  
• Four equal rectangular spans are drawn end-to-end in a single straight line. Each span is outlined in a uniform, thick blue line and is exactly the same width, giving the impression of a continuous beam supported on five supports (the supports themselves are not drawn).  
• Below the four rows of the beam, the caption “Figure 3.9: Four-span girder with four load distribution areas” is centered in plain text.

Row-by-Row Detail  
1. Top row – Span 1 LAR  
  – The load distribution area for the first (left-most) span is shown as a semi-transparent quadrilateral patch shaded in pastel blues, greens and purples.  
  – A very thick blue line outlines the patch, which slightly overhangs on the left side beyond the beam’s footprint, indicating an explicit free-defined area (possibly defined by four corner nodes with an overhang).  
  – Within the shaded patch you can see a fine grid of darker lines (roughly a 6×8 subdivision), signifying the mesh of M×N elements that SOFiLOAD has generated for distributing the load to the underlying beam.

2. Second row – Span 2 LAR  
  – The second span now carries the load distribution area, again drawn as a coloured grid-mesh patch.  
  – Its bounding box is centered squarely on the second span, without overhang.  
  – The mesh density appears similar (6×8), and the pastel colour pattern is identical in style, indicating the same type of load distribution area definition.

3. Third row – Span 3 LAR  
  – The third span’s load distribution area is shown in the same way, fully contained within the span’s footprint.  
  – The thick blue outline box again marks the four corner nodes of the quadrilateral; the internal grid lines represent the element subdivisions that will drive the equivalent beam loads.

4. Fourth row – Span 4 LAR  
  – Here the load distribution area is assigned to the right-most span.  
  – The semi‐transparent mesh patch again overhangs slightly beyond the right edge of the beam, implying an explicit area definition that extends outside the span limits.

Colour and Mesh Conventions  
• Each patch uses a tiled pattern of small squares shaded in a gentle colour gradient (light greens to blues to purples) against a faint grey background grid. That colouring visually distinguishes the load patch from the beam outline.  
• The fine grid lines within the patch show the local mesh: the number of elements in the longer direction uses the larger subdivision number, while the smaller edge uses the smaller one. If no “M” and “N” values had been provided, the program would generate a default mesh.  
• The thick outline (the same colour as the beam) marks the exact boundary of the user-defined load distribution area, which may be specified by absolute coordinates or by referencing GPT-point numbers and plane-increment literals (DXY, DYZ, DZX).

Contextual Notes (from accompanying text)  
• These illustrations demonstrate how separate LARs can be attached to each span to avoid “deductional loads” (i.e. unintended negative reactions) propagating into adjacent spans.  
• By defining each span’s load area individually—rather than one continuous area across the full four-span length—you ensure that a single span’s loads do not induce unwanted support forces in its neighbours.  
• The overhanging examples (spans 1 and 4) reflect cases where the defined quadrangle extends beyond the girder line; such overhangs are permitted but should be kept reasonably small to prevent numerical artifacts.  
• The text also notes that users can soften support stiffness with “CTRL LAR 0.3” if needed, and encourages validation of LAR definitions in the ANIMATOR module before running the analysis.

 Load distribution areas for beam systems can be generated with the record LAR. So it is possible to define forces as free point, line and area loads at their action position. These loads are converted then via load distribution areas into equivalent beam loads acting on the corresponding beams. Other load types (moments, temperature etc.) may not be treated.
 Single beam groups can be selected with GRP1, GPR2 and GRP3. Only the selected beam groups get then a loading. Thus e.g. a loading can be allocated only to the transverse or the longitudinal girders within a load distribution areas. Use of all beam groups is the default.
 The loading area may be defined as:
 • Existent QUAD elements of an area or a group
 • Explicit structures trinagular or quadrilateral mesh
 Every load distribution area gets a local z direction. The positive z direction results from the defined sense of rotation in analog mode to the QUAD elements. Thus it is possible to use free loads with the load type PZ - load in local z direction.
 An explicit load distribution area is described via three or four nodes which are the corner points of a triangle or quadrangle. This area is subdivided in M and N elements. Either the node coordinates or the numbers of already defined GPT points for X1, X2, X3, X4 are to be input. The highest subdivision value is used here for the greater edge length in the smaller one for the smaller edge. If no input for M and N was done or if a to coarse mesh was defined, then SOFiLOAD generates automatically a mesh.
 The coordinates of the four corners may be defined in absolute coordinates or taken from a structural node with the definition GPT nn. Further it is possible to enter for Z2, Z3 or Z4 one of the literals DXY, DYZ or DZX. The other two coordinates are then taken as increments within the specified plane to the first point. A definition of only the first two points will create a rectangle within the appropriate coordinate planes.

Further it is possible to enter for Z2, Z3 or Z4 one of the literals DXY, DYZ or DZX. The other two coordinates are then taken as increments within the specified plane to the first point. A definition of only the first two points will create a rectangle within the appropriate coordinate planes..
 The load distribution areas should not be defined too large, because otherwise deductional loads will arise. A load distribution area possibly with an overhang shown in the following pictures for a four-span bridge should be input per span.
 Four-span girder with four load distribution areas
 In case of one continuous load distribution area deductional forces can arise in the neighbour- ing span due to a single load.
 On the other hand deductional forces are generated as planned always inside for external loads, because they are necessary for the equilibrium.
 With e.g. CTRL LAR 0.3 the stiffness of the support can be softened to reduce possible negative support forces.
 It is recommended to check the LAR areas in the ANIMATOR.

The input table is the formal specification for defining a “POIN” (point) load in the RAG‐augmented vector store.  It consists of four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and is organized into three logical blocks:  
 1. Reference Definition  
 2. Spatial/Projection Parameters  
 3. Load Magnitude and Location  

Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown, with notes on context and usage rules drawn from the surrounding POIN documentation.  

1. Reference Definition  
   • REF (Reference type, unit=LIT, default=AUTO)  
     – AUTO: automatic selection of load location  
     – MOVE: automatic moving load  
     – LAR: load distribution area  
     – SLN: structural line  
     – SAR: structural area  
     – GFA: surface number for BRIC elements  
     – NODE: explicitly generated node  
     – BGRP: group of beam/cable/truss elements  
     – QGRP: group of QUAD elements  
     – VGRP: group of BRIC elements  
     Usage notes:  
       • If REF=NODE with a node number, that node’s coordinates become the default load point; any eccentricity about that node produces associated moments.  
       • If REF points at SLN or BGRP, stored eccentricities travel with the beam load or convert to moments on non‐beam lines.  
       • If REF is SAR or QGRP, the single POIN load is distributed as up to four nodal loads without eccentricity.  

   • NO (Reference or group number, unit=–, default=–)  
     – When REF refers to an existing object, NO specifies its numeric identifier or group index.  

   • TITL (Short title of loading, unit=LIT12, default=–)  
     – An optional 12-character label for easy identification.  

2. Spatial/Projection Parameters  
   • PROJ (Projection of load point, unit=LIT, default=N)  
     – N: project along the normal to the reference area (only relevant if REF=SAR)  
     – XX, YY, ZZ: project along global X, Y or Z axis  
     – Defines how the program finds the actual Cartesian location on or beside the referenced geometry.

Key Contextual Rules from the POIN Description:  
 • POIN loads are not true mathematical singularities but energetic equivalents attached to FE nodes; refining the mesh will reveal stronger local gradients.  
 • If element mesh size at the POIN site becomes smaller than the plate or shell thickness, all loads must revert to areal definitions and supports to areal supports with real dimensions.  
 • When multiple candidate elements exist under a projected point, the element with the lowest ID “wins.”  
 • For influence‐area analyses, a unit POIN load produces a Dirac-delta strain at the element center, with the mesh deformation defining the effective influence area—FE smoothing naturally regularizes the theoretical singularity.
