The table shown defines the fields you must supply whenever you create an AREA‐type load distribution in SOFiLOAD (PROG SOFILOAD).  It is organized into four columns – 1) Item (the keyword you type), 2) Description (what it means), 3) Unit, and 4) Default value – and can be read from top to bottom as follows:

1.  REF   (LIT; default = AUTO)  
    • “Reference type” – tells the program how to find the surface or elements you want to load.  
    • Valid literals are:  
      – AUTO  : search in all defined areas, QUADs, beams, etc., and pick the ones fully covered by your data points.  
      – MOVE  : for moving loads  
      – LAR   : load distribution area  
      – SAR   : structural area  
      – GFA   : BRIC surface number  
      – BGRP  : group of beam elements  
      – QGRP  : group of QUAD elements  
      – VGRP  : group of BRIC elements  

2.  NO    (–; no default)  
    • “Reference or group number” – the numeric ID of your chosen REF target.  

3.  TITL  (LIT12; no default)  
    • Short title or identifier for this loading case (up to 12 characters).

4.  PROJ  (LIT; default = N)  
    • “Projection of loading area” – defines the plane onto which your data points are projected before interpolation.  
    • Options:  
      – N    : project onto the normal of the REF surface (use for true‐surface loads)  
      – XX/YY/ZZ : global X-, Y- or Z-direction projection (e.g. snow load in plan view)  
      – XXL/YYL/ZZL : same as XX/YY/ZZ but the sign of P‐values is interpreted in the local axis  
      – LOAD : like N but suppresses eccentricity calculations  

5.  WIDE  ([m]₁₀₀₁; default = 0.0)  
    • “Range in direction of projection” – only meaningful if PROJ≠N. Specifies how far the load “smears” in the projection direction.

6.  NREF  (–; no default)  
    • “Reference node for coordinate values” – if you want point coordinates given relative to a particular nodal origin.

7.  TYPE  (LIT; default = PG)  
    • “Load type and direction” – e.g. P (surface pressure), PXX, PXP (projected pressure), M (moment), MX, PXPZ, etc.  
    • See the text for definitions.  PXX vs. PXP differ in whether the load is referenced to the true surface or its horizontal projection; PXPZ applies horizontal pressure in local Z, etc.

8.  P1…P6  (*; default = 0.0 or inherited)  
    • “Load value of point 1 … point 6” – give up to six magnitudes.  You may specify 1…6 on a single record.  Beyond six, use one or more CONT records to continue P7…P63.  

9.  X1…X6, Y1…Y6, Z1…Z6  ([m]₁₀₀₁; defaults X5/Y5/Z5 for P6)  
    • “Coordinates of point n” – the global X/Y/Z of each data point.  
    • Alternatively for the 2nd point you may supply DXY, DYZ, or DZX instead of X2, offsetting in that coordinate plane relative to point 1.  If you only give two points (and use D-literals), a rectangle is assumed.  

How it all works  
• Once you give 3…4 suitably placed points, SOFiLOAD will perform a bilinear surface‐fitting (4 coefficients).  
• If you define more points—at least 6 in each of two directions—it can go quadratic (6 coeffs) or bicubic (10 coeffs).  
• Any “kinks” in your loading must be split into separate AREA records.  
• If you need a simple uniform pressure over an area (no coordinates), you may omit X/Y/Z entirely and define only NO and P1.  
• For more than six points, append CONT records immediately after the main AREA record. CONT records must not contain any generation or list expressions.  

Projection rules and beam fallback  
• PROJ=N (the default) will project your data onto the curved SAR surface (or your chosen REF).  
• PROJ=XX/YY/ZZ project into a global plane, so load area can lie off the real geometry.  
• If you have no structural QUADs or SARs defined, SOFiLOAD will automatically distribute onto beam elements within the area, estimating transverse girders and eccentricities. You can tweak that with STOL/COTB.  

Load types  
The table does not expand TYPE’s full list, but common choices include:  
  – P, PXX, PXP, PXPZ (surface pressures)  
  – M, MX (moments per area)  
  – Temperature or initial stress loads (no equivalent nodal forces generated; element‐center test for inclusion)  

In summary, this table is your “input template” for defining arbitrary‐shaped, interpolated surface loads in an advanced FE preprocessor, covering everything from uniform pressures to bi/quadric distributions, in any projection you need.

This table (Table 3.37) defines all of the “free area” loading‐type codes you can use when you apply a surface load via AREA/SAR/LAR records (i.e. a polygonal loading region that is not tied to the element mesh). Its two columns are:

 1. Type of the Free Area Loading  
 2. Unit  

Entries fall into three logical groups:

1.   Special “factor” or CFD‐driven loads (unit “–”)  
     •  FACTOR: a pure multiplier.  
     •  Wall shear stress from a flow analysis (CTRL CFDL).  
     •  Distribution of the pressure field (CFD post‐processing).  
     •  Material‐type factor (see Chapter 7).  

2.   Pressure‐type surface loads (unit “kN/m²”)  
     •  P: uniform pressure applied normal to the free surface in the specified global direction.  
     •  PXX: pressure referenced to the true (possibly curved) area (e.g. self-weight on an irregular surface).  
     •  PXP: pressure referenced to the projection of that surface into the global XY plane (e.g. snow loading).  
     •  PXY, PXZ, PYX, PYY, PYZ, PZX, PZY, PZZ: other permutations of component‐wise pressures on true versus projected area, in global X, Y or Z directions.  
     •  PXXL, PYXL, PZXL: the same as above but using local element axes (“L” suffix forces you to treat sign/axis in the local coordinate frame rather than the global frame).  
     •  PXPZ (and analogous P*P*Z): a horizontally projecting pressure applied in the local Z‐normal direction of the area.  

   All of these are interpreted through the AREA load‐interpolation engine:  
     –  If you define 4 points, a bilinear (4-coefficient) load surface is fitted.  
     –  With 6–10 points (and at least two independent directions), you get quadratic or bicubic variation.  
     –  Any “kinks” (discontinuities) must be defined as separate AREA loads.  

3.   Moment loads per unit area (unit “kNm/m²”)  
     •  MX: moment about the local X‐axis.  
     •  MY: moment about the local Y‐axis.  
     •  MZ: moment about the local Z‐axis.  

Key cross-references and behaviors:  
–  If you omit the AREA number, the program searches all defined areas and applies loads only to areas whose projected volume fully contains the load polygon.  
–  PROJ options (e.g. “PROJ XY,” “PROJ XXL,” etc.) control whether a PXP load is treated in global or local space, and whether signage follows the global component or the local normal.  
–  For beam networks beneath the area, the code will automatically detect a primary girder direction and distribute “free area” loads transversely, unless you steer it with CTRL options STOL/COTB.  
–  Any P/M‐type surface load is eventually converted into equivalent nodal forces/moments via the element shape functions; other “initial stress” loads (e.g. thermal) are applied to any element whose centroid falls inside the AREA.  

All load‐type codes from this table are also valid under DOLFYN or HYDRA when you define QUAD loads.

The table shown is a continuation of “Table 3.37” and serves to document the units associated with the various AREA‐type load definitions (SAR, LAR, QGRP, etc.) and their related load‐type codes.  Its structure and content can be summarized as follows:

1. Two-column layout  
   - Left column: load‐type identifiers or descriptive qualifiers (e.g. global‐axis moments, in‐plane stiffness, curvature, temperature change, beam load components).  
   - Right column: the corresponding physical units.

2. Area-load (surface‐load) quantities (all per unit area)  
   • MX, MY, MXY, … (moment loadings about local axes, analogous to bending)  
     – Unit: kNm/m²  
   • PXX, PYY, PZZ, PXY, PXZ, PYZ (normal and shear pressures on the true area)  
     – Unit: kN/m²  
   • PXP, PYP, PZP (projections into a principal plane, e.g. snow load on XY)  
     – Unit: kN/m²  

3. Component‐load stiffness (for tendon, seismic, hydrostatic projections)  
   • “in xy plane”  
     – Unit: K (i.e. a nondimensional stiffness coefficient)  
   • “in local z-direction”  
     – Unit: K  

4. Angular or curvature parameters (used for geometric imperfections or warping)  
   • Rotation angles (e.g. for DXY, DYZ, DZX definitions)  
     – Unit: ‰ (per mille, shown as 0/00)  
   • Curvatures  
     – Unit: 1/km  

5. Temperature change across an area (initial‐stress or eigenstrain loading)  
   • ΔT  
     – Unit: mm (interpreted as a length offset or equivalent strain thickness)  

6. Beam‐equivalent loads (when AREA definitions are auto-projected onto beam elements in the absence of explicit LAR/QUAD meshes)  
   – Bending‐moment distributions about the local X, Y or coupled axis  
     • Units: kNm/m  
   – Axial or shear forces per beam length  
     • Units: kN/m  

Remarks and Contextual Notes (from the surrounding documentation):  
- Missing area‐load points are interpolated by a least‐squares bilinear (4 coefficients), quadratic (6 coeff.), or bicubic (10 coeff.) fit depending on how many points are provided.  
- You may specify up to 63 data points via continuation records (CONT), but must supply enough points in both coordinate directions to yield a full‐rank coefficient system.  
- If only two points are given and one uses the literal codes DXY, DYZ or DZX for the second (X) coordinate, the program interprets this as a rectangle in that plane.  
- AREA loads may project onto beams by defining a main girder direction; eccentricities and transverse distributions can be influenced by CTRL options STOL and COTB.  
- For P and M‐type loads, equivalent nodal forces are obtained by integrating element shape functions. For other loads (e.g. thermal), element centers are tested for inclusion in the AREA to assign the loading, so irregular meshes can yield slight deviations from the exact projected area.  

This table thus provides a quick reference for the engineer or script parsing SAR/LAR QGRP records to know exactly which units each load‐type field expects, ensuring correct interpretation and storage in a RAG vector database for later retrieval or parametric studies.

Thus up to four points with a suitable pattern will define a bilinear (4 coefficients) distribution, more points will allow a quadratic (6 coefficients) or bicubic (10 coefficients) distribution, but sufficient points have to be defined in at least two directions to allow the evaluation of all coefficients. The other two coordinates are then taken as increments within the specified plane to the first point. A definition of only two points will create a rectangle within the appropriate coordinate planes..
 For the projection of the load there are the principal rules:
 • Explicit references to an area is always unique. However if the number is not defined, the program will check all areas. So multiple instances of the loaded area might occur. However only those areas are used, where the load is completely within the volume defined by the elements of the area.
 • All Interpolations and geometric calculations will take place in the projected area. For SAR and PROJ N this is the region, which might be curved. The data points of the load should be on that surface therefore. For a global projection however the loading area may be situated somehow away from the real structure.
 • For a automatic reference, the program will start with any defined load distribution areas, then any defined QUAD elements and structural areas and finally work on beam elements.
 The loading on beam elements is best done via load distribution areas LAR or real QUAD ele-
 ments. If such are not present, the program will establish a main girder direction and distribute the load transverse to them on those beams fully or partial within the loading area. Eccentrici- ties of the load will be established as it would be without any transverse girders. However the user has CTRL options STOL and COTB to influence this processing.

 The difference between PXX and PXP is given by the fact, that PXX is a load referenced to the true area (e.g. dead weight) while PXP is referenced on the projection into the XY-plane (e.g. snow). However, for planar systems there will be no difference as the loads are always referenced on the true surface. The component loadings define a load direction derived from a projection of the normal of the area into the specified global projection plane (e.g. diverting forces of tendons). The local loads based on a global load projection are required to define earthquake loadings on fillings of tanks. A load type PXPZ will define a horizontal projecting pressure applied in the normal direction Z of the plane. In general the sign of the load value will be taken on the global component. However with projection XXL, YYL or ZZL the sign of the load value will define the local component. Thus specifying PXPZ on a circle with PROJ XX will define a load acting depending on the orienation of the local z-axis, while PROJ XXL will define a load acting everywhere in the same direction e.g. inwards.

However with projection XXL, YYL or ZZL the sign of the load value will define the local component. Thus specifying PXPZ on a circle with PROJ XX will define a load acting depending on the orienation of the local z-axis, while PROJ XXL will define a load acting everywhere in the same direction e.g. inwards..
 For load types P and M equivalent nodal forces and moments will be established by integrating the element shape functions.
 For all other loads, creating initial stress (like temperature) over the whole element, the selec- tion will be by hitting the loading area with the centre of the element. This is why for irregular meshes the sum of the loading area might deviate from the 100 % aim.
 Using load distribution areas with REF LAR a moment loading is not considered!
 For DOLFYN and HYDRA are the same load types available as specified for the record QUAD.

Left Sketch  
• Overall Form: A rectangular plan building footprint with a symmetric ridge running longitudinally. Two identical roof slabs slope down from the central ridge to the eaves on either side.  
• Perspective: Isometric-style view, with the front right-hand corner of the building cut away to reveal the right-hand sloping roof plane more clearly. The underside of the left roof plane is partly visible over the façade of the building.  
• Load-Point Markers: Six small numerals, each located at a vertex of the roof planes. The points are numbered 1 through 6 in counter-clockwise order when viewed from the outside of the roof plane:  
  1 – Located at the midpoint of the ridge on the right-hand roof plane (closest to the viewer)  
  2 – Front eaves of the right-hand roof slab  
  3 – Ridge end on the left-hand side, at the rear of the building  
  4 – Front eaves of the left-hand roof slab, near the viewer on the left side  
  5 – Lower left corner of the left roof slab, where it meets the building corner at the eaves  
  6 – Lower right corner of the right roof slab, adjacent to the façade cutaway  
• Edges and Surfaces: Roof edges are drawn as simple straight lines; the ridge is horizontal and central. Slopes are uniform and symmetric. Walls of the building are shown as vertical rectangular prisms beneath the roof.

Right Sketch  
• Simplified Geometry: A cleaner, slightly more exploded view, isolating the roof form without the building walls fully shown. One sidewall is sketched in to indicate the eaves plane.  
• Emphasis on Load-Point Sequence: Points 1–6 are again placed in counter-clockwise order when seen from outside the roof:  
  1 – Lower front right eaves intersection  
  2 – (Not explicitly visible in this particular view, but implied by continuity between points 1 and 3)  
  3 – Upper left end of the ridge (rear)  
  4 – Mid-ridge on the near side (left of point 1)  
  5 – Mid-eaves on the far left overhang  
  6 – Lower ridge-to-eaves intersection on the near right overhang  
• View Angle: Slightly rotated compared to the left sketch to highlight the slope and overhangs of the roof planes. The ridge line tilts upward leftward. Only minimal wall geometry is drawn, serving as context for the roof overhang.

General Observations  
• Numbering Convention: Meets the EN 1991-1-4 requirement that a double-pitched roof load area have at least six vertices, beginning with a point on the horizontal ridge, and proceeding counter-clockwise as seen from the outside.  
• Roof Symmetry: Both sketches emphasize the need for consistent inclination along all edges—identical slopes on both halves.  
• Purpose of Annotations: The numbered points define the polygonal load area for wind-pressure assignment. In practice these would be paired with pressure coefficients or copied and subdivided by the software per EN 1991-1-4 or DIN 1055 rules.  
• Contextual Note: The caption and accompanying text refer to how title codes (CP*, QP*, *MEAN) and colon-suffix values (for attic height or eave reduction) interact with wind load assignments in structural analysis software.  • The loading require the total outer extend of the building, defined by all groups active for wind loading.
 • A planar load area may have as many load points as possible, but all points have to be defined, that they are counter clockwise if you look from the outside on the surface.
 • A double pitched roof (saddle or through) requires at least six load points. The first point has to be on the ridge or groove, which is required to be horizontal and the inclination of the roof must match along all edges everywhere.
 • If a load area can not be treated an error message occurs, but it is strongly recommended to check the load values especially if the wind attack is not perpendicular to the structure.

The table defines the syntax and semantics of the VOLU record, which is used to apply volumetric loads to BRIC‐ and QUAD‐type finite elements (or to entire groups thereof).  It is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and enumerates all the parameters you can specify when declaring a VOLU load case.  Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown suitable for indexing in a RAG‐style vector store:

1. REF (Reference type)  
   - Description: Selects the geometric or group reference to which the volume load applies.  
     • LAR = Load distribution area  
     • GFA = Faces of BRIC elements  
     • SAR = Structural region  
     • SVO = Structural volume  
     • QGRP = Group of QUAD elements  
     • VGRP = Group of BRIC elements  
     • FGRP = Surface of BRIC elements  
   - Unit: Literal (LIT)  
   - Default: VGRP  

2. NO (Reference or group number)  
   - Description: Integer identifier of the chosen reference entity or element group.  
   - Unit: none  
   - Default: “–”  

3. TITL (Short title of loading)  
   - Description: Up to 12‐character text string for user reference.  
   - Unit: LIT12  
   - Default: none  

4. A/U (Reference value for silo loadings)  
   - Description: Only used when modeling granular (silo) loads; defines a reference magnitude.  
   - Unit: “*” (generic real)  
   - Default: none  

5. TYPE (Load type and direction)  
   - Description: Literal code that indicates which component or hydraulic loading to apply (e.g. PX, PY, PZ for pressure in X, Y, Z).  
   - Unit: LIT  
   - Default: PG  

6. P (Load value at reference point)  
   - Description: Scalar magnitude of the volumetric load at the “anchor” point.  
   - Unit: “*” (real)  
   - Default: 0.0  

7. X, Y, Z (Coordinates of reference point)  
   - Description: Cartesian coordinates of the reference point.  Alternatively, X (GPT) can be a grid point tag and Y the point number.  
   - Unit: metres [m]_1001  
   - Default: “*” (if omitted, entire volume or group is assumed)  

8. P1 (Load value of first point / increment)  
   - Description: Pressure (or body‐force increment) at the first corner of the sheared load domain.  
   - Unit: “*”  
   - Default: P/0 (inherit P or zero increment)  

9. X1, Y1, Z1 (Coordinates of first point)  
   - Description: Defines the first node of the parallelepiped (sheared cube) over which load is interpolated.  
   - Unit: [m]_1001  
   - Default: “*”  

…  

n. P5, X5, Y5, Z5 (Load value and coordinates for fifth point)  
   - Description: Up to five corner points may be specified to fully bound and shape the load domain.  Values are interpolated linearly in the local sheared coordinate system defined by point pairs (P–P1), (P3–P2), (P5–P4).  
   - Unit: P* values are “*”; coordinates are [m]_1001  
   - Default: P/0 for Pi, “*” for Xi, Yi, Zi  

Key behavioral notes (from context):  
- If no Xi/Yi/Zi are provided for any direction, the program automatically extends to the extreme of the model in gravity or perpendicular directions, treating the specified load as an increment.  
- For simple fluid‐pressure loading, only one plane (e.g. Z = free surface) and the weight P1 need be defined; all other corners default to the upper extent.  
- Partial loading on BRIC elements is not supported: any element whose centroid lies within the sheared domain is fully loaded. QUAD volumes will be clipped to the domain boundaries.  
- The same load types available to QUAD and BRIC records in DOLFYN or HYDRA solver formats also apply here.

The figure presents a three-dimensional, sheared parallelepiped (a “skewed cube”) that serves to illustrate how a user-defined volume is specified for the VOLU load in finite-element pre- and post-processors. Drawn in oblique perspective, four of the eight corner nodes of the volume are explicitly labeled and connected by solid and dashed edges; the remaining four corners are implied by the face outlines.  

Overall geometry  
• The outer boundary is a six-sided polyhedron whose faces are not orthogonal to one another but are “sheared” in space. Front and back faces appear as parallelograms rather than rectangles. Hidden edges on the near face are drawn as dotted or dashed lines to indicate depth, while visible edges are solid. The top and bottom faces slope gently from front to back and from left to right.  

Labeled points and axis directions  
• Point “P” marks the front-left corner of the volume. From P three noncolinear direction vectors emanate: one runs diagonally up toward the upper rear face, one runs diagonally down into the interior, and one runs horizontally across the top face. Each of these directions is represented by a short blue line segment.  
• Point “P2” lies on the left interior face, below and behind the front-left corner P. A blue segment from P2 slopes upward and to the right, indicating the second defining edge of the sheared coordinate system.  
• Point “P3” is positioned near the center of the top face, slightly toward the back. A blue segment along the top face connects P3 to the far-right top edge.  
• Point “P4” appears on the bottom face, roughly centered in plan, with a blue line slanting upward toward the front-right.  
• Point “P5” marks the upper-right rear corner of the parallelepiped.  

Key visual cues  
• Dotted shading on the interior indicates the volume that will be “loaded” or “activated” by the VOLU command.  
• The three blue segments through P, P2, P3 (and connecting onward toward P5 and P4) represent the sheared local coordinate axes (p1–p, p3–p2, p5–p4) that define how the program will interpolate loads across the solid. These must not lie in the same line or plane if the volume definition is to be valid.  
• Transparent rendering of the side and back faces ensures the viewer sees the interior orientation of these three defining directions.  

Caption  
Beneath the sketch, the text “Figure 3.11: The selected volume definition” calls out that this is the standard schematic for specifying a loaded volume in the input deck. In practice, the user supplies coordinates for P (the origin of the local sheared system), plus two additional points (often P1 and the free surface), and the other points default to the extents of the model in gravity or perpendicular directions. This diagram makes explicit how the six corner points or implied extents combine to establish the interpolated pressure or volumetric load within that sheared region.

The provided “Table 3.39: Type of the Volume Loading” summarizes all of the volume‐load formulations available when using the VOLU record (e.g. for DOLFYN or HYDRA).  In a RAG‐friendly, vector‐store description, one would store:

1. Table Identifier  
   • Title: “Type of the Volume Loading”  
   • Context: Applies to the VOLU keyword; load types available for QUAD (2-D) and BRIC (3-D) finite elements.

2. Column Definitions  
   • Column 1: Load‐Type Description—names or brief functional definitions of each volumetric‐loading variant.  
   • Column 2 (Unit QUAD): The engineering unit used when that load type is applied to QUAD (surface) elements. Because QUAD elements represent area‐based “shells,” all applicable loads appear in kN/m².  
   • Column 3 (Unit BRIC): The engineering unit used when that load type is applied to BRIC (solid) elements. BRIC elements occupy volume, so true volumetric loads appear in kN/m³; where a load concept does not make sense for a solid, the table marks “n.a.” (not applicable).

3. Row‐by‐Row Load‐Type Breakdown  
   1. Gravity direction (!)  
      – QUAD: kN/m²  
      – BRIC: kN/m³  
      – Notes: Automatic gravity loading; for BRIC this is a body‐force per unit volume, for QUAD an equivalent pressure per unit area.  
   2. Uniform pressure (constant)  
      – QUAD: kN/m²  
      – BRIC: n.a.  
      – Notes: A constant surface pressure only makes sense on QUAD elements.  
   3. Orientation‐dependent pressure  
      – QUAD: kN/m²  
      – BRIC: n.a.  
      – Notes: Varies with element normal/orientation; only for 2D shells.  
   4. Pressure referenced to an area  
      – QUAD: kN/m²  
      – BRIC: n.a.  
      – Notes: Loads defined relative to a reference area (AREA record).  
   5. Pressure referenced to a line  
      – QUAD: kN/m²  
      – BRIC: n.a.  
      – Notes: Loads “smeared” from a LINE record onto QUAD elements.  
   6. Volumetric load referenced to a plane  
      – QUAD: kN/m²  
      – BRIC: kN/m³  
      – Notes: For hydrostatic/fluid loads; plane sets a free surface, BRIC uses ρ·g so in kN/m³.  
   7. Volumetric load with linear gradient  
      – QUAD: kN/m²  
      – BRIC: kN/m³  
      – Notes: Linear variation along one direction (e.g. depth‐dependent).  
   8. Volumetric load with planar gradient  
      – QUAD: kN/m²  
      – BRIC: kN/m³  
      – Notes: Varies across two dimensions (e.g. sloping free‐surface fluid).  
   9. Custom load referenced to the element center  
      – QUAD: kN/m²  
      – BRIC: n.a.  
     10. User‐defined distribution (“incremental” type)  
      – QUAD: kN/m²  
      – BRIC: n.a.  
      – Notes: Applies only as an incremental (additive) surface loading.

4. Key Observations and RAG‐Meta  
   • “n.a.” flags that the concept of an area‐ or line‐referenced (2D) pressure has no counterpart inside a 3D, volumetric BRIC element.  
   • All gravity‐type and fluid‐pressure formulations that inherently involve volume density carry kN/m³ units for BRIC.  
   • The VOLU record interpolates load magnitudes within a “sheared cube” defined by up to six coordinate inputs (p1–p6); however, the table itself focuses solely on unit consistency.  
   • When populating a vector store, index each row by its load‐type keyword (e.g. “gravity,” “orientation‐dependent,” “plane‐referenced”) and store unit conventions under two separate fields: “unit_quad” and “unit_bric.”

By capturing the table in this structured form—explicit table title, column schema, per‐row load type plus units, and side notes—you enable downstream retrieval, filtering by element type, or schematic reconstruction for user guidance.

Below is a structured breakdown of the portion of Table 3.39 shown, which lists the units associated with the various load parameters when applied to quadrilateral (QUAD) or brick (BRIC) finite-elements under a VOLU loading definition. Note that this is a continuation of the full table; the first column (naming each load parameter) is not visible in the screenshot, but the two right-hand columns (“Unit QUAD” and “Unit BRIC”) are fully shown.

1. Overall Layout  
   • Two primary columns of interest:  
     – Unit QUAD – the physical unit to be used when the load parameter is assigned to QUAD (surface) elements.  
     – Unit BRIC – the physical unit when it applies to BRIC (solid) elements; “n.a.” indicates “not applicable.”  
   • Each row corresponds to one component or type of load or parameter used in the VOLU record.  
   • All loading types available for QUAD are carried over to BRIC only if meaningful; otherwise they are marked “n.a.”

2. Surface‐Pressure and Shear‐Type Loads (Rows 1–9)  
   • These first nine entries (not named in the screenshot but typically including P, P1, PX, PY, PZ, HS, HE, VG, VH in some formulations) share the same units:  
     – Unit QUAD: kN/m²  
     – Unit BRIC: n.a.  
   • Interpretation: these are all pressure‐type or distributed‐shear parameters defined per unit area on a QUAD element face; they have no direct analogue on a brick solid face.

3. Global Pressure Group Loads (Rows 10–11)  
   • Two further parameters read “from global PGG” and “from global PGP.” Again these refer to pressure lookup or amplification factors from predefined pressure groups.  
     – Unit QUAD: kN/m²  
     – Unit BRIC: n.a.

4. Distributed Moment Loads (Row 12)  
   • A moment‐per‐area quantity, often denoted for a local direction ℓ ∈ {x,y,z}.  
     – Unit QUAD: kNm/m²  
     – Unit BRIC: n.a.  
   • Used when a bending moment is distributed over a shell (QUAD) element.

5. Spring‐Stiffness Parameters (Rows 13–14)  
   • Two stiffness parameters—one for shear in the element’s plane, one for normal stiffness in the local z-direction.  
     – Both share “K” as the unit (i.e. a generic spring constant in force/displacement units).  
     – Unit BRIC: n.a.

6. Dimensionless or Ratio Parameters (Rows 15–16)  
   • The table’s final two rows carry a unit of “0 / 00,” signifying a per-thousand (per‐mille) ratio or dimensionless factor.  
     – Row 15: Unit QUAD = 0 / 00, Unit BRIC = 0 / 00 (both applicable).  
     – Row 16: Unit QUAD = n.a., Unit BRIC = 0 / 00 (only defined for BRIC).

Key Points for RAG Vectorization  
  • The table is purely a “unit lookup” for each load parameter—no numeric values are stored here, only the expected physical units.  
  • QUAD elements support pressure, shear, moment, stiffness, and dimensionless factors; BRIC elements in this context only use the last row’s per-mille factor.  
  • Whenever a parameter is marked “n.a.” under BRIC, it should be omitted from brick‐element load definitions in any automated schema.  
  • For retrieval—when a user requests “what unit must I use for parameter PZ on a BRIC element?” the answer is “not applicable”; for QUAD it is “kN/m².”  
  • The grouping of rows naturally splits into pressure‐type, moment‐type, stiffness‐type, and ratio‐type parameters, which may guide indexing or facet filtering in your vector store.

The table below defines two supplemental parameters—ID and TAG—that can be applied to any load entity (POIN, LINE, AREA, VOLU) within the CADiNP language. Both parameters appear immediately after the load definition and serve as properties for identification and grouping.

Table structure  
• Item  
  – The name of the parameter (ID or TAG).  
• Description  
  – A brief explanation of the parameter’s purpose.  
• Unit  
  – The data type used by the parameter: LIT32 indicates a literal string up to 32 characters in length.  
• Default  
  – The value used when no explicit parameter is supplied. A dash (“–”) means no default is defined; the field remains unset unless specified.

Items

1. ID  
   • Description: “Identifier of load.” This is the primary field for assigning a unique reference label to a load. In practice, this is often a GUID (Globally Unique Identifier) formatted as a 128-bit value in hexadecimal form, or any other user-defined label.  
   • Unit: LIT32  
   • Default: –  

   Usage context:  
   – When the GUID command is used, it implicitly populates ID with a globally unique 128-bit integer encoded as a string.  
   – The user may override or provide a custom identifier by writing GUID ID “<string>” immediately after a load statement (e.g. “poin p1 ... guid id ‘8c2bf9…’”).  
   – ID allows traceability of loads across CADiNP and external systems, ensuring that references remain consistent during data exchange.

2. TAG  
   • Description: “Marker.” This is an auxiliary label that the user can apply to group or categorize loads by arbitrary names (for example, “Column,” “Wall,” or “Slab”).  
   • Unit: LIT32  
   • Default: –  

   Usage context:  
   – TAG serves as a grouping key. Later in the script, the ECHO TAG command can filter loads by their TAG value and assemble them into summary tables. For example:  
     echo tag yes val1 “Column”  
     $Write table with all loads tagged “Column”  
   – Multiple loads can share the same TAG, enabling convenient batch operations, selective output, or analytical grouping in post-processing.

See also  
• POIN, LINE, AREA, VOLU: Core load-definition commands. Each of these statements may be followed by GUID and TAG property records.  
• GUID: A dedicated command that assigns a standard 128-bit global identifier. When GUID is used without an explicit ID clause, CADiNP generates and assigns the GUID automatically.  
• ECHO TAG: A scripting facility that scans all defined loads, filters them by their TAG value, and outputs a tabular summary of grouped loads.

Notes  
– Although ID and TAG are optional, it is good practice to supply meaningful identifiers and markers for any load that may need to be referenced or grouped later.  
– In text‐mode CADiNP models, it is not strictly necessary to set GUID if external referencing is not required; however, ID remains a flexible substitute.  
– The LIT32 type permits tags and identifiers up to 32 characters—enough for descriptive labels or full GUID strings.

The table summarizes the four parameters that the EXPO command accepts when exporting load‐case data from the CDB to a SOFiLOAD input file. Each row in the table defines one keyword, its meaning, its data type or “unit,” and its default behavior if the keyword is omitted. Below is a detailed breakdown:

1. NO  
   • Description  
     – Specifies the index (number) of a single load case to export.  
     – If set to 0, EXPO will export all load cases, including any associated actions or load areas.  
   • Unit / Data Type  
     – “—” (no text length limit but must be a nonnegative integer).  
   • Default  
     – “–” means there is no default numeric value; if you omit NO, EXPO behaves as if 0 were supplied and exports every load case.

2. TO  
   • Description  
     – Names the output file to which the EXPO command writes the extracted loads.  
     – If you do not supply TO, EXPO appends data to the most recently specified file or, if none exists, to the default file “project_LFD.DAT.”  
   • Unit / Data Type  
     – LIT96: a literal character string of up to 96 characters. Valid characters include letters, digits, underscores, periods, and path delimiters.  
   • Default  
     – “*” indicates “use the last specified file name or the built-in default.”  

3. PASS  
   • Description  
     – Provides the password of the CDB database. If the database is password‐protected, you must supply this argument so EXPO can gain read access.  
   • Unit / Data Type  
     – LIT16: a literal string up to 16 characters long. Case‐sensitive.  
   • Default  
     – “–” (no default). If the database requires a password and you omit PASS, the export will fail with an authentication error.

4. OPT  
   • Description  
     – A concatenation of option codes that control which subsets of data are exported. Multiple codes can usually be strung together without delimiters. The main options are:  
       • ACT – export only the action loads (skips nodal, elemental, and load‐area definitions)  
       • LAR – export only load‐distribution areas (skips actions, nodal, and elemental loads)  
       • … (other single‐letter flags may exist, see the EXPO documentation for full detail on less common flags, e.g. flags to include generated loads, free loadings <100 %, etc.)  
   • Unit / Data Type  
     – “—” (flags are parsed internally; no fixed text length but typically a short string up to 8 characters).  
   • Default  
     – “–” means “no special options”: EXPO exports all load data (nodal loads, elemental loads, load areas, actions, generated loads) for the specified load cases.

Usage Notes and Interactions  
- When TO is omitted, always check which file is “most lately defined”—you may inadvertently append to an older dataset.  
- Always verify that local‐to‐global transformations are handled correctly, as EXPO may lose coordinate‐system context.  
- Combining OPT flags allows fine‐grained control (for example, OPT=ACTLAR would export both actions and areas only).  
- Since EXPO can produce partial or overlapping data sets if misused, a post‐export review of the .DAT file is strongly recommended.

EXPO
 With the command EXPO you may write the loads form load cases in the database to a input file for SOFiLOAD. This may be useful in special cases, but you have to keep in mind that during the input processing always some information gets lost (e.g. local to global transformations), so the user should check the resulting data to be sure that nothing is missing.
 If the file name is not specified the data will be appended to the most lately defined file or set to project_LFD.DAT.
 If no load case is specified, all load cases including actions and load areas will be exported.
 OPT allows some extra options to be activated:
 ACT Only the actions will be also exported
 LAR Only the load distribution areas will be exported
 only nodal and elemental loads will be exported, but including all generated loads.
 only those free loadings are exported which have not been applied with 100 %.

The table below defines the keywords and parameters available on the EVAL input record in CADINP.  EVAL is used to post-process previously calculated load vectors, displacements or other response quantities, to evaluate integrals (influence areas, line integrals, etc.) or to assemble derived load cases for subsequent analysis.  Each column of the table means:

• Item – the name of the parameter on the EVAL record  
• Description – what that parameter controls  
• Unit – the expected data type or literal format  
• Default – the value assumed if you omit the parameter  

1. TYPE  
   – Type of evaluation to perform  
   – Unit: LIT (literal keyword)  
   – Default: RU  
   – Valid values (case-sensitive):  
     • RR   → compute the Euclidean norm of the load vector R  
     • RU   → compute the scalar (dot) product of R with displacement vector U  
     • RUU  → scalar product of R with U² (useful for energy estimates)  
     • RV, RVV → scalar products involving velocities V (first and second power)  
     • RA, RAA → scalar products involving accelerations A (first and second power)  
     • RP, RPP → scalar products involving support or reaction forces P  
     • RI, RII → scalar products involving incremental displacements  
     • TEQV → build an equivalent linear temperature load from thermal results  
     • TEIG → TEQV plus eigen-stress contributions (requires eigenforms)  
     • WCOH → compute coherent spectral density over all 3 directions  
     • WCOU → coherent spectral density in the u-component  
     • WCOV → coherent spectral density in the v-component  
     • WCOW → coherent spectral density in the w-component  

2. NO  
   – The second load case number to pull data from (for example U, V, A, P, etc.)  
   – Unit: none (integer index)  
   – Default: none (this field is mandatory – marked “!”)  

3. NAME  
   – A user-defined CADINP variable name in which to store the EVAL result  
   – Unit: LIT8 (up to 8 alphanumeric characters, no leading “#”)  
   – Default: – (if omitted, the result is not saved to a CADINP variable)  

4. IND  
   – Index for an array-type output variable (when NAME refers to an array)  
   – Unit: none (integer)  
   – Default: 0  

5. LEIG  
   – Load-case number of the first eigenform to include (used only if TYPE is TEIG or you are extracting eigen-mode contributions)  
   – Unit: none (integer)  
   – Default: 0  

6. NEIG  
   – Number of consecutive eigenforms to include, starting at LEIG  
   – Unit: none (integer)  
   – Default: 0  

Additional Context  
• When you specify TYPE = TEIG or you set LEIG/NEIG > 0, EVAL will fetch modal stresses or other eigen-mode results from previously computed dynamic load cases.  
• If you give TYPE = RU and apply a constant unit area load in the preceding block, the output RU is effectively the area integral over the specified region (i.e. the influence area).  
• EVAL expressions can be chained: after the END record, you may reference the saved NAME or array entries in subsequent CADINP blocks to drive further loading or parameter studies.  
• In beam or shell analyses (“See also: BEAM”), EVAL is particularly useful to evaluate deflection influence lines, reaction influence areas and to assemble equivalent temperature loads or spectral densities for fatigue or random‐vibration studies.

See also: BEAM
 EVAL
 NEIG
 number of eigenforms
 0
 With command EVAL one may evaluate expressions with the actual load vector of defined or generated nodal forces with displacements of other load cases in the database and supply these values to CADINP for the next input block (after the END-record) as a variable. This is an evaluation of an influence area or an integral over a given displacement function and is very helpful for some special loading.
 If for example a constant area load with value 1.0 is specified, the result of RU will be the integral of that area within the loaded area. EVAL may be also helpful for a fast evaluation of different loads on a calculated influence line.

The figure is divided into four schematic plots arranged left to right, linked by an “=” sign and two “+” signs, illustrating how an arbitrary through-thickness temperature profile ΔT(z) is decomposed into three parts: a constant (uniform) term, a linear term about the neutral axis, and a remaining non-linear correction.

1. Original temperature profile ΔT(z) (far left)  
   • Vertical axis: the local sectional z–axis, pointing downward. A dashed horizontal line marks the neutral axis.  
   • The total section depth is labeled h. Along the z-axis at discrete points z₁, z₂, …, zᵢ, …, zₙ, the local temperature excursions ΔT(z₁), ΔT(z₂), …, ΔT(zₙ) are plotted.  
   • These discrete ΔT values are connected by straight segments, producing a generally non-uniform, “polygonal” shape shaded solid blue. At some depths the profile bulges outward (positive ΔT), at others it tapers inward (negative or smaller ΔT).  
   • The overall envelope of this shape represents the given (possibly nonlinear) temperature change through the beam depth.

2. Constant (uniform) component ΔT_cons = ΔT_eq (center left)  
   • A simple rectangle of height h (same as the section) and uniform width equal to ΔT_eq, the equivalent average temperature change.  
   • The entire rectangle is shaded solid blue, indicating a constant shift applied equally at all z.  
   • This term represents the “mean” or zeroth-order part of the original profile.

3. Linear component ΔT_line(z) = (ΔT_z,eq)·(z/h) (center right)  
   • A symmetric triangular distribution about the neutral axis: above the axis a blue triangle (positive gradient), below the axis a mirrored orange triangle (negative gradient).  
   • The topmost width at z = h/2 equals +ΔT_z,eq, tapering linearly to zero at the neutral axis; below it mirrors with –ΔT_z,eq at z = –h/2.  
   • This term captures the first-order (linear) variation of the original profile and corresponds to an equivalent linear temperature gradient in the local z-direction.

4. Non-linear remainder ΔT_nonl(z) (far right)  
   • The difference between the original ΔT(z) and the sum of its constant and linear parts.  
   • Shaded with both blue (positive remainder) and orange (negative remainder) regions, its outline is a more complex polygonal shape that integrates to zero over the section.  
   • This correction term carries all higher-order deviations from uniform and linearly varying temperature across the depth.

Underneath the row of diagrams, the caption reads:  
“Figure 3.12: Temperature distribution decomposition into constant ΔT_cons, linear ΔT_line(z) and ΔT_nonl(z).”

Taken together, the series visually enforces the identity:  
   ΔT(z) = ΔT_cons + ΔT_line(z) + ΔT_nonl(z),  
highlighting how any arbitrary sectional temperature field can be split into an average shift, a pure gradient, and a zero-mean residual.

The table you provided defines the four “slots” (fields) that make up a single CTRL record when specifying control options for automated load‐generation.  Below is a detailed, field‐by‐field breakdown of its structure and contents, together with how it fits into the larger context of CTRL-based load‐case generation:

1. Overall Structure  
   • Four user‐supplied fields (OPT, VAL, V2, V3, V4) are laid out in columns beneath a standard 4-column header:  
     – Item  
     – Description  
     – Unit  
     – Default  
   • Each row corresponds to one of the five control parameters that can be specified on a CTRL line.

2. Columns Explained  
   • Item  
     – The mnemonic name of the control parameter (OPT, VAL, V2, V3, or V4).  
   • Description  
     – A concise narrative of what that parameter represents in the context of CTRL.  
   • Unit  
     – Indicates the expected “unit” or data type of the field:  
       · LIT = a literal text string (no blanks)  
       · – = no unit (numeric or no input)  
       · –/LIT = either a number or a literal token  
   • Default  
     – The value assumed if the user omits that field on the CTRL record.

3. Row-by-Row Detail  
   1. OPT  
      • Description: “Name of control option”  
      • Unit      : LIT (i.e. a keyword such as COMP, COPY, WIND, etc.)  
      • Default   : FULL  
        – If you do not explicitly supply an OPT, the system assumes “FULL,” meaning fully active or all‐options mode.  

   2. VAL  
      • Description: “Value of control option”  
      • Unit      : –/LIT  
        – Can be a numeric value (e.g. 0, 1, 64, 128, etc.) or another literal (e.g. MOVE, AUTO) depending on OPT.  
      • Default   : !  
        – The exclamation mark denotes that no explicit value has been set—typically interpreted as an error or a prompt for the user to supply a value when it is required by the given OPT.

   3. V2  
      • Description: “additional value for option”  
      • Unit      : –  
      • Default   : –  
        – A dash indicates “not applicable” by default. Certain OPT/VAL combinations (for example, COPY with a reference code N, or CFDL with pmin) can make use of this second free‐format slot.

   4. V3  
      • Description: “additional value for option”  
      • Unit      : –  
      • Default   : –  
        – Like V2, this slot is available when an option requires more than one or two parameters (for example, WIND with SUML fak1 fak2 fak3 alf).

   5. V4  
      • Description: “additional value for option”  
      • Unit      : –  
      • Default   : –  
        – The fourth free slot, used in rare cases where up to four coefficients or thresholds must be specified (such as PX, PY, PZ factors plus rotation angle for wind).

4. How It Fits Into CTRL Syntax  
   – A typical CTRL line looks like:  
     CTRL, OPT, VAL, V2, V3, V4  
   – For example:  
     “CTRL, COPY, 1, 0, —, —”  
     would instruct the system to use the COPY option with VAL=1 (point/line loads only), V2=0 (preferred area-load reference LAR), and no further arguments.  
   – All omitted fields revert to their “Default” in the table; input lines can therefore be kept concise wherever only OPT and VAL are needed.

5. Relation to the Preceding Context  
   – The long block of text before the table enumerates specific valid OPT keywords (COMP, COPY, DIST, WIND, SUML, LAR, CFDL, TOLG, TOLS, etc.), each with its own interpretation of VAL, V2…V4.  
   – This table simply standardizes how those parameters are laid out, what data type each accepts, and which defaults apply when you don’t explicitly specify a field.

In summary, the table functions as a schema reference for every CTRL record.  It tells you exactly (a) what field names you can use, (b) what each field means, (c) the type of data expected, and (d) which values will be assumed if you leave that field blank. This ensures consistent parsing of control‐option lines across all versions of the load‐case generation engine.

CTRL
 With CTRL you may specify some control options for the analysis. A definition for CTRL is evaluated sequentially within the input. The control values have to be input therefore before the load cases.

 Default: 0

 N=3 GFA N=7 VGRP
 N=8 AUTO

 Hint: EDG, SLN and BEAM imply option 1

 128 Clipping of load trains at lane width

 Default: 0

 0 on single beam elements only
 1 distributed between beam elements (AREA BGRP) (explicit direction dx,dy,dz definable with V2,V3,V4)

PX, PY, PZ in CRI1, CRI2, CRI3 of the load case header (see LC) the three consec- utive values are factors for the PX, Py and PZ, while the fourth value is an angle to rotate the resultants PX, PY (useful for drag coefficients).
 SUML fak1 fak2 fak3 alf genrates factorised and for 2D also rotated integrals of the forces from WIND.
 Default: 0
 LAR Variation of LAR-support
 > 1.0 rigid support

 For example LAR 2.0 creates a stiffer elastic support for the load distribution areas. LAR 0.0 will deactivate all LAR Areas for AUTO/MOVE loadings.
 Default: 1.0

 With a CTRL CFDL NODE lc pmin nodal loads will be generated which are more precise for the real pressure distribution.
 The following options are intended only for internal purpose up to now.

The table you provided defines the parameters available to the ECHO command, which controls what and how much information is printed out when working with lanes, actions, loadings, wind parameters, combinations, take-downs and tagged records. It is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—covering three parameters: OPT, VAL and VAL1. Below is a detailed, field-by-field breakdown.

1. Overall structure  
   • Item: the name of the command parameter.  
   • Description: what the parameter does and, when applicable, the literal values it accepts.  
   • Unit: the data type or literal type (LIT for short strings, LIT32 for 32-character literals).  
   • Default: the value assumed when the parameter is omitted.

2. OPT (option selector)  
   • Unit: LIT (short literal)  
   • Default: FULL  
   • Purpose: Specifies which subset of tables or data the ECHO command will print. If omitted, all available options are enabled (FULL).  
   • Allowed literals and their effects:  
     – FULL: Enable all sub-tables (lane geometries, actions, loadings, wind parameters, combinations, take-downs, tagged loads).  
     – LANE: Print only the traffic‐lane geometry table.  
     – ACT: Print only the actions table.  
     – LOAD: Print only the loading table.  
     – WIND: Print only the wind‐parameter table.  
     – COPY: Print only the load‐combination overview (COPY record).  
     – LTD: Print only the load take-down overview (LTD record).  
     – TAG: Print only tables of loads that have been assigned a tag in the GUID record. (Used alone, it excludes other tables unless OPT is FULL.)

3. VAL (volume of printout)  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: FULL  
   • Purpose: Controls the verbosity or “depth” of the chosen tables.  
   • Allowed literals and their effects:  
     – NO: Suppress printout entirely.  
     – YES: Standard, concise printout of the selected tables.  
     – FULL: Enhanced printout with additional columns or explanatory notes.  
     – EXTR: Extended printout including every possible detail, supplementary tables, and generated loads.

4. VAL1 (tag filter)  
   • Unit: LIT32 (up to 32 characters)  
   • Default: – (none)  
   • Purpose: When OPT=TAG (or when other tables include tagged entries), VAL1 restricts the output to only those items whose GUID record matches the specified tag value. If left blank, all tagged items are printed.

How these parameters interact:  
• You always supply OPT to choose which tables you want.  
• You supply VAL to adjust how much information each chosen table contains.  
• You can further refine TAG‐based outputs via VAL1, limiting them to a particular tag value.  

Use cases:  
• To print just the lane geometries in a standard format:  
   ECHO OPT=LANE VAL=YES  
• To get fully detailed load combinations and take-down data:  
   ECHO OPT=COPY LTD VAL=FULL  
• To list every tagged loading for tag “A123” with maximum detail:  
   ECHO OPT=TAG VAL=EXTR VAL1=A123  

This three-parameter schema gives you precise, orthogonal control over which datasets appear and at what level of detail, ensuring that ECHO’s output can be tailored for both quick checks and exhaustive reports.

ECHO
 With ECHO you my control the volume of the printout.
 LANE Table of traffic lanes
 NO do not print table
 FULL list of lanes
 ACT Table of actions
 NO do not print table
 YES Only list of actions
 FULL list of actions and their load cases
 LOAD Table of loadings
 NO do not print tables
 YES Load case + general infos
 FULL YES + defined loading
 EXTR FULL + generated loads
 Overview of the load combinations with record COPY
 NO do not print table
 YES load combinations
 Overview of the load take down with record LTD
 NO do not print table
 YES print table
 TAG Overview of the loads for which a tag was assigned with the record GUID. Several ECHO TAG records can be used to obtain tables for several tags. Not enabled with the OPT FULL command.
 NO do not print table
 YES print table
 VAL1 Filter for specific tag value from record GUID. If left empty, all loads with a tag are printed.

Dynamic loading may be accounted for among others with
 static equivalent loading
 •
 response or power spectra
 via a transient analysis with time functions.
 •
 In all cases you need a loading, in many cases generated by some unit accelerations (ACCE).
 A spectrum defines the response for a single degree of freedom system depending on the eigenfrequency period and may be used for systems with multiple degrees of freedom with statistical algorithms.
 For a dynamic analysis one or more load cases will be combined via time functions to a com- plete loading, which is then subdivided into discrete time steps. The tasks to do are:
 • Definition of the spectra (RESP)
 • Definition of time functions (FUNC)
 • Creating of loads for the single time steps (STEP)
 The last task is much more effective for linear dynamics (DYNA) within the time stepping al- gorithm, but for more general cases, like nonlinear dynamics with non conservative loading it will become necessary to save all the loading within the database for ASE with the command
 STEP.
 Hint
 The options RESP, FUNC and STEP are only available with a special license for dynamic effects.

The image is a schematic “Pushover analysis workflow” divided into three main stages, each labeled in a horizontal gray banner at the top. At the very bottom is the caption “Figure 4.1: Pushover analysis workflow.”

1. Stage 1 – “AQUA + SOFIMSH”:  
   • On the far left is a simple single‐column cantilever drawn as a vertical line fixed at its base. At the top of this column is a small red block indicating a hinge or nonlinear link element (plastic hinge).  
   • Below that are two small performance‐curve sketches:  
     – A moment–curvature diagram with horizontal axis φ (rotation) and vertical axis M (moment). Two curves, one red and one green, trace an idealized bilinear or multilinear backbone.  
     – A P–M interaction diagram showing vertical axis P (axial load) and horizontal axis M (moment). Again, two envelope curves (red and green) form a semi‐elliptical shape.  
   • To the right of these sketches is a four‐story frame: each floor consists of two columns and beams. At every beam–column intersection a small red circle marks the location of the assigned plastic hinges (nonlinear links).

2. Stage 2 – “SOFILOAD”:  
   • Centered in this panel is the same four‐story frame drawn in outline only, without hinges.  
   • Next to it on the left is a vector diagram of lateral forces: a curved shape of blue arrows of varying length, all pointing to the right. This illustrates the chosen pushover load pattern (proportional to a selected mode shape).  
   • The combination implies that the push‐load diagram (blue arrows) is applied to the outlined frame on the right.

3. Stage 3 – “ASE”:  
   • On the far right the same four‐story frame is shown in its deformed configuration under increasing lateral load. Each story level and column is bent into a smooth curve, exaggerating the drift shape.  
   • At the top right corner of the roof node is a red dot with a horizontal red arrow labeled “u_cnod,” indicating the control‐node (roof) displacement.  
   • At the bottom is a bold red arrow pointing left, labeled “Vb,” denoting the base‐shear force.  

Overall, the figure conveys how the engineer defines nonlinear hinges and material properties (Stage 1), prescribes a lateral load distribution (Stage 2), and then performs an incremental static push (Stage 3) to generate a capacity curve relating base shear Vb to control‐node displacement u_cnod. The use of red highlights for hinges, control points, and force envelopes, together with blue for applied load vectors, makes each element’s role clear in the pushover procedure.

The illustration is a three‐part schematic of a typical pushover analysis result for a multi-degree-of-freedom (MDOF) building model, labeled “Figure 4.2: Pushover curve (Vb-u diagram).” From left to right, the graphic conveys (1) the assumed lateral load pattern, (2) the deformed shape of the frame under increasing lateral forces, and (3) the global pushover curve relating base shear (Vb) to control‐node displacement (u_cnod).

1. Left panel – Lateral Load Distribution  
• Depicts a 2D frame’s elevation with vertical columns and horizontal beams, rendered as thin black lines.  
• To the left of the frame, a light blue outline traces a curved, increasing‐magnitude arrow shape, representing the lateral force pattern pᵢ assigned in SOFiLOAD. The arrow lengths grow with height, suggesting a modal‐shape‐proportional load (often the fundamental eigenmode).  
• Horizontal arrowheads on each floor level indicate the direction and relative magnitude of inertial forces applied during the pushover.

2. Center panel – Deformed Structural Configuration  
• Shows the same frame geometry now bent into a right‐leaning shape, sketched by black lines distorted into an S-curve. This represents the nonlinear static response under the applied lateral loads.  
• At the roof level, a single red dot marks the “control node” where displacement u_cnod is monitored. A short horizontal red arrow immediately above it points rightward and is labeled “u_cnod.”  
• At the base, a long red arrow points leftward and is labeled “Vb,” indicating the base‐shear reaction resisting the lateral loads.  
• Gray gridlines in the background highlight the increasing drift and global deformation pattern, illustrating how plastic hinges might form at beam–column ends.

3. Right panel – Pushover Curve (Vb vs. u_cnod)  
• A simple Cartesian plot with a vertical axis labeled “Vb” (base shear) and a horizontal axis implicitly representing control‐node displacement u_cnod.  
• A single red curve originates near the origin, rises steeply in the initial elastic regime, then gradually flattens as nonlinear yielding progresses, reflecting reduced stiffness and increasing ductility.  
• No numerical tick marks are shown; the general shape conveys the envelope of peak base‐shear forces corresponding to incremental displacement steps.

Overall, the figure encapsulates the key outputs of a pushover (nonlinear static) analysis: the assumed load distribution, the deformed frame geometry with its control‐point drift, and the capacity envelope (pushover curve) from which an equivalent single‐degree‐of‐freedom (SDOF) capacity diagram can be derived. This visual summary supports performance‐based seismic design by linking structural capacity (Vb) to displacement demand (u_cnod).

The image is a three-panel schematic labeled “Figure 4.3: Conversion of the pushover curve to capacity diagram (A-D format).” It illustrates how a multi-degree-of-freedom (MDOF) pushover curve (base shear vs. control-node displacement) is transformed into an equivalent single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) capacity diagram in spectral acceleration–spectral displacement coordinates, and then idealized as an inelastic SDOF model.

Panel 1 (left) – MDOF Pushover Curve  
• Horizontal axis: “u_cnod” (control-node displacement).  
• Vertical axis: “V_b” (base shear).  
• A red “capacity” curve originates at the origin, rises steeply, then gradually flattens, reflecting increasing inelastic deformation and eventual strength degradation.  
• This plot represents the incremental static pushover analysis result for the full structure, showing how base shear V_b grows with increasing lateral displacement at the chosen control node (often the roof node).

→ Conversion Arrow  
A bold rightward arrow connects Panel 1 to Panel 2, indicating the mathematical mapping step.

Panel 2 (center) – SDOF Capacity Diagram in ADRS Format  
• Horizontal axis: “S_d = u_cnod / (Γ·φ_cnod)” (spectral displacement). Γ is the modal participation factor, φ_cnod is the mode shape component at the control node.  
• Vertical axis: “S_a = V_b / (Γ²·m)” (pseudo-spectral acceleration), where m is the generalized modal mass.  
• The same red curve from Panel 1 is re-plotted in these normalized axes, producing the capacity diagram in the so-called ADRS (acceleration–displacement response spectrum) format.  
• This diagram represents the maximum inelastic SDOF resisting force (m·S_a) as a function of displacement demand S_d, and will be compared against the seismic demand spectrum.

Panel 3 (right) – Equivalent Inelastic SDOF Model  
• A simple mechanical model depicts a single mass–spring–dashpot system on a moving base.  
• Top: a rigid circular mass block labeled “m*.” An arrow “D(t)” indicates the relative displacement of the mass.  
• Middle: a vertical spring element is labeled “f_s*(D),” signifying the nonlinear resisting force vs. displacement (the capacity curve). A dashpot alongside is labeled “c*,” representing equivalent damping.  
• Bottom: the base rests on a fixed support; an arrow beneath the support labeled “ü_g(t)” denotes the ground acceleration input.  
• This idealization embodies the transformed pushover capacity (f_s*(D)) and damping of the MDOF system as an equivalent inelastic SDOF oscillator subjected to earthquake excitation.

Overall, the figure visually summarizes the four key steps of pushover-to-capacity conversion: (1) extract V_b–u_cnod pushover curve; (2) normalize to S_a–S_d axes using modal factors; (3) interpret the red curve as the SDOF capacity diagram; and (4) represent the structure as an equivalent mass-spring-dashpot responding to ground motion. This forms the basis for the capacity spectrum method or inelastic SDOF demand estimation in performance-based seismic design.

The image is a small, rectangular excerpt from a printed technical document—almost certainly a textbook or manual on seismic design—showing one centered equation labeled “(4.19)” and the first line or two of a figure caption beneath it. Everything is set in a standard serif typeface on a white background, with a narrow gray border or shadow at the very top (from the preceding page).

Detailed description of the contents:

1. Equation block (centered on the page):  
   - The equation is displayed in two equivalent forms, joined by an equals sign:  
       “S_d = S_a / ω² = S_a · (T / 2π)²”  
   - Immediately to the right of this equation is the equation number in parentheses:  
       “(4.19)”

   In plain text, the equation reads:  
     Sₐₗₜ: spectral acceleration (Sa) divided by the square of the circular frequency (ω²) gives spectral displacement (S_d). Equivalently, replacing ω = 2π/T yields S_d = S_a · (T / 2π)².

2. Caption text (just below the equation):  
   - The first line of the caption begins mid-sentence (it appears that the very beginning of the caption is on the previous page). What is visible reads:  
       “re 4.4 shows the conversion of the elastic response spectrum from traditional to … format. In A-D format the lines radiating from the origin have constant periods.”

   From context we infer this is referring to “Figure 4.4,” which illustrates how one converts a conventional acceleration-vs. period response spectrum into the so-called A–D (acceleration–displacement) or ADRS format, in which constant-period lines radiate out from the origin of the Sp–Sd plot.

Visual/style notes:  
- The page fragment has clean margins and no illustrations in this snippet—only text.  
- Mathematical symbols (subscripts, superscripts, division slash, multiplication dot) are all set in the same serif font but slightly larger when part of the equation.

Overall, the image conveys a fundamental relationship between spectral acceleration, circular frequency, period, and spectral displacement, and it leads into a figure caption explaining how that relationship is used when converting response spectra into the ADRS (acceleration–displacement response spectrum) format.

The figure is a two‐part schematic illustrating how a conventional elastic response spectrum (plotted against structural period T) is converted into the A–D (ADRS) format, i.e. spectral acceleration versus spectral displacement.  

Left‐hand plot (“Elastic response spectrum”):  
 • Axes: horizontal axis is labeled “T” (the vibration period); vertical axis is labeled “a” (acceleration).  
 • Response shape:  
   – From T≈0 the curve quickly rises to a constant plateau level of acceleration.  
   – Over a mid‐period range the curve remains essentially flat (constant acceleration region).  
   – Beyond that plateau it smoothly decays in a downward‐sloping, curvilinear branch (representing the long‐period, displacement‐controlled regime), eventually leveling off slowly.  
 • A dashed vertical line is drawn at a particular “T = const” value, indicating selection of a single‐degree period.  

Between the two plots is a bold right‐pointing arrow, indicating the transformation process.  

Right‐hand plot (“A–D format / elastic demand diagram”):  
 • Axes: horizontal axis is now labeled “Sd = Sa·(T/2π)²” (spectral displacement); vertical axis is labeled “Sa” (spectral acceleration).  
 • Transformed response shape:  
   – At low Sd the curve has a steep rise up to a constant Sa plateau (mirroring the flat region in the period‐based plot).  
   – Beyond that plateau Sa decreases along a similar curvilinear decay as before.  
 • Superimposed is a dashed diagonal line labeled “T = const,” which corresponds exactly to the vertical line in the left plot, now appearing as a straight line of slope equal to the chosen period in the Sd–Sa coordinate system. This line helps locate the point on the capacity or demand curve corresponding to that particular period.  

Caption beneath reads:  
“Conversion of elastic response spectrum to A–D format (elastic demand diagram).”  

Overall, the graphic shows how an elastic response spectrum originally defined as Sa versus T can be mapped into the capacity spectrum format (Sa versus Sd) by using the relation Sd = Sa·(T/2π)². This form is the foundation for performance‐based seismic design procedures—enabling direct comparison of the inelastic capacity curve and the elastic demand spectrum to locate the performance (target) point.

The figure is a schematic “capacity‐demand” plot in ADRS (acceleration–displacement) space used to find the seismic performance point of an equivalent SDOF system.  It is drawn with spectral displacement (Sd) on the horizontal axis and spectral acceleration (Sa) on the vertical axis.  Axes are both single‐headed arrows: the vertical axis, labeled “Sa,” points upward; the horizontal axis, labeled “Sd,” points right.

Three primary curves appear:

 1. Elastic Demand Diagram (black thick line):  
    - It starts at the origin and rises steeply into a near‐vertical branch (representing the elastic demand at very short periods).  
    - It then bends into a nearly horizontal plateau (constant Sa over a range of Sd), indicating the peak (yield) strength of the highly‐damped elastic spectrum.  
    - Beyond the plateau it slopes gently downward to the right (decreasing spectral acceleration with increasing displacement, reflecting longer‐period branch of the elastic demand spectrum).  
    - Small black arrowheads along its length indicate the direction of increasing ground‐motion intensity.

 2. Capacity Diagram (red curve):  
    - Plotted in red, starting from the origin and curving upward and to the right.  
    - This monotonic curve represents the inelastic “capacity” of the structure (pseudo‐acceleration Sp versus pseudo‐displacement Sd), derived by transforming the pushover curve of base shear versus roof displacement.  
    - No arrowheads are shown on the red curve in the sketch, but it is clearly labeled “Capacity Diag” in red.

 3. Inelastic Demand Diagram (blue curve):  
    - Drawn in blue, roughly parallel to the descending branch of the elastic demand but offset downward to account for inelastic energy absorption (i.e. reduction factor for damping and ductility).  
    - Begins at the same horizontal Sd as the elastic plateau, then slopes downward to intersect the capacity curve.  
    - Arrowheads on this curve indicate direction of increasing displacement demand.

Performance Point:  
  - Marked by a filled black circle at the intersection of the red capacity curve and the blue inelastic demand curve.  
  - From that point, dashed lines are drawn vertically down to the Sd‐axis (denoted Sdp, the target spectral displacement) and horizontally to the Sa‐axis (denoted Sap, the reduced spectral acceleration demand).  
  - The horizontal dashed line from the performance point to the Sa‐axis is labeled “Sap,” and the vertical dashed line down to the Sd‐axis is labeled “Sdp.”

Additional annotations:  
  - The legend in black text upward from the plateau labels the top branch “El. Demand Diagram.”  
  - Alongside the blue curve near its origin is a small label “Demand Diag.”  
  - Near the red curve is the label “Capacity Diag” in red.

Overall, the diagram visually conveys how the elastic demand spectrum is first drawn, then reduced (to account for inelastic behavior) into the inelastic demand.  The point where that inelastic demand intersects the structure’s capacity curve defines the performance point (Sdp, Sap).  That intersection then governs the target roof displacement and base‐shear demand for performance‐based design and for back‐calculating local and global response in the original MDOF system.

1.  Left panel: the idealized SDOF “stick‐model.”  
    •  A rigid horizontal base (grey rectangle) supports a single vertical column (black line).  
    •  A circular mass (grey sphere) sits atop the column.

      showing that the generalized mass m* times the spectral displacement S_ap is equal to the mass‐participation factor Γ times m·S_ap.

2.  Center panel: the assumed lateral‐load or mode‐shape distribution.  
    •  A vertical stack of equally spaced horizontal lines (black) on a transparent background represents story levels.  
    •  Superimposed in blue is a triangular‐shaped distribution of lateral forces (arrows pointing right), increasing toward the top.  
    •  This vector signifies the pushover load pattern proportional to the fundamental eigenmode or user‐specified shape ϕ.

3.  Right panel: the original MDOF frame “pushed” to the performance displacement.  
    •  A multi‐story frame is drawn as vertical columns and horizontal beams (black).  
    •  The deformed shape under the scaled load is shown with curved line segments inside each story.  
    •  At each column‐end there are small markers indicating nonlinear hinges or plastic links.  
    •  A red filled circle at the top story denotes the control node. A red double‐headed arrow above it is labeled:  
       u_cnod,p = ϕ_cnod · Γ · S_dp

At the bottom of the figure is a caption reading: “Transformation of the seismic demand of the SDOF system to the seismic demand of the MDOF system.” The three‐panel flow, connected by a right‐pointing arrow between the SDOF model and the load pattern and then directly to the full frame, visually reinforces the four‐stage pushover‐analysis process: (1) define SDOF capacity (SDOF model), (2) select load shape, (3) perform pushover, (4) map back to MDOF to obtain control‐node displacement and base‐shear demands. The use of color—grey for the SDOF, blue for the load vector, black for the undeformed frame, and red for the performance‐point indicators—makes each conceptual step distinct, aiding intuitive understanding of the capacity‐spectrum method described in the accompanying text.

Seismic design of structures is a challenging and demanding task for a structural engineer and the tools at his disposal range from a relatively simple multimodal response spectrum analysis (RSA) which has been incorporated into almost all modern seismic design codes to a rather complex and expensive direct nonlinear response history analysis (RHA). Despite its accuracy and rigorousness in estimating the seismic response of structures, direct nonlinear response history analysis still remains impractical for a wide range of problems encountered in earthquake engineering practice. On the other hand, the multimodal response spectrum analysis with its use of the estimated average ductility capacity based mostly on the type of the structure often provides a too crude estimation of the nonlinear seismic demand. In recent years, a turn from RSA towards performance-based seismic design based on the nonlinear static procedure (NSP) or pushover analysis has been evident. This procedure recognizes the fact that the capacity of the structure and a seismic demand are two inseparable parts of the performance-based design.
 Pushover analysis is a procedure whose purpose is to evaluate the performance of the struc- ture under a specified earthquake hazard by comparing the available capacity and estimated
 structural demands.
 Pushover analysis procedure comprises of the following stages (Figure 4.1):
 1. AQUA + SOFIMSHA/SOFIMSHC: First stage is the definition of the material properties, or what is more common in the pushover analysis definition of non-linear link elements, or plastic hinges (see AQUA: SMAT). Next the system is defined, with appropriate non-linear links assigned to e.g. ends of the beams.
 2. SOFILOAD: Next stage is the definition of the pushover lateral load case pattern. Choice of the load case pattern is an important point in the pushover analysis since these lateral forces should be able to represent the inertial forces that the structure will be experiencing when subjected to earthquake ground motion as accurately as possible. The load pattern is usually assumed to be proportional to some assumed displacement shape vector ϕ. Most commonly, the chosen load pattern is proportional to the fundamental eigenmode of the structure. However, any other reasonable displacement shape ϕ can also be used (e.g. constant or linear distribution of forces, etc.). Instead of a load driven pushover analysis, a displacement driven analysis might also be required (Figures 4.11 and 4.12). For more details about the definition of the pushover load see ACCE: Pushover Load.

However, any other reasonable displacement shape ϕ can also be used (e.g. constant or linear distribution of forces, etc.). Instead of a load driven pushover analysis, a displacement driven analysis might also be required (Figures 4.11 and 4.12). For more details about the definition of the pushover load see ACCE: Pushover Load..
 3. ASE: Pushover analysis is performed by subjecting the structure to a monotonically in- creasing load pattern of lateral forces defined in stage 2. As aforementioned, these lateral forces represent the inertial forces that the structure will be experiencing when subjected to earthquake excitation. The goal of this incremental nonlinear static analysis is to obtain the capacity of the structure.
 4. SOFILOAD: Based on the previous stages the structural capacity can be analyzed to- gether with the seismic demand and the structural seismic performance can be deter- mined.
