The table is the complete parameter‐list you feed into the RESP record (the “Response Spectrum” definition) of a seismic‐loading module.  It tells the program what kind of spectrum you want (code, soil, ductility, damping, etc.), how it is shaped, what site factors apply, and gives each parameter’s units and default.  

1. TYPE  
   • Description: Literal code or standard name of the spectrum you wish to use (for example “EC8” for Eurocode-8, “DIN”, “UBC”, “JRA”, custom, etc.).  Follow the hyper‐links or code list provided at the top of the RESP page for allowed values.  
   • Unit: LIT (alphanumeric literal)  
   • Default: “*” (undefined; you must choose one)

2. CLAS  
   • Description: Soil class or profile category (A, B, C, D, E or custom) that controls the shape of the response spectrum.  See the comments in the introductory text for shear‐wave‐velocity criteria for soil classes A–E.  
   • Unit: – (or LIT when selecting by name)  
   • Default: “*” (undefined; the code’s default per TYPE will be used)

3. MOD  
   • Description: Either the modal damping ratio ξ (for an elastic spectrum) or the behaviour (ductility) reduction factor q (for design spectra per EC8, UBC, etc.).  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 0.05 (5 % damping) for elastic spectra; 1.5 (q = 1.5) for EC8 design spectra

4. SA  
   • Description: Spectral ordinate at zero period (the rigid‐body acceleration).  
   • Unit: – (unless the code requires real units, then it may be a fraction of g or expressed in m/sec²)  
   • Default: “*” (taken from code default or computed from AG, AH, AV)

5. SB  
   • Description: Constant spectral acceleration plateau for short periods.  
     – For elastic spectra: S·η·β₀  
     – For design spectra: S·β₀ / q  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: “*”

6. SMIN  
   • Description: Minimum spectral acceleration threshold (flattening at very long periods).  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: “*”

7. TB, TC, TD, TE  
   • Description: Corner‐period values that define the piecewise shape of the spectrum.  
     – TB: lower‐period limit (sec)  
     – TC: transition period from plateau to descending branch (sec)  
     – TD: second corner (period where slope changes again) (sec)  
     – TE: cut‐off period beyond which no further decay (sec)  
   • Unit: sec  
   • Default for each: “*”

8. K1, K2  
   • Description: Exponents that control the slope of the spectral decay between the corner periods:  
     – K1 applies for TC < T < TD  
     – K2 applies for T > TD  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: “*”

9. ZONE  
   • Description: Seismic zone or map region literal.  This ties into code‐specific maps (e.g. US zone factor, Italian zones, Chinese zones, etc.).  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: (NORM) – the code’s normative zone mapping

10. AG  
   • Description: Free‐field basic ground acceleration at the site (usually as a fraction of g or in m/sec²).  Controlled by the ACCE record for direction.  
   • Unit: [m/sec²] or fraction of g  
   • Default: (NORM) – derived from code’s seismicity map for the chosen ZONE

11. AH, AV  
   • Description: Directional amplification factors: AH is the horizontal factor, AV is the vertical factor.  In codes that separate vertical spectra (e.g. Eurocode), only one factor is explicitly required.  Setting AH = 0.0 will force AV to the code’s default vertical factor.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: AH = 1.0, AV = – (use code default)

12. TITL  
   • Description: Title or user‐supplied descriptor for the response spectrum (up to 32 characters).  
   • Unit: LIT32  
   • Default: “*” (no title)

Usage notes:  
• If you define MOD > 1.0, the program assumes you are asking for a design (reduced) spectrum and will apply behaviour‐factor reductions accordingly.  
• All parameters marked “*” pick up default values from the chosen TYPE/CLAS combination but may be overridden for specialized studies or code‐comparison work.  
• The final spectral shape is a multi‐segment curve: flat from 0 to TB, plateau to TC, a decay of exponent K1 to TD, then K2 beyond TD, with a cut‐off at TE.  Soil classes A–E alter the breakpoints and amplitudes, while AG, AH and AV scale the absolute level.

The image is a hand-drawn, two-dimensional plot labeled “Figure 4.7: Shape of the response spectrum.” It represents the spectral acceleration S as a function of the natural vibration period T of a single-degree-of-freedom system. Below is a detailed, segment-by-segment description:

1. Coordinate System  
   • Horizontal axis: labeled “T,” the structural period. Four special period values are marked along it: TB, TC, TD and TF, equally spaced or at prescribed intervals. No numeric scales are shown, only these characteristic periods.  
   • Vertical axis: labeled “S” (spectral acceleration). Two key acceleration levels are marked: SA at a lower elevation, and SB at the top of the plateau. Again, no numeric values, only symbolic labels.

2. Overall Curve Shape  
   • Segment 1 (0 < T < TB): The curve begins at T≈0 with an acceleration approximately equal to SA. From SA it rises roughly linearly up to SB at T = TB. This first branch models the increase of spectral acceleration from short-period (rigid) structures toward the plateau.  
   • Segment 2 (TB ≤ T ≤ TC): A horizontal plateau at S = SB extends from period TB to TC. This plateau represents the maximum elastic spectral acceleration for structures with vibration periods in this mid-range.  
   • Segment 3 (TC < T < TD): Past TC the curve begins a smooth, monotonic decrease following a power-law envelope. Next to the declining branch, the formula “S = Tc / T^k1” is hand-written, indicating that for periods T greater than TC, spectral acceleration scales inversely with some exponent k₁.  
   • Segment 4 (around T = TD): A small change in slope or a slight “kink” appears near T = TD. From the main power-law descent the curve bends more gently, leveling off briefly before continuing to fall. This illustrates a secondary corner often included in code spectra to capture transitional damping or soil effects.  
   • Segment 5 (TD < T < TF): After the kink, the curve continues to decline toward TF.  
   • Segment 6 (beyond TF): At T = TF the response spectrum drops off sharply, indicating a cutoff period beyond which the code prescribes zero or negligible spectral acceleration.

3. Contextual Notes (from accompanying text)  
   • This generic spectrum shape corresponds to common design codes (Eurocode, UBC/IBC, Chinese/Japanese standards, etc.).  
   • The initial branch is associated with short-period structures; the plateau (SB) with mid-period ranges; and the descending branch models long-period behavior, often modified by soil class, modal damping and a behavior factor q.  
   • Key parameters TB, TC, TD and TF are functions of soil class (A–E), base acceleration (ACC record), importance factor and damping ratio.  
   • The hand-written equation and corner periods are adjustable via parameters in the RESP definition; vertical and horizontal spectra may be separately scaled via AH and AV factors.

Overall, this figure encapsulates the classic four-branch, piecewise spectral acceleration curve used for elastic seismic analysis and code-based design.

 RESP
 Earthquake loading is defined in most design codes as a basic acceleration dependant on the importance of the building and the seismic zone. The response of the structure is then defined as a response spectra depending on soil classes and the magnitude. RESP allows not only the selection of the standard spectra, but also variants with explicit parameters. For special cases even an individual curve may be defined with succeeding FUNC records.

 record ACCE. Please note that the spectra may be defined in absolute accelerations or as a fraction of the gravity acceleration g or a base acceleration g. The excerpted table (“Code Table 2”) assigns seismic “Zone Factors” (denoted ag) to different Building Site Classes. These factors represent the reference peak ground acceleration for each soil‐foundation condition and appear in the seismic design code as a base quantity to be scaled by building importance and response‐modification factors.

1. Table Layout  
   – Columns: After a row‐header column, the table lists four site classes—II, III, IV and V—across the top.  
   – Rows: A single data row labeled “Zone Factor, ag” provides the numeric ag value for each site class.  

2. Site Class Definitions (from adjoining code text)  
   – Class I: very stiff rock (not shown here)  
   – Class II: medium stiffness soil  
   – Class III: soft soil  
   – Class IV and V: progressively weaker or more variable ground conditions  

3. Numeric Values  
   – For Site Class II (medium soil) the zone factor ag = 0.10 g  
   – For Site Class III (soft soil) the zone factor ag = 0.16 g  
   – For Site Class IV the zone factor ag = 0.24 g  
   – For Site Class V the zone factor ag = 0.36 g  

4. How ag Is Used in Seismic Design  
   – ag is the “design ground‐motion parameter” that defines the horizontal spectral acceleration for zero period (PGA level) on rock or firm ground.  
   – Designers multiply ag by an Importance Factor I (Table 6: 1.5 for critical structures, 1.0 for ordinary buildings) and divide by a Response Reduction Factor R (Table 7, values typically 1.5–5.0) to obtain the design acceleration ACCE.  
   – Damping effects are introduced via additional reduction multipliers (Table 3), and the minimum spectral acceleration SMIN is set to R·g so as to satisfy Ah > g/2 under the code’s minimum shear-force requirement.  

5. Interpretation and Trends  
   – As the ground condition softens (from Class II to V), the prescribed ag increases, reflecting the greater amplification of seismic shaking.  
   – The code thus ensures that structures on weaker soils are designed for higher baseline accelerations before any ductility‐ or importance‐based reductions.  

In sum, this concise table ties each site class to its fundamental seismic intensity coefficient (ag), which serves as the cornerstone for all subsequent spectral‐based force calculations in the referenced standard.

The table at hand summarizes, for seismic intensities 6, 7 (and its subclass 7a), 8 (and its subclass 8a) and 9, three key coefficients used in Chinese seismic‐design practice (both GB 50011‐2010 and the earlier GBJ 11‐89).  Broadly speaking, these coefficients are:

 1. a∕g   – the basic seismic coefficient expressed as a fraction of gravitational acceleration g.  
 2. αmax (frequently) – the spectrum’s maximum acceleration, for the “frequent” (frequently‐occurring) earthquake level.  
 3. αmax (rarely)   – the spectrum’s maximum acceleration, for the “rare” (rarely‐occurring) earthquake level.  

Layout and contents  
•  Column headings list the seismic intensities:  
   – 6  
   – 7, 7a   (the code uses “7a” to denote a subclass of intensity 7 with slightly higher effects)  
   – 8, 8a   (similarly, “8a” is the higher‐severity subclass of intensity 8)  
   – 9  

•  Each row then gives the numerical value of the three coefficients for that intensity.  

Detailed entry by entry  
1. a∕g (row 1)  
   •  Intensity 6:   0.05 g  
   •  Intensity 7:   0.10 g  
   •  Intensity 7a:  0.15 g  
   •  Intensity 8:   0.20 g  
   •  Intensity 8a:  0.30 g  
   •  Intensity 9:   0.40 g  

   These “a∕g” values serve as the baseline spectral coefficients (SB in the codes) in the older GBJ 11-89 procedure, and as the “basic accelerations” in GB 50011-2010 Table 3.2.2.  Designers multiply these by g to obtain the reference spectral acceleration used in response‐spectrum generation.  

2. αmax (frequently) (row 2)  
   •  Intensity 6:   0.04  
   •  Intensity 7:   0.08  
   •  Intensity 7a:  0.12  
   •  Intensity 8:   0.16  
   •  Intensity 8a:  0.24  
   •  Intensity 9:   0.32  

   These factors define the spectral‐peak acceleration (αm in GB 50011-2010, Table 5.1.4-1) for the “frequently” design earthquake.  Under the new code, they are scaled by a site‐dependent factor η2 and by the fundamental period adjustments K1, K2, etc., to form the full response spectrum.  

3. αmax (rarely) (row 3)  
   •  Intensity 6:   0.28  
   •  Intensity 7:   0.50  
   •  Intensity 7a:  0.72  
   •  Intensity 8:   0.90  
   •  Intensity 8a:  1.20  
   •  Intensity 9:   1.40  

   These larger values correspond to the “rarely” design earthquake and are obtained by increasing the characteristic period by 0.05 s (per GB 50011-2010 §5.1.4), then applying the same factor scheme.  

Contextual notes  
•  Frequent vs. Rarely earthquakes.  GB 50011-2010 differentiates three seismic‐intensity groups (1, 2, 3) and for each group two occurrence levels—GBF (frequently) and GBR (rarely).  The table above provides the αmax values for both levels under the old GBJ approach as well as for the updated standard.  
•  Spectrum shape parameters.  Under GBJ 11-89, the response spectrum uses SA = 0.45 SB, K1 = 0.9, TD = 3.0 s, with Tg/TC user‐selected from Table 4.1.4-2.  Under GB 50011-2010, additional modifiers (damping ξ, K1, K2 negative for linear decay, SMIN for end‐range spectrum value) and site‐class periods (Table 5.1.4-2) must be applied to these αmax values.  
•  Design usage.  Designers first choose the seismic intensity for the project location, select frequent or rare design level, take the appropriate a/g and αmax values, and then build the response spectrum by applying the code’s period‐dependent shape factors and site conditions. This table is thus the cornerstone for deriving S_a(T) for both frequently and rarely occurring design earthquakes.

The table under review is excerpted from the old Chinese seismic code GBJ 11-89 (Type GBJ), Table 4.1.4-2, and defines the characteristic spectral period (denoted Tg or TC) in seconds for various combinations of “Design Seismic Group” and “Building Site Class.”  In seismic‐response spectrum analysis, Tg (sometimes called the characteristic period) marks the point beyond which spectral acceleration begins its long‐period decay.  This particular table is to be used in conjunction with a reference spectrum whose maximum ordinate SB equals the peak ground acceleration αm (i.e. SB = αm), a shape factor SA = 0.45·SB, a near‐source plateau factor K1 = 0.9, and a long‐period decay parameter TD = 3.0 s.  

Structure  
• Rows (Design Seismic Group 1, 2 and 3):  
 – These groups correspond to classifications of seismic intensity regions from GB 50011-2010 or its predecessor GBJ 11-89.  Group 1 refers to the lightest seismic zones (intensity VI), Group 2 to moderate zones (intensity VII) and Group 3 to stronger zones (intensity VIII–IX).  
• Columns (Building Site Class I0, I1, II, III and IV):  
 – Site Class I0 and I1 are rock or very stiff soil sites; Classes II, III and IV represent progressively softer ground conditions.  

Cell Values  
Each cell contains a single numeric value expressed in seconds.  This is the characteristic period Tg for the given seismic group and site class.  Practically, one reads across the row for the design seismic group that applies to the project’s geographic location, then down the column for the soil category at the building site.  Example entries:  
• Group 1 (light seismicity)  
 – Class I0: Tg = 0.20 s  
 – Class II: Tg = 0.35 s  
 – Class IV: Tg = 0.65 s  
• Group 2 (moderate seismicity)  
 – Class I1: Tg = 0.30 s  
 – Class III: Tg = 0.55 s  
 – Class IV: Tg = 0.75 s  
• Group 3 (higher seismicity)  
 – Class I0: Tg = 0.30 s  
 – Class II: Tg = 0.45 s  
 – Class IV: Tg = 0.90 s  

Intended Use in Spectrum Definition  
1. Identify the design seismic group (1–3) for your project’s location, per the seismic zoning map or code appendix.  
2. Determine the site class (I0–IV) based on in-situ soil or rock properties.  
3. Read off Tg from the table.  
4. Construct the elastic response spectrum using:  
 • SB = αm (peak ground acceleration factor, from Table 4.1.4-1: 0.04 for intensity VI, 0.08 for VII, 0.16 for VIII, 0.32 for IX)  
 • SA = 0.45·SB  
 • K1 = 0.9  
 • TD = 3.0 s  
 • Characteristic period Tg (this table)  

By anchoring the spectral plateau and the long‐period decay hinge point to soil conditions and seismic intensity, this table ensures that the elastic design spectrum adequately reflects both regional seismic hazard and local site amplification effects.

The table under discussion (from GBJ 11-89, Table 4.1.4-2) defines the reference characteristic period (Tg or Tc) to be used in the seismic design response spectrum, as a function of (a) the proximity of the seismic source and (b) the site‐class of the building foundation.  Below is a structured, detailed description suitable for feeding into a RAG/vector retrieval system.

1. Table title and context  
   - Title (implicit): “Characteristic Period (Tg = Tc) by Earthquake Proximity and Building Site Class”  
   - Source standard: GBJ 11-89 (often referred to as TYPE GBJ)  
   - Use: The structural designer or analyst selects Tg (sometimes noted Tc) from this table when constructing the elastic response spectrum for seismic load calculations.  

2. Row dimension – Proximity of the earthquake  
   • Near: Earthquakes occurring relatively close to the site (epicenters typically within ~50 km)  
   • Far: Earthquakes occurring at greater distances (epicenters beyond ~50 km)  

3. Column dimension – Building Site Class  
   • Class I: Extremely stiff rock or rock-like formations  
   • Class II: Stiff soil or very dense gravel and sand over bedrock  
   • Class III: Medium-stiff soil, less dense sands or gravels, weathered rock  
   • Class IV: Soft soil deposits, possibly with high plasticity clays, silts, or loose sands  

4. Table entries – Characteristic period Tg (seconds)  
   Each cell gives the period, in seconds, to be used as the corner period in the piecewise-linear response spectrum shape described elsewhere in GBJ 11-89 (see picture 4.1.4).  
   – Near, Site Class I: 0.20 s  
   – Near, Site Class II: 0.30 s  
   – Near, Site Class III: 0.40 s  
   – Near, Site Class IV: 0.65 s  
   – Far, Site Class I: 0.25 s  
   – Far, Site Class II: 0.40 s  
   – Far, Site Class III: 0.55 s  
   – Far, Site Class IV: 0.85 s  

5. How it ties into the overall seismic spectrum formulation  
   - The designer first determines the seismic intensity (6–9) and selects the corresponding spectral intensity factor αm (0.04 g to 0.32 g per Table 4.1.4-1).  
   - The response spectrum is then anchored to its peak spectral ordinate SB = αm.  
   - The spectrum shape uses SA = 0.45·SB up to Tg (selected from the table above), a plateau or other slopes defined in picture 4.1.4, and then a linear decay beyond TD = 3.0 s with K1 = 0.9.  
   - By choosing the correct Tg from this table, the designer accounts for local site amplification effects and the difference between near‐field and far‐field earthquake loading.  

6. Cross‐references and notes  
   - In GB 50011-2010 (the later Chinese code), a similar concept appears in Table 5.1.4-2 for Site Classes I0–IV, but with refined values and an added increment of 0.05 s for “rare” earthquake actions.  
   - Unlike GBJ 11-89 (TYPE GBJ), the modern code defines additional coefficients K2 (negative slope parameter), damping ξ, and spectral shape segments per picture 5.1.5.

The table shown is the definition of all fields that can appear in a “FUNC” record when you assign a time‐varying load in a dynamic response analysis.  In practice you will either define a single polygonal time‐history (pairs of (T,F) values which are linearly interpolated and are zero outside the first and last T), or you will superimpose/add multiple amplitude or harmonic components by using “FUNC ADD” or “FUNC MULT.”  If you supply a phase (T1) or both TMIN and TMAX, the loader will treat your data as one period of a periodic function with period T; outside the interval [TMIN, TMAX] the function is zero.  Below is a narrative description of each column in the table:

1.  Item “T”  
    – Description: “Time value” for a discrete polygonal point, or “type/mode number” if you are selecting a predefined modal shape  
    – Unit: seconds (sec)  
    – Default: mandatory (no default allowed, indicated by “!”)

2.  Item “F”  
    – Description: amplitude at the corresponding time T (first harmonic F1 if you’re doing a Fourier series)  
    – Unit: none (dimensionless)  
    – Default: none (you must supply it)

3.  Item “T1”  
    – Description: phase shift (in seconds) for a periodic function  
    – Unit: sec  
    – Default: blank (if omitted, assumed zero phase)

4.  Item “TMIN” / “TMAX”  
    – Description: windowing limits for a periodic record.  Between TMIN and TMAX you repeat the points every T seconds; outside that window, values are zero.  
    – Unit: sec  
    – Default: blank (infinite window)

5.  Item “S”  
    – Description: selects a special “built-in” function type or pedestrian impact factor.  You still supply F as a scale factor.  
    – Unit: none or LIT (dimensionless)  
    – Default: 0.0  
    – Interpretation of S:  
      • S = 0.0 → the points F, F2, F3, F4 define a Fourier series up to the 4th harmonic, with phases T1, T2, T3, T4.  
      • S < 0.0 → use the Bachmann pedestrian acceleration spectrum  
      • S > 0.0 → use the Seiler/Hüttner pedestrian spectrum  
      • S = “WALK” → equivalent to +0.4: sinusoid at 2.0 Hz (walking)  
      • S = “RUN” → +1.6: 2.4 Hz (running)  
      • S = “JUMP” → +3.0: 2.0 Hz (jumping)  
      • S = “FRUN” → treat the RUN case as a full Fourier series  
      • S = “FJUMP” → treat the JUMP case as a full Fourier series  
      • S = “COMP” → use a compound intensity function  
      • S = “EXPO” → use an exponential intensity function  

6.  Items “F2”, “T2”, “F3”, “T3”, “F4”, “T4”  
    – Description: amplitudes (F2–F4) and phases (T2–T4) of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th harmonics when S = 0 (Fourier series case)  
    – Units: F’s are dimensionless; T’s are sec  
    – Default: “*” (only valid if you have declared a Fourier series; otherwise blank)

7.  Item “TBLC”  
    – Description: time at which a baseline correction is applied (shifts the zero‐level of your time‐history)

The provided image is a schematic sketch of an “EXPO” impulse‐type load function I(t) plotted in a simple Cartesian coordinate system. No numerical scales or gridlines are shown—only two orthogonal axes, a bold curve and a single annotation marking the end of the event. Below is a breakdown of its visual elements:

1. Coordinate Axes  
   • A horizontal line representing time t runs from left to right; its right‐hand end carries a simple arrowhead.  
   • A vertical line representing the response magnitude I(t) or load amplitude rises from the same origin and carries an upward arrowhead.  
   • Neither axis carries tick‐marks or numeric labels except for a single endpoint label on the time axis.

2. Impulse Curve  
   • A thick, black stroke traces a smooth, single‐humped profile.  
   • Starting at the origin (t = 0, I = 0), the curve rises steeply but with a slight convex curvature, indicating a rapid lead‐in phase.  
   • It reaches a rounded maximum—this peak occurs at a time well before the end of the event, illustrating that the initial rise is faster than the subsequent decay.  
   • After the peak, the curve falls gradually and asymptotically toward the time axis, featuring a long “tail” that approaches zero more slowly than it rose.

3. End‐of‐Load Marker  
   • At the far right of the decay tail, the curve intersects a small vertical tick perpendicular to the time axis.  
   • Adjacent to this tick is the label “TMA” (interpreted as TMAX, the total duration). This visually denotes the moment when the impulse ends and I(t) returns to zero.

4. Intended Interpretation  
   • This shape corresponds to the analytic form  
       I(t) = F · [e^(–F₂·t) − e^(–F₃·t)]  
     (often cited in structural vibration literature as the “exponential” impulse).  
   • The rapid initial ascent is governed by the larger exponent coefficient F₃ (lead‐in), while the slower decay tail reflects the smaller exponent F₂ (lead‐out).  
   • The area under the curve (integral of I(t)) and the location of the peak depend on the ratio F₂/F₃ and the overall amplitude factor F.

5. Contextual Notes  
   • In pedestrian‐loading design codes, such transient impulses are sometimes called up when the impact factor s exceeds certain values (e.g., |s| > 1.0), triggering an EXPO‐type load definition.  
   • The simple form shown here omits intermediate plateau phases (present in multi‐phase definitions like COMP) but captures the essential two‐exponential behavior.

The table is a parameter‐definition schema for the FIMP command, which imports transient results from the database (HIST) as user‐defined functions. It is most often used in response spectrum evaluations of local components (see SIMR) but can also be applied in other situations. The table is organized in three columns—Item, Description, Unit, Default—and is divided into two logical sections: the core result‐selection parameters (TYPE, NO, LC, FACT) and auxiliary metadata (TEFF, TBLC, TITL).

1. Core Result‐Selection Parameters  
   • TYPE (Unit: LIT; Default: “!”)  
     – Specifies the literal code for the kind of results to import. Common codes include:  
       * U‐X, U‐Y, …, U‐RZ for nodal displacements in X, Y, rotational Z, etc.  
       * V‐X, V‐Y, …, V‐RZ for nodal velocities.  
       * A‐X, A‐Y, …, A‐RZ for nodal accelerations.  
       * U, V, W for fluid velocities.  
     – Beyond these, any literal defined in a HIST definition (e.g., most user-defined quantities) may be used.  
     – The default “!” acts as a placeholder, forcing the user to supply a valid literal.  
   • NO (Unit: LIT/—; Default: 1)  
     – Identifies the node or element number whose results are to be imported.  
     – May also be set to the literal “FUNC” to indicate that the command should sample from an existing load function (see STEP).  
     – When used with “FUNC,” FIMP essentially reuses or re-scales a previously defined forcing function rather than pulling raw nodal data.  
   • LC (Unit: —; Default: 1)  
     – The load case index for which the results are evaluated.  
     – Refers back to a load‐case definition in the database (e.g., static or dynamic load sets).  
   • FACT (Unit: [–]; Default: 1.0)  
     – A scalar multiplier applied to the imported time history or function.  
     – Useful for adjusting amplitude—for instance, scaling acceleration‐time histories up or down without redefining the original load case.

2. Auxiliary Metadata  
   • TEFF (Unit: [sec]; Default: –)  
     – The averaging (or effective) time window over which the transient data may be smoothed or averaged.  
     – When left blank, the raw data are used directly.  
   • TBLC (Unit: [sec]; Default: –)  
     – Time offset applied for baseline correction of the imported history.  
     – Enables shifting the time axis or removing initial bias before further processing.  
   • TITL (Unit: Lit32; Default: –)  
     – A text title (up to 32 characters) for the imported function.  
     – Useful for reporting, logging, or distinguishing multiple FIMP calls within the same analysis run.

How It Fits in RAG and the Broader Workflow  
- FIMP taps into HIST (the transient results database), making it a key building block for dynamic response analyses such as those handled by the RESP (response spectrum) and ACCE (acceleration time‐history) modules.  
- In workflows where you preprocess or correct time histories (via TEFF and TBLC) and then feed them into spectrum evaluators (RESP), FIMP provides the necessary bridge.  
- For cumulative analysis steps (STEP), one might first generate a derived load function via FIMP and then reference it by setting NO=”FUNC” in subsequent calls.  

By clearly defining TYPE, NO, LC, and FACT, along with optional time‐window and labeling controls, this table enables robust, reproducible function importation from transient result sets into virtually any post‐processing or advanced dynamic analysis routine.

See also: RESP, ACCE, STEP
 FIMP
 FIMP allows the definition of a function by an import of a transient result in the database (HIST). This is especially usefull for response spectra evaluation for local components (see SIMR), but may be usefull for other tasks as well.

Below is a structured, field-by-field description of the ACCE input table, suitable for ingestion into a RAG-style vector store.  It summarizes each parameter’s role, its units (where applicable), default value and any special behavior called out in the surrounding ACCE documentation.

1.  TYPE  
    – Description: Selects the form of acceleration or load to apply.  Common literals include:  
      •  NODA (translational & rotational accelerations → nodal accelerations in DYNA)  
      •  NODE (pure nodal loads = mass × acceleration)  
      •  NODC (adds nodal moments)  
      •  ELEM (element loads on beams, cables, trusses)  
      •  DIRN, DIRC, DIRE (direction only; references last RESP definitions)  
      •  DISP (prescribed nodal displacements for pushover analysis)  
    – Unit: LIT (literal)  
    – Default: NODA

2.  NO  
    – Description: Node number at which base acceleration or rotation is referenced.  NO = 0 uses the global origin (base).  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: ‑

3.  AX, AY, AZ  
    – Description: Global translational accelerations along X, Y, Z axes.  For “direction only” types (NODA/DIRN/DIRC), these define direction multipliers that will be scaled by the last RESP.  
    – Unit: m/sec²  
    – Default: 0.0

4.  AXX, AYY, AZZ  
    – Description: Angular accelerations about global X, Y, Z axes.  
    – Unit: rad/sec²  
    – Default: 0.0

5.  WXX, WYY, WZZ  
    – Description: Constant angular velocities about global X, Y, Z axes (for uniform rotation + centrifugal effects).  
    – Unit: rad/sec  
    – Default: 0.0

6.  REF  
    – Description: Reference node for defining rotation center (for rotational acceleration components).  “MBOD” can be used to refer to local beam‐axis rotations.  
    – Unit: – / LIT  
    – Default: *

7.  REFX, REFY, REFZ  
    – Description: Cartesian offsets [m] of the actual rotation center from the reference node.  Used when eccentricity is required (torsional moment generated if offset ≠ 0).  
    – Unit: m  
    – Default: 0.0

8.  GRP  
    – Description: Predefined group selection.  Limits application to the nodes or elements in that group.  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: ‑

9.  XMIN, YMIN, ZMIN, XMAX, YMAX, ZMAX  
    – Description: Defines an axis-aligned box in Cartesian space.  Only nodes within this box receive loads (only valid for TYPE=NODE or DIRN).  
    – Unit: m  
    – Default: ‑

10.  ARED  
    – Description: Depth‐dependent reduction factor (e.g. for underground).  See ARED/AH/GH rule per Indian code.  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: ‑

11.  AH  
    – Description: Z‐coordinate [m] at which the acceleration is reduced by factor ARED.  
    – Unit: m  
    – Default: 30.0

12.  GH  
    – Description: Z‐coordinate [m] of the ground surface.  At GH, no reduction (factor = 1.0).  
    – Unit: m  
    – Default: 0.0

13.  LINF  
    – Description: Load‐influence line (or vector) number.  Allows distinguishing multiple acceleration patterns or applying influence functions (e.g. soil‐structure interaction, mode shapes, pushover shape vectors).  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: ‑

Hints & Contextual Notes (from ACCE documentation):
- If only direction is needed and base accelerations were already defined via RESP, you may use DIR, DIRN, DIRC or DIRE; AX–AZ act as multipliers of the last RESP horizontal/vertical components.
- Uniform rotation (WXX/WYY/WZZ) and angular acceleration (AXX/AYY/AZZ) are combined with translational parts to compute total nodal/element accelerations.
- Eccentric reference offsets (REFX/Y/Z) automatically generate torsional moments about the mass center.
- Group/box selection lets you exclude soil nodes (for SSI analyses) or isolate specific stories (per EC8).
- LINF facilitates advanced patterns: base‐shear distribution from DYNA (ACCE BASE), pushover mode shapes (force or displacement based), or custom influence vectors.
- For pushover loads, negative LINF values point to stored displacement vectors (e.g. mode shapes) used for load pattern definition.

Therefore pushover load is defined and the necessary additional information are saved in database by specifying negative value for LINF.
 Depending on the type of the pushover analysis - force or displacement controlled - two possi- bilities for the definition of the pushover load exist:
 1. Forces - loads as external forces p. These loads are specified by selecting NODE as TYPE in the ACCE-command (Figure 4.11c).
 2. Displacements - loads as prescribed displacements of the nodes . These loads are specified by selecting DISP as TYPE in the ACCE-command (Figure 4.11d).
 The pushover static load should be able to represent the inertia forces that the structure will be experiencing when subjected to earthquake ground motion as accurately as possible. The load pattern is usually assumed to be proportional to some assumed displacement shape vector ϕ. Most commonly, the chosen load pattern is proportional to the fundamental eigenmode of the structure. However, any other reasonable displacement shape ϕ can also be used (Figure 4.12).
 For the displacement based pushover analysis (TYPE DISP), the load as the prescribed dis- placements is directly taken from the specified displacement shape vector ϕ (Figure 4.11d), that is
 = ϕ .
 (4.43)
 If the loads are in form of forces (TYPE NODE; force based pushover analysis), the displace- ment shape vector is additionally weighted by the mass matrix M in order to simulate the inertia forces (Figure 4.11c), i.e., the load pattern p is
 p=M-@¢.
 (4.44)

If the loads are in form of forces (TYPE NODE; force based pushover analysis), the displace- ment shape vector is additionally weighted by the mass matrix M in order to simulate the inertia forces (Figure 4.11c), i.e., the load pattern p is. p=M-@¢.. (4.44).
 Hint
 The mass matrix M is based on the masses which are currently active, i.e. which are specified before the current SOFiLOAD block. It is therefore recommended to run one ASE/DYNA eigenvalue analysis with all the necessary additional masses prior to the def- inition of the pushover loads, in order to ensure that the correct mass matrix is taken into consideration.
 Displacement shape vector ϕ is defined by specifying negative number of the load case con- taining displacements of the nodes for the LINF. For example, if the displacement shape vector corresponds to some eigenvector which is previously computed and stored in e.g. LC 9001, the input would read (Figure 4.12a)
 LC NO 101 TITL 'Eigenvector' ACCE TYPE NODE/DISP . . . LINF -9001
 Constant and linear displacement shape vectors can be defined by specifying the negative number of the running load case for LINF, e.g. (Figures 4.12b and 4.12c)
 LC NO 102 TITL 'Constant'
 ACCE TYPE NODE/DISP . . . LINF -102
 LC NO 103 TITL 'Linear'
 ACCE TYPE NODE/DISP . . . LINF -103 GH ... AH ... ARED
 As aforementioned any other displacement shape vector ϕ existing in the database can be used. For example, if an arbitrary static load case LC 501 which has been computed and for which the displacements of nodes are available in database is specified in LINF, then these dis- placements will be taken as the displacement shape vector ϕ for the definition of the pushover load pattern, e.g. (Figure 4.12d)
 LC NO 104 TITL 'Arbitrary' ACCE TYPE NODE/DISP . . . LINF -501

Below is a comprehensive description of the STEP input table, which governs how time‐dependent loads are generated for nonlinear dynamic analyses (ASE and DYNA) in a RAG-based workflow. Whenever you invoke a STEP block, you specify a combination of load cases and time functions; the table entries define how those functions are discretized in time.

Table Structure  
• Item: The keyword or parameter name you enter in the STEP line.  
• Description: A brief explanation of what that parameter controls.  
• Unit: Physical units or data type. A dash (“–”) means the parameter is dimensionless or user‐defined.  
• Default: Value assumed if you omit the parameter.

1. N  
   • Description: Number of time steps or divisor. If N > 0, STEP creates N successive intervals, each of length DT. If N < 0, STEP treats DT as the total time interval and divides it into |N| equal sub-steps.  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless integer)  
   • Default: 1  
   • Notes:  
     – Positive N yields fixed‐size increments. Total time = N×DT.  
     – Negative N automatically sets time step = (|DT|/|N|); total time still DT.  
     – N = 0 is not allowed; you must specify a nonzero integer.  

2. DT  
   • Description: Time step size (for N > 0) or total analysis duration (when N < 0).  
   • Unit: sec  
   • Default: Not applicable: you must supply a value (!)  
   • Notes:  
     – When N > 0: each increment is exactly DT seconds long.  
     – When N < 0: DT is interpreted as the overall time span, subdivided by |N| steps.  
     – Use physically meaningful time scales consistent with your RESP or FUNC definitions.  

3. LCST  
   • Description: Index of the first load case in the explicit‐history sequence. Subsequent load cases are numbered consecutively as STEP generates them.  
   • Unit: – (integer)  
   • Default: 1000  
   • Notes:  
     – All generated dynamic load‐case IDs run from LCST to LCST + (number of steps) – 1.  
     – Make sure this range does not overlap existing static or frequency cases.  
     – These cases are written to the database for ASE (single‐step analysis) or DYNA (time‐history analysis).  

4. TITL  
   • Description: User‐supplied title string for the history sequence. This appears in output listings and logs.  
   • Unit: Lit32 (32‐character literal)  
   • Default: “–” (blank)  
   • Notes:  
     – Useful for identifying sets of time histories when multiple STEP blocks are used.  
     – Avoid special characters that might conflict with downstream parsing.

Contextual Usage  
– In a typical nonlinear dynamic analysis, you first define static load cases (RESP) or time functions (FUNC) that describe how loads vary.  
– A STEP block “samples” those definitions over time, generating a sequence of transient load cases.  
– Each load case combines the base loads scaled by the corresponding function value at that time step.  
– The resulting cases are stored in the analysis database and executed in a loop (for ASE) or integrated continuously (for DYNA).  
– By judiciously choosing N and DT, you control temporal resolution and total simulation time, balancing accuracy against computational cost.

See Also  
– RESP: Definitions of static or transient loads.  
– FUNC: Time‐history functions (ramps, sine‐series, user‐defined tables).  
– ACCE: Post‐processing of accelerations and responses after dynamic runs.

See also: RESP, FUNC, ACCE
 STEP
 For a general dynamic analysis all selected load cases and time functions within an input block may be combined to generate the transient loading for all time steps to be used then in a load case loop for ASE and DYNA. Possibilities are:
 • A time interval of N time steps of size DT with a total length of N·DT
 • A total time interval of DT divided into time steps N·DT. This case is selected with a value of N < 0.
 All the load cases for a nonlinear dynamic analysis are created and saved to the database.

The table defines the key input parameters required by the SIMQKE‐derived module “SIMQ” for generating artificial earthquake accelerograms that match a prescribed target response spectrum. Each row corresponds to one keyword or card, with its meaning, unit of measure (where applicable) and a default value used when the keyword is omitted. Below is a detailed description of each parameter, grouped by function:

1. Target Spectrum Selection  
   • LSPE (Case number of target spectrum):  
     – Description: Index or identifier of the pre‐defined response spectrum (“RESP” data block) that the generated accelerogram must match.  
     – Unit: none (integer).  
     – Default: “!” (mandatory; user must supply a valid spectrum case number).  
   • LINT (Case number of intensity function):  
     – Description: Index of the intensity (energy distribution) function used to weight different frequencies during the time‐domain synthesis.  
     – Unit: none (integer).  
     – Default: 0 (zero selects a neutral or flat intensity function if available).

2. Time and Frequency Discretization  
   • DT (Time step of resulting function):  
     – Description: Increment in seconds between successive samples of the synthetic accelerogram.  
     – Unit: sec  
     – Default: 0.01 s.  
   • TMIN (Smallest period):  
     – Description: Lower bound of oscillator period (inverse frequency) for which the target response spectrum is defined.  
     – Unit: sec  
     – Default: 0.01 s.  
   • TMAX (Largest period):  
     – Description: Upper bound of oscillator period for the target spectrum.  
     – Unit: sec  
     – Default: 10.0 s.  
   • NFRE (Number of frequencies):  
     – Description: Number of discrete frequency samples between 1/TMAX and 1/TMIN used to compute the power spectrum and synthesize the accelerogram.  
     – Unit: none (integer)  
     – Default: 100.

3. Iteration and Convergence  
   • ITER (Number of iterations):  
     – Description: Maximum number of time‐domain/inverse‐spectral iterations to perform in order to drive the synthetic accelerogram’s response spectrum toward the target within a prescribed tolerance.  
     – Unit: none (integer)  
     – Default: 1 (one iteration; increase for tighter spectral matching).

4. Scaling and Damping  
   • AG (Base acceleration):  
     – Description: Global scale factor applied to the generated accelerogram. When positive, the accelerogram is normalized so that its spectral ordinates match the target at this base acceleration.  
     – Unit: m/sec²  
     – Default: * (an asterisk indicates no default; user choice or inherited from older code).  
     – Special cases:  
         • AG < 0 switches off scaling altogether, leaving the raw synthesized acceleration magnitudes intact.  
         • AG = 0 causes the program to output the power spectrum function rather than time‐history accelerations.  
   • D (Target damping for spectra):  
     – Description: Damping ratio (fraction of critical) assumed in the single‐degree‐of‐freedom response calculations used to define the target spectrum.  
     – Unit: none  
     – Default: 0.05 (5% damping).

5. Output Identification  
   • TITL (Title of history):  
     – Description: A 32‐character text label (Lit32) assigned to the accelerogram output for identification in plotting or archiving.  
     – Unit: none (string)  
     – Default: “–” (blank or user‐defined).

Hints and Cross–References  
 • After running SIMQ with these parameters, it is strongly recommended to validate the generated time history by invoking the REVA command (“see ACCE, REVA”) to compute a response spectrum from the synthetic trace and compare it against the original LSPE spectrum.  
 • For alternative spectral definitions or enhanced spectral‐matching functions, consult RESP (to define custom target spectra), FUNC (to load or define custom intensity functions), and ACCE (to handle raw acceleration spectra in lieu of time histories).

See also: RESP, FUNC, ACCE, REVA
 SIMQ
 The generation of artificial accelerograms for earthquakes follows the procedures published by the NISEE in 1976 for the software SIMQKE. From a given target spectra, defined as:
 - Powerspectra in [m?/sec?]
 • Velocity spectra in [m/sec]
 - Acceleration spectra in [ m/sec? |
 random phase values (based on the load case number) will be generated and with the help of an intensity function will yield an accelerogram, adjusted with a target damping D to the response spectra with an iterative process. The base acceleration AG has to be selected to match the spectra. The default is 9.81 [m/sec?]. However the most common case is to switch off the scaling of the accelerogram altogether. This can be achieved by specifying the negative value for AG (e.g. SIMQ ... AG -1) (see sofiload.dat/english/simg.dat). If the value AG is specified as 0.0, the function of the power spectra is created instead of the accelerations.
 Hint
 It is strongly recommended, as a way of checking the validity of the generated accelel- ogram, to always calculate a response spectrum from a generated accelerogram and compare it with a target spectrum (LSPE). This can be achieved with the help of the command REVA (see sofiload.dat/english/simq.dat).

The input table defines the parameters of a REVA/RESP response-spectrum analysis. It is organized by Item (the keyword), Description (semantic meaning and allowed values), Unit (physical units or literal), and Default (applied if the parameter is omitted). Below is a detailed breakdown:

1. TYPT  
   – Description: Determines how the results are plotted or processed.  
     • TIME: graph versus time  
     • FREQ: graph versus frequency  
     • LOGT: logarithmic time  
     • LOGF: logarithmic frequency  
     • DFT: discrete Fourier transform  
     • LDFT: DFT with a logarithmic frequency axis  
     • PDS: logarithmic power-spectral density  
     • PDSN: normalized logarithmic power-spectral density  
   – Unit: literal (LIT)  
   – Default: TIME  

2. TYPE  
   – Description: Selects which response quantity to compute or plot.  
     • P: force  
     • S: displacement  
     • V: velocity  
     • A: relative acceleration  
     • AA: absolute acceleration (ground + oscillator)  
     • AS: A as a function of S  
     • AAS: AA as a function of S  
     – You may also specify positive‐only (e.g. P+, S+, V+, A+, AA+) or negative‐only (P–, S–, etc.) components.  
   – Unit: literal  
   – Default: none (“–” meaning use the original function if TYPE is omitted)

3. LFUN  
   – Description: Identifies which load function to use for the response calculation. Syntax: loadcase.sequence_number (e.g. 3.2 for the second function in load case 3).  
   – Unit: none  
   – Default: 1

4. TMIN, TMAX, TDIF  
   – TMIN: lowest natural period or lowest frequency (sec or 1/sec). Default = 0.  
   – TMAX: highest natural period or highest frequency (sec or 1/sec). Default = “!” (automatically set to the maximum time/frequency of the input).  
   – TDIF: step size between successive periods or frequencies (sec or 1/sec). Default = (TMAX–TMIN)/50, or you can specify a negative number to indicate subdivisions relative to the first time step.

5. D1 through D5  
   – Description: Up to five modal damping ratios may be specified and plotted simultaneously.  
     • D1 marked by “.”  
     • D2 marked by “+”  
     • D3 marked by “*”  
     • D4 marked by “o”  
     • D5 marked by “x”  
   – Unit: none  
   – Defaults: D1 = 0.0; D2–D5 = none (off)

6. REF1, REF2, REF3 and RID1, RID2, RID3  
   – REF<n>: reference-curve number (optional). May point to a FUNC definition or a constant limit value with units.  
   – RID<n>: plotting style (colour and line type) for the corresponding reference.  
   – Unit: none  
   – Defaults: REF<n> = none; RID<n> = 2001 (standard line style)

Additional context (see FUNC, RESP):  
– REVA performs response‐spectrum analysis of a single‐degree-of-freedom oscillator across a defined range of natural periods or frequencies.  
– If the input LFUN originates from a DYNA transient analysis with base accelerations, you must request “acceleration” loading (ACCE) to include ground motion in the results.  
– For FFT or power-spectral‐density (PDS) evaluations, TDIF is mandatory to define the sampling interval of a general time function; otherwise the first time step is assumed.  
– Wind spectra require two scaling factors (one to convert natural frequency to the spectral ordinate, and one to de-normalize by the standard deviation σ); these are normally passed from WGEN→FIMP→REVA or via D1/D2.  
– If TYPE = FREQ, then TMIN, TMAX, and TDIF are treated as frequencies rather than periods.  
– Logarithmic (“LOGT”, “LOGF”, “LDFT”) or double-log (“LLGT”, “LLGF”, “LLFT”) scales may be requested; for PDS, only the frequency axis can be logarithmic if PDS0/PDS1 are set.

 REVA allows the calculation of a response spectra for a given load or acceleration function. Any load case may contain more than one function. The input selection can be done for LFUN or REF1 to REF3 with the syntax loadcase.sequencenumber.
 This is done by the response analysis of a single mass oscillator within a given frequency range. Then the maximum results depending on the frequency or period are visualized.
 If the LFUN has been established by a transient analysis with DYNA, it is strongly suggested to use the total accelerations. These can be only obtained if the loading is defined as accel- eration. (see ACCE) A transient analysis with eqvivalent forces will not allow to add the base accelerations to the results.
 For TYPE one can also enter P+, S+, V+, A+, AA+ as well as P-, S-, V-, A-, AA-. Then only the positive or negative components are evaluated. In the case of excitation through an acceleration, TYPE AA can be used to plot the total acceleration (ground+oscillator). This is usually the desired value. Without a specification for TYPE the original function is shown.
 The duration of the evaluation is determined by the highest time value of the excitation value. A somewhat longer time range with exciting function 0.0 should thus be defined in the case of high frequency excitation.
 For a FFT or PDS evaluation TDIF is required as constant time value for a genral time function. The default is the first time step of the selected function. It can be also specified with a negative number of the time steps. TMIN and TMAX will be the frequencies of visualized range of the resulting spectrum.
 Up to five different damping values can be examined simultaneously. The damping values D1 through D5 can be used arbitrarily according to the desired marking.

The table defines the complete set of input parameters required to configure a pushover (nonlinear static) analysis in the RAG framework. It is organized in four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and covers four logical groups of inputs: analysis type, additional behavioral options, load‐case specification, and performance limits. In practice these entries correspond to keywords in the “PUSH” section of the input deck; see also the related ACCE and RESP sections, and the theoretical background in Section 4.1.

1. Analysis Type (Item = TYPE, Unit = LIT, Default = VB-U)  
   • VB-U (“Base Shear – Control Node Displacement Diagram”): Pushover in base‐shear‐controlled mode, plotting roof/drift displacement at the control node against total base shear.  
   • A-D (“Spectral Acceleration – Spectral Displacement Diagram”): Capacity curve in spectral coordinates, used for capacity‐spectrum methods.  
   • ATC (“ATC-40 Procedure”): Performs pushover according to ATC-40 guidelines (Applied Technology Council).  
   • EC8 (“Eurocode 8 Procedure”): Eurocode 8 compliant pushover sequence.

2. Additional Option (Item = OPT, Unit = LIT, Default = “*” meaning none)  
   These optional flags permit the user to specify a structural behavior type that may alter the pushover sequencing or ductility calculation:  
   • SBTA: Structural Behavior Type A  
   • SBTB: Structural Behavior Type B  
   • SBTC: Structural Behavior Type C  
   If no option is specified, the analysis defaults to the solver’s built‐in behavior assumptions.

3. Load-Case Controls  
   • LCC0 (Basis load case for capacity curve): Integer index of the baseline load pattern used to trace the curve. Default = “–” (must be provided explicitly).  
   • LCC1 (First load case of the capacity curve): Index of the first incremental load case.  
   • NLCC (Number of load cases of the capacity curve): Total count of monotonic steps to apply in the pushover. Default = 1.  

4. Control Node and Damping  
   • CNOD (Control node): Node ID at which the lateral displacement is recorded as the control point. Essential for all pushover diagrams.  
   • DSTR (Viscous structural damping): Damping ratio (e.g. 0.05 for 5 % viscous damping); if omitted (“*”) a default from the global damping settings is used.  
   • LCDM (Demand load case): Index of the seismic demand record or envelope used for post-processing (optional).

5. Structural Performance Limits (Items SPL1–SPL5, Unit = [mm]₁₀₀₃, Default = “–”)  
   Up to five displacement (or drift) thresholds that define performance points—yield, ultimate, collapse, etc.—on the capacity curve. Each SPLi is specified in millimeters (as per unit code 1003) and is used to mark performance levels:

   – SPL1: Performance Limit 1  
   – SPL2: Performance Limit 2  
   – SPL3: Performance Limit 3  
   – SPL4: Performance Limit 4  
   – SPL5: Performance Limit 5  

In summary, this table standardizes all the LITeral flags, numeric indices and performance definitions needed to run and post-process a pushover analysis. It ensures reproducibility by fixing defaults and units, while allowing the user to tailor the control node, damping ratio, behavioral options and performance checkpoints.

See also: ACCE, RESP
 PUSH
 General workflow and theoretical background behind the pushover analysis are described in Section 4.1.

The input table defines the keywords, their meaning, units and default values for the PUSH command in SOFiSTiK’s RAG-oriented workflow. This command is used to transform an MDOF pushover curve into various capacity-type diagrams (e.g. VB-U, A-D, ATC, EC8). Below is a detailed breakdown of each column and row of the table:

1. Table Structure  
   • Columns  
     – PUSH: The keyword to be used on the PUSH command line.  
     – Description: A concise English description of the keyword’s function.  
     – Unit: The type or data‐type expected (e.g. LIT for literal, “—” for no unit).  
     – Default: The value assumed if the keyword is omitted.  

2. Row-by-Row Explanation  
   A. TYPE  
     • Keyword: TYPE  
     • Description: Specifies which capacity diagram to generate. The only listed option here is VB-U, which stands for “Base Shear – Control Node Displacement Diagram.” Other valid values (not shown) include A-D (Spectral Acceleration–Spectral Displacement), ATC or EC8 for inelastic spectrum procedures.  
     • Unit: LIT (literal string)  
     • Default: VB-U  

   B. LCC0  
     • Keyword: LCC0  
     • Description: The “basis” load case number containing modal‐participation data (participation factors, modal mass, assumed displacement shape, etc.). This case establishes the reference deformation degree‐of‐freedom for the control node.  
     • Unit: — (integer load‐case index)  
     • Default: – (no default; must be provided)  

   C. LCC1  
     • Keyword: LCC1  
     • Description: The first load case in the sequence of incremental pushover results. The pushover curve is assembled by reading NLCC successive load cases starting from LCC1.  
     • Unit: — (integer load‐case index)  
     • Default: –  

   D. NLCC  
     • Keyword: NLCC  
     • Description: Number of load‐case steps in the pushover sequence (i.e. how many load cases to read, starting at LCC1).  
     • Unit: — (integer count)  
     • Default: 1  

   E. CNOD  
     • Keyword: CNOD  
     • Description: The node number designated as the “control node.” Its displacement (or its directional component) is plotted against base shear to form the capacity curve.  
     • Unit: — (integer node index)  
     • Default: –  

   F. LCDM (optional)  
     • Keyword: LCDM  
     • Description: Control direction mask. When specified, it forces the algorithm to extract a single component of displacement and base shear rather than using the Euclidean norm of dominant DOFs.  
     • Unit: LIT (literal: X, Y or Z)  
     • Default: – (if omitted, the code computes the dominant DOF combination automatically)  
     • Suboptions:  
       - X: Global X direction  
       - Y: Global Y direction  
       - Z: Global Z direction  

3. How This Table Fits into the Workflow  
   – A user issues a PUSH line such as  
     “PUSH TYPE VB-U LCC0 301 LCC1 2301 NLCC 25 CNOD 4”  
     to extract a VB-U curve from cases 2301…2325 using control node 4 and reference case 301.  
   – Optionally, “LCDM X” would force the X‐component of displacement/shear.  
   – Further conversion to SDOF capacity (A-D) or inelastic demand (ATC/EC8) simply requires changing TYPE and supplying an elastic spectrum load case via LCDM.  

By clearly defining each keyword, its purpose, expected data and defaults, this table serves as the authoritative map for generating capacity and demand diagrams in a reproducible, parameterized RAG/vector‐store environment.

The figure is a classic pushover “capacity curve” plotting global base shear (Vb) against the lateral displacement of a single control node (U).  It is labeled “Figure 4.13: VB-U Diagram” and was produced by a SOFiLOAD PUSH TYPE VB-U run (e.g. LC 5001 PUSH TYPE VB-U LCC0 301 LCC1 2301 NLCC 25 CNOD 4).

1. Coordinate System and Labels  
   • Horizontal axis: control-node displacement U (presumably in millimeters).  Tick marks and grid lines at 0.000, 50.000, 100.000, … up to 300.000.  
   • Vertical axis: base shear Vb in kilonewtons [kN], with ticks at 0.0, 20.0, 40.0, 60.0, and 80.0.  
   • Both axes lie along black baseline and left edge; fine grey grid lines fill the interior for reference.

2. Curve Description  
   • A red polyline traces the pushover response, punctuated by small red “×” markers at each incremental load step (NLCC = 25).  
   • From the origin (0 mm, 0 kN) up to roughly (100 mm, 50 kN) the line is straight and steep, indicating the initial elastic stiffness of the structure.  
   • At about U ≈ 100 mm the slope visibly decreases—this “knee” marks the onset of yielding.  
   • Beyond yield, between 100 mm and 300 mm displacement, the base-shear continues to grow but at a much lower rate, reaching approximately 65 kN at the 300 mm tip displacement.  This gently upward trend reflects strain hardening or post-yield stiffness.

3. Incremental Markers  
   • Each red “×” denotes one nonlinear analysis increment (load cases 2301 through 2325); their nearly uniform spacing along the initial branch confirms linear behavior, while the clustering of later markers shows slower base-shear growth in the inelastic range.

4. Interpretation in Pushover Workflow  
   • This VB-U diagram is the direct output of Stage 4a in the pushover procedure.  It provides the MDOF capacity curve in terms of global shear vs. local displacement.  
   • In subsequent stages, this curve is transformed into an SDOF “capacity diagram” in A–D (spectral acceleration vs. spectral displacement) space via equations 4.45a–4.45b or into demand/capacity intersection (“performance point”) using ATC-40 or EC8 procedures.

5. Visual Style  
   • The background is white with light grey gridlines for clarity.  
   • Axes and tick labels are rendered in black, with the axis label “Vb [kN]” set vertically beside the y-axis.  
   • The bottom caption “Figure 4.13: VB-U Diagram” is centered beneath the plot in bold.

Overall, the plot succinctly illustrates an idealized push-over capacity curve: a linear elastic branch up to a yield point near (100 mm, 50 kN), followed by a reduced-stiffness plastic branch rising to about 65 kN at maximum displacement.

The excerpted table defines the key keywords, their meaning, units and defaults for the SOFiSTiK “PUSH” command. This command is at the heart of the pushover‐based capacity‐spectrum workflow (VB–U, A–D, ATC, EC8) and controls how the pushover curve is read, which control node is tracked, and, if requested, how that curve is transformed into a spectral‐acceleration versus spectral‐displacement (A–D) format or into inelastic demand formats. Below is a detailed description of each table entry, augmented by context from the surrounding documentation.

1. TYPE  
   • Description: Specifies the kind of diagram or capacity‐demand format to produce.  
     – “A-D” requests the Spectral Acceleration (Sp) versus Spectral Displacement (Sd) diagram.  
     – Other valid TYPE values include “VB-U” for Base Shear–Control Node Displacement, “ATC” for the ATC-40 capacity spectrum method, or “EC8” for the Eurocode 8 procedure.  
   • Unit: Literal (LIT)  
   • Default: A-D  

   In practice, “TYPE” determines whether the pushover curve remains in the MDOF VB-U coordinate system or is converted to an equivalent SDOF A–D format (Eqs. 4.45–4.46), or further processed by ATC-40 or EC8 inelastic demand methods (Eqs. 4.47–4.70).

2. LCC0  
   • Description: The Basis Load Case for the capacity curve. This load case (e.g. “301”) contains the assumed displacement shape, participation factors, modal mass, etc., needed to normalize base shear and control‐node displacement.  
   • Unit: —  
   • Default: —  

   LCC0 anchors the initial geometry of the capacity curve and defines the dominant DOFs for subsequent NLCC steps.

3. LCC1  
   • Description: The first Load Case of the incremental capacity analysis (e.g. “2301”). Following LCC1, the software reads NLCC sequential cases (LCC1 through LCC1 + NLCC − 1) to build the pushover curve.  
   • Unit: —  
   • Default: —  

4. NLCC  
   • Description: Number of Load Cases comprising the capacity (pushover) curve. It controls how many increments (steps) beyond LCC1 are read.  
   • Unit: —  
   • Default: 1  

   Setting NLCC to 25, for example, reads load cases 2301 to 2325 as one continuous capacity curve.

5. CNOD  
   • Description: Control Node number. The nodal displacement degree of freedom at this node is tracked throughout the pushover. Base shear Vb versus control node displacement Ucnod form the VB–U curve.  
   • Unit: —  
   • Default: —  

   CNOD is also used when transforming to A–D or inelastic demand formats: the same node displacement defines Sd before spectral conversion.

6. LCDM  
   • Description: Demand Load Case, typically the load case holding the elastic response spectrum (e.g. from RESP TYPE EC-1). This entry tells PUSH which spectrum to fetch in order to convert the capacity curve into a demand diagram (elastic or inelastic) when TYPE is A-D, ATC or EC8.  
   • Unit: —  
   • Default: —  

   When omitted, the Euclidean norm of the displacement and base‐shear components is used; when supplied, the spectrum direction fixes the global direction of Vb and Ucnod for the transformed diagram.

In summary, this compact parameter table provides all information needed by SOFiSTiK to locate the input pushover data, select the target diagram format or methodology (spectral, ATC-40, Eurocode 8), pick the control node, and—if spectral conversion is requested—identify the demand spectrum. Together, these keywords orchestrate the crucial Stage 4 and Stage 5 operations in the pushover‐based performance‐point determination workflow.

The table shown defines the input parameters of the SOFiSTiK PUSH command.  Each row corresponds to one keyword, its meaning, its unit (if any) and its default value.  This description is suitable for populating a RAG-enabled vector store, so that each parameter record can be retrieved by name, by function or by default setting.  

1.  Parameter: TYPE  
   • Description: Selects the analysis or conversion procedure for the pushover curve.  
   • Allowed values (literals):  
     – VB-U   (base shear vs. control-node displacement)  
     – A-D    (spectral acceleration vs. spectral displacement)  
     – ATC    (ATC-40 capacity-spectrum procedure)  
     – EC8    (Eurocode 8 inelastic spectrum procedure)  
   • Unit: LIT (literal)  
   • Default: ATC  

2.  Parameter: OPT  
   • Description: Additional option, only valid when TYPE=ATC.  Selects one of the three hysteretic behavior classes used by ATC-40 to compute effective damping.  
   • Allowed values (literals):  
     – SBTA  (Type A: stable, full loops)  
     – SBTB  (Type B: moderate loop degradation)  
     – SBTC  (Type C: severely pinched or degraded loops)  
   • Unit: LIT (literal)  
   • Default: SBTA  

3.  Parameter: LCC0  
   • Description: Basis load case number containing the MDOF‐system modal‐participation data, modal mass, assumed displacement shape, etc., used to compute the “zero” displacement degree‐of‐freedom for the control node.  
   • Allowed values: Integer load case ID  
   • Unit: – (unitless)  
   • Default: none (must be specified)  

4.  Parameter: LCC1  
   • Description: First load‐case index in which the incremental pushover analysis results have been stored.  The PUSH command will read successive load cases LCC1 .. LCC1+NLCC–1.  
   • Allowed values: Integer load case ID  
   • Unit: – (unitless)  
   • Default: none (must be specified)  

5.  Parameter: NLCC  
   • Description: Number of consecutive load cases to read, starting at LCC1, which represent increasing load steps along the pushover curve.  
   • Allowed values: Positive integer  
   • Unit: – (unitless)  
   • Default: 1  

6.  Parameter: CNOD  
   • Description: Control node for which displacements are extracted and plotted against base shear.  This node defines the “roof” or any monitoring point in the MDOF model.  
   • Allowed values: Integer node ID  
   • Unit: – (unitless)  
   • Default: none (must be specified)  

7.  Parameter: DSTR  
   • Description: Viscous structural damping fraction inherent in the MDOF system (used only by TYPE=ATC to form the total equivalent damping).  
   • Allowed values: Real number (fraction of critical damping)  
   • Unit: – (fraction)  
   • Default: 0.05  (i.e. 5 %)  

8.  Parameter: LCDM  
   • Description: Demand‐spectra load-case number.  When converting to A-D format (TYPE=A-D, ATC or EC8) or when plotting the elastic demand (TYPE=EC8, etc.), this load case must contain the response spectrum (created via RESP) whose direction also fixes the global sign of the base shear and control-node displacement.  
   • Allowed values: Integer load case ID  
   • Unit: – (unitless)  
   • Default: none (only needed for A-D/ATC/EC8)  

Usage notes:  
–  TYPE=VB-U does not require LCDM or OPT; it simply reads Vb vs. Ucnod data.  
–  For TYPE=A-D the table‐defined formula (Eq. 4.45) is used to convert Vb−cnod into Sp−Sd.  
–  For TYPE=ATC or TYPE=EC8, the pushover curve and the elastic 5 %-damped spectrum are transformed iteratively to locate the inelastic performance point in the Sp–Sd (A-D) coordinate system.  
–  All parameters except DEFAULT may be overridden at the command line.

The table in question—“Table 4.12: Values for damping modification factor, κ (ATC-40)” —provides the numerical relationships used in the ATC-40 capacity spectrum method to translate hysteretic energy dissipation into an equivalent viscous damping term.  Its primary role is to define κ, the so-called damping modification factor, as a function of two inputs:  
  1. The structural behavior type (SBT), which classifies the quality of the hysteretic loops observed in a nonlinear pushover analysis.  
  2. The equivalent viscous damping percentage ξ₀ [%], which represents the damping contribution attributed to hysteretic energy dissipation.  

Structure of the Table  
• Column 1 (SBT): Lists three discrete behavioral categories—A, B, and C—each reflecting a progressively more degraded hysteretic response:  
  – Type A (SBTA): “stable, reasonably full hysteresis loops.”  
  – Type B (SBTB): “moderate reduction of loop area.”  
  – Type C (SBTC): “poor hysteresis behavior with severely pinched or degraded loops.”  

• Column 2 (ξ₀ [%]): Defines ranges of equivalent viscous damping for each SBT.  These ranges split into sub-ranges for Types A and B and remain “any value” for Type C.  

• Column 3 (κ): Gives either a constant or a linear expression in ξ₀ to compute the damping modification factor.  

Detailed Rows  
1. SBT A (stable, full loops)  
   – For ξ₀ ≤ 16.25 % → κ = 1.00 (constant)  
   – For ξ₀ > 16.25 % → κ = 1.130 – 0.510·(ξ₀·π/2)  
     • Here the term “(ξ₀·π/2)” indicates that the damping percentage is multiplied by π/2 before applying the coefficient.  

2. SBT B (moderately reduced loops)  
   – For ξ₀ ≤ 25.00 % → κ = 0.67 (constant)  
   – For ξ₀ > 25.00 % → κ = 0.845 – 0.446·(ξ₀·π/2)  
     • As in Type A, the linear term reduces κ progressively as ξ₀ increases beyond the threshold.  

3. SBT C (poor, pinched loops)  
   – For any ξ₀ value → κ = 0.33 (constant)  

Interpretation and Use  
– In the ATC-40 capacity spectrum method, the total effective viscous damping ξ_eff is the sum of inherent (structural) viscous damping ξ_str and the hysteretic contribution ξ₀ scaled by κ:  
     ξ_eff = ξ_str + κ·ξ₀.  
– The factor κ accounts for the fact that not all hysteretic energy dissipation can be represented as viscous damping; it is reduced for severely degraded hysteresis (Type C) and adjusted linearly for higher ξ₀ in Types A and B.  
– Users select the appropriate SBT based on observed or assumed loop behavior, compute ξ₀ from the pushover curve (energy dissipated per cycle), then apply the formula from Table 4.12 to find κ.  This κ is then used to adjust the 5%-damped response spectrum to the effective damping level for performance-point iteration.  

By codifying κ in this way, the ATC-40 procedure embeds hysteretic characteristics into a single scalar modification factor, facilitating the conversion between nonlinear energy dissipation and an equivalent linear viscous model.

A brace at the top shows the defining piecewise formula for the reduction factor SR(T, ξ_eff, SBT):

 SR(T, ξ_eff, SBT) =  
  { SR_a(ξ_eff, SBT) for T ≤ T′_c = T_c  
  { SR_v(ξ_eff, SBT) for T ≥ T′_c  

Here SR_a is the constant-acceleration reduction factor (applied in the flat portion of the spectrum) and SR_v the constant-velocity reduction factor (applied in the descending branch). T_c is the corner period of the full 5 %-damped spectrum; T′_c is the reduced-spectrum corner, which remains coincident with T_c in the constant-acceleration range.

• A solid blue line showing the reduced spectrum for effective damping ξ_eff > 5 %:  
 – A lower constant plateau Sa_e = S′_B = SR_a·S_B for T ≤ T′_c  
 – A lower power-law decay Sa_e = S′_B·(T′_c/T)^k₁ for T > T′_c  

Vertical dashed lines mark T_c and T′_c on the T axis, and horizontal dashed lines mark the corresponding plateau values S_B (black) and S′_B (blue). Key labels such as “S_ae = S_B,” “S_ae = S′_B,” and the mathematical expressions for the decay branches are placed adjacent to each curve.

Two thin dashed lines emanating from the origin intersect the black curve in its descending branch, suggesting the slopes of constant-velocity decay.

At the bottom center, the figure caption reads:  
“Figure 4.17: Reduced response spectrum”  

Overall, this image clearly demonstrates how increased effective damping in an equivalent SDOF system (for instance when deriving the inelastic demand under ATC-40 or Eurocode 8 procedures) is accounted for by multiplying the elastic spectrum by spectral reduction factors SR_a and SR_v. The left panel gives the classical Sa–T view, while the right panel presents the same reduction in an alternate spectrum plot.

The table reproduced below (Table 4.13) defines the minimum allowable values for two spectral reduction factors—SRₐ and SRᵥ—corresponding to three different hysteretic “structural behavior types” (SBT). These minima are used in the ATC-40 (and similar) capacity-spectrum procedures to cap the computed spectral reduction factors so that they never fall below physically reasonable limits, regardless of damping or behavior‐type adjustments.  

Table 4.13: Minimum allowable SRₐ and SRᵥ values  
Columns:  
  • SBT: Structural Behavior Type (hysteresis‐loop classification)  
  • SRₐ,min: Minimum allowable spectral acceleration reduction factor  
  • SRᵥ,min: Minimum allowable spectral velocity (or displacement) reduction factor  

Rows:  
  • A: “Stable, reasonably full” hysteresis loops  
      – SRₐ,min = 0.33  
      – SRᵥ,min = 0.50  
  • B: “Moderate reduction” of loop area (some pinching or degradation)  
      – SRₐ,min = 0.44  
      – SRᵥ,min = 0.56  
  • C: “Poor hysteresis behavior” with severe pinching or degradation  
      – SRₐ,min = 0.56  
      – SRᵥ,min = 0.67  

Context and usage  
  – In the capacity-spectrum method (ATC-40), the elastic 5 %-damped acceleration spectrum Se(T, 5 %) is reduced to Se(T, ξ_eff) for higher damping levels using  
      Se(T, ξ_eff) = SR(T, ξ_eff, SBT) · Se(T, 5 %)  (Eq. 4.56)  
  – Analytical expressions (Eqs. 4.58a–b, based on Newmark & Hall) provide SR(T, ξ_eff) but the result must not be lower than the SBT‐specific minima in Table 4.13. That is, for each period range the computed SR is compared against SRₐ,min or SRᵥ,min (depending on whether acceleration or velocity reductions are sought), and the larger of the two is used.  
  – This ensures that even for very high damping or extreme hysteretic degradation the reduced demand spectrum does not become unrealistically low.  

Structural Behavior Type definitions (from ATC-40):  
  – Type A (SBTA): stable loops with minimal pinching  
  – Type B (SBTB): moderate loop area loss  
  – Type C (SBTC): severe pinching/degradation  

By enforcing these lower bounds, the method maintains conservative—and physically meaningful—spectral demands when transforming from an idealized elastic spectrum to one that accounts for inelastic energy dissipation.

   • Unit: LIT (a case‐sensitive literal text string)  
   • Default: EC8  
   – If you don’t specify TYPE, Eurocode 8 is assumed. For ATC‐40 you would write “PUSH TYPE ATC …”, for VB-U “PUSH TYPE VB-U …”, etc.  

2. LCC0  
   • Description: “Basis load case for capacity curve”  
   • Unit: — (integer index)  
   • Default: – (none)  
   – This is the load case number in which the static basis or reference mode is defined (e.g. modal participation factors, shape vector).  You always need to supply LCC0.  

3. LCC1  
   • Description: “First load case of the capacity curve”  
   • Unit: — (integer index)  
   • Default: – (none)  
   – After you run your incremental pushover analysis, the results are stored sequentially in load cases LCC1, LCC1+1, …, LCC1+NLCC–1.  

4. NLCC  
   • Description: “Number of load cases of the capacity curve”  
   • Unit: — (integer)  
   • Default: 1  
   – How many pushover steps (i.e. how many consecutive load‐case records) to read starting at LCC1.  If you omit it, SOFiSTiK assumes only one step is available.  

5. CNOD  
   • Description: “Control node”  
   • Unit: — (integer node number)  
   • Default: – (none)  
   – The node whose displacement you track as the “roof” or control‐point displacement.  Must match the node used in your Stage 2 ACCE/LCC0 definition.  

6. LCDM  
   • Description: “Demand load case”  
   • Unit: — (integer index)  
   • Default: – (none)  
   – The load case in which you defined the elastic (5 %-damped) response spectrum (via RESP) that you want to convert into the demand curve.  For A-D, ATC or EC8 PUSH types, this specifies the direction and magnitude of the elastic spectrum to be transformed alongside your capacity curve.

How to use in practice  
— Example for a pure VB-U pushover:  
   LC 5001  
   PUSH TYPE VB-U  
       LCC0 301  LCC1 2301  NLCC 25  CNOD 4  

— Example converting to A-D (ADRS) format using spectrum in load case 11:  
   LC 5002  
   PUSH TYPE A-D  
       LCC0 301  LCC1 2301  NLCC 22  CNOD 4  LCDM 11  

— Example invoking the EC8 (Eurocode 8) procedure:  
   LC 5004  
   PUSH TYPE EC8  
       LCC0 301  LCC1 2301  NLCC 22  CNOD 4  LCDM 11  

In a vector store you would index each parameter name, its description, valid values or units and default.  When a user or agent later asks “How do I form a PUSH command for ATC‐40?”, you retrieve the relevant rows (TYPE, LCC0, LCC1, NLCC, CNOD, DSTR, LCDM) and synthesize an example.

Axes and Annotations  
• X-axis: Period T in seconds, running from 0.0 to 8.0 s (tick marks at 2.00, 4.00, 6.00, 8.00).

Curves and Color Coding  
• A family of six piecewise curves represents increasing ductility ratios μ = 1 through μ = 6.  
• For T ≤ T_c each curve rises linearly from the origin, following the EC8 formula R_y(T,μ) = 1 + (μ – 1)·(T/T_c).  
• At T > T_c every curve flattens to a constant horizontal plateau equal to its target ductility μ (i.e. R_y = μ).  
• The “elastic” case μ = 1 is drawn as a single dark blue line: it grows from 1 at T=0 to R_y=1 at T_c and remains at 1 thereafter.  
• The higher ductility levels (μ=2, 3, 4, 5, 6) appear as successive green lines: each starts at R_y=1 for T=0, slopes up to its μ value at T_c, and then carries that constant value forward.

Interpretation in Context  
This R_y – μ – T plot is generated in the final step of the PUSH…TYPE EC8 analysis (e.g. “LC 5004 PUSH TYPE EC8 … CNOD 4 LCDM 11”). It provides the strength‐reduction factor that must be applied to the elastic spectral acceleration at each period in order to account for inelastic energy dissipation (ductility μ) under the EC8 procedure. By reading off the plateau level at a given T, the analyst obtains R_y; for short periods the linear segment gives the gradual buildup of inelastic demand. The intersection of this demand spectrum with the capacity curve in A–D coordinates defines the Performance Point (PP) of the structure.
