The figure is a classic capacity‐spectrum (a versus Sd) plot that illustrates both global structural performance demands and the user‐defined performance limits (SPL1–SPL5). The horizontal axis represents spectral displacement Sd (in millimeters, from 0 to about 400 mm), and the vertical axis is spectral acceleration a (in m/s², from 0 up to roughly 15 m/s²).  

Curves and lines shown:

  • Black solid line (“demand spectrum”): begins at a high initial acceleration (~15 m/s² at Sd≈0), is flat (constant‐acceleration branch) out to about Sd≈100 mm, then smoothly decays in a hyperbolic fashion toward lower accelerations (≈5 m/s² at Sd≈400 mm).  
  • Blue solid line (“damped/modified demand” or “inelastic demand spectrum”): starts at ≈8 m/s², remains nearly constant until about Sd≈60 mm, and then gradually decreases to around 2 m/s² by Sd≈400 mm.  
  • Brown/red piecewise line (“capacity curve”):  
    – Rises from the origin with a steep slope (elastic branch) up to a point labeled Py at roughly Sd≈50 mm and a≈4 m/s².  
    – Continues with a reduced slope through a yield‐to‐ultimate transition, reaching a second marker labeled PP (“performance point”) at about Sd≈100 mm and a≈6 m/s²—the intersection of capacity and demand.  
    – Beyond PP, a straight red line (post‐peak or ultimate capacity), labeled “Capa,” extends linearly upward to the right, reaching ≈7.5 m/s² at Sd≈400 mm.  

  • Green dashed radial lines (“constant‐period lines”): emanate from the origin at various slopes, each annotated with a period value (Tb = 0.1 s, T = 0.5 s, Tc = 0.6 s, Ty, T = 1.0 s, Tp). These trace constant‐period loci so that any point on the plot can be read in terms of its equivalent single‐degree‐of‐freedom period.  

  • Five vertical colored dashed lines mark the user‐specified global structural performance limits (SPL1–SPL5) in terms of spectral displacement (Sd):  
    – SPL1 (red) at Sd = 0.10 m (100 mm)  
    – SPL2 (blue) at Sd = 0.18 m (180 mm)  
    – SPL3 (yellow) at Sd = 0.25 m (250 mm)  
    – SPL4 (magenta) at Sd = 0.35 m (350 mm)  
    – SPL5 (cyan) at Sd = 0.45 m (450 mm)  

Key annotated points and labels:

  • “Py” marks the first yielding limit of the structural component (on the capacity curve).  
  • “PP” denotes the performance point—where the inelastic capacity and demand spectra intersect—representing the global seismic demand corresponding to a given hazard.  
  • “Tb,” “Tc,” “Ty,” “Tp” denote characteristic periods of the response spectrum: the beginning and end of the constant‐acceleration branch (Tb), the corner period between acceleration‐ and displacement‐controlled regions (Tc), the yield period (Ty), and the period at which the demand spectrum is again flat or trending (Tp).  

Caption (underneath the graphic): Figure 4.26: Structural performance limits.  

By plotting both the demand spectra (black and blue) and the capacity curve (brown/red), together with green constant‐period lines and red/blue/yellow/magenta/cyan vertical lines for SPL1 through SPL5, the diagram visually communicates how local and global performance thresholds (in terms of spectral displacement) relate to the expected seismic demand and the building’s inelastic capacity.

The performance point is used to compare the global response of structure and individual component deformations to limit values in context of the specific performance objectives for the building in question. The performance objective represents the desired building perfor- mance level under a given seismic hazard (earthquake ground motion). The performance levels are defined by the performance limits (ATC-40 [5]). The structural performance limits can be categorized as:
 • Local element and component acceptability limits. Each component (beam, column, slab, connections, etc.) of the structural elements (frames, seismic walls, diaphragms, foundations, etc.) should be checked to verify if its response under a given seismic demand (level of forces and deformations corresponding to the performance point) is within the acceptable limits (performance limits). Local performance limits for beam plastic hinges can be defined in AQUA (see AQUA: SFLA).
 • Global structural performance limits. Similar to local performance limits it is possible to define the global performance limits. Up to five global (structural) performance limits can be specified by the user (PUSH ... SPL1 ... SPL5).
 The following input will set the global structural performance limits (SPL1-SPL5) as the cnod displacements (VB-U coordinate system). If the analysis is of the type which works with the A- D coordinate system (e.g. PUSH TYPE ATC, EC8, etc. ), then the performance levels specified as the cnod displacements will be converted into the spectral displacements of the equivalent SDOF system Sd (Fig. 4.26).

Train loads for bridges are ruled by the fact, that the most unfavourable position of the loading is different for every single element and reaction and not known in advance.
 The base of the moving load process is a lane geometry, described in the plan view by straight, circular or clothoid segments and in the elevation as straight or quadratic parabola. This can be taken from the database as defined by SOFiMSHB or explicitly input with the record GAX. Each axis may have up to 99 separate lanes defined via LANE. For the dynamic impact coefficients an effective length may be specified and the extra width of the traffic area may be defined.
 Each lane has two coordinate systems. There is a local system (x) at the lane axis for real distances. However, the inputs for the positions along the lanes are entered in a global system of stations (s) which defines an alignment of the lanes to each other.
 There are three principal approaches for the problem of finding the most unfavourable load position:
 • One can generate numerous load cases with the train load at distinct positions and search for the maximum with the superposition tool MAXIMA. For some load definitions this ap- proach is not possible with acceptable effort however.
 • More general one can establish the influence lines for the forces and moments of all or selected locations within the structure. In a second step these influence lines may be eval- uated with the load trains. The result are direct extreme values of all forces and moments. This is performed with the program module ELLA, highly optimized for this task.
 Last not least a transient analysis of the load coursing the structure with the program DYNA is possible. For the animation of this process the record TREX is very helpful.
 •
 Depending on the system and the loading, the one or the other method will be better. Spe- cial effects like a load which is not bound to the lane in transverse direction (EC) or having independent wheels (DIN) may increase the number of needed load cases considerably.

Spe- cial effects like a load which is not bound to the lane in transverse direction (EC) or having independent wheels (DIN) may increase the number of needed load cases considerably..
 The commands available for the load train definition are:
 TRAI Specifying the load train
 TRPL, TRBL Explicit loading of a load train
 With this commands no loading will be applied to the structure yet. The load definitions are saved under a load case number which should not be used otherwise. It is the SOFiLOAD / COPY command that will transform the train to individual loading. With a reference to a geometric line (GAX) and an associated lane (LANE) the following transformations will take place:
 • The load train will be adopted to the geometry of the lane.
 • Centrifugal loading will be created based on the speed of the train and the curvature of the lane.
 • Variable eccentricities will be applied automaticallly in an unfaourable way.

The table at hand systematizes the “load groups” (gr0, grU, gr1 … gr6) used to assign partial‐load combination coefficients to the various components of a rail or road‐bridge load model under EN 1991-2 (or DIN FB 101).  Each row (gr­0 through gr6) defines which load component is taken as characteristic, frequent or permanent and whether it applies vertically (LM1(TS), LM1(UDL), LM4) or horizontally (braking, centrifugal).  Below is a detailed walk-through:

1.  Columns  
   • LM1(TS): “Train Static” concentrated wheel loads  
   • LM1(UDL): Uniformly distributed load along track  
   • LM4: Additional concentrated special traffic loads (e.g. exceptional vehicles)  
   • braking: longitudinal horizontal loads  
   • centrifugal: transverse horizontal loads  

2.  Load‐Group Definitions  
   • gr0 (Characteristic Train Loads)  
     – LM1(TS) is taken at its characteristic (“Charact.”) value  
     – All other columns blank (not active in this group)  
   • grU (Characteristic Uniform Load)  
     – LM1(UDL) is taken at its characteristic (“Charact.”) value  
   • gr1 (Combined Characteristic Model)  
     – Both LM1(TS) and LM1(UDL) at characteristic values  
     – braking and centrifugal marked “(*)”: these horizontal loads may be included under special rules or treated with ψ₁ coefficients per EN 1991-2/EN 1990  
   • gr2 (Frequent Load Case)  
     – LM1(TS) and LM1(UDL) at “frequent” levels (ψ₂‐reduced)  
     – braking and centrifugal both at their characteristic values (“Charact.”)  
   • gr2n (Non‐frequent Horizontal)  
     – Vertical loads as for gr2 (“frequent”)  
     – braking and centrifugal both at “non frequent” level  
   • gr2f (Permanent Case)  
     – LM1(TS) and LM1(UDL) taken as “permanent” (ψ₀-level)  
     – braking and centrifugal both at “Frequent”  
   • gr3 (Side‐walk or Pathway Loads)  
     – LM1(UDL) applies as characteristic but only on sidewalks; no LM1(TS)  
   • gr4 (Uniformly Distributed Live Load)  
     – LM4 replaces other vertical components as a “Charact. UDL on total area”  
   • gr5 (Mixed Lane Model)  
     – In the main lane, LM3 (special vehicle) is characteristic; on other lanes LM1 is at “frequent” value  
   • gr6 (Support‐Exchange Model)  
     – All loads (LM1(TS), LM1(UDL), braking, centrifugal) taken at 0.5 × Charact. value; used for “exchange of supports” per DIN FB  

3.  Combination Rules & Coefficients  
   – For any group other than the pure characteristic case (gr1), ψ₁ (for traffic loads) and ψ₂ (for UDL) from EN 1991-2 or BS EN 1990 are applied.  
   – Special additional LM1 loads may carry bespoke ψ₁(TS) or ψ₂(UDL) values in the train’s load‐case record, but special‐vehicle loads (LM3) are always taken full without reduction.  
   – Any deviation or bespoke combination must be implemented via a dedicated group plus an explicit FACT multiplier.  

4.  Additional Constraints (DIN FB 101, Appendix C)  
   – LM2 and single‐wagon loads must not combine with other live loads.  
   – Snow or wind may never be combined with braking or groups gr2/gr3.  
   – Snow or wind exceeding ψ₀·FWk cannot go with gr1 or LM1.  
   – Wind and temperature actions cannot be applied concurrently.  
   – Railway‐bridge groups 11–31 in table 6.6 (not shown here) should be evaluated by sophisticated envelope tools (ELLA or MAXIMA) rather than explicit sum cases; wind and train loads only act together at the train’s position and only if wind remains below a threshold.

There are possibly different combination coefficients within one load train. Therefore we have load groups within the EN 1991-2 or the DIN FB. For road bridges they are given in table 4.4, for railway bridges in table 6.6. From these definitions the following table is deducted:
 Traffic area
 The selection of a group will select individual factors for the components from a complete load train definition. gr6 is used for the exchange of supports according to DIN FB. For all combi- nations with other than the characteristic values the PSI1-coefficients of EN 1991-2 resp. BS EN 1990 are used. Other coefficients for the additional LM1 may be specified with coefficients PSI1 (TS) and PSI2 (UDL) in the train’s LC record. But the loading of the special vehicle will always be taken without those coefficients. All other deviations to this have to be build up with the special groups and an explicit factor FACT.

 • Neither snow nor wind should be combined with braking or load group gr2 or gr3.

Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown of the “input table” schema used to define geometric axes (GAX records) in SOFiMSHC, SOFiLOAD/ELLA/TENDON and related modules. This description will help you build a RAG‐ready vector store by capturing each column’s purpose, data type and default behavior.

1. NO (Axis identifier)  
   • Description: A four‐character literal (LIT4) that uniquely names the axis segment. Typical values are “A1”, “B2”, etc.  
   • Unit: LIT4  
   • Default: “A1”  
   • Notes: The first record in an axis definition usually sets NO; subsequent records that continue the same axis may omit NO if it remains unchanged.

2. S (Total arc length / station)  
   • Description: The accumulated length along the axis from its start point, measured in the plan view (2D) or along the curve (3D).  
   • Unit: meters (m)  
   • Default: 0.0  
   • Notes:  
     – For the very first record this is the length of the first segment.  
     – In subsequent records, S gives the length of the next segment only.  

3. X, Y, Z (Real‐world coordinates of point)  
   • Description: The absolute coordinates of the axis point in global space (Cartesian).  
   • Unit: meters (m)  
   • Default: 0.0 for each coordinate  
   • Notes:  
     – In purely 2D definitions, Z may remain zero or undefined; in full 3D definitions all three must be set.  

4. R (Radius of the lane axis)  
   • Description: The radius of the circular arc that connects the previous point to the next.  
   • Unit: meters (m)  
   • Default: – (calculated automatically if omitted)  
   • Notes:  
     – Positive R bends to the right (driver’s right), negative R to the left.  
     – If R is omitted and no clothoid parameter A is given, the software computes R from the given length.

5. A (Clothoidal transition parameter)  
   • Description: A controls the rate of change of curvature: R·L = A² for a clothoid spiral.  
   • Unit: meters (m)  
   • Default: – (no spiral if omitted)  
   • Notes:  
     – Positive A produces increasing curvature, negative A decreasing curvature.  
     – If A is nonzero and R is omitted, the end curvature is calculated automatically.  
     – Setting A=0 with a given R yields a constant‐curvature (circular) “basket arch” segment.

6. NX, NY, NZ (Direction vector for 3D curves)  
   • Description: A unit‐direction vector defining the local z-axis around which circular arcs are revolved.  
   • Unit: — (unitless direction cosines)  
   • Default: * (not used for standard 2D alignments)  
   • Notes:  
     – Only required when doing full 3D axis definitions (e.g. vertical curve elements).  
     – If omitted, the “plan view” XY‐plane is assumed.

7. TYPE (Type of axis)  
   • Description: Literal (LIT) specifying the semantic category of the alignment.  
   • Allowed values:  
     – AXIS = general geometric axis  
     – LANE = traffic lane center line  
     – BGEO = bridge geometry alignment  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: AXIS  
   • Notes: This field helps downstream modules (e.g. load‐train, LANE) interpret the axis appropriately.

8. TITL (Designation of lane or axis)  
   • Description: Variable‐length literal (LIT32) for a human-readable name or description of this axis segment.  
   • Unit: LIT32  
   • Default: blank (no title)

Contextual remarks:  
• The first GAX record defines the start point (X,Y,Z), the initial direction (NX,NY,NZ), the first segment length S and, if required, curvature (R) or clothoid (A).  
• Each following GAX record for that same NO may only specify the new S, optional R and A, and title or type fields if they change.  
• When both R and A are specified on the same record, the start‐point curvature is derived rather than the end‐point radius.  
• Transitions between segments (if R changes) are automatically handled by inserting a short spiral when A ≠ 0; if A=0 you get a piecewise constant curvature.  
• Although SOFiLOAD/ELLA/TENDON only accept a simplified (2D) definition, SOFiMSHC can process full 3D axes with elevation and cross-fall options.  
• After assembling the axis records into a dynamic axis (WinGRAF or WING), users should always perform a graphical validation to ensure the intended geometry.

The image (labelled “Figure 5.1: Lane axis”) is a clean, black-and-white schematic illustrating how a single lane axis is built up from a straight (linear) segment into a clothoid (spiral) transition and then into a circular arc.  Visually it consists of three main portions laid end to end:

1. On the left, a long straight line is drawn at a slight incline and is annotated with the word “linear” in italic type.  This represents the initial tangent segment of the lane, with zero curvature.

2. As the straight segment gives way to the curved portion, a small tick mark is placed on the curve to indicate the exact station where curvature begins.  From that point, the line bends gradually upward into what is implied to be a clothoidal spiral.  Above this spiral section is the label “+A,” signifying the clothoidal parameter A that controls the rate of change of curvature (positive A means curvature is increasing in the chosen direction).

3. Further along the curve, another vertical bar (drawn as a thick straight stroke crossing the curve) marks the end of the spiral and the beginning of the circular arc.  Immediately to its right the curve is labelled “+R,” signifying a constant radius parameter R (positive values meaning the lane turns to the right-hand side).

At roughly the midpoint of the transition between straight and spiral, a local coordinate triad is sketched.  A bold line segment roughly tangent to the curve is drawn in heavy weight; an arrow-tipped line continues that direction and is labelled “x.”  Perpendicular to it, a thinner arrow points downward (toward the center of curvature) and is labelled “y.”  This local x-y frame illustrates the local axis orientation used when defining curvature in 3D: x is the tangential (forward) axis and y is the lateral (normal) axis into which positive curvature bends.

Beyond the circular‐arc section, the curved line would proceed toward further elements, but only the three‐part sequence is shown here.  All line work is crisp, with no color or shading, and text labels are upright sans-serif except for the italicized “linear.”  The overall style matches engineering-drawing conventions: clear demarcation of segment boundaries, small tick marks for station points, plus-sign prefixes to curvature parameters, and a miniature orthogonal axis for local directions.

Contextually, this figure supports the “GAX” command definitions in the SOFiMSHC / SOFiLOAD / ELLA / TENDON grammar.  In that context:

• The initial straight segment corresponds to a GAX record with an S‐value only (length), zero curvature R, and zero clothoid A.  
• The spiral transition uses the same S station plus a nonzero A parameter (clothoidal spiral).  
• The circular arc section uses an S station plus a nonzero R (and A = 0) to lock in constant curvature.  

Together, the drawing conveys how a general geometric axis is constructed from linear, clothoidal, and circular elements, how positive A and R affect curvature direction, and how the local coordinate axes align with the tangent (x) and normal (y) at any point along the lane.

The input table specifies all parameters needed to define one or more traffic or railway loading lanes in a SOFiLOAD model. Each row in the table represents a single lane segment; each column controls a particular geometric or loading attribute. Below is a detailed description of its structure and fields:

Table structure  
• Four columns:  
  – Item: parameter keyword as used in the lane definition record  
  – Description: what the parameter controls or represents  
  – Unit: physical units (m, mm or literal)  
  – Default: value assumed if the parameter is omitted  

1. Identification parameters  
  • NO (lane_ident.nummer)  
    – Literal label for the lane: “axisID.laneNumber.”  
    – Example: “A1.3” denotes the third lane on axis A1.  
    – If only the axis is given, it refers to the entire traffic area (all lanes).  
    – Unit: literal; Default: must be supplied (“*”).  
  • TYPE  
    – Predefined section type. When one of the standard RQ-literals or country codes is used, secondary lanes are generated automatically.  
    – Available presets: RQ7.5, RQ9.5, RQ10.5, RQ15.5, RQ20, RQ26, RQ29.5, RQ33, RQ35.5; or EN, BS, TMH7, CAN, IRC, JRA, AS.  
    – Unit: literal; Default: must be supplied (“*”).  

2. Curbstone coordinates  
  • WR – ordinate of the right-hand curbstone (y-coordinate)  
  • WL – ordinate of the left-hand curbstone (y-coordinate)  
    – Defines lane width = WL – WR.  
    – Units: meters; Default: WL = –WR.  

3. Longitudinal segmentation  
  • SA, SE  
    – Start and end station along the lane axis.  
    – Must be specified (“!”).  
    – No units label (interpreted in the model’s length unit).  

4. Transverse and center‐line offsets  
  • YCA, YCE – transverse offset of the lane centerline at SA and SE  
    – Units: meters; Default: YCE = YCA.  
  • YRA, YLA – right and left boundary ordinates at SA  
  • YRE, YLE – right and left boundary ordinates at SE  
    – Units: meters; Defaults: YRA = YCA, YRE = YRA; YLA = (WL–WR)/2, YLE = YLA.  

5. Segment length for impact calculation  
  • L  
    – Effective length used to compute dynamic impact coefficients and length‐dependent loading.  
    – Optional; if “CONT” is entered, this segment is combined with the previous one.  
    – Units: meters; Default: user must supply or leave blank (“*”).  

6. Vertical and cross‐fall attributes  
  • HSA, HSE – deck or rail height above lane surface at SA and SE  
    – Units: meters; Default HSA = 0.0, HSE = HSA.  
  • INCA, INCE – cross fall (dz/dy or Δh) at SA and SE  
    – Units: millimetres; Default INCA = 0.0, INCE = INCA.  

7. Railway‐specific effective dimensions  
  • HEFF – effective height of rail plus sleeper  
  • BEFF – effective length of sleeper  
  • DEFF – effective width of sleeper  
  • INCD – spread angle for stress distribution  
    – Unit for INCD: none; Default = 0.25.  
  • ASL – spacing between mounting points (e.g. rail fasteners)  
    – Units: meters; Default: must be defined if EM load is used.  

Key notes  
• Lane 0 is compulsory. If it is the only lane, its width is governed solely by the load‐train dimensions and any eccentricities apply absolutely. If additional lanes exist, lane 0 spans the full traffic area including footpaths; the moving‐load width is then governed by the maximum width of lanes 1…n.  
• Residual areas between the moving‐load edges and lane boundaries are treated only for lane 0. Gaps between lanes carry no residual load.  
• Predefined TYPE literals automatically create secondary lanes and curbstone coordinates in accordance with international codes. New lane definitions always overwrite prior ones for the same axis.

The drawing labeled “Figure 5.2: Single lane loaded and residual area” is a plan‐view schematic of a curved traffic lane and the way its loading is subdivided into the actual moving‐load footprint and the so-called residual (or “additional basic”) areas. The entire lane is bounded by two concentric arcs (an inner and an outer edge), each drawn as a smooth curve following the same center of curvature. Between these two arcs lies a constant‐width band that represents the full lane width. That band is filled with diagonal hatching at roughly 45° to emphasize the primary loaded zone.

Within the hatched band, a series of short line segments—drawn perpendicular to the arcs—depict the path of the moving load train (the wheelsets or tire contact patches). In this snapshot those “train” lines do not span the full width of the lane; they occupy only a narrower sub-band centered within the lane’s boundaries. Where the load train is narrower than the lane itself, the gaps between the outer edges of the moving‐load footprint and the full lane boundaries become “residual areas.” A leader arrow labeled “additional basic area” points to one of these unhatched gap zones on the outside of the curve, indicating that SOFiLOAD (or GAX) will assign a constant basic loading to those portions whenever the load train width falls short of the defined lane width.

Below the graphic one can just make out the partial text “constant width l…” which alludes to the “constant width loading” concept: the lane edges are fixed, even if the actual train footprint varies. The boundary arcs are shown as solid lines, while the load‐train centerline or reference axes (not fully visible here) would typically be drawn dashed or with lighter weight. The figure thus encapsulates the rules stated in the accompanying EN 1991-2 / DIN-FB 101 guidance:  

- The total loading area (lane 0) is defined first.  
- If the load train is narrower than the lane, residual zones between the train and lane edges receive a uniform basic load.  
- If the train exceeds lane width, reductions in applied loading are permitted (not shown in this figure).  

By visualizing a curved segment, the illustration also hints at the need for correctly handling torsional effects when lane‐edge curves intersect or converge. In sum, Figure 5.2 provides a clear plan‐view representation of how SOFiLOAD subdivides a single, constant‐width curved lane into the moving‐load footprint and the supplementary residual areas that ensure consistent structural loading.

   • The space between the red polyline and the central axis line corresponds to the combined width of lane 0 (including pathways) plus lanes 1 and 2; any regions not directly occupied by the moving load train are residual areas where a constant basic load may be defined.

The illustration (labelled “Figure 5.6: Ballast and sleepers”) is a schematic cross‐section through a ballasted railway track showing how sleeper loads are transferred into the ballast prism.  At the very bottom runs a thick, solid horizontal baseline representing the subgrade or foundation.  Centered on that base is a vertical line marked “z” with a small filled circle at its intersection, indicating the vertical axis and the point of application of the wheel‐set or sleeper load.

Above and straddling the centerline are two rectangular sleeper blocks (drawn as narrow, slightly tilted bars) upon which the rails (two thin, almost parallel lines) rest.  The sleepers lean marginally, suggesting possible track cant or crossfall.  Midway between the two sleeper blocks is the label “BEFF,” denoting the effective width of loading that the sleeper imposes on the ballast.  

Flanking the sleeper at left and right are two identical, sloping wedge shapes of ballast.  Each side is bounded by a straight line inclined downward and outward; each of those lines is annotated “INCD” (inclination of ballast side).  At the base of the slope on the left is the coordinate “YL” marking the lateral extent of the ballast prism on the left, and on the right “YR” similarly marks the right‐hand limit.

The table under discussion defines the complete set of input fields available for configuring a “load train” within a structural-analysis context (for example in the ELLA or SOFILOAD programs). Each row identifies one parameter (the “Item”), offers a concise “Description,” specifies the physical “Unit,” and gives a “Default” value where applicable. Below is a detailed walkthrough of every entry:

1.  TYPE  
    – Description: Literal identifier of the load-train pattern to apply (e.g. CONS for a constant load, or any named standard such as LM71, SW/0, HB, etc.).  
    – Unit: LIT (literal text)  
    – Default: CONS  

2.  P1, P2, P3, P4  
    – Description: Up to four primary magnitudes defining wheel or axle loads (classes or absolute values depending on TYPE). These form the moving concentrated loads.  
    – Unit: kN (for forces) or m (for moments, in certain train definitions)  
    – Default: user-supplied (*)  

3.  P5  
    – Description: Residual area load applied to spare zones (no dynamic factors or centrifugal forces). Used to cover:  
      • The triangular/rectangular areas outside the constant-width train footprint but inside the lane edges,  
      • Pathway strips between parallel lanes,  
      • Entire lane area for pedestrian or similar group loads.  
    – Unit: kN/m²  
    – Default: (*)  

4.  P6, P7  
    – P6: Wind loading (area or line load, depending on code convention).  
    – P7: Height of wind attack area (for horizontal loads) or elevation of line load.  
    – Units: P6 is code-specific (–), P7 is [m].  
    – Default: (*)  

5.  P8  
    – Description: Parameter controlling braking or acceleration loads, sign determined by the train’s moving direction. ELLA/SOFILOAD can vary or disable it programmatically.  
    – Unit: code-specific (–)  
    – Default: (*)  

6.  P9  
    – Description: Vertical height of the mass center for centrifugal effects or cross-fall brake moments.  
    – Unit: [m]  
    – Default: (*)  

7.  PFAC  
    – Description: Global multiplier for all concentrated and residual loads of the train. Commonly selected from a standard list (0.75…1.46 per EN 1991–2).  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: 1.0  

8.  PFAV  
    – Description: Factor for favorable (reducing) load effects. Applied only to wheel loads for road trains; defaults vary by code (e.g. 0.0 for LM71, 1.0 for others).  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: (*)  

9.  WIDT  
    – Description: Overall transverse width of the load train pattern. If zero, no residual area loads are generated.  
    – Unit: [m]  
    – Default: (*)  

10. PHI, PHIS  
    – PHI: Explicit impact factor for bending moments.  
    – PHIS: Explicit impact factor for shear forces.  
    – Units: –  
    – Defaults: (*) for both  

11. V  
    – Description: Running speed of the load train for dynamic‐amplification computations.  
    – Unit: km/h  
    – Default: (*)  

12. FUGA  
    – Description: Amplification factor for train masses to compute centrifugal forces.  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: 1.0  

13. XCON  
    – Description: Minimum spacing (convoy distance) when the same train is repeated behind itself. Defines the gap between the last axle of one set and the first axle of the next.  
    – Unit: [m]  
    – Default: 0  

14. YEX  
    – Description: Eccentricity of the entire train pattern within the lane (positive/negative lateral shift). For rail codes, a default of ±r/18 is recommended.  
    – Unit: [m]  
    – Default: 0.0  

15. DIR  
    – Description: Longitudinal direction in which the train is applied:  
      • B = both directions (default)  
      • R = positive (rightward in model)  
      • L = negative (leftward)  
      • N = suppress application (no dynamic factors)  
    – Unit: LIT  
    – Default: B  

16. DIRT  
    – Description: Transverse‐loading direction control, same code as DIR. “N” will completely suppress lateral loads.  
    – Unit: LIT  
    – Default: B  

Notes on Usage and Interactions:  
• If XCON>0 the train pattern repeats automatically at that spacing.  
• Residual area loads (P5) only appear if WIDT>0 and according to lane topology.  
• PFAC and PFAV allow consistent scaling of standardized trains for classification or code adjustments.  
• DIR=N disables all dynamic, braking, velocity, and wind loads—but user may override impact filters via ELLA options.  
• For multi-body dynamics (TREX record), masses and springs can be generated instead of prescribing P-values.  
• Custom or “USER” TYPE definitions may bypass standard axle patterns but retain PFAC/PFAV and other tuning parameters; the user must then manually ensure proper P5 deduction and convoy spacing.

The table “TRAI” defines all the parameters needed to generate, position and scale moving‐load models (trains, road convoys, pedestrian bands, wind‐and‐traffic combinations, multi‐body dynamic assemblies) in a finite‐element or influence‐line analysis tool.  For a Retrieval‐Augmented Generation (RAG) vector‐store you can think of each row as one “load train definition” with these key fields:

1. Load‐Train Identifier (P1)  
   • A code or literal: e.g. HA, HB (pedestrian, per BS 5400/BD 37‐01), IRC AA/B, BRO types (Swedish), LM71, SW/0, HSLM, RFAT, ASRT, RL, UIC71, USER (a purely custom set of axle‐loads).  
   • Use this to group or filter all subsequent parameters.  

2. Convoy Spacing (XCON)  
   • If present, causes the same train pattern to repeat, maintaining at least XCON distance from end‐of‐last‐load to start‐of‐next.  
   • Units: length (m).  

3. Residual Area Load (P5)  
   • Uniform area pressure applied outside the train’s constant‐width footprint:  
     – Between train width and lane polygon,  
     – Between lane 0 and any other lanes,  
     – Entire area for load group GR4.  
   • No dynamic impact factors, no centrifugal forces.  
   • Units: force/area (kN/m²).  

4. Global Multipliers (PFAC, PFAV)  
   • PFAC: standard load‐group multiplier (e.g. 0.75, 0.83, … 1.46 per EN 1991-2 6.3.2(3)).  
   • PFAV: favorable‐loading factor (EN 1990 GRP 13/14 & 23/24).  
     – Road loads: only applied to wheel loads.  
     – Defaults: railway LM71 → 0.0, other rail → 1.0, most road → 0.0.  

5. Lateral Eccentricity (YEX)  
   • Offset of the entire train from lane center (±r/18 default for rail per EN 1991-2 6.3.5).  
   • A positive value shifts to the right (in traffic direction), negative to the left.  

6. Movement Direction (DIR)  
   • “+” (forward), “–” (reverse), “N” (neutral) or “B” (bidirectional).  
   • Influences brake‐load sign, whether impact factors apply (none if DIR=N), preset wind and velocity to zero, and internal load‐sequence ordering.  

7. Wind Load (P6, P7, DIRT)  
   • P6: wind pressure magnitude (line or area load).  
   • P7: height of wind attack band.  
   • DIRT: optional override of sign convention (default: positive = from right).  
   • Combined traffic+wind may be defined as area load (P6 on height band P7) or line load (AASHTO style).  

8. Braking/Acceleration Load (P8)  
   • Magnitude and sign follow DIR: positive→braking, negative→accelerating.  
   • If DIR=B, the solver (ELLA/SOFILOAD) may toggle or suppress this load.  

9. Multibody‐Dynamics Extension (TREX)  
   • When performing MBD analysis, TREX can produce rigid‐body masses (bogie, wheel), connecting springs/dampers.  
   • Masses may be absolute (+) or fractional (–) of total mass.  
   • See record TREX for full syntax.  

10. Supplemental Definitions (TRPL, TRBL, LANE, COPY)  
    • TRPL / TRBL let you append extra loads (point, line, bracket loads) to any train.  
    • LANE assigns the train to a specific traffic lane or path.  
    • COPY duplicates a previous TRAI line with modifications.  

11. Special Notes for USER Trains  
    • When P1=USER, no axle or area patterns are auto‐generated, but dynamic‐factor and eccentricity rules still apply.  
    • The default P5 must be subtracted for areas now loaded by USER.  
    • Check inter‐load distances carefully—user patterns can shift standard spacing.  

12. Units, Defaults & References  
    • Lengths in meters, forces in kN or kN/m², frequencies (FRB) in 1/s.  
    • Default eccentricity ±r/18, PFAC and PFAV defaults per load type (rail vs. road).  
    • See EN 1990/1-2, BS 5400/BD 37-01, AASHTO, AS 5100, French Fascicule 61, Indian IRC 6-2000, Japanese Road Assoc., Swedish BRO, UIC71, EC Annex 2, etc.  

In indexing this table for a RAG system, each field can be vectorized to allow similarity searches by load‐train type, dynamic factor requirements, multi‐body‐dynamics flags, wind/traffic interactions, and regional code standards. Using the “See also” pointers (COPY, TRPL, TRBL, LANE, TREX) lets you pull in related definition tables. By mapping every parameter to a semantic key (e.g. “PFAC→impactMultiplier”), you ensure any query for “heavy railway fatigue trains” or “multi‐body dynamics wheel mass” will return exactly the TRAI rows, plus any TREX extensions, that match.

The table “Parameters for multibody dynamics” defines seven key quantities you can pass (for example, via the TREX record) when setting up a moving‐train model composed of rigid bodies (car body, bogie, wheels) interconnected by springs and dampers. All entries share the same four‐column structure:

 1. Item  
    – A short, unique code used in the input deck.  
 2. Description  
    – A brief English label of what the parameter represents.  
 3. Unit  
    – Physical units (or “–” if dimensionless).  
 4. Default  
    – The value assumed if the parameter is omitted.

Below is a parameter‐by‐parameter breakdown:

• DAB  
   – “Modal Damping of body support.”  
   – Unit: dimensionless (–).  
   – Default: 0.0  
   – Comments: Represents the damping ratio at the car-body mounting; zero means purely undamped if not explicitly set.

• BOGI  
   – “Load value of bogie.”  
   – Unit: –/kN (a multiplier acting on a reference load, expressed in kN).  
   – Default: 0.0  
   – Comments: Defines the static preload or equivalent mass of each bogie. Zero disables inertial effects unless overridden.

• FRBO  
   – “Frequency for bogie Spring Cbo.”  
   – Unit: 1/sec (natural frequency).  
   – Default: ∞ (infinite)  
   – Comments: An infinite default effectively makes the bogie‐to‐body connector infinitely stiff (no relative translation) if no finite value is supplied.

• DABO  
   – “Modal Damping of bogie support.”  
   – Unit: dimensionless (–).  
   – Default: 0.0  
   – Comments: Damping ratio in the bogie mounts; with zero default, energy loss in that joint is inactive.

• WHEE  
   – “Load value of wheel.”  
   – Unit: –/kN (multiplier on wheel load).  
   – Default: 0.0  
   – Comments: Defines each wheel’s equivalent static load or mass contribution; must be specified for dynamic wheel effects.

• FRWH  
   – “Frequency for wheel spring Cwh.”  
   – Unit: 1/sec (natural frequency).  
   – Default: ∞ (infinite)  
   – Comments: Infinite stiffness at the wheel‐bogie interface if not otherwise defined, i.e., no suspension deflection.

• DAWH  
   – “Modal Damping of wheel support.”  
   – Unit: dimensionless (–).  
   – Default: 0.0  
   – Comments: Damping ratio in the wheel suspension; zero implies no damping at the unsprung mass.

Usage Notes:  
– In a multi‐body dynamics analysis (record TREX), you would normally specify at least the load values (BOGI, WHEE) and spring frequencies (FRBO, FRWH). If you leave frequencies infinite and damping zero, you collapse the model into a single rigid system without spring–mass–damper dynamics.  
– All damping coefficients (DAB, DABO, DAWH) are modal ratios; to introduce physical energy dissipation you must provide nonzero values.  
– Because default load and damping values are zero, omission is equivalent to disabling that component’s dynamic contribution.  
– The choice of units (1/sec for frequency, dimensionless for damping, –/kN for loads) follows standard conventions in EN 1991-2 and related multi‐body‐dynamics formulations.  
– For more elaborate train definitions—including axle spacings, track irregularities, centrifugal, braking or wind loads—you would combine these TREX parameters with TRAI, TRPL or TRBL records as described in the surrounding specification.

The provided table, titled “Table of most important Standard Load Trains,” is a two-column reference listing the most commonly used predefined traffic and area‐loading patterns (P1 codes) in the TRAI/TRPL/TRBL records of the RSTAB/SCIA Engineer environment.  Each row associates a short identifier (first column) with a concise description of the corresponding load train or area loading (second column).  These entries cover railway models, fatigue spectra, heavy goods vehicles according to various national standards, and highway/bridge design loads.

Columns  
• P1 Code: A mnemonic tag for each standard load train or area loading.  These codes are entered in the TRAI record’s first parameter to invoke the predefined pattern.  
• Definition: A brief textual description of the load train, including references to the governing design standard (e.g., Eurocode, BS 5400, AASHTO, CSA, NBR).

Rows (key entries)

1. USER  
   – Constant Area Loading P5 or fully user-defined load train.  Use this when you want to impose a uniform area load or specify every wheel/axle position manually, but still retain impact factors, dynamic allowances, etc.  

2. Railway Load Models (Eurocode 1 Part 2 & BS EN 1991-2)  
   – LM1: Double‐axle load model 1 (Eurocode 1-2).  
   – LM2: Single‐axle load model 2 (Eurocode 1-2).  
   – LM3: Special case load model 3 (Eurocode 1-2).  
   – SV, SOV: Special vehicles (BS EN 1991-2).  
   – LM4: Pedestrian load model 4 (Eurocode 1-2).  

3. Fatigue Load Models (Eurocode 1 Part 3)  
   – FLM1 to FLM4: Fatigue load models 1 through 4, for long-term spectral or repetitive loading checks according to Eurocode 1-3.  

4. Heavy Goods and Truck Loading  
   – SLW: Heavy load truck (DIN / ÖNORM / IAB).  
   – LKW: Standard truck per national country code.  
   – LKWD: German truck definition when working in Austrian projects.  
   – LKWA: Austrian‐specific truck model.  
   – NBR: Brazilian load trains according to NBR 7188 / NB6 (analogous to SLW).  

5. Highway and Bridge Live Loads  
   – HS: Highway live load (AASHTO).  
   – HT: Highway truck load (AASHTO).  
   – CAN: Highway live load (Canadian Standard CSA).  

Usage Notes  
• Any of these P1 codes can be combined with TRPL (axle positions) and TRBL (wheel patterns) records to refine spacings or include auxiliary loads.  
• Impact factors, braking/acceleration loads, wind or centrifugal forces, and residual area loads (P5) are managed by supplementary TRAI parameters (PFAC, PFAV, XCON, DIR, etc.) but reference the same baseline train pattern.  
• If “USER” is chosen, the modeler must manually ensure:  
  1. Deduction of default P5 loads from areas redefined by the USER train.  
  2. Verification of convoy spacing, since automatic elements may alter the nominal end-to-end distance of the train.  

By selecting one of these codes in your load definitions, the software automatically applies the correct axle loads, spacings, widths and dynamic allowance factors in accordance with the stated standard—streamlining the setup of railway, truck, pedestrian, or fatigue analyses.

The image is entitled “Figure 5.7: Load model 1” and consists of two distinct parts—a simplified cross‐section at the top and a plan-view sketch of possible axle positions across three parallel traffic lanes in the lower portion.

1. Cross-section (top strip):
- A heavy, hatched rectangular block represents the pavement or bridge deck slab in section.  
- Two black downward arrows penetrate the slab from above. Each arrow is annotated “αQi Qi,k” (or a slight variation in subscript on the second arrow), indicating that the characteristic axle load Qik is multiplied by a dynamic/amplification factor αQi before being imposed on the deck.  
- This strip establishes how vertical wheel forces are applied through the thickness of the structure.

2. Plan view of lane layout and tandem axle placements:
- Three horizontal bands, each bounded by thin parallel lines, represent three adjacent notional lanes. The middle band is filled with a fine dot pattern, denoting the “active” or loaded lane in a typical scenario; the top and bottom bands are drawn as plain (unshaded) lanes to show alternative positions.  
- In each lane band a pair of identical wheel clusters is shown—a tandem axle system. Each cluster consists of two small solid squares side-by-side, each with a tiny crosshair overlay to mark the wheel contact point. Short radial lines extend from each square to suggest loading direction or wheel orientation.  
- The two wheel clusters in a given lane lie on the lane’s longitudinal centerline. Dimension arrows between clusters in the same lane indicate a longitudinal spacing of 2.00 m.  
- Transverse offset dimensions of 0.5 m are shown from each cluster to the nearest lane boundary, illustrating the Eurocode requirement that consecutive loads must remain at least 0.5 m apart when traveling in adjacent lanes.  
- By repeating the same tandem-axle symbol in the top, middle, and bottom lane bands, the diagram makes clear that Load Model 1 may be applied independently to any one of several parallel lanes, without synchronizing the positions across lanes.  

Altogether the sketch communicates:  
• A single tandem axle (two wheels per axle) moving centrally in a notional 2.5–3.5 m-wide carriageway lane.  
• Axle spacing of 2 m and a minimum 0.5 m clearance to the lane edge (or to another loaded vehicle in an adjacent lane).  
• The applied force per wheel is the characteristic axle load Q multiplied by an impact factor αQi, applied vertically to the deck.  

These graphical conventions align with EN 1991-2 § 4.3.2, where global effects of tandem systems are assessed by placing them centrally on notional lanes and ensuring the specified minimum eccentricity and clearance criteria.

The excerpted table defines the parameter set for Load Model “FLM3,” a complete truck configuration used primarily in fatigue‐based design checks. FLM3 represents a truck with two double‐axle groups spaced 6.0 m apart; all values are applied concurrently and none may be omitted even if one axle position produces more favorable results. Below is a structured description suitable for inclusion in a RAG (Retrieval‐Augmented Generation) vector store:

1. Table Identity  
   • load_model: “FLM3”  
   • description: “Complete truck with two double axles at 6.0 m spacing, for fatigue design”  

2. Column Definitions  
   – P1 = Class (dimensionless)  
     · Identifies one of three standardized load‐classes.  
     · Values: [300, 200, 100]  
   – P2 = Axle load [kN]  
     · Nominal vertical force per axle group.  
     · Matches P1 class values: [300 kN, 200 kN, 100 kN].  
   – P3 = Reserved [kN]  
     · Placeholder parameter; currently zero for all classes.  
     · Values: [0, 0, 0].  
   – P4 = Traffic lane uniformly distributed load [kN/m²]  
     · Represents the additional distributed load over the deck area occupied by the vehicle.  
     · Values: [9.0, 2.5, 2.5] correspond to P1 classes 300, 200, 100 respectively.  
   – P5 = Residual area load [kN/m²]  
     · Background (“residual”) uniform load applied to the remainder of the deck beyond the immediate wheel paths.  
     · Constant: [2.5, 2.5, 2.5] across all classes.  
   – P8 = Brake loading [kN]  
     • Represents concentrated braking forces.  
     • Values: [“*”, 0.0, 0.0]. The asterisk on the 300 kN class indicates a special or user‐defined brake load; classes 200 and 100 impose no brake load.

3. Units and Conventions  
   • All forces (P2, P3, P8) are in kilonewtons.  
   • Surface loads (P4, P5) are in kN per square meter.  
   • Placeholder or user‐specified entries are marked with “*” and must be defined prior to analysis.

4. Contextual Notes (Eurocode EN 1991-2)  
   • This FLM3 definition supplements the standard Model 1 load trains by focusing on fatigue effects under repeated truck passages.  
   • No axle load reduction is allowed: both axles of each double assembly contribute fully to permanent stress cycles.  
   • Synchronization or clipping of loads in adjacent lanes is managed separately; FLM3 itself does not enforce lateral offsets.  
   • Brake loads are only activated when P8 is explicitly defined; otherwise, dynamic amplification and distributed braking actions are omitted.

5. Usage in Software (e.g. ELLA)  
   • The class parameter P1 drives selection of axle spacing, dynamic amplification factors, and any transverse offsets needed should P2 exceed standard lane width.  
   • P3 remains reserved for future extensions or national‐annex customization.  
   • P4 and P5 feed directly into the UDL (uniformly distributed load) generators for live‐load envelope calculations.  
   • P8 is passed to concentrated‐force routines when nonzero.

By indexing each parameter name, unit, permitted values and intended function, this description enables RAG‐based systems to retrieve and apply FLM3 data consistently across analysis scenarios.

The image is a schematic, plan-view illustration of the “Load Train SLW,” as defined in various European bridge design codes (DIN 1072, ÖNORM B 4002, Spanish IAP, Brazilian NBR). It shows how concentrated wheel (axle) loads and complementary lane loads are arranged across a traffic lane for static and dynamic analysis. Below is a step-by-step description:

1. Coordinate System and Orientation  
   • At the top left of the drawing is the origin “O” with an arrow pointing right, indicating the positive x-direction along the lane.  
   • The horizontal baseline represents the centreline of the bridge deck or lane axis.

2. Side (“Rest-of-Traffic”) Loads – P3  
   • On both the far left and far right of the diagram, immediately adjacent to the deck edges, are two rectangular blocks labeled “P3.”  
   • These blocks represent the uniform area loads (basic traffic band) that fill the remainder of the lane outside the concentrated axle loads.  
   • P3 is the load intensity applied to the portions of the lane not occupied by the heavy train axles.

3. Concentrated Axle Loads – 3.33 × P1  
   • Between the two P3 regions are three downward-pointing arrows, evenly spaced, which represent the successive wheel (axle) loads of the train.  
   • A text label “3.33 × P1” is placed above the centreline of the three arrows, indicating that each arrowed load is 3.33 times the basic axle load P1 (to account for dynamic amplification or code-specified grouping effects).  

4. Geometry and Spacing  
   • Beneath the baseline are distance markers showing uniform 1.5 m spacings:  
     – From the inner face of the left P3 block to the first axle load arrow: 1.5 m  
     – Between the first and second arrow: 1.5 m  
     – Between the second and third arrow: 1.5 m  
     – From the third arrow to the inner face of the right P3 block: 1.5 m  
   • Thus, the entire “train” width (axle-loaded zone) spans 4 × 1.5 m = 6.0 m.

5. Caption and Reference  
   • Centered below the drawing is the caption: “Figure 5.17: Load Train SLW.”  
   • This identifies the schematic as part of a larger set of figures detailing standard load configurations for bridge analysis.

6. Interpretation in Bridge Design Context  
   • P1 refers to the characteristic axle load of the train (e.g. 100 kN or 150 kN, depending on the national code variant).  
   • The factor 3.33 accounts for grouping of multiple axles and any dynamic or impact factor applied per code.  
   • The P3 regions carry the uniform distributed “complementary” traffic load in the rest of the lane.  
   • Designers use this layout to ensure the bridge deck is checked for worst-case bending and shear under both concentrated and distributed rail loads.

Overall, this figure conveys the required positions, magnitudes, and spacings of train axle loads (enhanced by a 3.33 × P1 factor) and the adjacent uniform lane loads (P3). It is a fundamental reference for setting up load cases in structural models of railway bridges under the SLW (standard traffic) loading regime.

The provided figure is a clean, two-dimensional schematic of the so-called “Load Train LKW” (heavy-truck load pattern) used in many European bridge-design standards. Visually, it consists of a single horizontal line (the bridge deck surface) on which three load regions are imposed: two uniformly distributed side strips and two concentrated central loads. Below is a step-by-step breakdown of what you see:

1. Coordinate Reference  
   • Above the drawing is a small axis indicator: the point “0” marks the origin, and an arrow pointing to the right is labeled “x,” showing that all horizontal distances are measured in the positive x-direction.

2. Uniform Side Loads (P3)  
   • At the leftmost and rightmost portions of the deck line are two upright rectangular blocks, each labeled “P3.”  
   • These blocks represent a uniform area load (traffic band) filling the remaining lane width outside the moving load train.  
   • Each P3 zone sits directly on the deck line and extends vertically a modest amount (purely schematic) to indicate that this region is covered by the basic, static traffic loading P3.

3. Concentrated Central Loads (Dynamic Wheel Action)  
   • Between the two P3 blocks are two large downward arrows, denoting the tandem wheel loads of a heavy vehicle’s axles as they pass over the bridge.  
   • The left arrow is thicker and is annotated “6.66 * P1.” The right arrow is slightly thinner (or simply drawn the same but labeled differently) and is annotated “3.33 * P1.”  
   • Here P1 is the base characteristic wheel load intensity; the multipliers (6.66 and 3.33) distribute the total vehicle load between its two axles according to standard axle-spacing rules for trucks (heavier on the lead axle, lighter on the trailing axle).

4. Dimensional Layout  
   • Directly beneath the deck line, three horizontal dimensions are indicated in meters:  
     – From the face of the left P3 block to the centerline of the left arrow: 1.5 m  
     – Between the two arrows: 3.0 m  
     – From the centerline of the right arrow to the face of the right P3 block: 1.5 m  
   • These distances define a total dynamic‐loading width of 6.0 m (1.5 m + 3.0 m + 1.5 m), matching typical heavy-truck lane widths in DIN and ÖNORM standards.

5. Caption  
   • Below the diagram is the text “Figure 5.18: Load Train LKW,” identifying it as the reference illustration for the heavy-truck load pattern LKW in the document.

Contextual Notes (from the accompanying text):  
- “Load Train LKW” is one of the classical moving-load arrangements specified by standards such as DIN 1072, ÖNORM B 4002, Spanish IAP or Brazilian NBR.  
- P3 represents the static, uniform traffic band that occupies the remainder of the lane outside the moving axles.  
- P1 is the wheel-load intensity for the dynamic train; the total combined axle load (6.66 + 3.33)·P1 approximates the standard design axle forces (e.g., 390 kN with impact factor).  
- The central moving loads span a 3.0 m width (per most codes), while the side bands are each 1.5 m wide.  
- National variants may alter these widths (2.5 m in ÖNORM or minimum 4.0 m in IAP), but the sketch here follows the classical LKW geometry.

The table presents a concise summary of standard “load trains” as specified in various bridge‐loading norms (German DIN 1072, Austrian OENORM B 4002, Spanish IAP and Brazilian NBR). It is organized in three columns—“Axial Loads [kN]”, “P3 [kN/m²]” and “P5 [kN/m²]”—and one row for each train designation. Below is a detailed description of its structure and content:

1.  Train Designation (first column)
    •  SLW 30, SLW 60  
       –  SLW = “Standard Live Load” trains per DIN 1072 / OENORM.  
    •  LKW 3, 6, 9, 12, 16  
       –  LKW = Truck loads with dual‐axle configurations, numbers roughly indicate total axle load in tonnes.  
    •  LKWA 16, 25  
       –  “A” variants of the LKW series, slightly higher total loadings.  
    •  NBR 24, 30, 36, 45, 12  
       –  Brazilian norms (NBR) referencing either SLW‐equivalent (e.g. NBR 24 uses 80 kN = SLW 30 axle) or LKW‐equivalent (NBR 12 uses 80 kN + 40 kN).

2.  Axial Loads [kN] (second column)
    •  Single‐value entries (e.g. SLW 30 → 100 kN; SLW 60 → 200 kN) denote one concentrated load per axle, applied on the moving load band.  
    •  Dual‐value entries separated by “+” (e.g. LKW 3 → 20 + 10) denote two axles: first (primary) axle load and second (secondary) axle load.  
    •  NBR lines specify which reference they follow: “80(SLW)” means use the 80 kN SLW axle, “80/40(LKW)” reproduces the 80 + 40 kN truck combination.

3.  P3 [kN/m²] (third column)
    •  Surface load intensity applied over the “traffic band” outside the wheel contact area.  
    •  Values vary from 3.0 to 5.0 kN/m² depending on the train type and standard:  
       –  SLW trains always use 5.0.  
       –  Light trucks (LKW 3) use 3.0, mid‐range trucks (LKW 6–12) use 4.0, heavier variants rise to 5.0.  
       –  Brazilian NBR SLW-equivalents mirror the SLW P3 values (4.0 or 5.0 depending on the nominal axle load).

4.  P5 [kN/m²] (fourth column)
    •  Uniform “background” load on all remaining areas within the lane (basic area load).  
    •  Generally set between 2.0 and 3.0 kN/m²:  
       –  SLW and heavy‐truck variants default to 3.0.  
       –  LKW 3/6 use 2.0.  
    •  The SLW 60 entry bears an asterisk on “3.0*” indicating that under OENORM B 4002 this band width is 2.5 m (P5=2.5 kN/m²) and under Spanish IAP the band is widened to 4.0 m (P5=4.0 kN/m²).

Additional contextual notes (drawn from the accompanying text):  
•  Standard band width for moving loads is 3.0 m (2.5 m in OENORM, 4.0 m for Spanish IAP).  
•  P3 loads cover the “traffic band,” P5 covers the rest of each lane.  
•  Secondary lane loading (DIR N) can be applied without dynamic impact factors.  
•  For advanced software modules, rather than stacking P2/P4 trains use two synchronized lanes, each with its own load train; the secondary lane must deactivate its dynamic impact factor (set to 1.0), using P5 as defined for P3.  
•  All trains split their loads symmetrically to left and right of the lane axis.  
•  Brake loads (P8) and wind (P6) are handled separately: P6=1.25 kN/m², P7=3.50 m (gust length), P8=1.00 (horizontal brake‐force factor), with DIN specifying 30–100 % brake‐load ratios (max 900 kN) and IAP 140–720 kN.

The image is a schematic, one‐dimensional “plan‐view” of the standardized Load Train designated HB (heavy loading) or NB (normal loading).  It is labeled in the caption as “Figure 5.20: Load Train HB, NB.”  In essence the diagram shows a straight reference line (representing the lane centerline of a bridge or roadway) on which two types of loads are superimposed:

 1. Traffic band (uniform distributed) loads at the ends, each of magnitude P3, represented by two short vertical “risers” topped by horizontal caps on both the far left and far right of the baseline.  The blocks are labeled “P3.”

 2. Concentrated axle loads in the central span, represented by four identical downward‐pointing arrows arrayed in a row.  Each arrow is labeled “P1” (the standard single‐axle load intensity).

Beneath the baseline, the spacing is dimensioned in meters as follows (from left to right):

 • From the face of the left P3 block to the first axle arrow: 25.0 m  
 • From the first axle arrow to the second axle arrow: 1.8 m  
 • From the second axle arrow to the third axle arrow: x m (variable, user‐defined distance)  
 • From the third axle arrow to the fourth axle arrow: 1.8 m  
 • From the fourth axle arrow to the face of the right P3 block: 25.0 m  

Thus the total loaded length (including end band loads and axle spacings) is 25.0 + 1.8 + x + 1.8 + 25.0 = P3‐zone + P1‐zone + P3‐zone, giving a symmetric arrangement around the central pair of axles.

Above the left and right blocks is the text “P3,” and above each of the four arrows is the text “P1.”  There are no further dimensions on the vertical risers other than their implied infinitesimal thickness; the focus is entirely on the longitudinal layout.

Contextually, this configuration is used to represent the simultaneous application of  
• A heavy (HA/HB) or normal (NB) axle pattern, determined by a default axle‐loading parameter P1 (commonly 30.0 kN, but selectable between 24.0 and 45.0 so that actual axle load = 10 × P1), and  
• A uniform traffic‐band load P3 (magnitude varies with eccentricity factor P2 and band‐position factor P3, per standards such as BS 5400 or BD 37/88).

In the BS 5400 variant, four positions of the P3 band are available (centered, doubly centered, offset right or left by one‐quarter lane width), controlled via P2 (offset) and P3 (load multiplier).  NB loading in TMH7 is applied without additional life‐load combinations, thus only P1 and P3 are relevant here; any other parameters (P2–P4) are ignored for NB.

The image is a simplified side‐elevation sketch of a bridge deck under the so-called “Load Train HS” (one- or two-axle truck) from the HL-93 loading specification. At the very bottom, nearly the full width of the deck is indicated by two closely spaced horizontal lines; these represent the top flange of a girder or the underside of the deck slab. Sandwiched between those two lines, a long, narrow rectangular band is shaded by the label “P3,” signifying the uniform, longitudinally distributed lane load (traffic band) acting on the deck surface.

Above the deck, two vertically downward‐pointing arrows of equal length are drawn side by side. Each arrowhead sits directly on the upper deck line, marking the positions of two wheel‐loads (either a tandem‐axle or single‐axle configuration). Each arrow is labeled “P,” denoting the magnitude of the concentrated point load (in the full HL-93 model, each wheel is 32 kip or 145 kN).  

To the left of those arrows, a hollow circle with the letter “O” inside it sits slightly above the deck. A dimension line runs horizontally from the circle to the location of the first (front) wheel‐load arrow. This denotes the longitudinal offset, P₀ (often called the origin offset), between the start of the loaded area and the first axle. Although the numeric value is not shown in the sketch, in practice P₀ is specified to position the axle loads with respect to the girder ends or reference section.

Beneath the entire figure, the caption reads “Figure 5.21: Load Train HS.” The sketch encapsulates the two essential components of the HS loading model:  
  • A uniform strip load P3 (fixed width, typically 3.048 m or 10 ft) that runs the full length of the vehicle path.  
  • One or two concentrated wheel loads P, spaced by the axle distance P4 (which in design models can vary or be fixed).  

In a design program, P3 would actuate the lane‐load model across all girders in its width, while the two discrete Ps would produce peak shear and moment envelopes at the axle positions. Together, they form the classic AASHTO HS loading pattern used for ultimate‐limit and shear checks.

The table summarizes five standardized load-train options—three older AASHTO “HS” classes from 1944 and two versions of the modern HL-93 model (one in U.S. customary units, one in SI). Each row is indexed by P1, the “load train” selector, and supplies three key parameters:

1. P2 (HS or HL-93): axle or total concentrated loads  
2. P3: uniform (lane or distributed) load intensity  
3. P4: axle-spacing or inter-axle distance  

Detailed breakdown:

1. P1 = 10 → Load train HS10-44  
   • P2 = (13.0, 9.0) kip  
     – Represents a two-axle configuration: 13.0 kip on the lead axle, 9.0 kip on the rear axle.  
   • P3 = 0.32 klf (kips per linear foot)  
     – Uniform, strip-width loading for longitudinal design.  
   • P4 = 0  
     – No variable spacing; the HS loads are applied at the actual axle locations without additional offset.

2. P1 = 15 → Load train HS15-44  
   • P2 = (19.5, 13.5) kip  
     – Tandem-axle pair: 19.5 kip on the front axle, 13.5 kip on the second.  
   • P3 = 0.48 klf  
   • P4 = 0  

3. P1 = 20 → Load train HS20-44  
   • P2 = (26.0, 18.0) kip  
     – Heavier tandem pair: 26.0 kip and 18.0 kip.  
   • P3 = 0.64 klf  
   • P4 = 0  

   Notes on HS classes:
   - These three “HS” trains originate from AASHTO’s 1944 standard.  
   - P1 (10, 15, 20) also serves as the old-class identifier for shear checks.

The table before you defines a series of design load “trains” used in bridge and girder analysis.  Each row corresponds to one load‐train variant, and the four columns (P1 through P4) specify the key parameters you would store or index when building a RAG-backed vector store.  Here is a detailed breakdown:

1.  Column headings and their meanings  
    •  P1 (Load-Train Code)  
       –  For the old AASHTO vehicles (1944): codes 10, 15, 20 correspond to H10-44, H15-44, H20-44.  
       –  For the modern HL-93 family: “US,” “SI” for the standard vehicles, “US2,” “SI2” for the compact two-axle variants, and “USF,” “SIF” for the fatigue-specific versions.  
    •  Load Train (Name/Type)  
       –  Identifies the official load model designation: H10-44, H15-44, H20-44 or HL 93 (with “(fat)” appended for fatigue versions).  
    •  P2 (Total Concentrated Load)  
       –  The total axle load applied by the vehicle model.  
       –  Units: kip in US-English entries; kN in SI entries.  
    •  P3 (Lane or Line Load)  
       –  A uniform line load representing a continuous traffic band or per-lane loading.

    •  P4 (Axle/Truck Spacing)  
       –  Distance(s) between axle groups.  A “–” indicates no prescribed spacing (the model may assume a single spacing or is governed by another rule).

The figure is a simple 2-D schematic of the “LM 71” (also called UIC 71 or RU under BS 5400) design train load model. It shows, laid out along the horizontal (x-) axis, both the constant line—“lane”—loads and the concentrated axle loads that together define LM 71 for bridge and track structural checks.  

Key graphic elements:  
• Horizontal baseline: a thin line representing the track level (sleepers and ballast interface).  
• Distributed lane‐load blocks: two solid rectangular blocks (one on the far left, one on the far right) sitting on the baseline. Each block is labeled “80 kN/m,” indicating a uniform load intensity applied along the rail seat (this is P3 in the code).  
• Four vertical arrows: between the two distributed‐load blocks there are four identical downward‐pointing arrows. Above the arrows the legend reads “250 250 250 250 kN.” Each arrowhead represents a concentrated wheel‐set load of 250 kN (code parameter P2).  
• Dimensional annotations under the arrows: from the left edge of the left lane‐load block to the first concentrated load is 0.8 m; between each adjacent pair of axle loads is 1.6 m; and from the fourth axle load to the right lane-load block is again 0.8 m. The pattern therefore is 0.8 – 1.6 – 1.6 – 1.6 – 0.8 m.  
• Coordinate arrow: at upper right, a small “0 → x” arrow denotes the positive x-direction along the track.  
• Caption: centered beneath the diagram is “Figure 5.31: Load train LM 71 = UIC 71 = RU (BS5400).”  

Interpretation in the context of the code:  
- This loading corresponds to the default four‐axle model (P1 = 0 → “four single loads”) for an excellently maintained track under LM 71.  
- Each concentrated load of 250 kN represents one axle reaction, spaced at the code’s standard 1.6 m centers.  
- The uniform 80 kN/m lane load covers the rail seat areas immediately outside the outermost axles to capture the effect of the remainder of the train’s wheel sets and overall static load distribution.  
- No nosing load (P4) is shown here; if required, a horizontal‐to‐vertical eccentricity or additional lateral action would be superposed separately.  

By superimposing these discrete and distributed loads in a moving‐load analysis, engineers check bending moments, shear forces, deflections and track‐structure interface pressures in bridges and other rail support structures under the specified LM 71 standard.

1. Top band (vehicle outline and dimensions)  
   – A simplified side-elevation silhouette of a tracked armored vehicle (tank) rendered in light grey. It shows a low, rectangular hull, slightly angled front glacis plate, a small turret atop the hull, and a long gun barrel projecting to the left.  
   – Directly above this side view is a rectangular annotation reading “136,08 t,” indicating the vehicle’s total mass.  
   – Below the hull, a double arrow spans the tank’s contact width on the track pads, annotated “–7,32–” (in meters), denoting the total track-to-track width.  
   – To the right of the side view is a front elevation of the same tank: turret in the center, two track units flanking the hull. A double arrow beneath the tracks reads “–4,67–,” marking the distance between the outer edges of the track shoes. A single arrow from the vehicle’s centerline to the outer track face is marked “1,27,” indicating half-track width.

2. Bottom band (rail flatcar load train)  
   – Centered below is a schematic of a multi-axle flat rail wagon supporting the tank. Above the wagon is a second mass annotation, “154,22 t,” representing the combined weight of wagon plus vehicle.  
   – Five vertical arrows drop from the load (from front to rear) onto individual wheelsets or bogie pivots. Each arrow carries a small rectangular label with a load value (in tonnes). From left to right these read approximately:
     • “29,96”  
     • “38,10”  
     • “38,10”  
     • “29,03”  
     • “29,03”  
   – Below the wheelset symbols, a horizontal linear scale shows inter-axle and bogie spacing in meters:  
     • 3,66 m between the first and second wheelset  
     • 2,13 m between the second and third pivot  
     • 6,71 m between the third and fourth wheelset
