   – The flatcar itself is drawn as a long, flat rectangular deck with simple single-line rail track on top; wheelsets are represented by black‐filled circles underneath.

Contextual Note (from STANAG 2021, App. A):  
This figure illustrates one of the standardized military load trains used for determining axle loads and bridge/trainway capacities under NATO’s MLC (Military Load Classification) system. In the sixth edition of the STANAG, Appendix A defines classes P1 (gross vehicle mass: 4, 8, 12… up to 150 t) and for each P1 class three P2 sub-categories:
 – P2 = 1: Single-axle loads (column 4 in the STANAG table)  
 – P2 = 2: Tracked vehicles (column 2)  
 – P2 = 3: Wheeled vehicles (column 3)  
The 136.08 t combat weight and even distribution of axle loads shown here correspond to a tracked-vehicle load train (P2 = 2) for a P1 class appropriate to that mass. This diagram is used to extract per-axle loads and spacings when analyzing rail bridge or track capacity under NATO standardized procedures.

MLC Load trains of the STANAG are given in the sixth edition in appendix A. There are the classes P1 = 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 30 up to 150. For every class we have available:
 P2 = 1 Values from column 4 (Single Axles)
 P2 = 2 Values from column 2 (tracked vehicles)
 P2 = 3 Values from column 3 (Wheeled vehicles)

The table defines all the parameters you need to specify a “free” or arbitrary loading sequence (a load‐train) in ELLA/SOFILOAD.  Every row (“Item”) is one input parameter; the columns give a concise label, a human‐readable description, the unit (when applicable) and a default value.  Below is a structured walkthrough:

1.   P  (kN)  
     – Vertical wheel or axle load. Default = 0.  
2.   PB  (kN)  
     – Longitudinal load component. Positive = braking in travel direction, negative = acceleration. Default = 0.  
3.   PW  (kN)  
     – Transverse horizontal load (e.g. bump, wind). Default = 0.  
4.   PF  (kN)  
     – Equivalent vertical load for centrifugal effects. Default = copy of P if not overridden.  
5.   PFAC  
     – Factor applied to “favourable” load components. Dimensionless. Default = 0.  
6.   DIST  
     – Interpretation of distance metric A.  “ABS” = absolute spacing from reference, “MIN” = minimum spacing constraint. Default = ABS.  
7.   A  (m)  
     – Distance from the previous load point. For the first load this fixes the reference x=0. Default = 0.  
8.   DPOS  (m)  
     – Minimum allowed spacing of this load from the reference point (only applies when DIST=MIN). Default = 0.  
9.   DMIN  (m)  
     – Upstream influence window for special evaluation regions in ELLA. Default = 0.  
10.  DMAX  (m)  
     – Downstream influence window for special cases. Default = 0.  
11.  Y  (m)  
     – Transverse eccentricity of the load relative to the lane centerline. Positive to the right. Default = 0.  
     •  Note: ELLA assumes symmetric load trains.  If you specify a non-zero Y you must also supply a mirrored negative Y at the same A location.  
12.  HW  (m)  
     – Total height of wind attack area (for transverse loads). Default = 0.  
13.  ZW  (m)  
     – Height of purely horizontal forces (torsion lever arm). Default = HW/2.  
14.  HF  (m)  
     – Height of the mass center for centrifugal loads. Default = 0.  
15.  PHI  
     – Impact and special handling bit‐mask. Common bits:  
     1 = apply code UDL impact factor to P,  
     2 = apply code factor to PB,  
     8 = split transverse load if it’s “unfavourable,”  
     16 = treat as area load over full lane width,  
     32 = force centric loading (YEX ignored).  
     Default = 1.  

Wheels and Contact Area  
16.  NW  
     – Number of wheels on this axle (0–7). If zero, P/PB/PW are converted to a line load over lane width WIDT (clipped at lane boundary or distributed by PHI). Default = “*” (see TRAI).  
17.  B  (m)  
     – Span between wheel contact points across lane. If B < WIDT you have a wheel pair; B = WIDT yields full‐width distribution. Default = 0.  
18.  BW  (m)  
     – True width of each wheel contact patch (for area loads or internal COPY uses). Default = 0.  
19.  LW  (m)  
     – Length of wheel contact patch in direction of travel. Default = 0.  

Animation / Multi‐Body Dynamics  
20.  SNO  
     – Section number for visualization/animation. Default = none.  
21.  FRB  (1/s)  
     – Natural frequency of primary body spring (Cb). Default = from TRAI.  
22.  DAB  
     – Modal damping ratio of body support. Default = from TRAI.  
23.  BOGI  (−/kN)  
     – Bogie mass or fraction (positive absolute in kN or negative fraction of total). Default = TRAI.  
24.  FRBO  (1/s)  
     – Natural frequency of bogie spring (Cbo). Default = TRAI.  
25.  DABO  
     – Modal damping of bogie support. Default = TRAI.  
26.  WHEE  (−/kN)  
     – Wheel mass or fraction (same sign convention). Default = TRAI.  
27.  FRWH  (1/s)  
     – Frequency of wheel spring (Cwh). Default = TRAI.  
28.  DAWH  
     – Damping of wheel support. Default = TRAI.  

Additional Records  
•  TRPL  
     – Use this record for free‐form loading trains (the subject of the table above).  
•  TREX  
     – Emits multi‐body‐dynamics entities (masses, springs, dampers).  
•  CONT  
     – Contact node index in a user‐defined train‐structure model. Positive = slave node (receives deformations), negative = just offset for visualization. All non-bridge‐contact nodes of the train must be defined.  

Remarks:  
– The first “A” position uses x=0.  Subsequent A’s accumulate from the last.  
– For distributed loads over lanes (e.g. KEL of HA in BS), PHI bit-flags override the NW logic.  
– ELLA does not use the true contact patch shape for influence line evaluation; only the resultant forces matter.  
– PFAC, DMIN and DMAX allow you to carve out special influence regions for advanced checks (e.g. fatigue, special code clauses).

sections: 5.6 TRPL – Point Load of load train

content:
The diagram is a schematic representation of a user-defined (freely defined) load train as used in the ELLA influence-line evaluation module. It consists of two parallel horizontal lines (representing the lane or beam axis) and a series of point loads, dimension markers, and coordinate references along an x-axis. Below is a detailed breakdown of each element:

1. Coordinate System and Reference Point  
   • A bold arrow at the top right points to the right and is labeled “x,” indicating the positive direction of the longitudinal axis along which the loads travel.  
   • Immediately to the left of the arrow is a small “o” symbol on the top line, marking the first load location, which also serves as the reference point (x = 0.0) for all subsequent distance measurements.  
   • A “+” sign on the top and bottom lines further left marks the origin alignment of the two lane/beam representations.

2. First Load Position and A1  
   • The distance from the origin (“+” sign) to the first load location is shown by a double-arrow bracket labeled “A1” at the far left of the top line.  
   • Directly below this first load position is a single vertical downward arrow labeled “P,” denoting the magnitude of the first point load.

3. Subsequent Point Loads and Inter-Load Distances  
   • Two additional point loads, each represented by a vertical arrow labeled “P,” appear successively to the right on the beam.  
   • Between these arrows, double-headed dimension lines identify the distances from one load point to the next:  
     – The span between the first and second loads is marked “A2.”  
     – The span between the second and third loads is marked “A3.”  
     – A further span beyond the third load is marked “A4,” leading toward the right-hand end of the diagram.

4. Minimum Distance Constraint (DPOS)  
   • On the top line, just to the right of the third point load, a text “≥ DPOS(4)” indicates that the separation from the last defined load to the next load reference point must be at least the minimum distance DPOS associated with load index 4.  
   • This notation highlights the possibility of enforcing either a fixed spacing or a variable spacing (with DPOS as a lower bound) when users define load positions.

5. Symmetry and Coordinate Reinforcement  
   • A second “+” sign on the bottom line aligns with the origin indicator on the top line, underlining that both horizontal lines share the same coordinate system.  
   • Double-headed arrows labeled A2, A3, and A4 also appear on the bottom line, mirroring the top measurements to emphasize that all loads and distances are measured along a single axis common to both lines.

6. Caption  
   • Centered beneath the graphic is the caption “Figure 5.38: Freely defined load train,” providing the figure number and a concise description of the content.

Overall, the image conveys how a sequence of vertical point loads P is positioned along a beam or lane according to user-defined distances (A1, A2, A3, A4), with the very first load establishing the reference origin at x = 0.0. The annotation “≥ DPOS(4)” reminds the user that any spacing to subsequent loads can be constrained by a minimum distance value (DPOS) when defining variable-spacing load trains in ELLA.

sections: 5.6 TRPL – Point Load of load train

content:
The illustration is a schematic from the ELLA user documentation (Figure 5.39) showing how a “single load” is resolved into its constituent force components when applied to a bridge or lane surface. Key elements and annotations are as follows:

1. Bridge/Lane Geometry and Local Axes  
   - A gently curved line across the top of the figure represents the plan or elevation of the bridge deck (or lane surface).  
   - A small right-angle symbol is drawn on that line, with the horizontal leg labeled “x” (the local longitudinal axis, tangent to the deck surface) and the vertical leg labeled “y” (the local normal axis, pointing down through the deck).  

2. The Load Point  
   - A solid black circle immediately beneath the deck line marks the point of application of the concentrated (single) load.  

3. Vertical Component (P, PF)  
   - A vertical arrow, pointing straight down from the load point, is labeled “P, PF.”  
   - “P” denotes the static vertical load (wheel or axle load), while “PF” refers to the dynamic or impact‐factored vertical load (i.e., P multiplied by the code’s UDL factor or v²/g term).  

4. Longitudinal Component (PB)  
   - A horizontal arrow, drawn along the x-direction and pointing to the right, is labeled “PB.”  
   - This represents the longitudinal force at the wheel‐rail interface: positive values correspond to braking loads (in the direction of travel), negative values represent traction or acceleration loads (in the reverse direction).  

5. Transverse Component (PW)  
   - A slanted arrow, directed downward and to the right from the load point, is labeled “PW.”  
   - This arrow indicates the lateral (cross‐track) force component of the wheel load, acting at the plane of the deck.  

6. Eccentricity and Torsion (hs, PF·v²/g)  
   - To the right of the main sketch, a separate small inset shows the same wheel‐load point with a horizontal arrow labeled “PF·v²/g” and a vertical offset “hs.”  
   - This illustrates that the dynamic vertical force PF, applied at the height hs above the lane surface, produces a torsional moment about the deck plane. If the load has finite width B, that moment is modeled as a pair of lateral forces; if the load is truly centric, it becomes a pure twisting moment along the lane axis.  

7. Caption and Cross-References  
   - Below the drawing is the caption “Figure 5.39: Single load and its components.”  
   - The text surrounding the figure (not shown in the sketch but provided in the user context) explains how these force components are entered into the ELLA input records (e.g. TRPL, TREX, CONT) and how options (OPT flags) affect distribution, symmetry, minimum/maximum distances, multi‐body model coupling, etc.  

Overall, this diagram underpins ELLA’s treatment of wheel and axle loads as concentrated forces resolved in three orthogonal directions (vertical, longitudinal, transverse), with additional considerations for dynamic amplification, height‐induced torsion, eccentricity, and distribution over multiple wheels or lane width.

 A freely defined loading by the user comprises an arbitrary number of loads defined relative to
 each other. The first load determines the load reference point (x=0.0). Each further loading is defined with a distance to the previous one.The distance of the point load to the last load point may be either constant or variable with a minimum value. In the latter case and additional minimum distance to the load reference point may be defined with DPOS. For the evaluation in ELLA two additional values DMIN and DMAX may be specified for special cases describing an influence region before and behind the load.
 For the evaluation of the load trains in ELLA symmetric load trains are expected. Thus, any definition of Y should be complemented with a second definition at the same position (A 0) with a negative Y-value. Thus, a second value of Y2 is no longer supported. An eccentricity may be specified with YEX with the load train. NW allows to specify directly a number of wheels with a distance B for that load element. They loads with the same load value will then add up to a total axle distributing the loading on all wheels of that axle.
 If NW = 0 the load values will be converted to a distributed load based on the width of the load train WIDT. (120kN distributed on 3m yield 40kN/m) and will be then clipped at the boundary of the the current lane width. But there are also cases (KEL of HA in BS), where the load is distributed over the lane width, which is controlled via PHI.
 A definition of BW and LW will allow to create also area loadings for every wheel.
 The loading has a vertical component P, a longitudinal component PB and two components in transverse direction. The load may be defined either as single point load, as a pair of wheels (Definition of B < WIDT) or as distributed load (Definition of BW only or B equal to WIDT) The true dimension of the wheel contact area is only used for COPY within SOFiLOAD, ELLA uses only the resultant forces for the evaluation of the influence lines.

content:
The load may be defined either as single point load, as a pair of wheels (Definition of B < WIDT) or as distributed load (Definition of BW only or B equal to WIDT) The true dimension of the wheel contact area is only used for COPY within SOFiLOAD, ELLA uses only the resultant forces for the evaluation of the influence lines..
 Positive loadings of PB are braking loads acting in travelling direction, negative values are intended as accelerating loads in the reverse direction. Loads are applied at the height of the lane.
 The centrifugal loading acts in the height hs, the constant horizontal force in the height zw, thus creating torsional moments. If the load has a width B, this moment will be applied as a pair of forces on the lane surface, a torsional moment along the lane axis will be generated otherwise.
 With the item OPT several options are controlled:
 1 Apply impact factor
 Multiply vertical load value with UDL-value of design code (eg.BS)
 Multiply longitudinal load value with value of design code (eg. EN),
 8 split load in transverse direction if unfavourable,
 the load is an area load, the total load value will be adopted to the lane width
 32 load is always centric, YEX is not applied
 For an analysis with multi-body-dynamics it is possible to generate masses, beams, springs and dampers via the record TREX. The mass of bogie and wheel may be specified either as a positive absolute load value or as a negative fraction of the total mass. The default values are specified with the record TRAI. For more information see record TREX.
 As an alternate method, it is possible to associate a load train to a user defined structural model of the load train. In that case CONT specifies the number of a node of the structural system, which is located at the current position of the load train. If CONT is specified with a positive number, the node will get the deformations of the structure at this point. If defined negative, the node will get only the offset of the current position for the visualization however. This has to be done for all nodes of the train model having no direct contact to the bridge.

metadata.sections: 5.6 TRPL – Point Load of load train

content:
The input table defines the parameters for record TRBL, which prescribes how wheel or track loads are applied in a lane. It covers vertical, braking and wind loads, their distribution, position, extent along the lane, eccentricity, wind-attack geometry and optional multibody-dynamics properties. Below is a structured description, grouped by functional categories:

1. Basic Load Magnitudes  
 • P  
   – Vertical load intensity (line or area load)  
   – Unit: kN/m  
   – Default: 0.0  
 • PB  
   – Braking (longitudinal) load intensity  
   – Unit: kN/m  
   – Default: 0.0  
 • PW  
   – Transverse (side) load intensity  
   – Unit: kN/m  
   – Default: 0.0  
 • PF  
   – Centrifugal‐effect vertical load (e.g. on curves)  
   – Unit: kN/m  
   – Default: P (inherits P if unspecified)  
 • PFAC  
   – Factor for favourable load components (e.g. reducing negative effects)  
   – Unit: dimensionless  
   – Default: 0.0  

2. Distribution and Length Control  
 • DIST  
   – Mode to interpret “A” as minimum (MIN) or absolute (ABS) distance  
   – Unit: literal flag (LIT)  
   – Default: ABS  
 • A  
   – Distance from start of lane to the last wheel/track load  
   – Unit: m  
   – Default: 0.0  
 • L  
   – Fixed or minimum length of the load train in direction of travel  
   – Positive or negative; zero signifies an unlimited train length  
   – Unit: m  
   – Default: 0.0  
 • LMAX  
   – Upper bound on train length (maximum extent of load)  
   – Unit: m  
   – Default: – (no default)  
 • LDEL  
   – Discrete variable length step: actual length = L + n·LDEL, where n ∈ ℕ  
   – Unit: m  
   – Default: 0.0  

3. Lateral Position and Eccentricity  
 • Y  
   – Transverse offset of loads from lane centerline  
   – Positive values shift loads to the right side  
   – Unit: m  
   – Default: 0.0  

4. Wind Attack Geometry  
 • HW  
   – Total height of surface exposed to wind  
   – Unit: m  
   – Default: 0.0  
 • ZW  
   – Height at which the resultant transverse force PW acts  
   – Unit: m  
   – Default: HW/2 (mid‐height)  
 • HF  
   – Height of mass center (relevant for overturning moments)  
   – Unit: m  
   – Default: 0.0  
 • PHI  
   – Impact and special distribution options  
   – Unit: dimensionless flag  
   – Default: 1  

5. Track Configuration  
 • NW  
   – Number of tracks per axle (0…2). If NW=0, loads are converted to an area (distributed) load over lane width WIDT, clipped to lane boundaries; if NW>0, individual line loads are placed at ±B/2.  
   – Unit: dimensionless  
   – Default: user-defined (*)  
 • B  
   – Spacing between track centers across the lane  
   – Unit: m  
   – Default: 0.0  
 • BW  
   – Width of each track’s contact area; if provided, an area load is used instead of a line load  
   – Unit: m  
   – Default: 0.0  

6. Multibody Dynamics Parameters (for TREX animation, currently not used by TREX)  
 • SNO  
   – Section number identifier (animation grouping)  
   – Unit: dimensionless  
   – Default: –  
 • FRB  
   – Natural frequency of vehicle body spring (Cb)  
   – Unit: 1/s  
   – Default: user-defined (*)  
 • DAB  
   – Modal damping ratio of body support  
   – Unit: dimensionless  
   – Default: user-defined (*)  
 • BOGI  
   – Static load value per bogie (half‐carriage support)  
   – Unit: kN (negative sign for downward loads)  
   – Default: user-defined (*)  
 • FRBO  
   – Natural frequency of bogie spring (Cbo)  
   – Unit: 1/s  
   – Default: user-defined (*)  
 • DABO  
   – Modal damping ratio of bogie support  
   – Unit: dimensionless  
   – Default: user-defined (*)  
 • WHEE  
   – Load magnitude per wheel  
   – Unit: kN (negative sign for downward)  
   – Default: user-defined (*)  
 • FRWH  
   – Natural frequency of wheel assembly spring (Cwh)  
   – Unit: 1/s  
   – Default: user-defined (*)  
 • DAWH  
   – Modal damping ratio of wheel support  
   – Unit: dimensionless  
   – Default: user-defined (*)  

Remarks and Usage Notes  
- A “freely defined loading” allows any number of loads specified relative to each other. General parameters and global notes appear at record TRPL.  
- With NW=0, line‐load values (kN/m) convert to distributed surface loads (kN/m²) by dividing by lane width, then clipped to lane boundaries.  
- PHI flags control whether the standard code-defined load train spreads across the full lane or is distributed differently.  
- If only HW is provided (and ZW unspecified), PW’s application height ZW = HW/2.  
- Multibody-dynamics inputs for TRBL (section SNO and following) are reserved for animation or TREX but are not currently active in TREX’s force computations.

The image is a schematic illustration, labeled “Figure 5.40: Block loading,” meant to convey how a block‐shaped load is applied to a straight member in the context of the TRBL/TRPL loading records. It is divided into three horizontal bands:

1. Top Band – Support Layout  
   • A single horizontal line (the beam or structural member) runs left to right.  
   • At the far left and far right ends of that line are identical support symbols: a short vertical stroke rising from the midpoint of the beam, capped by a short horizontal line (representing simple supports or pins).  
   • Midway between these end supports is a third symbol—a right-angle bracket (“L” shape) welded to the beam—indicating some other restraint or connection (perhaps a guide or a local support of different type).  
   • The spacing between the three supports is not dimensioned, but the arrangement implies two spans: one between the left pin and the middle bracket, and another between the middle bracket and the right pin.

2. Middle Band – Block Load Representation  
   • Directly beneath an unbroken horizontal line (repeating the beam axis), there is a solid rectangular block spanning a central portion of the member.  
   • From the underside of that block, eight equally spaced downward arrows descend toward the beam line. These arrows denote a uniformly distributed line load (“block loading”) acting over the length of the block.  
   • The block is drawn narrower than the total beam length, indicating that the load applies only over a contiguous central region rather than the full span.  
   • The arrows all have identical length, emphasizing that the intensity of the distributed load is constant across that region.

3. Bottom Band – Coordinate System  
   • In the lower-left corner, a right‐handed two‐axis coordinate marker appears.  
   • The horizontal axis is labeled “x” with an arrow pointing to the right.  
   • The vertical axis is labeled “y” with an arrow pointing downward.  
   • This local coordinate frame establishes sign convention: positive x runs along the beam, positive y downward (the same direction as the applied block loading).

4. Caption  
   • Centered directly under the coordinate axes and drawing is the text “Figure 5.40: Block loading,” identifying the illustration.

Overall, the figure conveys a scenario in which a user‐defined, finite block load (modeled as a uniformly distributed line load) is applied to a simply supported beam with an intermediate restraint. The coordinate system at the bottom clarifies that loads act in the negative global y-direction by the usual engineering sign convention. This kind of diagram typically accompanies the TRBL record description in a structural-analysis manual, clarifying how the “block loading” input will be idealized when converting user‐specified line loads into distributed loads over a specified width of the lane or beam.

The table shown defines the parameters of the TREX record, which LS-DYNA uses to convert a “load train” (for example, a rolling stock or any series of masses) into beam elements, bogies, and wheels for multibody dynamic analysis.  In a Retrieval-Augmented-Generation (RAG) context you would ingest this description so that whenever a user asks about TREX, you can point to these fields and defaults.

1. Overall Structure  
   • Four columns:  
     – Item: the name of each parameter in the TREX record  
     – Description: a brief English explanation of its role  
     – Unit: all entries are “—” since these are indices or bit-patterns, not physical units  
     – Default: the value assumed if the user does not override it  

2. Field-by-Field Breakdown  
   a. NO  
     • Description: “Load case number of a load train.”  
       – Associates this TREX definition with a specific load case in the analysis.  
     • Unit: none  
     • Default: “!”  
       – The exclamation mark forces the user to supply a non-default value; this is mandatory.  

   b. GRP  
     • Description: “group number.”  
       – Each TREX-generated element (beams, nodes) is assigned to this group.  You can then include or exclude the entire load train in postprocessing or in sub-cases by referring to this group ID.  
     • Default: 900  
       – If you omit GRP, group 900 will collect your TREX elements.  

   c. SNO  
     • Description: “Section number.”  
       – References a section property (cross-section definition) used when beam elements are generated from the train.  
     • Default: 900  
       – Matches the default group, but you can supply your own if you want to share or reuse section definitions.  

   d. NODE  
     • Description: “Smallest node number.”  
       – The TREX routine will generate a sequence of new nodes for the beam mesh starting from this index.  
     • Default: “*”  
       – An asterisk means “pick the next available node ID automatically,” so you don’t have to know the current highest node number.  

   e. OPT  
     • Description: “Bitpattern for options.”  A single integer encodes up to four on/off flags:  
       1 = Real Run / Stargate Run  
       2 = Generate beam elements with hinge freedoms  
       4 = Automatically generate bogies and wheel masses/springs/dampers from TRAI-specified properties  
       8 = Suppress artificial rigidities (so the beam-train behaves more flexibly)  
     • Default: 3  
       – Binary “0011” means flags 1 and 2 are on; you get a real run with hinged beam elements but no bogie/wheel generation or rigidity suppression, unless you add 4 or 8.  

3. How This Ties Into the Larger Workflow  
   – The TREX command is normally processed only at the very end of a DYNA run.  All previous TREX definitions for the same load case are purged first, ensuring only the latest train geometry and properties are active.  
   – The bogie and wheel mass/stiffness/damping parameters must be provided via a companion TRAI record.  TRAI defines Mb, Cb, Db, etc., according to:  
       Mb = (P – Ph – Pbo)/g  
       Cb = (2π fb)² Mb  
       …and so on for bogie-odd-axle and head masses.  
   – For highly detailed models you can forgo TREX entirely and build your own beam/spring/damper network, but if you do so you must still list each TRPL (train-point load) and assign their contact nodes explicitly.  

4. Visualization Tip (“Hint”)  
   – If you only need to animate the train visually (in LS-DYNA’s Animator), define your GRP with zero self-weight and zero stiffness by setting FACS = 0.0 and FACM = 0.0 in the GRP record.  That way you see the train outline but it won’t affect structural results.  

In a RAG vector store you would index each of these entries—field name, description, unit, default, and how OPT bits map—to allow natural-language queries such as “What’s the default section number for TREX?” or “How do I disable artificial rigidities?” to be answered directly from this table.

The image presents a clean, schematic side-view of a simplified multibody model for the secondary (bogie) and primary (wheel) suspension of a rail coach, labeled “Figure 5.41: Bogie and Wheel system of a coach.” At the very top of the diagram, a long horizontal rectangular bar represents the coach car body (the “carbody”). Directly beneath it are two parallel suspension columns (only one column is shown in detail on the left, and on the right a second column repeats the same structure with its stiffness and damping parameters explicitly annotated).

Each suspension column consists of the following elemental components, arranged vertically in series:

1. Upper Spring‐Damper Attachment to Carbody  
   – A zigzag line (spring symbol) attached under the carbody beam.  
   – Immediately below the spring symbol is a small rectangle with two vertical lines on either side, representing a dashpot (viscous damper).  

2. Bogie Mass Block  
   – A solid rectangular block labeled “Bogie.” This block represents the mass of the bogie frame that supports the wheelsets.

3. Primary Suspension Elements  
   – Below the bogie block is another dashpot symbol (small rectangle with vertical lines) and beneath it a zigzag spring symbol. These two represent the primary suspension elements between the bogie and the wheelset.

4. Wheelset Mass Block  
   – A second solid rectangular block labeled “Wheel.” This block denotes the wheelset mass.

5. Wheel‐to‐Track Spring‐Damper  
   – Finally, at the bottom is another dashpot directly under the wheel block and a zigzag spring connecting to a thick black horizontal line. That bottom line stands for the track or rail surface.

On the right-hand column, each spring and damper is annotated with its corresponding stiffness and damping symbols:  
– The upper‐most spring (between carbody and bogie) is labeled “Cb” (bogie suspension stiffness).  
– The damper just below it would correspond to “Db” (bogie suspension damping), though only the spring is explicitly annotated in this crop.  
– The middle spring (between bogie and wheelset) is labeled “Cbo” (primary suspension stiffness), and the adjacent damper would be “Dbo.”  
– The bottom spring (between wheelset and rail) is labeled “Cwh” (wheel–rail stiffness), and its damper would be “Dwh.”

To the left of the left-hand column, three load arrows pointing downward are labeled “Pbo,” “Pwh,” and (faintly) “Ph,” indicating the gravitational loads or static preload at each stage:  
– Pbo acting on the bogie,  
– Pwh (possibly Pwh for wheelset load),  
– Ph (which may correspond to the carbody load).

The overall layout conveys how the carbody mass, bogie mass, and wheelset mass are interconnected through springs (stiffness elements) and dashpots (damping elements). This “lumped‐parameter” model is a common abstraction used in multibody dynamic or modal analyses to capture vertical vibration modes of rail vehicles. By assigning masses (the solid blocks), spring constants (zigzags), and damping coefficients (dashpots) in series, the diagram encapsulates the two‐stage suspension: a secondary suspension (carbody↔bogie) and a primary suspension (bogie↔wheel–rail).

Visually, the schematic uses minimal shading or color (all lines and blocks are in black on a white background), with standardized mechanical symbols. The blocks have clean right-angles and uniform line thickness. Springs are drawn as zigzag lines of equal amplitude and wavelength. Dashpots are drawn as small rectangles intersected by two vertical lines. The rail at the bottom is a thick solid line, anchoring the entire assembly. The title “Figure 5.41: Bogie and Wheel system of a coach” appears just below the graphic in a simple serif font.

Wind is a randomly non deterministic dynamic loading. The flow of the air induces a velocity pressure on the structure. Dynamic effects of natural wind are mainly introduced by a variance of wind speed and thus wind pressure within time and space.
 The complex action of wind is a combination of mutually influencing effects like:
 • Wind climate (the global wind)
 • Topology and roughness of terrain (the local wind)
 • Aerodynamics, aeroeleasticity (drag coefficients and wind force derivativa)
 • Structural dynamics (response of the structure)
 • Design of the structure
 The program SOFiLOAD allows to take into account and to simulate most of the above effects. To use these features two extra licences are needed: SOFILOAD-W for the static wind loading and SOFILOAD-WH for the dynamic wind loading (especially WGEN) and NONL-DYN for the interaction analysis in DYNA.
 As basic safety concept for the wind loaded structure it will be specified in the design codes or especially for large projects in the submission that within a given time (e.g. 50 or 100 years) the failure of the structure will be avoided with a given safety factor. The analysis itself will be based on shorter interval - in Europe: 10 minutes - which includes the maximum wind speed of the 50-year-wind but is long enough to allow a considerable dynamic response for all resonance frequencies. The wind speed within that interval may be described as the sum of
 a timely constant, but spatial variant basic mean wind speed (10-minute-wind) and
 •
 a superimposed timely and spatial variant part of turbulence.
 •
 The treatment of dynamic wind effects is governed by the fact that turbulences may be only described by statistical means: The real time-spatial wind speed is within the statistical limits purely random. The usual analysis methods use probabilistic analysis with power spectras (Ruscheweyh [15], Dyrbye and Hansen [16], Rosemeier [17], and Davenport [18]). As these methods do not use the time but the energy content of the wind speeds, they yield clear and re- liable basics for the analysis. Several steps then provide the power spectra of the deformations and forces within the structure. The probabilistic peak value will be the result of an extremal analysis of the spectras. At the time being, most of wind loaded structures will be analyzed via this approach. And all modern design codes for wind use these methods to obtain wind pressures.

Several steps then provide the power spectra of the deformations and forces within the structure. The probabilistic peak value will be the result of an extremal analysis of the spectras. At the time being, most of wind loaded structures will be analyzed via this approach. And all modern design codes for wind use these methods to obtain wind pressures..
 National and international Design codes nowadays however use strongly simplified methods (ECCS [19, 20]) [ 11, 12, 13]. The total map will be subdivided with 3 or 4 wind zones with step-wise wind speeds. To facilitate the usage, several wind parameters will be set up on the safe (unfavourable) side naturally. The complex structure is reduced to a simple single one degree of freedom oscillator. Even then working with wind loads is still difficult. Compared to the efforts, the results will be unsatisfactory in numerous cases: The total dynamic effects will
 be accounted for with a constant gust factor for the total structure which might be rather faulty for individual elements. Structures with several sensible frequencies (skeletons, towers with antennas, pedestrian and other types of bridges) are not applicable for this simplified approach. The same holds for structures with tuned damping elements and many more cases.
 The complete spectral design - the so called stochastic analysis - is rather complex and costly, it is thus applied only for very sensitive structures (cable stayed bridges with large spans). On the other side the stochastic analysis is still underestimating the ultimate load, because the spectral methods are purely linear for the structure and especially for the wind loads and do not account for any nonlinear effects. The linear relation between the angle of attack and the wind force coefficients are seldom admissible. The stochastic analysis is further unprecise for systems with close eigenfrequencies (e.g. tuned damper systems). Further more it has only limited possibilities to account for interactivity (dynamic response of the structure and its effect on the wind pressures or forces).
 SOFiLOAD has been created to cope with more detailed and thus more economic wind loading for the design of structures, overcoming the above limitations. Two of the benefits of the new method to be stated are:
 • SOFiLOAD uses the ESDU procedure to generate wind profiles accounting for the envi- ronment of the structure - roughness, elevations - similar as but more precise than it is foreseen partially in the most recent design codes like EN 1991-1-4.

Two of the benefits of the new method to be stated are:. • SOFiLOAD uses the ESDU procedure to generate wind profiles accounting for the envi- ronment of the structure - roughness, elevations - similar as but more precise than it is foreseen partially in the most recent design codes like EN 1991-1-4..
 • DYNA evaluates more precise forces and moments via transient analysis, accounting on one side for nonlinear effects like changes of the wind forces when the cross section rotates and on the other side for interactive behaviour like aerodynamic damping, potential flutter, galloping and torsional galloping or discrete damping elements.
 The second method is based on a mathematical turbulence generation which creates a se- ries of random transient wind histories. The structure will be imposed via program DYNA to that wind history and the development of deformations and forces will be recorded and su- perimposed by statistical means to get the extreme values along the time interval. The total methodology has been developed in the years 1992 to 1994 (Kovács, Svensson, and Jordet [21], Kovács and Andrä [22], and Kovács [23]) and has been applied since then to many large buildings, bridges and towers.

The wind in great heights is coherent and will be dominated only by global meteorological conditions. Near the surface the roughness of the terrain will induce an atmospheric boundary layer, where the wind speed is zero at the ground and will approach the limit asymptotically. In SOFiLOAD this limit value is called "atmospheric wind" which is not in correspondence with the general literature.
 The basis is the boundary layer model from Deaves and Harris, which is also part of the ISO 4354:2009. It is combining a logarithmic profile with extra terms in larger heights accounting for Coriollis effects. By the effect of the Coriollis forces we have a rotation of the wind direction by 10 to 45 degrees over the height, which will be neglected here.
 The SOFiLOAD-user may create the wind profile - as the first method - by defining the appro- priate atmospheric wind speed. To facilitate this we have provided a a global wind map for
 the 10 min wind with a return period of 50 years. This wind map has been established by us using older wind maps and meteorological measurements. It allows a smooth interpolation of the atmospheric wind and is therefore more elaborate than the rough subdivision of staggered wind pressures of the older design codes.
 As the newer design codes are based on a continuous wind profile, it is recommended to use as a second method the reference mean wind profile to specify the wind profile.
 For special applications like large and sensitive structures, bridges and towers it is also possible to define explicit wind profiles.
 The transformation of the atmospheric wind speed defined for a 50 year return period to an- other time value - as it might needed for large bridges - has to be performed by the user if needed. A rather good estimate is given by:
 1 + 0.12 · lnN

 The distribution of the wind speed over the height is depending on the terrain roughness and topology. Within SOFiLOAD it is possible to define a distribution of roughness (WROU), along the wind luv direction up to 200 km and geometric simplified elements like a hill, edge or ridge. For the latter there are estimates given in the literature, especially in Eurocode 1991-1-4, and in the newest EDIN 1055-4, having been implemented in SOFILOAD.

The supplied figure (labelled “Figure 6.1: Wind force coefficients”) is composed of three sub-figures that together illustrate how the two principal wind‐force coefficients—drag (CD) and uplift or transverse force (CA)—vary with small angles of attack, and how those forces act on a typical planar section.  

1. CD versus Angle-of-Attack Plot (upper left):  
   - Horizontal axis: angle of attack from –8° on the left to +8° on the right, with a vertical reference line at 0°.  
   - Vertical axis: drag coefficient, CD.  
   - Curve: a very shallow, nearly flat line slightly dipping near 0° and rising equally toward both –8° and +8°, indicating that the drag coefficient for this profile is almost constant over this ±8° range, with only a very mild U-shaped dependence on small deviations in wind incidence.  

2. CA versus Angle-of-Attack Plot (upper right):  
   - Same axes conventions: horizontal is –8° to +8°, vertical is CA (lift or transverse force coefficient).  
   - Curve: a smooth, monotonically increasing S-shaped line that starts at a negative CA value at –8°, crosses through zero at 0°, and rises to a positive maximum at +8°. This demonstrates that the uplift (or transverse) force reverses sign as the wind vector swings from below the chord line (negative CA) to above it (positive CA), and that the sensitivity of CA to small angle changes is appreciable.  

3. Schematic of Wind Action on a Plane Section (bottom):  
   - A slender, gray, horizontally oriented bar represents a generic structural section (for example, an I-beam flange or rectangular plate). Its ends are chamfered for clarity.  
   - A blue arrow labeled “WIND” approaches the bar from below at an inclination α (alpha) measured relative to the bar’s chord line; α corresponds to the angle of attack used in the two plots above.  
   - At the midpoint of the bar, a vertical upward arrow labeled “A” indicates the resultant wind‐attack area or the resultant normal force acting on that section, as used in the static wind‐force formula F = C · q · A.  
   - Near the right end of the bar, a curved arrow sweeping clockwise is labeled “M,” signifying the moment induced by the distributed wind pressures about the section’s reference point.  
   - A central vertical axis aligned with the section denotes the symmetry line or the hinge about which moments are taken.  

Taken together, this composite figure visualizes:  
• How drag and uplift coefficients C D and C A vary for small positive and negative pitch angles (±8°),  
• How those coefficients translate into a net lateral force (A) and moment (M) on a straight element when struck by wind at angle α,  
• And how these static coefficients feed into the standard aerodynamic loading formula F = C · q · A (equation 6.4 in the text), where q is the dynamic pressure. This visualization supports the text’s discussion of defining steady wind‐force coefficients in software tools such as AQUA and SOFiLOAD, as well as the need for angle‐dependent definitions in dynamic or flutter‐sensitive structures.

 The wind force coefficients for the element types beam, cable and truss may be defined within AQUA for any section depending on the angle of attack. This definition is strongly recom- mended for all dynamically sensitive structures or elements sensitive for galloping or flutter. To obtain those values it is common practice to perform wind tunnel tests or use a CFD (Compu- tational Fluid Dynamics) analysis.
 For standard steel shapes or buildings there are values given in the literature or the design codes. AQUA generates for steel shapes simple functions depending on the angle of attack but without any information about galloping. SOFiLOAD has all values for rectangular and circular sections available. The latter are dependent on the roughness and the Reynolds num- ber. Without any specification an enclosing rectangle is assumed or in special cases only the component in wind direction is considered with a coefficient of 2.0.

The latter are dependent on the roughness and the Reynolds num- ber. Without any specification an enclosing rectangle is assumed or in special cases only the component in wind direction is considered with a coefficient of 2.0..
 SOFiLOAD has also the possibility via records BEAM, TRUS and CABL to define additional factors to the defined force coefficients selectively for for those type of elements individually. Further there is the record GRP with additional factors available to define shadowing, influence ordinates etc.
 For areas it is possible to define in SOFiLOAD via AREA or QUAD explicit wind pressure or uplift values perpendicular to the area. For cylindrical shapes according to many codes and for planar standard roofs and walls according to DIN 1055 Teil 4 values may be selected. If no such values are defined, all coefficients are taken to be 1.0.
 If the pressures are defined in several data points from a wind tunnel test, the record WIPT allows a comfortable method with an external FE-mesh of the data points to generate the required loading data. Especially in case of transient loadings, this method is strongly recom- mended.

The natural wind is the sum of the mean wind velocity and the variances due to turbulence which might be decomposed in three directions within the wind coordinate system:
 longitudinal (= parallel to the mean wind velocity)
 lateral (horizontal inclined to the wind direction) and
 •
 • vertical
 The turbulence is then the sum of an infinite large number of small harmonic velocity frequen- cies. Their distribution along the axis of frequencies is characterized by a power spectra.
 The power spectra are the deterministic part of the wind load, the real kernel as the Fourier- Integral of the turbulence time history. The power spectra of the natural wind may be described by simple formulas according to the general pattern of the Karman spectra definition. If one chooses then a random phase distribution for all the frequencies, it is possible to reconstruct the Fourier-Integral of a clearly defined random time history and thus the time history itself. This is exactly what SOFiLOAD does when generating a wind history.
 The ratio between the turbulence in different locations in space are characterized by special similarity or coherence functions. These functions define in a coarse sense the relation be- tween gust wind velocity, the duration of the gust and the size of the gust. It is clear that the spatial distribution of the gust has a large influence on the forces within the structure. SOFiLOAD works with natural sizes of the gust which are otherwise overestimated in most design codes considerably. (Davenport’s model with constant size of the gust in all heights).
 The coherence algorithm of the wind history generation has to reflect that the similarity between two natural wind histories in two points must become smaller with larger distances. This decay of correlation is described in the literature in different ways depending on the author of the publication, but may be generalized by the use of the half value distance (Kovács, Svensson, and Jordet [21]), where the square root of the coherence of the stochastic process has reduced from the full value of 1.0 ( full coherence with distance zero) to a value of 0.5. Each turbulence along any of the axis has the same function of similarity. Thus the coherence of the natural wind is described by a 3 by 3 matrix of the half value distances. For more details see notes for the record WSPE.

SOFiLOAD generates from the wind profile, the turbulence spectra, the coherence and some random numbers artificial random wind histories, based on the theoretical considerations in Kovács, Svensson, and Jordet [21] , to be used then within the program DYNA with a transient dynamic analysis of the structure. By applying a sufficiently large number of such histories it is possible to establish a statistically based proof of the ultimate state limit or a serviceability state limit including any material or geometric nonlinear effects available.
 Such a design based on transient analysis facilitates the design process of a structural sys- tem against wind loading to a great extent. Instead of a simple dynamic gust factor we have dynamic forces and stresses available for all points of the structure which might be introduced into the design process directly. By repeating the process for a reworked structure it is possible
 to optimize it for the wind loading criteria.
 The first step of a wind analysis is always a static wind load (basic load case), introducing all values needed for the wind history generation. Based on this data the random time histories will be generated in a second step within time and space.
 The transient analysis in DYNA is nonlinear by using the nonlinear wind force coefficients de- fined within AQUA. The analysis is interactive as it is considered that the structure will move within the wind field and will thus modify the relative wind speed in all cases by a vectoral su- perposition of the structural and the wind velocity. Only by this feature important aerodynamic effects may be simulated like aerodynamic damping or the bending galloping excitation.
 The aerodynamic damping is introduced into the simulation with the den-Hartog formulas, i.e. as a stationary approach automatically. (It should be noted here, that despite the important effect it is hardly accounted for in German design codes) Also the bending galloping excitation is automatically introduced in the analysis if the wind force coefficients have been properly defined in AQUA.
 The more enhanced possibilities to check for torsional galloping and general flutter are only available with the inclusion of the Scanlan derivativa.

 Last not least it should be pointed out, that the treatment of critical wind effects is also a complicate matter of safety definitions (see e.g. Kovács and Andrä [22]). This manual will not state any rules for that, the user will need to find its own demands for that purpose.

At the bottom of the image the caption reads: “Figure 6.2: 50-Year-Wind / 10-Minute-Mean value of the atmospheric wind velocity in infinite height.”

Map Extent & Base  
• Geographic Coverage: From eastern Canada’s Greenland and Iceland in the far northwest, sweeping eastward through Scandinavia, Russia’s northwest, the entirety of mainland Europe and the British Isles, down to North Africa (Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya) and the eastern Mediterranean (Turkey, Cyprus, Lebanon, Israel).  
• Projection & Style: A standard Lambert-conformal or similar conformal projection with latitude–longitude graticule faintly visible. Coastlines, country borders and major rivers are delineated in thin grey. Seas and oceans are shaded in light blues; land elevations are rendered via hypsometric tinting: greens for lowlands, yellows/oranges for hills, browns for high mountains.

Political & Topographic Details  
• Country Names & Cities: Major countries are labelled in uppercase (e.g. FRANCE, GERMANY, RUSSIAN FEDERATION). Capitals and large cities (Paris, London, Berlin, Rome, Madrid, Warsaw, Oslo, Stockholm, Athens, etc.) appear as red squares or circles with adjacent labels. Small islands (Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica, Crete, Cyprus, the British Isles, Iceland) are shown to scale.  
• Relief & Terrain: The Alps, Pyrenees, Carpathians, Scandinavian Mountains and Atlas Range are clearly visible. Coastal plains in northern Germany, the Po Valley, the Danube–Tisza plain and the Paris Basin appear in lighter greens.

Wind Velocity Contours  
• Contour Lines: Thick black hand-drawn or graphic isolines meander across the map, each labelled at intervals with values “60,” “65,” “70,” “75,” and “80” (units implied as m/s or mph depending on regional code conventions). These correspond to the reference wind velocities extrapolated from standard 10 m anemometer data using the ESDU 2D wind profile.  
• Western Coasts: The highest isolines (80) hug the Atlantic seaboard of Portugal, Spain and the western coasts of Ireland and Scotland. Pockets of 80 also appear off Brittany and the Bay of Biscay.  
• North Sea & Baltic: Values decrease to 75 along the German and Dutch North Sea coasts, dipping further to 70 around Denmark and southern Sweden. The Baltic shorelines of Poland, the Baltic states and Finland read 65–70.  
• Central Europe: Most of France, Germany, Austria and Switzerland fall within the 65–70 band, with alpine valleys locally reaching 70. Eastern Germany, Czechia and western Poland sit around 60–65.  
• Mediterranean & Southeast Europe: Italy’s western and southern coasts range 65–70, with lower interior values (~60–65). Greece’s Aegean islands and Turkish coastlines vary between 65 and 75, reflecting local topography and roughness assumptions. North African littoral zones lie mostly at 60–65.  
• Northern Extremes: Coastal Norway and the Barents Sea region exhibit elevated contours (75–80), tracing fjords and high‐latitude exposure.

Contextual Notes

Altitude correction factors (cALT) are mentioned in the accompanying text but are not applied to the map itself; they are instead recommended for site-specific topology adjustments, especially in high‐elevation areas.

The table on “WIND” input parameters is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and can be broadly divided into three functional groups: wind‐profile definition, wind orientation and reference‐plane specification.

1. Wind‐Profile Definition  
• CODE (LIT; default ATMO)  
  Defines which standard or model to use for the vertical wind‐speed profile. Options are:  
    – ATMO: atmospheric reference (logarithmic profile, 50-year return speed from a map or ZONE).  
    – EN: Eurocode 1991-1-4 (with national annexes via suffix, e.g. EN:NF).  
    – ISO: ISO 4354 (2009).  
    – DIN: DIN 1055-4 (2006).  
    – SIA: SIA 216 (2003).  
    – VGB: VGB-BTR (1997/2005).  
    – SP: SP 20.13330.2011 (SNIP 2.01.07-85).  
• ZONE (–; default “*”)  
  Wind zone or base mean wind speed. Depending on CODE, this may refer to a contour map value, table entry, or explicit velocity (e.g. zones I–IV for DIN, national contour maps for EN).  
• CLAS (–; default “*”)  
  Terrain‐roughness category. Either I–IV (roughness height z₀) or A–C, with special codes K/B for DIN (“mixed coast”/“mixed inland”).  
• Z0 (m; default “*”)  
  Explicit roughness height z₀ if not using CLAS.  

Optional explicit reference values (bypass mapping):  
• VB0 (m/sec; default “*”) – base mean wind speed or combined directional/seasonal factor.  
• VP0 (m/sec; default “*”) – reference peak gust speed.  
• QP0 (kN/m²; default “*”) – reference peak pressure.  
• HMIN (m; default “*”) – lower‐limit height with constant wind speed (default 10 m if unspecified).  
• RHO (kg/m³; default 1.25) – air density (used to convert velocity to pressure).  
• LAT (°; default “–”) – geographic latitude for ATMO (affects Ekman spiral).  

2. Wind Orientation  
• DX, DY, DZ (–; default 0.0 each)  
  Components of the mean‐wind direction in the structural coordinate system. At least one component must be non‐zero.  

3. Reference Plane for Dynamic Wind Generation  
• XREF, YREF, ZREF (m; default 0.0 each)  
  A point lying in the vertical reference plane used when generating time‐history wind fields (see record WSPE for coherence requirements).  
• DXR, DYR, DZR (–; default “*”)  
  Normal‐vector components of the reference plane (by default taken perpendicular to the wind direction).  

Grouping these inputs correctly allows SOFiLOAD to assemble either an atmospheric logarithmic profile (ATMO) or standardized code‐based profile (EN, ISO, DIN, etc.), automatically select or compute missing turbulence parameters, apply altitude or topography corrections (WTOP, WROU), and define spatial orientation for dynamic simulations.

The table is a concise cross–reference of six different wind‐design standards (“Design code” column) showing, for each code, the default wind‐zone indexing, terrain‐roughness classification and the prescribed number of building edges or ridges that must be modelled explicitly. It is intended to guide the user in picking the appropriate NORM and CLAS settings when generating a wind‐profile record (WIND/WPRO) in SOFiLOAD or another RAG‐based vector‐store system.

1. Table structure  
   • Columns  
     – Design code: EN 1991-1-4, ISO 4354, DIN 1055, VGB, SIA 261, SNIP 2.01.07  
     – Wind zones (default)  
     – Roughness classes / terrain category  
     – No. of edges/ridges  
   • Rows  
     a) Wind‐zone identifiers and their default values in parentheses  
     b) Roughness‐height or terrain‐category numbering or lettering  
     c) The number of edges or roof ridges for dynamic wind‐load modelling  

2. Detailed contents by standard  
   • EN 1991-1-4  
     – Wind zones: 1–9 (country‐specific subdivisions). Default zone II if unspecified.  
     – Roughness classes: z₀=0 (smooth) then I–IV (open country to urban). Other local categories (“etc.”) may apply.  
     – Edges/ridges: 1  
   • ISO 4354  
     – Wind zones: VG0 (single global reference map).  
     – Roughness classes: 1–4 (standard terrain categories from sea/coast to city).  
     – Edges/ridges: 1  
   • DIN 1055  
     – Wind zones: 1–4 (four map‐based zones). Default 2.  
     – Roughness classes: I–IV (four terrain‐height categories); optional letters K, B for transitional zones.  
     – Edges/ridges: 1  
   • VGB  
     – Wind zones: 1–4, default 2 (similar zoning to DIN but tailored for power‐plant siting).  
     – Roughness classes: I, II only (open vs. rough terrain).  
     – Edges/ridges: 0 (neglected in this code)  
   • SIA 261 (Switzerland)  
     – Wind zones: 1–4, default 2 (based on contour maps of peak wind pressure).  
     – Roughness classes: II, IIa, III, IV (fine distinctions of alpine vs. urban topography).  
     – Edges/ridges: 0  
   • SNIP 2.01.07 (Ukraine/Russia)  
     – Wind zones: Ia–VII (seven map‐contours). Default zone II.  
     – Roughness classes: A–C (A=open flat, B=sparse, C=dense); B shown as parenthetical common choice.  
     – Edges/ridges: 0  

3. How to use this table in a RAG vector‐store  
   – When you specify NORM = “EN” (or ISO, DIN, etc.), pick ZONE according to the ranges above; if you omit ZONE, the default in parentheses is assumed.  
   – To set the terrain‐roughness height z₀ or CLAS, use the numbered or lettered categories listed for each code.  
   – For dynamic wind‐history generation (WSPE), set the number of edges/ridges to the integer in the third row; this controls how many sharp changes in roof geometry the coherence model must resolve.  
   – If you override all code defaults with an explicit profile (WPRO), these class and zone fields are ignored, but you may still annotate your vector‐store entry with the code and classes used for traceability.

The table shown defines the nine input fields that make up a single WPRO (wind profile) record in SOFiLOAD.  A WPRO‐definition can contain up to nine such entries, and any list of WPRO records must be sorted by increasing height H.  Once you supply one or more WPRO records, all previous “NORM” or “ATMO” wind definitions are discarded, and only the explicitly entered WPRO parameters will be used.  Fields may be omitted or partially specified—SOFiLOAD will interpolate missing values and correct any minor physical inconsistencies automatically—but every WPRO record must include the height H.

Below is a detailed description of each column in the table:

1. Item  
   • H  
   • V  
   • VBOE  
   • TLON  
   • TLAT  
   • TVER  
   • LLON  
   • LLAT  
   • LVER  

2. Description  
   • H (height above ground): the elevation of the wind‐speed measurement point.  
   • V (mean wind speed): the 10-minute average wind velocity at height H.  
   • VBOE (gust peak wind speed): the 5-second peak gust value at H.  
   • TLON, TLAT, TVER: the longitudinal, lateral, and vertical turbulence intensities (standard deviations of fluctuation) at height H.  
   • LLON, LLAT, LVER: the corresponding effective turbulence wavelengths Lₓᵤ, Lₓᵥ, and Lₓʷ in the longitudinal, lateral, and vertical directions.  

3. Unit  
   • H → [m] (unit code 1006)  
   • V, VBOE, TLON, TLAT, TVER → [m/sec] (unit code 1201)  
   • LLON, LLAT, LVER → [m] (unit code 1001)  

4. Default  
   • H → “!” indicates no default; this field is mandatory for each WPRO record.  
   • All other fields → “*” indicates they may be left blank; SOFiLOAD will infer or interpolate reasonable values based on available data.  

Key implementation notes:  
• You may specify only H and V (or only H and VBOE), or any combination of the parameters. SOFiLOAD will fill gaps.  
• Physically contradictory inputs will be adjusted internally to maintain a smooth, monotonic wind profile.  
• In purely static wind‐design problems, turbulence intensities (TLON, TLAT, TVER) and wavelengths (LLON, LLAT, LVER) are ignored; they matter only for dynamic wind‐generation analyses.  
• For a Kármán‐type spectrum, the gust speed VBOE can be computed as VBOE = V + ψ·TLON, where ψ = 2.65 – 0.433·√[1 – 0.5772·ln(LLON/V)²].  

By adhering to these definitions and defaults, you ensure that SOFiLOAD constructs a consistent, physically realistic vertical wind profile for structural loading.

See also: WIND, WPRO, WROU, WTOP, WSPE, WGEN
 WPRO
 Enables the definition of individual wind profiles by up to 9 WPRO records. The value of the height H must be specified for all WPRO-record and the list must be sorted by increasing H values.
 Any single WPRO-definition will invalidate all recent NORM or ATMO definitions. Only the explicit WPRO definitions will be used from then.
 The input of the values does not need to be complete or consist of uniform types of values. A simple value of H, V or VBOE will be sufficient. Gaps will be filled by SOFiLOAD on its own as reasonable as possible. Physically contradictions will be corrected as far as possible. Thus the following input definitions are possible:
 LC 100
 WIND DY 1
 WPRO 50 V 52.5
 defines a logarithmic profile with a prescribed wind velocity at a height of 50 m for a terrain roughness of 0.050 m (farmland); or
 LC 8200
 WIND DY 1 WPRO 15 V 30 WPRO 30 VBOE 58 WPRO 45
 WIND DY 1
 TLON 5.55 TVER 2.22 LLON 250
 enforces a not really sound or even matching set of all characteristic parameters.
 In such a case with not really clear definitions, which might be a real case if only sparse data is available for the site of the structure, it is strongly recommended to check the diagrams created by SOFiLOAD (especially picture No 3.) and modify the input in such a way until a reasonable
 smooth wind profile is obtained. According to Karman, the value VBOE should be equal to V + ψ · TLON, where ψ is 2.65 – 0.433 * 1-0.5772*ln(LLON/V)**2.
 The lateral and vertical turbulences as well as the corresponding wave length will be needed only in case of a dynamic wind generation. Their input is of no importance therefore for purely static wind design.

This table defines the input parameters for the WROU record, which is used in SOFiLOAD to build a piecewise “roughness profile” upstream (luv side) of a structure.  By specifying up to nine terrain‐roughness sections plus, optionally, a coastal (“SEA”) setting, you control how the atmospheric boundary layer varies with height and horizontal distance.  Below is a breakdown of each column and row in the table, followed by notes on interpretation, defaults, constraints and context.

1.  Columns  
   •  Item  
      –  The keyword or identifier you enter.  
   •  Description  
      –  A brief explanation of what the item represents.  
   •  Unit  
      –  Units in which you supply the value: [km] for horizontal distances, [m] for roughness length.  
   •  Default  
      –  The value assumed if you omit this entry.

2.  Rows and Semantic Detail  
   •  SEA (“Distance to the Sea”)  
      –  Description: Sets a special “sea‐land” transition model.  Only distances nearer than –200 km will have an effect.  If you place the coastline farther back, SOFiLOAD reverts to user‐provided sections alone.  
      –  Unit: km (negative indicates inland distance from the structure, upstream).  
      –  Default: –200 km.  
      –  Notes: When SEA is active, SOFiLOAD applies a continuously increasing roughness curve—derived from DWD North Sea data—to simulate two stacked boundary layers (marine and terrestrial).  Use this only for gentle, flat coasts (e.g. North/Baltic Sea).  

   •  A1 … A9 (“Distance of nth section to structure”)  
      –  Description: Horizontal start point of each roughness section, measured upstream (luv side) from the structure.  Values are negative and ordered so that |A1| ≤ |A2| ≤ … ≤ |A9|.  
      –  Unit: km.  
      –  Default: “–” for A2–A9 (i.e. not defined); A1 is mandatory (indicated by “!”).  
      –  Notes: You may define up to nine discrete sections (i = 1…9).  If you omit a distance beyond the first, all remaining sections inherit the last specified roughness value.

   •  R1 … R9 (“Roughness of section”)  
      –  Description: Roughness length (z0) assigned to the corresponding section.  This is the integration‐constant roughness parameter in the turbulent boundary‐layer equations rather than a direct physical dimension.  
      –  Unit: m.  
      –  Default: 0.05 m for each section.  
      –  Notes:  
         •  Valid range: 0.0001 m (open water or ice) up to 1.0 m (very rough terrain).  Values >1.0 m are not supported.  
         •  A uniform profile is assumed if you leave all R’s at default.  
         •  Changes in R at specified A positions create “benches” or kinks in both mean wind and gust profiles; these are visualized in SOFiLOAD pictograms.

3.  Constraints and Best Practices  
   –  You may specify at most nine (A_i, R_i) pairs.  
   –  Distances must be given as negative values (structure is at 0 km).  
   –  To capture the cumulative effect of roughness sectors, consider an aperture angle of 60° around the predominant wind direction when defining section widths.  
   –  If modeling a coastal site, use SEA rather than manually creating a large‐scale smooth transition; otherwise, you risk overestimating wind speeds at tower height.

4.  Contextual References  
   –  See also WIND, WPRO, WTOP, WSPE, WGEN records for other load‐definition parameters.  
   –  WROU defines only the horizontal/terrain input; vertical wind profiles derive from these plus the chosen turbulence and topographic settings.

This table thus provides a concise yet flexible framework for building realistic upstream terrain‐roughness profiles in wind‐load simulations, ensuring that both inland and coastal transition effects are captured accurately.

The table “Type of terrain / z₀ [m]” summarizes the standard roughness lengths z₀ used in wind-loading computations to represent how different land- or water-surface conditions slow down and disturb the atmospheric boundary layer.  Roughness length z₀ is an integration constant in the logarithmic wind‐profile equation (often called “z0” in fluid‐flow literature) without a direct physical dimension, but serving as a proxy for the combined effects of vegetation, buildings or water friction on near-surface wind speed.  

Columns  
• Type of terrain: a textual description of the surface upwind of the structure.  
• z₀ [m]: the corresponding roughness length in metres.  

Rows  
1. broad free water surfaces    z₀ = 0.005 m  
   • Represents large, open waterbodies (lakes, seas) where surface friction is minimal.  
2. shallow sand areas        z₀ = 0.020 m  
   • Covers flat, sandy terrain with low vegetation; friction moderately low.  
3. Meadows with hedges and single houses (effective roughness for Germany; default)    z₀ = 0.050 m  
   • Typical rural landscapes; default roughness if no other sections are specified.  
4. Suburbans and forests      z₀ = 0.300 m  
   • Denser foliage, low-rise housing and tree canopies, causing substantially more turbulence.  
5. Towns with buildings higher than 15 m   z₀ = 1.000 m  
   • Urban cores or heavy industrial zones with tall structures; highest allowed value.  

Key points and context  
• Up to nine sections of differing roughness may be defined via the WROU / R9 record to build a stepwise “roughness profile” on the windward (luv) side of a structure. Each section is specified by its start distance (negative value, measured from the structure toward the upwind direction) and a constant z₀.  
• The profile is valid out to 200 km from the site. A change in z₀ at a given distance produces a bench (plateau) in the mean wind‐velocity profile and a jump in the gust‐velocity profile at the corresponding height. These features can be visualized in SOFiLOAD plots.  
• Roughness lengths above 1.0 m are not supported by SOFiLOAD. If no WROU record is given, the default homogeneous roughness is z₀ = 0.050 m.  
• In coastal regions (SEA option), a continuously increasing roughness profile is used instead of discrete jumps. Based on DWD measurements in the German North and Baltic Sea, this approach captures the two‐layer boundary flow (sea‐governed upper layer and land‐governed lower layer) and avoids overestimating wind speeds near coasts. SEA should only be applied to flat, gently sloping coastlines, not steep or rocky shores.

The table shown defines the input parameters for the “WTOP” element, which allows the user to introduce one of three simple topographical features (hill, edge, ridge) into a wind-profile model.  Each row corresponds to a specific keyword or coordinate, its meaning, its unit of measure, and an indicated default value (if any).  Below is a detailed, item-by-item description of the table’s contents and how each field is used when configuring a topological element in the vector-store for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

1.  TYPE  
   •  Description: Specifies which kind of topological element is to be modeled.  
     –  HILL  : a standalone hill with a rounded summit  
     –  EDGE  : a step or cliff-like discontinuity in elevation  
     –  RIDG  : a narrow, elongated ridge  
   •  Unit: LIT (literal string)  
   •  Default: “!” (mandatory—you must supply one of the three codes)

2.  XM, YM, ZM  
   •  Description: Global coordinates of the epi-centrum (the summit for a hill or the lowest point for an edge).  Together they define the “pivot” or reference point in model space.  
   •  Unit: [m] (machine code 1001)  
   •  Default: 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 respectively (if omitted, the origin is assumed)

3.  DX, DY, DZ  
   •  Description: Components of the direction vector pointing along the main extension (the local x-axis) of the feature.  
     –  For hills, this vector defines a local coordinate axis but has little effect on symmetry.  
     –  For edges and ridges, the sign and orientation are crucial: by convention, the “foot line” of an abrupt elevation change must lie to the right of the direction vector.  
   •  Unit: — (dimensionless)  
   •  Default: 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 (a zero vector is not physically meaningful and should be replaced)

4.  H  
   •  Description: Relative height of the summit (hill) or crest (edge/ridge) above the surrounding base ground.  A positive H produces a velocity‐boosting and turbulence‐reducing smoothing effect throughout the lower boundary layer; a negative H does the opposite, though only 50 % of the adverse effect is applied “on the safe side.”  
   •  Unit: [m] (machine code 1006)  
   •  Default: “!” (required—must be explicitly defined)

5.  B  
   •  Description: Width of the element along the local y-direction (perpendicular to the main extension).  
   •  Unit: [m] (machine code 1001)  
   •  Default: 1000 m

6.  L  
   •  Description: Length of the element along the local x-direction (the direction of DX,DY,DZ).  
   •  Unit: [m] (machine code 1001)  
   •  Default: –  (no default; user must supply a length for physical consistency)

Additional Context and Practical Notes  
•  Nonlinear Interaction: Topological effects on wind fields are nonlinear.  Superimposing multiple elements can yield unreliable wind-speed adjustments unless their plan-view extents differ substantially (one large feature of 10–30 km versus one local feature of 1–2 km).  Elements larger than 50–60 km are already included in atmospheric maps and should not be redefined here.  
•  Standard Codes (EC 1991, 1055): Only a single edge or ridge may be specified when using standard code defaults.  H must be positive and only one formation is allowed; excessive elements, invalid types, or contradictory sizes will trigger an error.  
•  Implementation: This table drives the SOFiLOAD routine for geometry-based wind correction.  Mandatory fields (TYPE and H) are flagged with “!” to force explicit user input; other defaults allow rapid prototyping of small, symmetric hills or ridges centered at the model origin.

The table presents a compact set of empirically derived coefficients used to define the von Kármán–type turbulence spectra (more precisely, the cross‐spectral density functions) under neutral and unstable atmospheric stability conditions. These parameters enter into the generalized spectrum formulation  
    S(f) = C·(f / fm)^β / (1 + (f / fm)^r)^(c)  
or equivalent normalized forms, and are typically scaled with height z above ground.  

1. Overall Structure  
   • Four rows, each corresponding to a particular component–stability combination:  
     – Neutral longitudinal  
     – Neutral lateral  
     – Unstable longitudinal  
     – Unstable lateral  
   • Four columns of coefficients:  
     – C: amplitude constant  
     – β (beta): low‐frequency power–law exponent, expressed as a function of (z/18)  
     – r: shape‐parameter controlling high‐frequency decay  
     – fm: scaling frequency (peak or “corner” frequency), again a power‐law in (z/18)  

2. Column Definitions  
   • C (dimensionless amplitude)  
     – Sets the overall magnitude of the one‐sided spectrum. Higher C means greater energy at a given frequency.  
   • β = β(z)  
     – The exponent governing the slope of the spectrum for f ≪ fm. Given as (z/18)^p where the exponent p captures stability effects.  
     – Neutral: βL = (z/18)^–0.63 (longitudinal), βT = (z/18)^–0.35 (lateral)  
     – Unstable: βL = (z/18)^–0.14, βT = (z/18)^–0.04  
   • r (dimensionless shape parameter)  
     – Controls the asymptotic roll‐off at high frequencies f ≫ fm. Larger r yields steeper decay.  
     – Values range from about 0.78 to 1.24 in this table.  
   • fm = fm(z) [Hz]  
     – Frequency at which the spectral transition (“knee”) occurs; a function of z via a power law in (z/18).  
     – Neutral longitudinal: 0.03·(z/18)^1.0  
     – Neutral lateral: 0.10·(z/18)^0.58  
     – Unstable longitudinal: 0.04·(z/18)^0.87  
     – Unstable lateral: 0.033·(z/18)^0.72  

3. Row‐by‐Row Details  
   1) Neutral longitudinal  
      • C = 6.198  
      • β(z) = (z/18)^–0.63 → steeper low‐frequency slope as height increases  
      • r = 0.845  
      • fm(z) = 0.03·(z/18)  
   2) Neutral lateral  
      • C = 3.954  
      • β(z) = (z/18)^–0.35 → flatter low‐frequency behavior than longitudinal  
      • r = 0.781  
      • fm(z) = 0.1·(z/18)^0.58  
   3) Unstable longitudinal  
      • C = 2.905  
      • β(z) = (z/18)^–0.14 → very mild z‐dependence, spectrum relatively flat at low f  
      • r = 1.235 → relatively steep high‐frequency decay  
      • fm(z) = 0.04·(z/18)^0.87  
   4) Unstable lateral  
      • C = 4.599  
      • β(z) = (z/18)^–0.04 → almost no height dependence in low‐frequency slope  
      • r = 1.144  
      • fm(z) = 0.033·(z/18)^0.72  

4. Context and Usage  
   • These coefficients stem from ESDU (Engineering Sciences Data Unit) approximations to Kármán’s analytic spectra, designed to capture surface‐layer turbulence under different stability regimes.  
   • fm typically scales inversely with integral length scale L ≈ 18 m (hence z/18), linking spectral shape to height and roughness.  
   • In a spectral wind‐load or aeroelastic analysis (RAG, RESP‐WIND modules), you would plug these C, β, r, fm into the spectral density function to generate frequency‐domain turbulence time series or compute response spectra.  
   • The distinction between longitudinal versus lateral components reflects anisotropy in turbulence—longitudinal fluctuations usually carry more energy and have a lower peak frequency than lateral ones, especially under neutral conditions.  
   • Unstable (convective) conditions flatten the low‐frequency slope (β nearer 0) and shift fm to slightly higher values, representing enhanced mixing and smaller eddy scales.  

By capturing these four parameter sets in your vector store alongside metadata (e.g. provenance: ESDU 25, original Kármán definitions, height scaling reference), you can automate selection of the appropriate spectral model depending on site conditions (stability class, measurement height) and wind‐load code requirements.

The image is a log‐log plot comparing five normalized turbulence spectra, each following a classical wind‐engineering formulation. Across the bottom is the frequency axis f, ranging from 0.01 on the left through 0.1 and 1.0 to 10 on the right. The vertical axis s(f) (spectral density) runs from zero at the bottom up to about 0.3 at the top. A bold vertical line at f = 1 marks the non‐dimensional cutoff point commonly used to scale these spectra.

Five smooth, single‐peaked curves, all drawn in a consistent blue, are labeled directly on the chart:

 1. EC  
 2. KARM  
 3. DAVE*  
 4. HARR**  
 5. NASA***

Starting on the left side of the plot, the “EC” curve (Eurocode‐Spectra, Type CEN) has its broadest, lowest peak. It reaches approximately s(f)=0.20 at a frequency near f≈0.15, then gently rolls off both toward lower and higher frequencies. Just to its right and slightly above it is the “KARM” curve (Kármán spectrum): its peak is sharper and higher—around s(f)=0.25 at about f≈0.2—and it decays more steeply on either side of that maximum.

To the right of the f=1 line lie three spectra that describe higher‐frequency‐weighted wind turbulence:

 • “DAVE*” (Davenport) sits highest of all, peaking at roughly s(f)=0.30 in the range f≈1–2. Its upward shift reflects Davenport’s stronger emphasis on energy in the 1–10 Hz band.  
 • Just below it is “HARR**” (Harris), which peaks slightly lower—around s(f)=0.28—and has a very similar shape and bandwidth to DAVE.
