The image is a black-and-white line sketch labeled “Figure 6.6: wind reference systems.” At its core it shows three overlapping, rectangular “slices” of a turbulence field—drawn as lightly dotted boxes—sliding past a fixed point in space. Key elements are:

1. Global Vertical Axis  
   - At the far left of the drawing there is a single, bold vertical arrow labelled “Y.” This represents the global or real-world vertical direction (gravity).

2. Local (Skewed) Coordinate Axes  
   - From the first (leftmost) box emerges a thick arrow, tipped upward and to the right, labelled “WX.”  
   - From the third (rightmost) box a second thick arrow, tipped more horizontally to the right, is labelled “WY.”  
   - Although not explicitly drawn, the third axis WZ (vertical in the skewed system) lies in the plane of the paper and coincides with the global Y direction, thus making WY–WZ the local reference plane.

3. Reference Plane and Reference Point  
   - A dashed diagonal line cuts through all three boxes. This line indicates the intersection of the local reference plane (defined by WY and WZ) with the drawing plane.  
   - The middle box is annotated underneath with the word “Referenzpunkt” (reference point), marking the fixed spatial location at which turbulence history is recorded.

4. Wind Direction  
   - A large, bold arrow in the lower-left quadrant points up and to the left, labelled “Windrichtung” (wind direction). This shows that the stack of dotted boxes is translated “frozen” along the wind vector, so that each box represents the same two-dimensional turbulence pattern at successive phases.

5. Overlapping Boxes  
   - The three dotted rectangles are arranged in a row, overlapping slightly. They symbolize the identical turbulence snapshot being carried by the flow. Because coherence along the wind direction is set to unity, the pattern in each box is the same except for a phase shift.

Overall, the figure illustrates how SOFiLOAD constructs a frozen‐turbulence field: a 2D pattern generated in the skewed WY–WZ plane (shown by the dashed line and WY arrow) is carried unchanged along the wind vector (Windrichtung arrow). The WX axis indicates the remaining local direction perpendicular to that reference plane. By moving this slice past the fixed reference point, the software enforces unity coherence in windward direction while allowing realistic lateral and vertical turbulence correlations.

The turbulence field generated by SOFiLOAD is mainly the result of a 2D-turbulence generation within the reference plane defined within the WIND-record:
 The axis WX, WY and the vertical gravity direction WZ define a skewed coordinate system where the longitudinal, lateral and vertical turbulence is calculated along the reference plane defined by WY and WZ following the coherence within that plane. This pattern of turbulence moves than along the wind direction in a frozen form passing the structure, ie. the coherence in wind direction is always 1.0, the history is identical only with a different phase. This approach may be in rare cases to much on the safe side. Examples for this are structures repeating itself along the wind direction showing a resonance with the frequency of the excitement not observed in nature. In those cases a correction with a slightly change of value C3D ̸= 1.0 may help.

Below is a structured, field-by-field description of the table you provided. It defines the keyword inputs required for a coherence‐of‐wind-fluctuations calculation (often invoked as WTST in some solver decks), and it also documents default settings, units, and allowable values. This summary is written so that it can be indexed in a RAG vector store or used as metadata in a knowledge base.  

1. Table Purpose  
   • Specifies all input parameters to compute the coherence between two points in a turbulent wind field, either as a function of nondimensional frequency (n·r/U) or at a set of discrete frequencies.  
   • Allows selection of one of several empirical coherence curves (Davenport 1968, Davenport 1977, Krenk 1995) for comparison.  

2. Column Definitions  
   – Item: the keyword or parameter name you must supply in the input deck.  
   – Description: what the parameter controls in the coherence calculation.  
   – Unit: physical unit or data type (e.g. [m] for meters, LIT for literal strings).  
   – Default: the value assumed if you omit the keyword.  

3. Parameter Details  

• TYPE  
  – Description: selects which component of the coherence tensor to calculate. You may enter any one of the nine combinations of U, V, W:  
  KUU, KUV, KUW  
  KVU, KVV, KVW  
  KWU, KWV, KWW  
  – Unit: LIT (literal)  
  – Default: “!” (required)  

• NEIG  
  – Description: number of discrete frequencies at which to compute coherence.  
  – Unit: dimensionless  
  – Default: 0  
  – Notes:  
  ◦ If NEIG = 0, the code returns a continuous coherence curve versus nondimensional frequency n·r/U.  
  ◦ If NEIG > 0, exactly NEIG frequency points are read from the next lines of the deck.  

• LC  
  – Description: load-case number (eigenvalue set) from which to pull the wind field modal data.  
  – Unit: dimensionless  
  – Default: 1  

• XREF, YREF, ZREF  
  – Description: coordinates of the reference point in the global coordinate system. This is the “first point” from which you measure.  
  – Unit: meters [m]  
  – Default: 0.0, 0.0, 0.0  

• RX, RY, RZ  
  – Description: components of the offset vector from the reference point to the second point, given in global X, Y, Z.  
  – Unit: meters [m]  
  – Default: 0.0, 0.0, 0.0  

• COMP  
  – Description: which empirical “comparison curve” to overlay on your calculated coherence.  
  – Allowed values (LIT):  
  DAV1 → Davenport, Journal of Wind Engineering (1977)  
  DAV2 → Davenport, Proc. Royal Society (1968)  
  KREN → Krenk, Wind Engineering Journal (1995)  
  – Default: KREN  

• CU, CV, CW  
  – Description: numerical coefficients in the Krenk/Davenport formulations. If you supply CU, CV, and CW, the code will compute and plot the selected empirical coherence law.  
  – Unit: dimensionless  
  – Default: “–” (absent)  
  – Notes:  
  ◦ In the Krenk formulation, CU, CV, CW scale the decay rate in each principal direction.  
  ◦ In Davenport’s original papers two conventions exist: some authors tabulate the coefficient for √(coherence) rather than the coherence itself. Choose the convention you have coefficients for.  

4. Usage Notes  
   • If you omit COMP or its coefficients, only the computed coherence curve appears—no empirical reference is plotted.  
   • To run a spectral-only check (no discrete freqs), leave NEIG = 0 and specify XREF, YREF, ZREF plus RX, RY, RZ.  
   • When NEIG > 0, you must supply NEIG frequency values immediately following these keywords in your deck.  
   • See also related wind spectral cards: WIND, WPRO, WROU, WTOP, WSPE.  

This description can be stored as a text embedding to help users understand what each input does and how the solver uses it to produce coherence curves.

The input table is a parameter reference for the WGEN “wind‐generation” module in a structural analysis environment. It is organized in four columns—Item, Description, Unit, Default—and arranged into five functional groups: 1) basic wind‐case definition, 2) time‐ and frequency‐domain settings, 3) explicit time‐functions, 4) wind‐history visualization, and 5) database I/O. Below is a detailed description of each entry.

1. Basic Wind‐Case Definition  
• LCG  
  – Description: Load case number of the selected basic wind case (the seed for turbulence and randomization).  
  – Unit: none  
  – Default: “!” (an internal placeholder requiring user assignment)  
• SPEC  
  – Description: Selects which wind loading to generate—static or transient fields.  
  – Unit: literal (LIT)  
  – Default: MEAN  
  – Options:  
    · GUST – static wind loads using peak pressures  
    · MEAN – static wind loads of reference mean wind speed νb  
    · TLON, TLAT, TVER – quasi‐static turbulent unit loadings in longitudinal, lateral, or vertical directions  
    · U, V, W – single‐component wind fields (longitudinal, lateral, vertical)  
    · Combinations – UV, UW, VW, UVW for multi‐axis fields  
• LCOH  
  – Description: Account for local coherence (decay of turbulence along an element)  
  – Unit: literal (LIT)  
  – Default: ON  
  – Options: ON or OFF  

2. Time‐ and Frequency‐Domain Parameters  
• T  
  – Description: Total duration of wind‐loading history  
  – Unit: seconds  
  – Default: 600  
• DT  
  – Description: Time increment for discrete history generation  
  – Unit: seconds  
  – Default: 0.2  
  – Notes: DT = 0.0 is allowed for steady wind  
• FMIN  
  – Description: Minimum frequency in generated spectra  
  – Unit: Hertz  
  – Default: 0.0  
• FMAX  
  – Description: Maximum frequency in generated spectra  
  – Unit: Hertz  
  – Default: 1.0  
  – Notes: Should exceed key structural resonance frequencies  
• FDEL  
  – Description: Frequency resolution (spectral increment)  
  – Unit: Hertz  
  – Default: 0.001  
  – Notes: Must be small enough to avoid artificial periodicity  

3. Explicit Time‐Functions (Overrides)  
• FLON, FLAT, FVER  
  – Description: Provide user‐defined time functions in longitudinal, lateral, or vertical directions instead of random‐field generation  
  – Unit: none  
  – Default: “–” (not specified)  

4. Wind‐History Visualization Controls  
• HTYP  
  – Description: Element type(s) selected for wind‐history output  
  – Unit: literal  
  – Options: BEAM, TRUS, CABL, QUAD, NODE  
• NR0 … NR9  
  – Description: Up to ten element or node IDs to save for visualization in DYNR (historical wind velocity components V-X, V-Y, V-Z)  
  – Unit: none  
• SHOW  
  – Description: Interval (in time steps) at which to record visualization snapshots  
  – Unit: none  
  – Default: 10  

5. Database Input/Output  
• FROM  
  – Description: Name of an existing database from which to import wind spectra or complete histories  
  – Unit: literal (Lit*)  
  – Default: none  
• TO  
  – Description: Name of a new or clone database to receive generated histories (often used to preserve master database)  
  – Unit: literal (Lit*)  
  – Default: none  

Together, these parameters steer the two‐step process of WGEN—first creating discrete Fourier spectra for each turbulence component at every node, then transforming them into time histories. Proper selection of T, DT, FMIN, FMAX and FDEL ensures statistical accuracy without undue computational cost, while LCOH, SPEC and the explicit functions enable fine‐tuning of coherence and loading types. Visualization (HTYP/NR*) and database cloning (FROM/TO) facilitate post‐processing and result integration.

 WGEN
 Based on the wind profile and parameters including, turbulence and integral length distribu- tions, defined with the basic load case LFG a transient sequence of loadings will be generated with measured or random wind loading.
 The random properties are assured by the load case number, which is also used as the ini- tialization value for the random sequence. The required number of wind histories has to be derived from the safety concept of the building. For the common design codes and safety factors for wind a number of 11 histories should be adequate in most cases.
 The wind definition thus starts with the basic wind load case, e.g..
 LC 300 W TITL 'Wind basic load case'
 WIND DY 1 XREF 0 0 0 DXR 0.1 1.0 GH 5.0 WROU 0.02 ; WPRO H 100 VBOE 65 ; WTOP ... WSPE EN:DIN
 For a spectral analysis the options TLON, TLAT and TVER create the quasi-static loading based on the turbulence intensity. If the base case has been analyzed, the obtained mean rotations of the sections will be accounted for. The background response may be specified with PSI0 at the load case.
 Selecting components with SPEC, the generation of the individual spectra and wind histories ist triggered. As this is somehow time consuming, it is highly recommended to check first the base load case thoroughly in all details. With the above defined base load case 300 we have:
 LC 301 W TITL 'Dynamic Wind' ; WGEN 300 SPEK UVW T 620 0.1 LC 302 W TITL 'Dynamic Wind' ; WGEN 300 SPEK UVW T 620 0.1 LC 303 W TITL 'Dynamic Wind' ; WGEN 300 SPEK UVW T 620 0.1 ....

metadata.sections: 6.13 WGEN – Generation of Wind Spectra and Histories

content:
LC 301 W TITL 'Dynamic Wind' ; WGEN 300 SPEK UVW T 620 0.1 LC 302 W TITL 'Dynamic Wind' ; WGEN 300 SPEK UVW T 620 0.1 LC 303 W TITL 'Dynamic Wind' ; WGEN 300 SPEK UVW T 620 0.1 .....
 It is possible to change the spectra individually for some histories. In that case WSPE has to be defined with all parameters between the LC and the WGEN definition again. It is also possible to import wind spectra or even complete histories from a secondary data base FROM.
 The generation of the wind history has two steps. The first step (spectra generation) will create form the energy spectra based on the theory given inKovács and Andrä [22] and Kovács [23] an individual Fourier-spectrum for this load case (a discrete Fourier-Integral) for all turbulence components of all nodal points of the structure. The second step (history generation) will then create the discrete wind history via a discrete Fourier-transformation. The spectra generated once may be used for different wind histories: e.g. variant durations of wind, variant time steps or the selection of lower or higher frequencies of turbulence etc..
 The generated windhistories for selected elements may be saved in the database for graphical visualisation with DYNR. The individual components are then available with types V-X, V-Y and V-Z, CFD-Boundary conditions with types U, V and W.
 Some parameters of wind generation (e.g. DT, FMAX, FDEL) may be selected by the user, they have to match however. The frequency step FDEL has to be small enough, otherwise a non natural periodicity of the wind load may be obtained. DT has to be chosen in such a way that all important frequencies of the structure are properly addressed. An optional value of FMAX has then to be larger that those important structural resonance frequencies. For the case of a steady wind it is possible to specify DT 0.0 as special case.
 The wind generation will become very costly on the other side if the parameters are chosen to generous, thus it might be necessary to choose a best compromise. FMAX and FDEL may
 be also changed for tests or prechecks in the evaluation phase of a project to have shorter response times. For the final design however, the parameters should match the statistic nec- essaries. The defaults are selected based on the needs for large bridges. for smaller structures modifications are necessary, e.g. reducing the value of DT, enlarging the value of FMAX.

be also changed for tests or prechecks in the evaluation phase of a project to have shorter response times. For the final design however, the parameters should match the statistic nec- essaries. The defaults are selected based on the needs for large bridges. for smaller structures modifications are necessary, e.g. reducing the value of DT, enlarging the value of FMAX..
 Within the generation of turbulence a decay of turbulence for the end point of an element based on the local decay of coherency along the beam axis is implemented allowing an easier generation of beam loading. For checks of the turbulence it might be requested to switch this option off via the definition of LCOH OFF.
 It is also recommended to start with a primary load case based on the static wind to keep the disturbances of the start up period as low as possible. The best start is to use the same wind field of the mean wind directly as a static load case for this purpose.
 For the static wind generation the wind velocities will be converted to classical loadings, which can be used in other programs as well. If the literal MEAN or GUST has an appendix ":E" the loads will be generated separately, thus the transverse loading is acting with a possible eccentricity in the WPAR referenece point.
 The volume of the data may become rather large, because a nonlinear history will create an own load case for every time step. That is why we recommend to use a separate copy of the database for every history. With the definition of the TO item, a clone of the current database is created containing all necessary data for the wind history analysis. After performing the analysis and all superpositions, the extreme values may be imported into the master via the program DBMERG.

Below is a structured, detailed description of the WIPT table and its fields, explaining how each parameter is used in the wind-tunnel load-case generation process. This text is intended to be ingested by a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store so that later queries about wind-loading setup, influence functions and mesh point definitions can be answered precisely.

1. Context and Purpose  
   • In a wind-tunnel experiment, discrete pressure or force measurements are taken at selected points on a scale model surface.  
   • Each measurement “point” is turned into its own load case: a unit pressure is applied at that point only, and the resulting areal distribution is used as that point’s influence function.  
   • WIPT defines the geometric location of each measurement point and controls how it is projected onto the finite-element mesh (constant or bilinear distribution).  
   • Downstream tools (SOFILOAD, DYNA or STEP) read WIPT entries to create static or transient load cases for analysis.

2. Table Overview  
   The table has four columns:  
   – Item: the keyword or parameter name used in the input deck.  
   – Description: a short text on what the field represents.  
   – Unit: the physical units or data type expected.  
   – Default: the value assumed if the field is omitted.

3. Fields Detail

  • X  
    – Description: X‐coordinate of the measurement point in the global model (hull) coordinate system.  
    – Unit: meters [m].  
    – Default: 0.0.  
    – Notes: Together with Y and Z, this locates the data point in 3D space; critical for determining the element containing or neighboring the point.

  • Y  
    – Description: Y‐coordinate of the measurement point in global coordinates.  
    – Unit: meters [m].  
    – Default: 0.0.

  • Z  
    – Description: Z‐coordinate of the measurement point in global coordinates.  
    – Unit: meters [m].  
    – Default: 0.0.

  • GRP  
    – Description: Optional grouping index for the wind mesh (e.g. to assign the point to a particular surface patch or façade group).  
    – Unit: integer or dash (no units).  
    – Default: “–” (not assigned).  
    – Notes: If used, SOFILOAD may restrict the influence shape to elements belonging to that group.

  • TOL  
    – Description: Tolerance for projecting the measurement point onto a shell or surface element.  
    – Unit: meters [m].  
    – Default: 0.01.  
    – Notes: If the projected distance from the point to the element plane is within this tolerance, the point is considered “inside” that element.

  • ELIM  
    – Description: Edge-detection limit; controls whether the influence shape is treated as constant over the element or bilinear.  
    – Unit: dimensionless.  
    – Default: 0.4.  
    – Notes:  
       • Value = 0.0 ⇒ the point is at the element center ⇒ constant pressure over the element.  
       • Value = 1.0 ⇒ the point is exactly on the edge ⇒ bilinear shape function across the four nodes.  
       • Intermediate values set the threshold for categorizing the point as “edge” or “interior.” An “edge” point causes node loads to be extrapolated, sometimes exceeding unity.

  • MNAM  
    – Description: Name of the database or file containing the wind mesh definition (the FEM shell or solid model describing the hull surface).  
    – Unit: literal string (Lit*).  
    – Default: “!” (a placeholder indicating no external mesh file).  
    – Notes: When specified, SOFILOAD pulls element and node connectivity from the named database to build the areal load pattern.

4. Workflow Integration  
   • After all WIPT lines are read, SOFILOAD generates one static or transient load case per point.  
   • If a point lies inside an element (inside TOL, ELIM criterion), a single‐element constant pressure patch is used.  
   • If the point is near an edge (ELIM threshold exceeded), a bilinear interpolation shape spanning the four neighboring nodes is built.  
   • The real measured pressure time history for that point multiplies the unit‐pressure influence shape in either DYNA (directly) or is unbundled into ASE load cases via STEP.

5. Retained Defaults  
   Once TOL, ELIM and MNAM are set in the first WIPT definition, subsequent WIPT entries inherit those values unless overridden. This ensures consistency across many measurement points without repetitive specification.

The image, labeled “Figure 6.7: Meshing of measurement points,” presents two side-by-side, isometric views of a planar surface subdivided into finite‐element cells with superimposed wind-tunnel pressure measurement locations (blue dots). It illustrates two strategies for placing measurement points relative to a coarse mesh of quadrilaterals (or triangles) when preparing input for SOFILOAD/WIPT in a wind‐load analysis.

Left panel (a):  
 • The overall shape is an oblique quadrilateral sketched in solid black, giving a slight three-dimensional perspective.  
 • Interior mesh lines are drawn as dashed green strokes, creating a 3 × 3 grid of rectangular cells (nine cells total).  
 • Within each cell sits a single blue circular marker, positioned roughly at the geometric center of the element.  
 • This arrangement corresponds to the approach “(a)” described in the text, where each measurement point lies well inside one element. Under WIPT, such an internal location yields a constant influence function across that element—applying the measured pressure uniformly over the entire cell.

Right panel (b):  
 • The same parent quadrilateral is now subdivided by only two dashed mesh lines—one vertical, one horizontal—bisecting it into four large quadrilateral elements.  
 • Here the measurement points (blue dots) are located near or on the element corners and edges rather than at the centers. In the sketch, five dots appear: two near the top corners, one midway up on the left edge, and two near the bottom corners.  
 • This corresponds to approach “(b),” where each data point falls at or close to a node of the bilinear element. WIPT’s bilinear shape functions then assign a value of 1.0 at the measurement point and 0.0 at the opposite nodes, producing a linearly varying pressure distribution within each surrounding element. A node nearest the data point may receive an extrapolated factor greater than 1.0 if the point lies outside the strict convex hull of that element’s interior.

Together, the two illustrations emphasize:  
 • How to generate one load case per data point by zeroing all other pressures and applying a unit pressure at the point in question.  
 • That interior points yield constant (“flat”) element loads, while corner‐adjacent points invoke bilinear interpolation with potentially amplified nodal weights.  
 • How these influence functions can then be used directly in DYNA or converted into discrete ASE load cases via STEP, with default settings for ELIM, TOL, and MNAM carried through all definitions.

See also: WIND, WPRO, WROU, WTOP, WSPE
 WIPT
 Using a wind tunnel experiment a model of the building is tested yielding integral forces or pressures in discrete points. They vary along time and it is depending on the structure if the loading may be taken as quasi static mean value or if the dynamic effects should be modelled. To convert those pressures to loadings the recommended procedure is as follows:
 • For every measured data item a separate load case is defined.
 • Then a unit pressure of 1.0 is applied in that data point while all other data points have the value of 0.0. This yields a areal distribution of pressure to be taken as influence function of the pressure in that point.
 • Each of this load cases may be taken as static or defined with FUNC as transient. In both cases the applied factors are the real pressures in that data point.
 Assuming that we have an area of the hull of our structure with several measurement data points, we may create a coarse mesh of triangles or quadrilaterals in two ways. We have either the possibility to create this mesh to have each data point near the center of one element (a) or in the corners or near the corners of a bilinear mesh (b):
 Than the coordinates of that selected data point are specified with WIPT. SOFILOAD will create an areal load pattern with the selected shape of the influence function. If the point is inside
 the element a constant pressure for the whole element is created. if the point is near the edge (ELIM) a bilienar shape function is assumed with the value 1.0 in the data point and 0.0 in the distant nodes. Thus the node nearest to the data point will have an extrapolated value > 1.0.
 The influence functions may be then used directly within DYNA or may be converted with STEP to single load cases for ASE.
 Values for ELIM, TOL and MNAM are retained as default for all following definitions.

The image is divided into two main parts: at the top, the Morison‐type loading equation is given in symbolic form; below it, a cross‐sectional schematic (Figure 7.1) illustrates how a regular wave and its associated velocity field impinge on a vertical cylinder of diameter D.  

1. Mathematical formulation (upper part)  
   - The total inline wave force F per unit length is split into a drag component Fd and an inertia component Fi:  
     F = Fd + Fi = ½·ρ·Cd·D·U²   +   (π/4)·ρ·Chyd·D²·(∂U/∂t)  
   - Here ρ is the water density, Cd the drag coefficient, Chyd the inertial (hydrodynamic) coefficient, D the cylinder diameter, U the local water velocity, and ∂U/∂t the local water‐particle acceleration.  

2. Schematic illustration (lower part – Figure 7.1 “Wave Loading”)  
   - A single vertical cylindrical pile (dark gray shading) of width D is founded on a bed (hatched pattern) and immersed in water. The mean waterline is shown by a horizontal dashed line; above it, the free‐surface wave profile is drawn in outline.  
   - To the left of the cylinder a propagating wave crest is sketched. An arrow marked “c” above the crest indicates the wave celerity traveling from left to right.  
   - Within the fluid domain, velocity vectors develop beneath the wave. A curved blue line depicts the spatial variation of the instantaneous horizontal velocity U(z): it is zero at the seabed, increases with elevation z, and reaches a maximum near the free surface.  
   - Two sets of colored arrows along this velocity profile distinguish the two force contributions:  
     • Blue arrows (pointing largely to the right, slightly upward) represent the distributed inertial force Fi arising from fluid acceleration acting on the structure.  
     • Red arrows (horizontal) represent the distributed drag force Fd proportional to the square of the relative velocity. A thicker red vector drawn adjacent to the cylinder indicates the resultant drag at the structure’s surface.  
   - A local coordinate system (vx to the right, vy upward) is drawn near the bed to emphasize the sign convention for velocities and accelerations.  
   - On the right, the cylinder width is explicitly dimensioned by “D,” and on the vertical edge the elevation coordinate “z” is indicated to remind that both U and ∂U/∂t vary with depth.  

Taken together, the formula and schematic illustrate how, in a decoupled (two‐step) analysis, a software tool first computes the undisturbed wave kinematics (as if no structure were present) and then evaluates the local drag and inertia forces on the embedded member by inserting the relative velocities and accelerations into the Morison equation. These loading components are later assembled in SOFiLOAD under a dedicated wave‐load case for subsequent structural analysis.

Waves on the ocean are primarly created by wind over longer distances. They are an essential loading for embedded structures in the coastal regions or offshore. Similar to the wind a large scale stochastic wave field is generated, influenced substantially by sea currents and the shape of the coast. For these problems special software (e.g. SWAN) is available.
 For the loading of a structure a local design wave or wave spectra is provided, which is saved in SOFiLOAD in an individual load case number. The SOFiSTiK solution separates the wave model from the structure similar as in the previous chapter. The water flow is calculated as if there is no structure present. For the evaluation of the forces however the movement of the structure will be accounted for by taking the relative velocities and accelerations by the Morison equation.

Oceanic waters are deep waters, such that the waves are unaffected by the seabed, with- out currents or obstacles such as islands, headlands and breakwaters. In contrast with the treatment of coastal waters, a limited but constant water depth, i.e. a horizontal bottom, is considered [29].
 Waves on the surface of the ocean, with periods usually between 3 to 25 sec, are a funda- mental feature of coastal regions. Other wave motions exist on the ocean including internal
 waves, currents, tides, and edge waves. The term waves will here apply only to surface gravity waves, to water with idealized physical properties and motions and with gravitation as the only external force [30].
 Knowledge of these waves and the forces they generate is essential for the design of offshore structures. An overview of the theories and mathematical formulas for describing ocean surface waves and the forces, accelerations, and velocities due to them, is given here, and two main wave categories are treated: regular waves and irregular waves.
 In the Regular Waves section, the objective is to provide a detailed understanding of the kine- matics of a wave field through examination of waves of constant height and period. In the Irregular Waves section, the objective is to describe the methods involved for analyzing irregu- lar waves which are more descriptive of the waves seen in nature.

Wave theories are approximations to reality. When looking at the sea surface, it is typically irregular, three-dimensional and changes in time. The complexity of this time-varying 3 − D surface cannot be adequately described in its whole, and thus simplifying assumptions must be employed in order to arrive at estimates able to represent it.
 The simplest mathematical representation of oceanic waves is provided by the linear wave theory. Linear theory is described by freely propagating, small in amplitude, harmonic waves. The main requirement for the linear theory to apply is that the amplitudes of the waves are small, i.e. small compared with the wave length and small compared to the water depth. This linear theory is also called Airy and can cover many engineering problems with reasonable accuracy.
 When wave heights become larger, the linear theory may not be adequate and finite amplitude wave theories have to be used. These theories are nonlinear and allow formulation of waves that are not purely sinusoidal in shape. For steep waves or waves in shallow water, e.g. waves with flatter troughs and peaked crests, higher order theories will be described such as the Stokes wave theory and the Cnoidal wave theory. Furthermore, the stretching of linear theory is introduced, which compensates for the small amplitude assumption and maps the results into the finite region of their extent.
 Adopting a wave theory, care must be taken to ensure that the wave phenomenon of interest is described reasonably well by the theory, since offshore design depends on the ability to predict sufficiently wave surface profiles and water motion.
 A regular wave, may be described by a periodic deterministic function controlled by three es- sential parameters:
 a wave height H (difference between crest and trough)
 a period of the wave T (mostly between 3 and 25 sec)

The input “Table 7.2” is a compact one-column listing of four different “stretching” (or “compression”) formulas for the instantaneous horizontal particle velocity vₓ in linear water-wave theory. All four expressions share the same basic variables and parameters:

• vₓ(x,z,t): horizontal velocity component  
• ω: angular frequency of the wave  
• α: wave amplitude scale (often equals surface elevation η at crest)  
• k: wave number (2π/wavelength)  
• d: still-water depth  
• z: vertical coordinate measured from mean water level (z = 0)  
• η = η(x,t): instantaneous free-surface elevation  
• t and x: time and horizontal coordinate  

Because classical Airy theory (linear wave theory) prescribes a vertical profile of velocity valid only from the bottom (z = –d) up to the still-water level (SWL, z = 0), these formulas are introduced to “stretch” or “compress” that profile so that it can be applied through the instantaneous surface z = η(x,t). They are used in Random Wave (RAG) or near-surface kinematics modules to avoid the overestimation of velocity above SWL when naïvely extrapolating Airy results.

Structure of the table  
– The single header cell “Horizontal Velocity” precedes the list of four vₓ expressions.  
– No separate columns of description are given; each row is a formula, with trailing remarks on its domain of validity.

Row 1: Instantaneous-depth hyperbolic stretching  
  vₓ = ω α [ cosh( k·d·(z + d)/(η + d) ) / sinh(k d) ] · cos(k x – ω t)  
  • The classic depth-profile cosh(k(z+ d))/sinh(kd) is replaced by cosh scaled with the ratio of current depth (η+d) to still depth d.  
  • As η fluctuates, the vertical coordinate z is nonlinearly mapped into the cosh argument so that vₓ remains finite at the moving surface.

Row 2: Instantaneous-depth stretching with full cosh/sinh  
  vₓ = ω α [ cosh(k·(z + d)) / sinh(k·(η + d)) ] · cos(k x – ω t)  
  • Similar goal as Row 1 but here both numerator and denominator involve instantaneous total depth (η+d) in the sinh term.  
  • Ensures exact Airy profile at the mean surface when η=0, and automatically “compresses” the velocity‐decay scale when the water shallows or steepens.

Row 3: Two-layer hybrid (stretch–Airy)  
  vₓ = ω α [ cosh(k d) / sinh(k d) ] · cos(k x – ω t)  for z > 0  
        Airy‐theory profile (standard linear)             for z ≤ 0  
  • Above SWL (z>0) the profile is “frozen” at its SWL value (cosh(kd)/sinh(kd)), so no further decay; below SWL, one simply uses classic Airy distribution.

Row 4: Linear correction above SWL  
  vₓ = ω α [ cosh(k d) / sinh(k d)  +  k·z ] · cos(k x – ω t)  for z > 0  
        Airy‐theory profile                             for z ≤ 0  
  • Builds on Row 3 by adding a linear-in-z term to adjust velocity above SWL.  
  • This gives a first-order correction that increases vₓ linearly toward the free-surface elevation.

How to read and use this table  
1. Identify your range of interest in the water column—whether you need velocities just above the mean water line, all the way up to the instantaneous crest, or only below SWL.  
2. Choose the stretching scheme that best matches your application:  
   – Fully nonlinear hyperbolic stretching (Rows 1 or 2) for smooth profiles into the crest region.  
   – Simpler frozen-profile or linear corrections (Rows 3 or 4) when computational simplicity is paramount.  
3. Substitute your instantaneous η(x,t) into the appropriate formula to compute vₓ(x,z,t) at any elevation z.  

Contextual notes from the surrounding text:  
– Airy‐theory velocities above z=0 are known to overestimate particle speeds at crests if extrapolated naively.  
– Stretching schemes preserve the small-amplitude assumptions below z=0 (Airy valid) while providing a plausible extension into finite crest amplitudes.  
– They are essential in design and analysis of near-surface kinematics in offshore structures, where loads depend sensitively on horizontal velocities at or above the free surface.

The image is a two‐dimensional chart (Figure 7.4) that maps out the ranges of validity for Stokes‐type (periodic, finite‐amplitude) versus Cnoidal (long, shallow‐water) wave theories, and it also shows the theoretical maximum normalized wave height Hm∕d as a function of the nondimensional wavelength L∕d. 

Axes  
• Horizontal axis: Wavelength‐to‐depth ratio, L∕d, running roughly from 1 (deep water limit) through about 10 (intermediate/transitional depth) and extending off to the “solitary” or infinite‐wavelength limit on the right.  
• Vertical axis: Normalized wave height, H∕d, from 0 up to 1.0.  

Curves and Regions  
1. Thick black curve (labelled “Hm∕d”):  
   – Represents the upper theoretical limit of wave height relative to depth, as derived by Williams (1981) and given by Fenton’s Equation 7.17.  
   – Starts near Hm∕d ≃ 0.14 at L∕d = 1, rises fairly steeply in the transitional region (around L∕d ≃ 3–10), and asymptotes toward Hm∕d ≃ 0.78 as L∕d → ∞ (the solitary‐wave limit).  
2. Thin black curve (labelled “U > 40”):  
   – Marks the locus where the Ursell number U (which quantifies the importance of nonlinearity via U = (3/4) (H∕L)/(kd)³ sinh³(kd)) just reaches 40.  
   – To the right of this curve (longer L∕d, shallower relative depth), U exceeds 40 and therefore Cnoidal theory is more appropriate.  
   – To the left (shorter L∕d, deeper relative depth), U < 40 and Stokes‐type expansions remain valid.  

Regions:  
• “Stokes Theory” zone occupies the lower‐left portion, beneath both the thick and the thin curves, typically for L∕d less than about 5–10.  
• “Cnoidal Theory” zone lies to the right of the thin U > 40 curve, beneath the thick Hm∕d envelope, and extends toward the solitary wave limit.  

Dashed reference lines:  
– A horizontal dashed line at H∕d = 0.55 indicates the empirically observed maximum wave‐height‐to‐depth ratio (Nelson, 1994) just before breaking, which in practice is lower than the theoretical 0.78 limit.  
– A faint dashed extension near the “Solitary” label on the top‐right shows the asymptotic Hm∕d ≃ 0.78 for infinitely long waves in the inviscid limit.  

Labels and Notation:  
• Key annotations identify the two primary theoretical frameworks (“Stokes Theory” on the left, “Cnoidal Theory” on the right) and specify the solitary‐wave asymptote.  
• Both axes and curves are clearly marked; the thick line is captioned “Hm∕d,” the thin one “U > 40.”  

Interpretation:  
This diagram succinctly delineates (1) the maximum nondimensional wave height one can expect before breaking (thick curve), (2) the degree of nonlinearity at which a Stokes‐series expansion ceases to converge effectively (thin Ursell‐number curve at U = 40), and (3) the empirical breaking limit of H∕d = 0.55. It thereby provides practical guidance on when to apply Stokes expansions (shorter waves, deeper water) versus Cnoidal theory (longer waves, shallower water) in steady‐wave modeling.

The results of these load cases are then taken mutually exclusive for the most unfavorable case. This will be achieved in SOFILOAD with the COPY command and a shift by DX,DY.

The image is a Cartesian‐style line plot entitled “Figure 7.5: Jonswap Spectra,” showing how the JONSWAP spectral density E(ω) varies with angular frequency ω for different values of the peak‐enhancement parameter γ. Key elements of the figure are as follows:

1. Axes and scales  
   • Horizontal axis (abscissa): ω, ranging roughly from 0.2 on the left to 1.2 on the right. Tick marks appear at 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, and 1.2.  
   • Vertical axis (ordinate): E(ω), the spectral energy density, from 0.0 at the bottom up to 12.0 at the top. Major gridlines or ticks appear at 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12.  

2. Curves for different γ values  
   Five distinct curves are overlaid, each corresponding to a different value of the JONSWAP peak‐enhancement coefficient γ. Each curve is smooth and unimodal, peaking near ω ≈ 0.7 (the estimated peak frequency ωpek). As γ increases, the peak of E(ω) becomes both sharper and taller, illustrating the effect of the enhancement factor on the narrowness and amplitude of the spectrum. Specifically:  
   • γ = 1.0 (blue curve): the broadest, lowest peak—this case effectively reduces the JONSWAP spectrum to the Pierson–Moskowitz form for fully developed seas.  
   • γ = 2.0 (green curve): a slightly higher, narrower peak than γ = 1.0.  
   • γ = 3.3 (teal or cyan curve): the “average” JONSWAP formulation often quoted in literature; the peak is more pronounced.  
   • γ = 5.0 (golden‐yellow curve): a noticeably sharper and taller crest.  
   • γ = 7.0 (light gray curve): the most acute, highest peak of all five, rising above 10 on the E(ω) axis.

3. Peak‐frequency marker  
   A vertical dashed line is drawn at ω ≈ 0.7 to denote the spectral peak frequency ωpek. This visually anchors where all curves attain their maximum energy density.

4. Annotations  
   Each curve is labeled at or near its crest with its corresponding γ value (for example, “γ = 7.0” next to the topmost, gray line; “γ = 1.0” on the lowest, blue line). These text labels are placed slightly above or to the side of each peak to aid identification without a separate legend box.

5. Overall appearance  
   The five curves are plotted on a light grid or plain white background, allowing clear color differentiation. The transition from broad (γ = 1) to narrow (γ = 7) spectral shapes is visually striking. The figure neatly encapsulates how increasing the peak‐enhancement factor in the JONSWAP spectrum concentrates energy closer to the peak frequency, a phenomenon directly tied to the statistical methods and wave‐spectra theory discussed in the surrounding text.

In the context of linear wave theory and spectral sampling (e.g., constant vs. irrational frequency intervals), this plot demonstrates the JONSWAP spectrum’s flexibility via its γ parameter. The input table defines all of the wave‐and‐current parameters a user must supply when setting up a hydrodynamic loading case.  It is organized into four columns:  
• Item – the keyword the user types in.  
• Description – what that keyword controls.  
• Unit – the physical unit in which the value must be given.  
• Default – the value assumed if the user does not override it.  

Below is a row-by-row breakdown:

1. TYPE  
   • Description: Selects the basic wave formulation. Two main categories – Regular Waves and Irregular Waves – each with multiple sub-options.  
     – Regular Waves:  
       • AIRY: Linear (first-order) wave theory  
       • STOK: Fifth-order Stokes theory  
       • CNOI: Fifth-order cnoidal theory  
       • You can override the perturbation order by appending “:2” (second order Stokes) or “:3” (third order cnoidal) to the above codes.  
     – Irregular Waves (spectral):  
       • JONS: JONSWAP spectrum  
       • TMAS: TMA shallow-water extension of JONSWAP  
       • Wave‐stretching variants applied to AIRY baseline:  
         – :W Wheeler stretching  
         – :C Chakrabarti stretching  
         – :V Vertical stretching  
         – :E Linear extrapolation  
       • Frequency‐sampling option:  
         – :I Irrational frequency spacing instead of uniform ∆f  
   • Unit: literal text (LIT)  
   • Default: “*” (none – must be specified)

2. H  
   • Description: Significant wave height.  
   • Unit: meters [m]  
   • Default: user must supply (!)  

3. T  
   • Description: Wave period. For a spectrum this is the spectral peak period.  
   • Unit: seconds [sec]  
   • Default: user must supply (!)  

4. D  
   • Description: Water depth (still-water depth measured from datum to seabed).  
   • Unit: meters [m]  
   • Default: “∞” (deep water)  

5. SWL  
   • Description: Sea Water Level (e.g. storm tide elevation above datum).  
   • Unit: meters [m]  
   • Default: 0.0  

6. DX  
   • Description: Main wave propagation direction (degrees from north or as defined).  
   • Unit: nondimensional (—)  
   • Default: 0.0  

7. DY  
   • Description: Main current direction (if a superimposed constant current is applied).  
   • Unit: nondimensional (—)  
   • Default: 0.0  

8. DZ  
   • Description: Magnitude of any superimposed tidal current.  
   • Unit: meters per second [m/sec]  
   • Default: 0.0  

9. UC (often labeled Uc)  
   • Description: Background constant current speed (used together with DZ).  
   • Unit: meters per second [m/sec]  
   • Default: 0.0  

10. EXPU  
   • Description: Exponent α for an exponential current‐profile distribution, i.e. U(z) ∝ exp(α·z). Literature suggests α=0.17.  
   • Unit: nondimensional (—)  
   • Default: 0.17  

11. RHO  
   • Description: Density of the water.  
   • Unit: kilograms per cubic meter [kg/m³]  
   • Default: 1025  

12. NF  
   • Description: Number of discrete frequencies to represent the spectrum.  
   • Unit: nondimensional (—)  
   • Default: 100  

13. TMIN  
   • Description: Smallest wave period in the spectrum. Used only in irregular (spectral) cases.  
   • Unit: seconds [sec]  
   • Default: 3.0  

14. TMAX  
   • Description: Largest wave period in the spectrum. Also only for irregular waves.  
   • Unit: seconds [sec]  
   • Default: (not shown in the snippet; often set so that TMAX > T)

Additional contextual notes (from the manual text):  
- When using a spectrum (JONS, TMAS, etc.), H refers to the significant wave height and T to the spectral peak period.  
- The seed for the random phase generator is the load-case number, ensuring repeatability. NF, TMIN, TMAX apply only in spectral cases.  
- Appending “:I” to the spectrum keyword (e.g. JONS:I or JONS:IW) invokes an irrational frequency spacing for amplitude calculation instead of a constant interval.  
- For the TMA spectrum, default γ and α (the peak enhancement and scale parameters) follow Hughes’s shallow-water parameterization (Eq. 7.23). If you prefer standard JONSWAP values (γ=3.3, α=0.0081), you may specify them explicitly.  
- A constant current can be added to wave kinematics. Its vertical distribution may use an exponential law with exponent EXPU=0.17 unless overridden.

The table in question defines all of the wave‐related input parameters required to model a single design wave or—alternatively—an entire irregular wave spectrum for offshore and coastal engineering analyses. It is laid out in columnar form with each column heading representing one independent variable or control parameter. Below is a detailed description of each column, its purpose, and how it interacts with the accompanying explanatory text.

1. Item  
   • A running index or label for each wave “load case.”  
   • Serves two purposes: identifying the case in printouts and acting as the seed for the random-number generator when building an irregular spectrum.

2. TYPE (Wave model)  
   • Specifies the kind of wave representation. Examples include:  
     – MONO (single‐period sinusoid)  
     – JONSWAP (standard Pierson-Moskowitz–type spectrum)  
     – TMA (shallow-water version of JONSWAP)  
     – Custom spectra indicated by literal suffixes such as “:I” for irrational frequency spacing or “IW” for frequency stretching.  

3. H (Wave height)  
   • If TYPE is a single wave (MONO), H is the amplitude (peak‐to‐trough).  
   • If TYPE is a spectrum, H is the significant wave height (Hs), i.e. the average height of the highest one-third of all waves.

4. T (Wave period)  
   • For a regular wave, T is the period.  
   • For a spectrum, T represents the peak spectral period (Tp), at which energy density is maximal.  
   • When T is part of an irregular spectrum run, multiple subintervals may be generated according to NF and TMIN/TMAX (see below).

5. D (Wave direction)  
   • Mean propagation direction in degrees (meteorological convention or mathematical convention as stipulated by the solver).

6. SWL (Still Water Level)  
   • Reference water elevation at which the wave kinematics are superimposed.  
   • Can be used to model tides or set a datum.

7. DX, DY, DZ (Spatial offsets)  
   • Phase‐shift distances in the global X, Y, and Z directions.  
   • Used to shift the wave field in space, important for arrays of load cases or for initializing multiple sensors/structures.

8. UC (Uniform current)  
   • A constant background current that modifies wave kinematics.  
   • Can be positive or negative, in line with the global coordinate system.

9. EXPU (Exponential current distribution exponent)  
   • When a depth‐varying current profile is desired, wave kinematics are computed with an exponential decay law:  
     U(z) = UC · exp(–α · z/H),  
     where α is typically 0.17 (literature value) and z is the local vertical coordinate.

10. RHO (Water density)  
    • Defaults to 1025 kg/m³ (seawater) unless overridden for special fluids or temperature/salinity cases.

11. NF (Number of frequency intervals)  
    • Only applies when TYPE denotes a spectrum.  
    • Controls the discretization of the frequency domain:  
      – If NF = N, the spectrum is split into N bands.  
      – Irrational (“:I”) or stretched (“IW”) spacing schemes ignore the default constant Δf.

12. TMIN (Minimum wave period)  
    • The lower bound of the spectral band.  
    • Relevant only if NF is specified, otherwise ignored for single‐period runs.

13. TMAX (Maximum wave period)  
    • Upper bound of the spectral band for irregular spectra.

14. Notes and defaults from the accompanying text  
    • When using TMA, default parameters γ and α are set per Hughes Eq. 7.23, enabling equilibrium wind-sea conditions to be modeled directly.  
    • For a standard JONSWAP spectrum, users may override defaults (e.g. γ = 3.3, α = 0.0081) to generate a shallow-water form.  
    • The seed for random phase generation is the load case number, ensuring reproducibility.  

In practice, the user selects either a regular wave or an irregular spectrum by setting TYPE. For regular waves, only H, T, D, SWL, DX, DY, DZ, UC, EXPU, and RHO are needed. For irregular waves, NF, TMIN, TMAX (and optional spectral parameters) are activated to sample the spectrum. The ability to append “:I” or “IW” to the TYPE allows the engineer to request nonuniform frequency spacing, which can reduce sampling error in certain bands. Finally, the table may continue on the next page with further cases or additional explanatory footnotes.

The provided table defines a set of spectral‐model parameters used whenever an irregular wave spectrum (for example JONSWAP or TMA) is specified instead of a single “design” wave. Each row represents one input item, giving its mnemonic code (“Item”), a brief description, the units (here none are dimensionalized), and the default value applied if the user does not override it. Below is a detailed breakdown.

1. Columns  
   • Item  
     – A short alphanumeric code that identifies each spectrum parameter.  
   • Description  
     – A concise English phrase explaining the physical or mathematical role of the parameter.  
   • Unit  
     – Indicates measurement units. All entries are marked “—” because these parameters are dimensionless or implicitly defined by the spectral formulation.  
   • Default  
     – The value used in the absence of user input. Some defaults are derived from standard JONSWAP practice; others are computed internally (see “*”).

2. Rows / Parameters  
   • TMAX  
     – “highest wave period.” In spectrum generation, this is the maximum wave period considered in the frequency domain. Default = 25 s. It effectively truncates the spectrum at long waves.  
   • GAM  
     – “Peak-enhancement coefficient,” also known as γ in JONSWAP. Controls the sharpness of the spectral peak. Default = 3.3, the classical JONSWAP choice for a moderately peaked wind-sea spectrum.  
   • ALF  
     – “Energy scale parameter,” commonly denoted α in spectrum equations. It sets the overall energy level of the spectrum. Default = “*,” indicating that α is calculated internally (for example using Eq. 7.23 in Hughes [40] for TMA) to match a given significant wave height.  
   • SIGA  
     – “Peak-width parameter,” σa in JONSWAP. Defines the spectral bandwidth on the low-frequency side of the peak. Default = 0.07.  
   • SIGB  
     – “Peak-width parameter,” σb in JONSWAP. Defines the spectral bandwidth on the high-frequency side of the peak. Default = 0.09.  
   • S  
     – “Exponent directional distribution.” A parameter in the directional spreading function, controlling how narrowly waves are clustered around the mean direction. Default = 0 (isotropic or very broad distribution).  
   • PHI  
     – “Resolution for direct. distribution.” The angular step (in degrees) used when discretizing the directional spread. Default = 5°.

3. Contextual Notes  
   – These parameters tie back to the additional text’s discussion of using a full spectrum (with H as the significant wave height and T as the peak period) and the possibility of applying an irrational frequency spacing (“:I” option) or a stretching scheme (“:IW”).  
   – For the TMA spectrum, the defaults for γ and α are those given by Hughes [40], which allow seamless transition from deep-water JONSWAP to shallow-water forms.  
   – Directional spreading can be further modified by a constant current profile (exponential with exponent ≃ 0.17) when wave kinematics are enhanced by currents (UC, EXPU in the broader input set).  

In practice, users may override any of these defaults to tailor the spectral shape, peak sharpness, energy level, and directional characteristics to site-specific or design requirements.

 Instead of the single design wave a complete spectra of an irregular wave field may be used. In that case H is the siginficant wave height, while T is the peak period of the spectra. The seed for the random generator is the load case number. Values of NF, TMIN, TMAX etc. are used only for that case.
 Furthermore, the irrational frequency, rather than the default constant frequency interval, can be applied for the calculation of the amplitudes, when using a spectrum. This is done by specifying the literal :I after the input spectra type, e.g. JONS:I or with a stretching scheme JONS:IW.
 For the TMA spectrum, the default values used here for the parameters γ and α are given by Eq. 7.23, as described by Hughes [40]. The main advantage of this parameterization is the ability to specify the equilibrium wind sea spectrum associated with a given energy level. Otherwise a standard input could be given as in JONSWAP spectra, such as for example γ = 3.3 and α = 0.0081, which will just transform the corresponding JONSWAP to a shallow water spectrum.
 The wave kinematics may be enhanced by a constant current. For this an exponential distribu- tion may be specified. For the exponent α a value of 0.17 is found in the literature.

The snow loading in SOFiLOAD is just at the beginning of the total development.
 Wehen defining the design code with NORM it is possible to define the snow zone and the alti- tude about sea level. From those values a basic snow load is derived according the provisions of the design codes.
 • The basic snow load is defined in SOFiLOAD according to EN-1991-1-3 for the climate regions following appendix C according to table C.1 dependant on the country code and the Z-value defined at NORM SNOW (1,2,3,4 or 4.5), and the altitude.
 • For Germany, Austria and Switzerland the national documents have been provided instead: DIN (Zones 1,1a,2,2a and 3), OENORM (2*,2,3,4) and the SIA 261.
 • For Italy the national document DM 2005 with Snow Zones I,II,III according table 3.5 has been implemented.
 Snowloads are available for all free loadings of type LINE and AREA as load type SNOW. The load value then defines the form factor wich is used to be multiplied with the basic snow load on the ground, depending on the inclination of the roof and local aglomerations.
SOFiLOAD enables the transfer of support forces from another database (source) to the cur- rent model (target). This makes it possible, for example, to model the floors of a building independently.

There are essentially two different ways to assign support loads of the source geometry to target geometries: i) manually, by linking the respective involved structural lines (SLN) and structural points (SPT), or ii) (partially) automatically.
 The magnitude and shape of the resulting point and line loads result from the load transfer function and whether the target geometries act independently or as a unit (see modes for target geometries).

The image is a schematic, two-part figure (labeled “a)” and “b)”) illustrating a 1:1 assignment of support loads from a source geometry (SLN) to a target geometry (SLN or SPT). Each part shows a simple structural element, its applied support loads (in green), and the corresponding transferred loads (in red) on the target line or point.

Part a) (left half of the figure):  
– At the very left, a simplified plan-view of a floor slab with a rectangular opening (shown as a white rectangle with a black, irregularly shaped inset) sits between two darker gray bands (indicating beam zones). This contextual graphic suggests the overall structural slab.  
– To the right of the slab, a straight horizontal line segment represents the source structural line SLN 201. At its four equally spaced end-nodes (indicated by small crosshair symbols), green upward arrows are drawn, each arrow pointing vertically up from the line. These arrows represent the support reactions that the slab applies to SLN 201. Above the line, the number “201” is centered in bold.  
– Directly below the source line, a second horizontal line segment depicts the target structural line SLN 101. At its two end-nodes (also marked with crosshairs) and at one intermediate point, red downward arrows are drawn from a red, polygonal “chain” that slopes from left to right, illustrating how the individual support loads from SLN 201 are mapped exactly—one for one—onto SLN 101. The red chain segments connect the nodes in sequence, showing the nonuniform distribution of transferred loads. Beneath this line, the label “101” is centered.  

Part b) (right half of the figure):  
– At the far left of this half, a simplified T-shaped cross section represents a column-beam junction: two large, light-gray flanges separated by a slender web. This again provides context for the structural element.  
– Immediately to the right, a straight horizontal line with four equally spaced green upward arrows indicates the source geometry SLN 202. The arrows and node symbols are identical in style to part a); above the line is the bold label “202.”  
– Further to the right, a single crosshair-node symbol stands alone. A single red downward arrow attaches to that node, indicating the equivalent support force transferred to target support point SPT 11. Below the node, the label “11” is printed.  

Along the bottom of the image runs the caption “Figure 9.1: 1:1 assignment: Support loads transferred from a) SLN 201 to SLN 101 and b) SLN 202 to SPT 11.” The overall graphic emphasizes that in a 1:1 assignment, each support reaction on the source line (or group) is directly assigned to a corresponding node on the target line (or point), preserving both magnitude and relative position of the original loads.

1:1 assignment is the simplest (but most elaborate) form of load transfer. Here, support forces of a source geometry are directly assigned to a target geometry, typically source-SLN ↔target- SLN, or source-SPT ↔target-SPT. It is also possible to concentrate support forces of structural lines on a column or to ’smear’ individual support forces on a wall. Whole groups can also be linked together (see Figure 9.1).
 $ Loads from SLN 201 are transferred to SLN 101
 LTD OPT TASK SRLC 1 SRCT SLN SRC 201 TRGT SLN TRG 101 TYPE MOMT FROM $$
 "source.cdb"
 $ Loads from SLN 202 are transferred to SPT 11
 LTD OPT TASK SRLC 1 SRCT SLN SRC 202 TRGT SPT TRG 11 FROM "source.cdb"
 $ Loads from group 1 are transferred to group 2
 LTD OPT TASK SRLC 1 SRCT GRP SRC 1 TRGT GRP TRG 2 FROM "source.cdb"

The image is a two-part schematic (labeled “a)” and “b)”) illustrating an N:M assignment of support loads from source geometries (SLNs) to target geometries (SLNs or SPTs). Both parts consist of a simple gray-shaded outline of the structural element, annotated load arrows, and numeric labels for source and target segment IDs.

Part a) Wall-to-wall assignment  
- On the left, a single rectangular block represents a wall element in the source model. Visually the wall is shown in light gray with darker gray edging at its top and bottom to suggest its thickness or flanges. On the face of this wall is a small black-and-white trapezoidal inset (likely representing a cutout or detail), but this inset is decorative and not part of the load assignment.  
- Directly above that wall block are two equally spaced green upward arrows. Each arrow roots at a small crosshair symbol on a horizontal reference line. Above each arrow is a bold label “201” over the first arrow and “202” over the second. These denote two source load segments (SLN 201 and SLN 202) in the source geometry. A double-headed horizontal dimension line with arrowheads at its ends spans over the two arrows, indicating the span of the combined load segments.  
- To the right of that is a second rectangular block representing the target wall geometry. Beneath it is a red polyline connecting three downward red arrows, each anchored to its own crosshair on a reference line. The three red arrows are labeled “101”, “102” and “103” from left to right. A sloping red line drawn above them indicates that the total load is being redistributed unevenly among the three target segments (101, 102, 103). A horizontal dimension line with arrowheads spans them and aligns with the source’s double-headed dimension line, communicating that the entire width of SLNs 201+202 is being assigned across SLNs 101, 102, 103.  

Caption for a): “Support loads of two SLNs (201, 202) are assigned to three SLNs 101, 102, 103.”

Part b) Wall-to-columns (SLN to SPT) assignment  
- On the left, another gray block assembly shows a thick slab-beam-slab configuration: a top slab (light gray), three vertical columns or webs in the middle (slightly darker gray pillars), and a bottom slab. This assembly represents the source geometry.  
- Above the top slab is a horizontal reference line with five small crosshairs, three of which have green upward arrows inserted. Only one arrow at each of three positions, equally spaced, is colored green. Above the group of three arrows is the label “203”, and a double-headed dimension line spans their outermost crosshairs, denoting the source load segment SLN 203 distributed across that width.  
- To the right is a simplified column model in gray: a top flange, a single central web, and a bottom flange (representing a column element in the target geometry). Beneath its bottom flange, on a horizontal line with three crosshairs, are three red downward arrows. Each arrow corresponds to a separate support point (SPT) and is labeled “11”, “12” and “13” from left to right. A straight horizontal red line above the arrows indicates that the total load from SLN 203 is equally or uniformly assigned to SPTs 11, 12 and 13. A double-headed dimension line again spans the outermost support arrows, tying back to the source span.  

Caption for b): “Support loads of SLN 203 are assigned to three SPTs 11, 12, 13.”

Overall, the figure visually communicates how an N:M mapping can split or combine structural loads: in example (a) two contiguous wall loads map into three target wall segments, and in example (b) one distributed wall/beam load maps into three column support loads. Each assignment uses one LTD OPT TASK record plus multiple LTD OPT SEL records to specify source and target segment IDs.

The N:M assignment allows n source geometries to be assigned to m target geometries. For this purpose, any number of LTD OPT SEL records can be specified after the main LTD OPT TASK record. Possible use cases are e.g. the assignment of a wall to several columns or walls that are divided differently in the source and target geometry (see Figure 9.2).

The illustration is divided into two halves. On the left is a three-dimensional, shaded-gray model of a simple structural assembly. It consists of top and bottom horizontal slabs (floor and roof) connected by three vertical elements: a rectangular column at the front right, a slightly inclined (leaning) rectangular column toward the front left, and a thin rectangular web or wall element set back toward the rear right. The top slab is a flat, horizontal plate that overhangs slightly beyond the supporting elements. The bottom slab is of matching plan size. The middle web element is positioned close to the right side, leaving an open span on its left; the front-left column is visibly tilted outward at its top. All components have uniform thickness and are rendered in light gray, with darker shading on their vertical faces to convey depth.

On the right is a schematic diagram showing how support reactions and applied loads “fall” from a source ground plan down onto a target geometry. The source geometry is depicted by a dashed-line outline in plan view at two elevation levels, one near the top and one near the bottom of the diagram. Three white circular symbols with center-crosshair (⊕) mark source support nodes, labeled (from left to right) “22,” “202,” and “21.” They lie along a dashed horizontal line at the top. Beneath each source node, vertical dashed lines drop down through the diagram, indicating the gravity direction.

• At source node “22” (left), a short vertical dashed line descends to the lower dashed outline.  
• At “202” (middle), a dashed line extends further downward past the mid-height into the bottom dashed plan, aligning with the central column location in the 3D view.  
• At “21” (right), its dashed line also goes straight down, aligning roughly under the back-right wall element in the 3D model.

Green upward arrows of varying lengths are clustered beneath the horizontal dashed source line on each branch. Under “22” and “202” there are multiple small green arrows pointing up, as though indicating existing support loads captured at the source. Under node “21” there is one tall central green arrow flanked by several smaller ones—this suggests a higher magnitude reaction at that support.

Red arrows and triangular arrowheads depict how those source reactions are “dropped” to the target geometry:  
• Beneath each dashed-line branch, a single long red arrow points straight down from the source level into the target plan.  
• At the bottom, red “inverted-V” shapes illustrate redistributed support forces forming a triangular support mechanism on the target slab. The left cluster (under “22” and “202”) shows two supports bridging between two red base points on the dashed-line bottom plan. The right cluster (under “21”) shows a single inverted-V anchored at two base points flanking the vertical red arrow.

Dashed outlines represent the target ground plan geometry. The middle dashed bottom plan is offset slightly from the right bottom plan, indicating that the target may have openings or a different footprint than the source. The annotation in the caption reads: “Figure 9.3: ALL → FALL: All support forces from the source are dropped onto the target geometry.”

Overall, the left half provides a concrete structural example in 3D, while the right half uses schematic symbols (⊕ nodes, dashed plans, green and red arrows) to visualize the “SRCT ALL, TRGT FALL” operation: capturing all loads (ALL) from the source and transferring them downward (FALL) onto a potentially mismatched target geometry, aware that loads can “fall through openings” if the plan differs.

sections: 9.1.3 All Loads – Falldown of Source Geometries

content:
Selecting all sources (SRCT ALL) ensures that all loads from the source geometry are cap- tured. With TRGT FALL, all load bearing SLNs and SPTs of the source geometry are duplicated (see Figure 9.3). If the source and target groundplan differ, it is not guaranteed that all loads will be transferred correctly – so loads may fall through openings.
 $ All loads from the source fall down
 LTD OPT TASK SRLC 1 SRCT ALL TRGT FALL TYPE MOMT FROM "source.cdb"

The image is a composite of three small schematic views (labelled a), b) and c)) illustrating how a line‐load (SLN 203) on a plate is automatically or semi‐automatically mapped to a set of support points (SPTs 11, 12, 13) on a target line (SLN 103) under different “ignore” (IGN) or “modify” (MOD) options. Along the left edge a generic I‐beam cross‐section is shown for context, but the focus is on the three detail sketches to its right.

1. Common Elements in All Three Views  
   • Top line: a solid horizontal line labelled “203” with a series of green downward arrows evenly spaced beneath it. This represents the source geometry (SLN 203) carrying a distributed moment or load.  
   • Bottom line: a fine dotted horizontal line labelled “103,” punctuated by three black circle symbols at its base, labelled “11,” “12” and “13.” These denote the candidate target geometries—structural points (SPTs) or a meshed line—onto which the source load might be assigned.  
   • Red arrows and/or red connector lines showing how the green source‐line arrows are actually mapped down to the three support points.

2. Subfigure a) “Initial situation – automatic distribution”  
   • All loads (green arrows) on SLN 203 are automatically distributed to SLN 103.  
   • A single red, slightly skewed line running from the leftmost source‐arrow to the rightmost source‐arrow spans above the dotted target line, illustrating a 1:N mapping of the entire source line onto the entire target line.  
   • Three red arrows drop from that skewed red connector onto points 11, 12 and 13. In effect the software “sees” SLN 103 (including any spurious meshed line segments) as the proper target and distributes the moment across all three supports—even though two of them (11 and 13) may actually be columns, and the middle one (12) is really part of the plate mesh.

3. Subfigure b) “IGN TRGT SLN 103 – ignore target line”  
   • The target line SLN 103 is explicitly ignored via “LTD OPT IGN TRGT SLN TRG 103.”  
   • The software then finds the closest valid structural points (SPTs 11, 12, 13) to each source arrow on SLN 203 and applies each load directly downward in a true 1:1 fashion.  
   • Visually, the red connector from SLN 203 has disappeared; instead, each green arrow now has a red downward arrow aligned beneath it, pointing straight onto the nearest support point.

4. Subfigure c) “IGN SRCT SLN 203 – ignore source line”  
   • The source line SLN 203 is ignored (“LTD OPT IGN SRCT SLN SRC 203”), and the engineer must reselect or combine the target points by hand.  
   • A dashed‐red line, parallel and directly beneath the original SLN 203, represents a reconstructed “source” shape that will be manually linked to the supports.  
   • Three red arrows drop vertically from that dashed line onto SPTs 11, 12, 13, indicating that the user has chosen to treat the three columns as a combined unit (TRGM COMB) and transfer the moment accordingly.  
   • In practice, commands such as “LTD OPT SEL TRGT SPT TRG 11,12,13” would follow to finalize the assignment.

Together, these three mini‐diagrams illustrate the pitfalls of fully automatic load‐to‐geometry mapping (a), and how the IGN TRGT (b) and IGN SRCT (c) options allow an analyst to correct mis‐assignments—either by excluding stray meshed targets or by manually reestablishing the source‐to‐target links.

The figure is a composite sketch showing how SOFiLOAD handles three different “TYPE”s of load‐transfer between a set of support (source) geometries and one or more target geometries. Visually it is divided into two parts: at top, a schematic of a rigid “resultant” R picking up support forces from a “source” beam or wall; below that, three separate red‐colored load‐distribution diagrams labeled (a), (b) and (c), corresponding to the three transfer methods.

1. Top schematic—source supports and resultant R  
   • A horizontal line represents the “target” element onto which loads will ultimately be applied.  
   • Directly above the beam is a single thick blue arrow pointing downward, labeled “R,” indicating the resultant force vector computed from all of the selected source supports.  
   • Beneath the same horizontal line (representing the source geometry), six small triangular supports are drawn at regular intervals. Each of these has a green arrow attached, pointing downward toward the beam; these green arrows depict the individual support reactions that are being collected. One of the end supports on the right shows a green arrow pointing upward—indicating that that particular support contributes an upward reaction, opposite in sign to the others.  
   • Below the row of supports is a horizontal dimension line spanning the full distance between the first and last support, labeled “ℓ.” A secondary dimension line immediately beneath breaks ℓ into two parts, “ℓ₁” on the left and “ℓ₂” on the right.  
   • A small coordinate arrow at the left end, labeled “x,” denotes the positive direction along the length of the beam.

2. Method (a): Constant force transfer (“CONST”)  
   • Directly below the top schematic is a single black baseline (the target geometry) with two short red arrows at its ends pointing downward—these represent a uniformly distributed load of constant intensity.  
   • A red rectangular “band” drawn above that baseline conveys the idea of a constant pressure p(x).  
   • At center of the red band is the formula p(x) = R / ℓ, indicating that the total resultant force R is spread evenly over the entire length ℓ.

3. Method (b): Force‐and‐moment transfer (“MOMT”)  
   • The next diagram down again shows a black baseline with red arrows at each end—this time the left arrow is taller than the right one, and the red band above is sloped downward from left to right.  
   • Centered above the band is the equation p(x) = R/ℓ + (M/J)·x. Here M denotes the equivalent moment transmitted, J denotes the cross‐sectional second moment (or analogous polar moment), and x is the distance from the reference end. Because of the additional M/J·x term, the distribution is linear rather than constant.

4. Method (c): Trapezoidal load transfer (“TRAP”)  
   • The bottom diagram is a simplified trapezoid: a black baseline with two red arrows at its ends, one labeled p₁ on the left (taller) and one labeled p₂ on the right (shorter).  
   • A single red slanted band connects the two arrows, forming a trapezoidal shape. No explicit formula is written inside this shape—it “qualitatively represents an influence of the moment” without generating any upward (lifting) forces. The positions of p₁ and p₂ are determined purely by geometry—i.e. the location of the resultant force relative to the supports—so that the trapezoid captures moment effects without a direct moment term.

Together, these four sketches encapsulate how SOFiLOAD can transfer:  
• A constant resultant force (pure R),  
• A combination of force and moment (R plus M, producing a triangular distribution), and  
• A qualitatively moment‐influenced trapezoidal load (avoiding any locally lifting segments).

SOFiLOAD provides three different methods (TYPE) to transfer loads (see Figure 9.7).
 CONS In the simplest case – constant load transfer – the resultant R is formed from all the support forces of the selected source geometries and applied as a constant load to the target geometries.
 MOMT As a second method, both the resultant force and the moment can be transferred. For a straight wall, only the moment about the normal direction of the wall can be transmitted. For the case of a curved wall or several non-collinear walls together, moments can be transmitted in both spatial directions.
 TRAP Under certain circumstances, lifting forces, as they can occur during moment trans- mission, are not desired – however, the influence of the moment should not be com- pletely neglected. For this case, there is a transfer function that qualitatively repre- sents an influence of the moment. The position of the resultant force determines the trapezoidal load purely geometrically. It applies:
 over the length . b) In addition to the force, the moment is also transferred. c) Positive trapezoidal load to qualitatively represent an influence of the moment.

The figure consists of two side-by-side, three-dimensional schematic views of a rectangular “building-core” formed by four planar walls. The slab edges above and below the walls are suggested by thin, dashed‐brown lines, while the walls themselves are drawn in solid red. Blue lines and arrows indicate the direction and point of application of the transferred forces. Each wall is numbered 1 through 4 in bold black type, corresponding to the four faces of the core.  

View (a), labeled “TRGM INDI,” shows each wall acting and being loaded independently:  
 • Wall 1 (upper left in plan view) is represented by a red vertical plane rising between two dashed lines. A thick blue arrow labeled “1” sits on the top dashed slab line, pointing inward toward the wall, and a blue vertical drop line at the bottom slab transfers the load down.  
 • Wall 2 (upper right) likewise has a blue arrow labeled “2” at its top edge, and a matching vertical vector at its base.  
 • Wall 3 (lower right) is shown with its load vector “3” on the lower dashed slab, slanting upward from the bottom edge of the wall to the slab, and the corresponding vertical reaction at the top slab.  
 • Wall 4 (lower left) mirrors this arrangement, with a sloping blue arrow labeled “4.”  

Because each red wall is treated in isolation, the slab’s dashed outline remains unbroken, and each pair of blue arrows attaches directly to its own wall.  

View (b), labeled “TRGM COMB,” depicts all four walls combined into a single structural cross-section. The red walls are now rigidly connected at their corners. Only three blue arrows are shown:  
 • Load 1 acts on the top slab edge of the combined section, centered between walls 1 and 2.  
 • Load 2 lies on the right slab edge between walls 2 and 3.  
 • Load 3 is on the bottom edge between walls 3 and 4.  

A fourth reaction arrow (in blue) at the lower right corner represents the resultant of biaxial bending. The dashed‐brown slab outlines remain, but the individual vectors no longer tie back to individual walls; instead they distribute across the composite section.  

Together, these two diagrams illustrate:  
 1. TRGM INDI (left): Each wall transfers forces separately, with its own load path and reaction.  
 2. TRGM COMB (right): The four-wall core behaves as one unit, redistributing loads through biaxial bending across the combined geometry.

In most cases, a wall will transfer loads independently of other walls (TRGM INDI). However, there are also cases where several walls are to act as one ’cross-section’, such as in a stiffening building core. For this case there is the possibility to combine several target geometries (TRGM COMB) and consider them as unit (see Figure 9.8).
